<h2>FOREWORD</h2><p>Under the leadership of the Royal Government of the 7<sup>th</sup> Legislature of the National Assembly of the Kingdom of Cambodia, the Ministry of Health pays high attention to the health and well-being of the entire population. The Ministry of Health is strongly committed to ensuring the provision of equitable, safe and quality patient-centered health services for the Cambodian population in line with the Health Strategic Plan 2025-2034 and the Royal Government Roadmap Towards Universal Health Coverage in Cambodia 2024-2035.</p><p>This Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPG) for General Medicine provides national guidance on the management protocols of priority health problems with a focus on diagnosis and care, including curative and preventive care, as well as follow-up of health problems.</p><p>The Guidelines, published for the third time in Cambodia in three parts, Part 1, Part 2 and Part 3; was developed by the Technical Working Group of the Ministry of Health with participation from various stakeholders and individuals, including experts from relevant fields ranging from clinicians working in hospitals at all levels to district health officers, Provincial Health Departments, national programs, health professional associations, as well as partner organizations.</p><p>The Guidelines is intended for use by health professionals and other relevant professionals, especially health care providers, including doctors and other health practitioners in both public and private health facilities as well as trainees, policymakers, relevant individuals, professional councils and professional associations.</p><p>The Ministry of Health guides all health professionals and relevant individuals to use this Guidelines in their professional practice with the aim of improving effectiveness, efficiency and quality in patient care and safety, as well as contributing to human resource capacity building.</p><div style="text-align: right;"><p>Phnom Penh, 31. December, 2025</p><p><img alt="Seal of the Ministry of Health of Cambodia"/></p><p>Minister of Health</p><p><img alt="Signature of Prof. CHHEANG RA"/></p><p>Prof. CHHEANG RA</p></div>

Professor <b>Koy Vanny</b>, Secretary of State, Chair and all Vice-chairs and members of the Technical Working Group of Clinical Practice Guidelines for General Medicine, under the overall leadership and guidance of the Steering Committee for National Medical Care and Therapy of the Ministry of Health.</p><p>We would also like to express our deep gratitude to all partners involved, including the World Health Organization and other partners, for their technical and financial contributions to the formulation of the guidelines.</p><p>This Clinical Practice Guidelines for Medicine represent another significant and commendable achievement of the Ministry of Health of the Kingdom of Cambodia.</p><p>Phnom Penh, 31 December, 2025</p><p>Chair of the Steering Committee for National<br/>Medical Care and Therapy</p><p>[Signature]</p><p>H.E Prof. Yit Sunnara</p>

<h1>INTRODUCTION</h1>
<h2>I. BACKGROUND</h2>
<p>The Ministry of Health of Kingdom of Cambodia is committed to improving the health and well-being of all Cambodian population through the provision of quality, safe, acceptable, equitable and affordable healthcare services. Implementing evidence-based, appropriate, and cost-effective health interventions within care packages at various levels of the health system, guided by contextually relevant best practices in clinical practice guidelines (CPGs), can significantly enhance population health.</p>
<p>Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPGs) are essential diagnostic and care tools in achieving UHC by ensuring that healthcare services are provided timely, effectively, safely, continuously and with patient-centeredness. The guidelines provide evidence-based and or up-to-health services at different levels of the health system. They ensure that health problems are appropriately diagnosed and clinical decisions are based on the best available evidence and experiences, leading to improved patient diagnosis and care outcomes as well as more efficient use of resources. By adhering to CPGs, healthcare providers can offer consistent, high-quality care that meets national and international standards.</p>
<p>The 1st Clinical Practice Guidelines (CPGs) for Medicine and Pediatrics were published in 2013. They are the only existing CPGs in Cambodia. Since then, many new developments have taken place, especially in the area of laboratory tests, medical imaging, diagnosis tools and treatment options. Regularly reviewing and updating the CPGs offer up-to-date and more evidence-based recommendations for health services and interventions tailored to Cambodia's current and future needs. Updating the clinical practice guidelines aims to enhance both quality and coverage by providing a solid evidence-based foundation for changes in services. This includes the diagnosing, treatments, and support necessary to deliver these services as defined in the essential packages of care under the CPA guidelines.</p>
<h2>II. DEVELOPMENT PROCESS</h2>
<p>This Clinical Practice Guidelines was formulated by “Technical Working Group of Clinical Practice Guidelines for General Medicine” of the Ministry of Health through face-to-face and online meeting of the working group and small group meeting and discussions with guidance and endorsements from the Steering Committee for National Medical Care and Therapy of the Ministry of Health mainly through its meeting. The development process of the guidelines was actively participated by various stake holders and individuals, including experts from related fields ranging from clinicians working in hospitals at all levels, district health officers, Provincial Health Department, national institutes, national programs, health professional associations as well as experts and officials partner organizations. Each health section follows standard format except in few cases. These guidelines contain three parts-Part I, Part II and Part III with each separate volume presented in its hard copy division and publication. The guideline covers 174 topics/diseases/conditions within 11 specialized chapters. The guideline do not cover the national programs topics/diseases/conditions such as HIV/AIDS, TB,</p>

<!-- PAGE 15 -->

<div><p>Malaria, Dengue, Schistosomiasis and vaccine preventable diseases. The list of the protocols/guidelines of these national programs are included in the annex B of the CPGs.</p><h3>III. PURPOSE AND USERS</h3><p>The main aim of these guidelines is to assist health care providers and practitioners make informed decisions on clinical diagnosing and treatment based on recommended protocols based on systematic review of evidence and an assessment of the benefits and harms of alternative care options. The guidelines is used for health professionals and relevant stakeholders in both public and private sectors, including doctors, related health professionals, trainees and medical students, policy makers, professional societies, in both public and private health facilities and institutions, including Provincial and district hospitals, private clinic, training and research institutions.</p><p>The main end users of the CPG are clinicians, managers and other health professionals practicing in patient care settings in both private and public sectors, particularly at referral hospitals and private clinics to support the delivery of consistently safe, quality and cost effective and equitable health care. They should be harmonized with the CPA guideline, IPC guideline, AMR guideline, Cambodian Hospital Accreditation Standards (CHAS) and Quality Enhancement Monitoring Tool (QEMT) and other MoH guidelines to motivate and facilitate their relevance and use. CPG can also be used by other relevant bodies and people such as in training and research institutions as well as by other organization or institutions as per the relevancy of their mandates.</p></div>

<h1>ASSESSMENT THE PATIENTS IN EMERGENCY ROOM</h1>
<p>Dr. HUN Vanasola, Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Asst. TAING Sovanna,<br/>Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha,<br/>Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy,<br/>Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya</p>
<h2>I. INTRODUCTION</h2>
<p>Patients who present to the Emergency Room (ER) are typically unselected on arrival. A critical function of all ERs is to have reliable processes that can sort patients, in accordance with their clinical need. This process is termed “Patient Assessment” which is an important part of emergency patient evaluation. Even though it may seem time-consuming, it is necessary to properly and completely examine the patient to determine what care the patient requires. It is required not only to detect life-threatening conditions and correct them as quickly as possible but also detect problems that may become life-threatening if they go unnoticed.</p>
<h2>II. TRIAGE</h2>
<ul>
<li>Triage is a French verb meaning to sort.</li>
<li>Most patients entering an emergency room (ER) are greeted by a triage nurse, who will perform a brief evaluation of the patient to determine a level of acuity or priority of care.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Priorities of Care and Triage Categories:</h3>
<ul>
<li>Standardized triage categories are usually developed within each ER.</li>
<li>Most common triage systems consist of five levels of acuity:
        <ul>
<li>Triage Level I - Resuscitation</li>
<li>Triage Level II - Emergent.</li>
<li>Triage Level III - Urgent.</li>
<li>Triage Level IV - Less Urgent.</li>
<li>Triage Level V - Non-urgent.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<table border="1">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Level I</td>
<td>Resuscitation</td>
<td>see patient immediately</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Level II</td>

<td>within 15 minutes</td>
</tr>

<h3>Triage Level I - Resuscitation:</h3>
<ul>
<li>Conditions requiring IMMEDIATE nursing and physician assessment.</li>
<li>Any delay in treatment is potentially life - or limb - threatening.</li>
<li>Includes conditions such as:
        <ul>
<li>Airway compromise.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 18 -->

<ul><li>Cardiac arrest.</li><li>Severe shock.</li><li>Cervical spine injury.</li><li>Multisystem trauma.</li><li>Altered level of consciousness (LOC) (unconsciousness).</li><li>Eclampsia.</li></ul><p><b>Triage Level II - Emergency:</b></p><ul><li>Conditions requiring nursing assessment and physician assessment within 15 MINUTES of arrival.</li><li>Conditions include:<ul><li>Head injuries</li><li>Severe trauma</li><li>Severe asthma</li><li>Lethargy or agitation</li><li>Severe allergic reaction</li><li>Chest pain</li><li>Back pain</li><li>GI bleed with unstable vital signs</li><li>Stroke with deficit</li><li>Abdominal pain in patients older than 50</li><li>Severe headache</li><li>Vomiting and diarrhea with dehydration</li><li>Any pain greater than 7 on a scale of 10</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>Triage Level III - Urgency:</b></p><ul><li>Conditions requiring nursing and physician assessment within 30 MINUTES of arrival.</li><li>Conditions include:<ul><li>Alert head injury with vomiting.</li><li>Mild to moderate asthma.</li><li>Moderate trauma.</li><li>Abuse or neglect.</li><li>GI bleed with stable vital signs.</li><li>History of seizure, alert on arrival.</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>Triage Level IV - Less Urgency:</b></p><ul><li>Conditions requiring nursing and physician assessment within 1 HOUR.</li><li>Conditions include:<ul><li>Alert head injury without vomiting.</li><li>Minor trauma.</li><li>Vomiting and diarrhea in patient older than age 2 without evidence of dehydration.</li><li>Minor allergic reaction.</li><li>Corneal foreign body.</li><li>Chronic back pain.</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>Triage Level V - Non-urgent:</b></p><ul><li>Conditions requiring nursing and physician assessment within 2 HOURS.</li><li>Conditions include:<ul><li>Minor trauma, not acute.</li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 19 -->

<ul><li>Sore throat.</li><li>Minor symptoms.</li><li>Chronic abdominal pain.</li></ul><h3>III. ASSESSMENT</h3><p>The primary and secondary assessment ensure that life-threatening conditions can be identified and treated early, in order of priority.</p><h4>1. Primary Assessment:</h4><ul><li>Primary assessment is meant to identify life-threatening conditions and treated early, in order of priority.</li><li>It is an initial, rapid, A-B-C-D-E (airway, breathing, and circulation, neurologic disability and exposure). It should be performed in the first 5 minutes and repeated whenever a patient's condition changes or worsens.</li><li>A problem discovered (A-B-C-D-E) must be addressed immediately before moving on to the next step.</li></ul><table border="1"><thead><tr><th>A</th><th>B</th><th>C</th><th>D</th><th>E</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><ul><li>Obstruction: foreign body</li><li>Obstruction: burns</li><li>Obstruction: anaphylaxis</li><li>Obstruction: trauma</li></ul></td><td><ul><li>Tension pneumothorax</li><li>Opiate overdose</li><li>Asthma/COPD</li><li>Large pleural effusion/haemothorax</li></ul></td><td><ul><li>Pulselessness</li><li>Shock</li><li>Severe bleeding</li><li>Pericardial Tamponade</li></ul></td><td><ul><li>Hypoglycaemia</li><li>Increased pressure on the brain</li><li>Seizures/convulsions</li></ul></td><td><ul><li>Snake bite</li></ul></td></tr></tbody></table><p><b>Figure 2: Acute Life-Threatening Conditions</b></p><h4>A (Airway):</h4><ul><li>Can the patient talk normally? If YES, the airway is open.</li><li>If the patient cannot talk normally:<ul><li>Look to see if the chest wall is moving and see if there is air movement from the mouth or nose.</li><li>Listen for abnormal sounds (such as stridor, grunting, or snoring) or a hoarse or raspy voice that indicates a partially obstructed airway. Stridor plus swelling and/or hives suggest a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis).</li><li>Look and listen for fluid (such as blood, vomit) in the airway.</li><li>Look for foreign body or abnormal swelling around the airway, and altered mental status.</li><li>Check if the patient is able to swallow saliva or is drooling.</li></ul></li></ul><h4>B (Breathing):</h4><ul><li>Look, listen, and feel to see if the patient is breathing.</li><li>Assess if breathing is very fast, very slow, or very shallow.</li><li>Look for signs of increased work of breathing (such as accessory muscle use, chest in drawing/retractions, nasal flaring) or abnormal chest wall movement.</li><li>Listen for abnormal breath sounds such as wheezing or crackles.</li><li>With severe wheezing, there may be limited/no breath sounds on examination because narrowing of the airways may be so severe that breathing cannot be heard.</li><li>Listen to see if breath sounds are equal on both sides.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 20 -->

<ul><li>Check for the absence of breath sounds and dull sounds with percussion on one side (large pleural effusion or hemothorax).</li><li>If there are no breath sounds on one side, and hypotension, check for distended neck veins or a shifted trachea (tension pneumothorax).</li><li>Check oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter when available.</li></ul><p><b>C (Circulation):</b></p><ul><li>Obtain a blood pressure (in both arms if chest trauma is suspected).</li><li>Look and feel for signs of poor perfusion (cool, moist extremities, delayed capillary refill greater than 3 seconds, low blood pressure, tachypnoea, tachycardia, absent pulses).</li><li>Look for both external AND internal bleeding, including bleeding: into chest; into abdomen; from stomach or intestine; from pelvic or femur fracture; from wounds.</li><li>Look for hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds that might indicate pericardial tamponade.</li></ul><p><b>D (Disability):</b></p><ul><li>Assess level of consciousness using the AVPU scale:<ul><li>A: The patient is aware of the examiner and can respond to the environment around them independently. The patient can also follow commands, open their eyes spontaneously, and track objects.</li><li>V: The patient's eyes do not open spontaneously. The patient's eyes open only in response to a verbal stimulus directed toward them. The patient can react to that verbal stimulus directly and in a meaningful way.</li><li>P: The patient's eyes do not open spontaneously. The patient will only respond to the application of painful stimuli by an examiner. The patient may move, moan, or cry out directly in response to the painful stimuli.</li><li>U: The patient does not respond spontaneously. The patient does not respond to verbal or painful stimuli.</li></ul></li><li>In trauma cases, check consciousness using the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS).</li><li>The AVPU scale correlates to distinct GSC ranges, as outlined below<ul><li>GCS Score 15 - Alert</li><li>GCS 12 to 13 - Verbally Responsive</li><li>GCS 5 to 6 - Physically Responsive</li><li>GCS 3 - Unresponsive</li></ul></li><li>Always check glucose level in the confused or unconscious patient.</li><li>Check for pupil size, whether the pupils are equal, and if pupils are reactive to light.</li><li>Check movement and sensation in all four limbs.</li><li>Look for abnormal repetitive movements or shaking on one or both sides of the body (seizure/convulsion).</li></ul><p><b>E: Expose/environmental control</b></p><ul><li>Examine the entire body for hidden injuries, rashes, bites or other lesions.</li><li>Rashes, such as hives, can indicate an allergic reaction</li><li>Other rashes can indicate infection</li></ul>

<p><b>Figure 4: The ABCDE Approach</b></p>
<h2>2. Secondary Assessment (F-G-H-I-J):</h2>
<ul>
<li>Do not begin the secondary assessment until the primary assessment is complete and resuscitation procedures have been initiated as indicated.</li>
<li>Continue to monitor ABCDE during the secondary assessment. If any life-threatening problems arise, return to the primary assessment and intervene as indicated.</li>
<li>Prioritize and initiate interventions for injuries or conditions discovered in the secondary assessment after the entire head-to-toe examination is complete.</li>
<li>Perform the secondary assessment using a systematic: the mnemonic F-G-H-I-J</li>
<li><b>F: Full set of vital signs/Five interventions/Facilitate family presence</b>
<ul>
<li>Full Set of Vital Signs
<ul>
<li>Obtain a full set of vital signs including blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and temperature.</li>
<li>Obtain blood pressure in both arms if chest trauma is suspected.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Five interventions
<ul>
<li>Pulse oximetry to measure the oxygen saturation.</li>
<li>Indwelling urinary catheter (do not insert if you note blood at the meatus, blood in the scrotum, or if you suspect a pelvic fracture).</li>
<li>Gastric tube (if there is evidence of facial fractures, insert the tube orally).</li>
<li>Laboratory studies frequently include type and crossmatching, hemoglobin and hematocrit, urine drug screen, blood alcohol, electrolytes, prothrombin time (PT) and partial thromboplastin time, and pregnancy test if applicable.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Facilitate family presence
<ul>
<li>It is important to assess the family's needs.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 22 -->

<ul><li>If any member of the family wishes to be present during the resuscitation, it is imperative to assign a staff member to that person to explain what is being done and offer support.</li><li><b>G: Get monitoring devices and Give comfort measures.</b><ul><li>Do not forget to give comfort measures to the family during the resuscitation process.</li><li>Follow the mnemonic L-M-N-O-P when obtaining resuscitation monitoring devices and supports.<ul><li>L= Laboratory studies: ABG analysis, lactic acid level, type and crossmatch if indicated</li><li>M= Monitoring (Cardiac): arrhythmia may indicate a blunt cardiac injury</li><li>N= Nasogastric or orogastric tube: to relieve gastric distention, optimize lung inflation and prevent vomiting and aspiration. Avoid in patients with a suspected head injury or mid-face fractures.</li><li>O= Oxygenation and Ventilation: Assess SpO2 by pulse oximetry and plethysmography if any doubt, Monitoring ETCO2 via capnography</li><li>P= Pain assessment and management: using pain assessment scale then initiate pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic as indicated.</li></ul></li></ul></li><li><b>H: History and Head to Toe examination.</b><ul><li>Obtain prehospital information of the incident or illness. A helpful mnemonic M-I-S-T:<ul><li>M: Mechanism of injury:<ul><li>It is helpful to understand the mechanism of injury to anticipate probable injuries. It is particularly helpful in motor vehicle accidents to know such information as external and internal damage to the car and the period of time elapsed before the patient received medical attention.</li></ul></li><li>I: Injuries sustained or suspected:<ul><li>Ask prehospital personnel to list any injuries that they have identified.</li></ul></li><li>S: Signs and symptoms before arrival</li><li>T: Treatment<ul><li>What treatment did the patient receive before arriving at the hospital and what was his response to those interventions?</li></ul></li></ul></li><li>Obtain the patient's history. A helpful mnemonic is S-A-M-P-L-E.<ul><li>S- Signs/symptoms associated with the injury or illness</li><li>A- Allergies and tetanus status</li><li>M- Medications currently used, especially anticoagulants</li><li>P- Past medical history (including hospitalizations and surgeries)</li><li>L- Last oral intake and output (last menstrual period if female of childbearing age)</li><li>E- Events and environmental factors related to the illness or injury?</li></ul></li><li>Assess the patient from head to toe (Physical Examination)</li></ul></li><li><b>I: Inspect posterior surfaces</b><ul><li>In the injured patient, obtain assistance to maintain cervical spine alignment and support injured extremities while log rolling the patient to the side.</li><li>Avoid rolling the patient onto an injured extremity or side if possible. If necessary, for adequate assessment of posterior surfaces, roll the patient to both sides.</li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 23 -->

<ul><li>The log roll maneuver can result in spinal and pelvic movement. Carefully consider the risks and benefits of performing this maneuver, especially if the potential for spinal cord injury or pelvic fracture is significant.</li><li>When spinal or pelvic injuries are suspected, radiographs are recommended before logrolling the patient.</li><li>Inspect the posterior surfaces for wounds, deformities, or discolorations. Palpate all posterior surfaces for wounds, deformities, or muscle spasms.</li><li>Remove the backboard or transferring device as indicated.</li><li><b>J: Just keep reevaluating</b><ul><li>Continue ongoing monitoring and evaluation of the patient. Reevaluation should include the primary survey, vital signs, level of pain and any injuries identified. A helpful mnemonic is V-I-P-P:<ul><li>V = vital signs</li><li>I = injuries sustained and interventions</li><li>P = primary survey</li><li>P = level of pain</li></ul></li></ul></li><li><b>Physical examination</b><ul><li><b>Head and Neck</b><ul><li>Observation face, head, neck &amp; scalp</li><li>Palpation lymph node, parotid and salivary gland regions</li><li>Assess auditory acuity (crude test hearing loss)<ul><li>If hearing loss, perform Weber &amp; Rinne Tests 512 Hz fork (CN 8)</li></ul></li><li>Ear: external and internal (otoscope)</li><li>Nose: observation, nares/mucosa (otoscope)</li><li>Oropharynx:<ul><li>Inspect w/light from otoscope &amp; tongue depressor( uvula), tonsils, tongue, mucosa</li><li>“Ahh” to help see back of throat</li><li>Inspect teeth &amp; salivary gland ducts</li><li>Thyroid: Observation, palpation</li></ul></li></ul></li><li><b>Eye Exam, Including Ophthalmoscopy:</b><ul><li>Observe external eye structures – lid, sclera, pupil</li><li>Visual acuity (hand-held card – CN2)</li><li>Visual fields (confrontation – CN 2)</li><li>Extra-ocular movements (CN 3, 4, 6)</li><li>Using Ophthalmoscope:<ul><li>Examine external eye structures (lids, sclera, pupil, iris, conjunctiva)</li><li>Check pupillary response to light – direct and consensual (CN 2 &amp; 3)</li><li>Red reflex</li><li>Retinal exam – identifying: Optic disc, arteries, veins, color of retina, and macular area.</li></ul></li></ul></li><li><b>Pulmonary</b><ul><li>Observation and Inspection<ul><li>General observation of breathing, note if using accessory muscles/general respiratory effort</li><li>Note shape of chest and spine</li></ul></li><li>Palpation<ul><li>Assess chest excursion</li><li>Assess tactile fremitus</li></ul></li><li>Percussion</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul>

MANAGEMENT</h3><h4>1. A = Airway management</h4><p>If the patient is unconscious and not breathing normally and:</p><ul><li>NO TRAUMA: open the airway using the <i>head-tilt and chin-lift maneuver</i>.<ul><li>Place one hand on the patient's forehead and the other under the chin.</li><li>Tilt the forehead back whilst lifting the chin forward to extend the neck.</li></ul></li><li>CONCERN FOR TRAUMA: maintain cervical spine immobilization and open the airway using the <i>jaw thrust maneuver</i>.<ul><li>Identify the angle of the mandible</li><li>Place two fingers under the angle of the mandible (on both sides) and anchor your thumbs on the patient's cheeks</li><li>Lift the mandible forwards</li></ul></li><li>Place an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway to maintain the airway.</li><li>If a foreign body is suspected: – If the object is visible, remove it– be careful not to push the object any deeper.</li><li>If the patient is able to cough or make noises, keep the patient calm and encourage coughing.</li><li>If the patient is choking (unable to cough, not making sounds) use age-appropriate chest thrusts/ abdominal thrusts/back blows.</li><li>If the patient becomes unconscious while choking, follow relevant CPR protocols.</li><li>If secretions or vomit are present, suction when available, or wipe clean. Consider placing patient in the recovery position if the rest of the ABCDE is normal and no trauma is suspected.</li><li>If the patient has swelling, hives or stridor, consider severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), and give intramuscular adrenaline.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 27 -->

<ul><li>Allow the patient to stay in a position of comfort and prepare for rapid handover/transfer to a center capable of advanced airway management, if needed.</li></ul><div><img alt="Figure 5 shows two side-by-side images demonstrating airway maneuvers. The left image shows the Head-Tilt maneuver, where the provider tilts the patient's head back by lifting the chin. The right image shows the Chin-Life Maneuver, where the provider lifts the chin while maintaining a neutral head position."/></div><p><b>Figure 5: Head-Tilt (Left) and Chin-Life Maneuver (Right)</b></p><div><img alt="Figure 6 shows a single image demonstrating the Jaw-Thrust Maneuver. The left image shows the insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA). The middle image shows the NPA in place, with an overlay diagram highlighting the airway path. The right image shows the placement of an oropharyngeal airway (OPA), also with an overlay diagram."/></div><p><b>Figure 7: Nasopharyngeal Airway and Oropharyngeal Airway</b></p>

<!-- PAGE 28 -->

<div><p><b>2. B = Breathing Management</b></p><ul><li>If unconscious with abnormal breathing, start bag-valve-mask ventilation and follow relevant CPR protocols.</li><li>If not breathing adequately (too slow for age or too shallow), begin bag-valve-mask ventilation with oxygen. If oxygen not immediately available, DO NOT DELAY ventilation. Start ventilation while oxygen is being prepared. Plan for rapid handover/transfer.</li><li>If breathing fast or hypoxic, give Oxygen.</li><li>If wheezing, give salbutamol.</li><li>Repeat salbutamol as needed.</li><li>If concern for severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), give intramuscular adrenaline.</li><li>If concern for tension pneumothorax, perform needle decompression immediately and give IV fluids and oxygen. Plan for rapid handover/transfer.</li><li>If concern for large pleural effusion or hemothorax, give oxygen and plan for rapid handover/transfer.</li><li>If cause unknown, remember the possibility of trauma.</li></ul><div><img alt="Figure 8 shows two images illustrating the one-hand bag mask ventilation technique. The left image shows a person applying a bag valve mask to an adult patient's face. The right image shows a person performing head tilt/chin lift on a child or infant patient."/></div><p><b>Figure 8: One-Hand bag mask ventilation technique</b></p><p><b>3. C = Circulation Management</b></p><ul><li>For cardiopulmonary arrest, follow relevant CPR protocols.</li><li>If signs of poor perfusion, give IV fluids and oxygen and:<ul><li>For external bleeding, apply direct pressure or use other technique to control.</li><li>If internal bleeding or pericardial tamponade are suspected, refer rapidly to a center with surgical capabilities.</li></ul></li><li>If cause unknown, remember the possibility of trauma: Bind pelvic fractures and splint femur fractures, or any fracture with compromised blood flow.</li></ul><p><b>4. D = Disability Management</b></p><ul><li>If altered mental status and no evidence of trauma, place in recovery position.</li><li>If glucose low (&lt;3.5 mmol/L) or glucose test not available and patient has altered mental status, give glucose.</li><li>For active seizures, give a benzodiazepine.</li><li>If pregnant and having seizures, give magnesium sulphate.</li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 29 -->

<ul><li>If pupils are small and breathing slow, consider opioid overdose and give naloxone.</li><li>If pupils are not equal, consider increased pressure on the brain and raise head of bed 30 degrees if no concern for spinal injury.</li><li>Plan for rapid transfer to an advanced provider or facility with neurosurgical care.</li></ul><p><b>5. E = Exposure Management</b></p><ul><li>If snake bite is suspected, immobilize the limb, 20mn WBCT, give appropriate antivenom if available.</li><li>Remove constricting clothing and all jewelry.</li><li>Cover the patient as soon as possible to prevent hypothermia by using warm blankets, overhead warmers, and warmed I.V. fluids. Acutely ill patients have difficulty regulating body temperature.</li><li>Remove any wet clothes and dry patient thoroughly.</li><li>Respect the patient and protect modesty during exposure.</li><li>If cause unknown, remember the possibility of trauma: Log roll if suspected spinal injury.</li></ul><p><b>V. <h1>OXYGEN THERAPY AND RESPIRATORY SUPPORTS</h1>
<p>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda,<br/>Prof. Asst TAING Sovanna, Dr. Pen Phallkun, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak,<br/>Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara,<br/>Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya</p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>The administration of supplemental oxygen is necessary when a patient has low blood oxygen levels, termed hypoxemia. Untreated, acute hypoxemia can lead to tissue hypoxia (low level of oxygen at the cellular level), organ dysfunction and death. Delivery of oxygen to tissues also relies on adequate cardiac output and hemoglobin to carry oxygen to the tissues.</p>
<p>Oxygen therapy improves oxygen delivery to the tissues by increasing oxygen content in the blood. Oxygen content in the blood is frequently measured indirectly by pulse oximetry as oxygen saturation (SpO<sub>2</sub>).</p>
<ul>
<li><b>oxygen content in arterial blood</b> (CaO<sub>2</sub>) = 1.34 × (Hb) × SpO<sub>2</sub> + (0.003 × PaO<sub>2</sub>)</li>
</ul>
<p>Arterial oxygen partial pressure (PaO<sub>2</sub>) measured in mmHg by arterial blood gas analyzer.</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Oxygen concentration</b> (% O<sub>2</sub>) from the oxygen source (i.e. wall outlet, bedside concentrator...) is the purity of oxygen produced by the device. It can range widely depending on the quality of the source but generally should range from 0.82–1.0 (82–100%).</li>
<li><b>Fraction of inspired oxygen</b> (% FiO<sub>2</sub>) is the oxygen concentration that is inspired by the patient, usually a result of mixing the oxygen source and ambient air and can range from 0.21–1.0 (21–100%). This varies depending on the delivery device and the patient's respiratory drive.</li>
</ul>
<p>Oxygen saturation (% SpO<sub>2</sub>) and oxygen partial pressure (PaO<sub>2</sub>) are the measured oxygen levels in blood, the former measured by pulse oximeter and the latter by blood gas analyzer.</p>
<h2>II. INDICATIONS FOR OXYGEN THERAPY</h2>
<ul>
<li>Respiratory distress</li>
<li>Sepsis with hypoperfusion or shock</li>
<li>Alteration of mental status</li>
<li>Hypoxemia</li>
</ul>
<p>The following conditions may require airway management in addition to oxygen.:</p>
<ul>
<li>obstructed or absent breathing,</li>
<li>severe respiratory distress,</li>
<li>central cyanosis,</li>
<li>shock,</li>
<li>coma and/or convulsions</li>
</ul>
<p>Supplemental oxygen therapy should be provided immediately to achieve the following SpO<sub>2</sub> targets:</p>
<ul>
<li>SpO<sub>2</sub> ≥ 90% in adults and children</li>
<li>SpO<sub>2</sub> ≥ 92–95% in pregnant patients</li>
<li>SpO<sub>2</sub> ≥ 94% if child or adult with signs of multi-organ failure, including shock, alteration of mental status, severe anemia, and/or during resuscitation.</li>
<li>Once stabilized, resume target SpO<sub>2</sub> ≥ 90%.</li>
</ul>
<h2>III. RESPIRATORY (VENTILATION) SUPPORT</h2>
<p>Respiratory failure type 1 or hypoxic-respiratory-failure, as well as patients who have dyspnea and low SpO<sub>2</sub> need supplemental oxygen therapy. Most of the time, the standard oxygen delivery devices (nasal cannula, mask) or HFNC can help. When patients have also hypercapnia (respiratory failure type 2), then NIV is more helpful. In cases where the oxygenation disorder is</p>

<!-- PAGE 31 -->

<div><p>severe (e.g., in ARDS with PaO<sub>2</sub>/FiO<sub>2</sub> &lt;150), often, only invasive mechanical ventilation may help. Note that the NIV is the first-choice modality of ventilation support in Exacerbations of COPD and acute congestive heart failure.</p><h3>A. Oxygen delivery devices</h3><h4>a. In adult</h4><table border="1"><thead><tr><th></th><th>O<sub>2</sub> flow</th><th>FiO<sub>2</sub></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td rowspan="4"><strong>Non-invasive O<sub>2</sub> delivery devices</strong></td><td>Nasal canular</td><td>1 - 5L/min</td><td>0.23 - 0.35</td></tr><tr><td>Face mask</td><td>5 – 10L/min</td><td>0.30 – 0.50</td></tr><tr><td>Venturi face mask</td><td>2 – 15L/min</td><td>0.24 – 0.6</td></tr><tr><td>Face mask reservoir bag</td><td>10 – 15L/min</td><td>0.5 – 0.95</td></tr><tr><td rowspan="4"><strong>Advanced non-invasive O<sub>2</sub> delivery devices</strong></td><td>High-flow nasal oxygen</td><td>10 – 60L/min</td><td>0.23 – 1.0</td></tr><tr><td>BiPAP/CPAP oronasal</td><td rowspan="3">10 – 80L/min</td><td rowspan="3">0.21 – 1.0</td></tr><tr><td>BiPAP/CPAP nasal</td></tr><tr><td>BiPAP/CPAP full face</td></tr><tr><td></td><td>BiPAP/CPAP Helmet</td><td></td><td></td></tr></tbody></table><h4>b. In children</h4><p>Nasal cannula is the preferred method of delivering oxygen to infants and children &lt; 5 years of age with hypoxemia who require oxygen therapy.</p><table border="1"><thead><tr><th>Age of child</th><th>Nasal canula size</th><th>Maximal oxygen flow rates</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Neonates</td><td>Neonatal</td><td>0.5 – 1L/min by nasal canula</td></tr><tr><td>Infants</td><td>Infant</td><td>1 – 2L/min by nasal canula</td></tr><tr><td>Pre-school aged</td><td>Child</td><td>1 – 4L/min by nasal canula</td></tr><tr><td>School-aged</td><td>Child to adult</td><td>1 - 5L/min by nasal canula</td></tr></tbody></table><h4>c. Humidification</h4><p>When oxygen is delivered at standard flow rate (0.5–1 L/min for a neonate, 1–2 L/min for an infant, 1–4 L/min for an older child) through nasal prongs, humidification is not necessary. Higher flow rates without effective humidification may cause drying of nasal mucosa with associated bleeding, airway obstruction and may cause bronchoconstriction in some conditions (e.g. asthma, COPD).</p><p>Bubble humidifiers reduce the dryness of the oxygen supplied by bubbling the gas through water at room temperature. They must be filled with clean water at least once a day (distilled water or tap water that has been boiled and cooled). The water level in the humidifier should be checked twice daily and topped up as necessary. The humidifier equipment must be washed and disinfected regularly to prevent bacterial colonization.</p><h3>B. Choosing the modality of respiratory support</h3><ul><li><strong>Standard oxygen therapy:</strong><p>Simple mask and nasal cannula provided low FiO<sub>2</sub>, can be used on patients with mild hypoxia. FiO<sub>2</sub> varies and depends on minute ventilation. Use cannula with O<sub>2</sub> flow &lt; 5LPM; simple mask needs the O<sub>2</sub> flow 5-10LPM<br/>Venturi-mask provides constant FiO<sub>2</sub> as marked on the device, different color gives different FiO<sub>2</sub>. Usually, the color red gives FiO<sub>2</sub>=40% with O<sub>2</sub> flow 10-12LPM, the green one gives FiO<sub>2</sub> = 60% with oxygen flow 12-15 LPM.<br/>Use a non-rebreathing mask with reservoir bag and the highest possible oxygen flow to the patient who is remarkable hypoxic (SpO<sub>2</sub> &lt;90%), It may provide FiO<sub>2</sub> up to 80-95%</p></li><li><strong>High Flow nasal canula (HFNC):</strong><p>The main use of HFNC is to provide relatively high FiO<sub>2</sub> to patients with severe non-hypercapnic-hypoxemic respiratory failure. Most devices can provide maximum FiO<sub>2</sub>= 100%</p></li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 32 -->

<div><p>and flow 60LPM. Sometimes HFNC can help hypoxic-respiratory-failure patient avoid intubation, but it is important to detect failure and move early to invasive mechanical ventilation if indicated.</p><p>The ROX score = SpO<sub>2</sub>/FiO<sub>2</sub> ÷ RR, may help to decide whether to continue HFNC or change. Score &lt; 2.85 at 2h, or &lt; 3.47 at 6h, or &lt; 3.85 at h12 are predictors of failure. Score ≥ 4.88 after 2h, or 6h, or 12h predicts the success, and HFNC may continue.</p><ul><li><b>Non-invasive ventilation (NIV):</b></li></ul><p>NIV with a mask delivering continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bilevel positive airway pressure (BiPAP) can increase minute ventilation, reduce the work of breathing, recruit alveoli, and improve hemodynamics.</p><p>Contra-indication of NIV:</p><ul><li>Cardiac / respiratory arrest</li><li>Medically unstable (hypotensive shock, uncontrolled cardiac ischemia, or arrhythmias)</li><li>Severe upper gastrointestinal bleeding</li><li>Unable to protect airway (impaired cough or swallowing)</li><li>Excessive secretions</li><li>Unable to apply mask due to facial surgery, trauma, burns, or facial deformity</li><li>Agitated or uncooperative</li><li>Undrained pneumothorax</li><li>Multiorgan system failure</li></ul><p>NIV helps to improve oxygenation (increase PaO<sub>2</sub>) and ventilation (decrease PaCO<sub>2</sub>). Using ICU ventilator, in CPAP mode, CPAP = PEEP, in BiPAP mode EPAP=PEEP, delta P = PS, PS + PEEP= IPAP. (EPAP: expiratory positive airway pressure, IPAP: inspiratory positive airway pressure)</p><p>Initial setting usually PEE=5 cmH<sub>2</sub>O, PS=5-10 cmH<sub>2</sub>O</p><p>Increase level of PEEP usually helps to increase PaO<sub>2</sub>, and increase the PS usually decreases PaCO<sub>2</sub>.</p><ul><li><b>Mechanical ventilation:</b></li></ul><p>Endotracheal intubation and controlled mechanical ventilation should be pursued aggressively when ventilatory support is needed and NIV is not expected to improve outcomes, such as for acute exacerbations of asthma and diseases that do not respond rapidly to medical therapy (e.g., pneumonia and ARDS).</p><p>Endotracheal intubation is an aggressive procedure that should be done by trained personals. Some anesthetic drugs (hypnotic, opioids, myorelaxant) often used during intubation and for neuro sedation. The intubation tube-cuff pressure should be between 20 - 30cmH<sub>2</sub>O.</p><p>Modern ventilators have many settings and choices to adapt with patient conditions. The most frequent initial setting in emergency is:</p><ul><li>Mode: V-ACV (volume target-assist-control-ventilation)</li><li>Vt: 6-8ml/kg (Ideal body weight), ~ 400ml for adult 60-70kg actual body weight.</li><li>PEEP: 5 cmH<sub>2</sub>O</li><li>FiO<sub>2</sub>: start 100%, then reduce progressively as condition improved</li><li>Frequency: 12-18/min (varies to PCO<sub>2</sub>, increase Frequency if PCO<sub>2</sub> high)</li><li>Plateau pressure: &lt; 30 cmH<sub>2</sub>O</li><li>Trigger: -2 cmH<sub>2</sub>O, or – 2L/min</li></ul><p>Most often, after putting on mechanical ventilation in ER, the patient was transferred to operation room or ICU where the team adapt the ventilation setting and follow up accordingly. The control of mechanical ventilation is guided by arterial blood gas analysis or PetCO<sub>2</sub> and SpO<sub>2</sub> measures, the surveillance of respiratory mechanic and clinical response.</p><p>The main objectives of mechanical ventilation are:</p></div>

<!-- PAGE 33 -->

<div>
<p>(1) normalization of oxygenation and ventilation</p>
<p>(2) Avoid or limit the complications of ventilation. And</p>
<p>(3) wean patients from ventilator as soon as possible</p>
<h4>IV. OXYGEN SUPPLY</h4>
<p>At the facility level, there are many considerations required to estimate oxygen demand, including:</p>
<ul>
<li>Oxygen source type:
        <ul>
<li>pressure swing adsorption (PSA),</li>
<li>vacuum pressure swing adsorption (VPSA) plants,</li>
<li>bulk liquid tank,</li>
<li>bedside oxygen concentrators,</li>
<li>distribution manifolds with high-pressure cylinders, or</li>
<li>a combination of sources.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Distribution system: Oxygen may travel from the source to the patient's bedside in two main ways: pipe network or bedside high-pressure gas cylinders (or bedside concentrators). Accessories for monitoring and regulation of the medical gas should be included (e.g. pressure regulators and flowmeters).</li>
<li>Delivery equipment and devices: This refers to biomedical equipment connected to the network (e.g. patient ventilators, or direct interfaces such as nasal cannula).</li>
</ul>
<h5>Oxygen concentrator</h5>
<p>There are multiple devices available and approved, with different power efficiencies and a range of minimum and maximum oxygen output between a minimum of 0.125 L/min to a maximum of 10 L/min. Few portable oxygen concentrators can deliver more than 10 L/min, and many oxygen concentrators may claim a wide range of flows but only with low oxygen concentrations.</p>
<h5>Oxygen cylinders</h5>
<p>Many hospitals use oxygen cylinders, the pressure is in Bar. A full compressed cylinder is 120-130 Bar. A cylinder size J, has 47.2L water capacity, full compressed to 120 bar have oxygen = 47.2 × 120 = 5664L. A pressure release manometer is needed to reduce the outlet pressure to a constant pressure usually from 3.5-5 Bar to run the ventilator. Some model ventilators (e.g., Hamilton T1) can be connected also to low pressure O<sub>2</sub> flow outlets.</p>
</div>

<p>YES → Intubation and mechanical ventilation</p>
<p>Intubation and mechanical ventilation</p>
<p>Use lung protective ventilation or Highest level of support available and transfer to a ward or facility where mechanical ventilation can be done safely</p>
<p>Assess response (Increased distress or SpO2 &lt; 90% ?)</p>

<p>5 - 10L/min</p>
<p>Max FiO2 ≤ 0.5</p>

<p>Non-rebreathing mask + reservoir</p>

<p>Max FiO2 0.5-0.95</p>
<p>Assess response (Increased distress or SpO2 &lt; 90% ?)</p>

<p>YES → Consider 1 – 2h trial of one of the following based on patient &amp; local context</p>
<p>Consider 1 – 2h trial of one of the following based on patient &amp; local context</p>

<div><p><b>VI. SAFETY MEASURES FOR USING CYLINDERS</b></p><ul><li>Check cylinder pressure: Before use, verify that the cylinder has sufficient oxygen by checking the pressure gauge.</li><li>Open valve slowly: When opening the cylinder valve, do so slowly to prevent rapid gas release.</li><li>Use correct flow rate: Set the oxygen flow rate according to the patient's needs and medical prescription.</li><li>Monitor patient: Continuously monitor the patient's oxygen saturation levels and adjust the flow rate as needed.</li><li>Secure oxygen delivery device: Ensure the oxygen delivery device (nasal cannula, mask, etc.) is securely fitted to the patient.</li><li>Close valve when finished: Close the cylinder valve when the oxygen is no longer needed.</li></ul><p><b>VII. MONITORING AND ADJUSTMENT OF OXYGEN THERAPY</b></p><ul><li><b>Assess response</b><br/>Re-evaluate patient every hour initially, then every 2-4h once the condition is stable or improving. Check for:<ul><li>Increased/continued distress?</li><li>SpO<sub>2</sub> &lt; 90%, pH &lt; 7.30, PaCO<sub>2</sub> &gt; 45,</li><li>declining or altered mental status?</li></ul></li><li><b>Titration and SpO<sub>2</sub> goal</b><ul><li>SpO<sub>2</sub> ≥ 90% in adults and children</li><li>SpO<sub>2</sub> ≥ 92–95% in pregnant patients</li><li>SpO<sub>2</sub> ≥ 94% if child or adult with signs of multi-organ failure</li><li>Avoid SpO<sub>2</sub> &gt; 96% to avoid ill effects of hyperoxia and to conserve O<sub>2</sub> supply.</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</b></p><p><b>A. Chronic Obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD),</b></p><ul><li>Acute exacerbation of COPD<br/>medical therapy including bronchodilators, corticosteroids, and antibiotics when indicated.<br/>For patients presenting to the emergency department, provide supplemental oxygen if the patient is hypoxemic, and perform an assessment to determine the optimal treatment setting and whether noninvasive ventilation is indicated (due to increased work of breathing or impaired gas exchange).<ul><li>Titrate oxygen to a target saturation of 88%-92% to improve hypoxemia and prevent worsening partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PCO<sub>2</sub>) levels.</li><li>Carbon dioxide retention can occur, especially if higher saturations are achieved.</li><li>Perform arterial blood gas (ABG) measurements 30-60 minutes after starting oxygen.</li><li>Venturi masks (high-flow devices) are more accurate than nasal cannula but less likely to be tolerated.</li><li>Use pulse oximetry or ABG to track or adjust supplemental oxygen and monitor for carbon dioxide retention and/or worsening acidosis</li></ul></li><li>Post exacerbation long term use of oxygen<br/>At least 2 months after exacerbation, Check if patient need long term supplemental oxygen. Perform 2 times ABG check in 3 weeks apart.<br/>Prescribe oxygen at least 15h/day for long time in patients with stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who have “severe chronic resting hypoxemia”, defined as any one of the following:</li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 40 -->

<ul><li>arterial oxygen partial pressure (PaO<sub>2</sub>) ≤ 55 mm Hg</li><li>oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry (SpO<sub>2</sub>) ≤ 88%</li><li>PaO<sub>2</sub>: 56-59 mm Hg, SpO<sub>2</sub>= 89% or arterial oxygen saturation (SaO<sub>2</sub>) ≤ 88%, if evidence of peripheral edema, right heart failure, P pulmonale on electrocardiogram (ECG), polycythemia (hematocrit ≥ 55%), or pulmonary hypertension.</li></ul><p>Long term oxygen therapy (at home) should be initiated at a flow rate of 1 L/minute and titrated up by 1 L/minute increments until oxygen saturation measured by pulse oximetry (SpO<sub>2</sub>) is &gt; 90%. Consider arterial blood gas testing after initial titration to SpO<sub>2</sub> &gt; 90% to confirm target resting arterial oxygen partial pressure (PaO<sub>2</sub>) ≥ 60 mm Hg has been achieved (If available).</p><p>Oxygen flow should be sufficient to achieve PaO<sub>2</sub> &gt; 60 mm Hg or 90% SpO<sub>2</sub> without causing hypercapnia or acidosis (Strong recommendation).</p><h3>B. Patient with Central nervous System lesion (stroke, brain injury)</h3><ul><li>Patient with ischemic stroke</li></ul><p>Patients with adequate ventilation should have their oxygen saturation monitored. Patients who are hypoxic should receive supplemental oxygen to maintain oxygen saturation &gt;94%. Supplemental oxygen should not routinely be given to nonhypoxic patients with acute ischemic stroke.</p><ul><li>Brain injury (traumatic)<ul><li>Pre-hospital: Patients who are not intubated should receive supplemental oxygen as necessary to maintain an SpO<sub>2</sub> &gt;90% to 93%</li><li>In Emergency department: Endotracheal intubation should be performed at this time for all patients with a GCS score &lt;9, inability to protect the airway, inability to maintain SpO<sub>2</sub>&gt;90 % despite the use of supplemental oxygen, or clinical signs of cerebral herniation. Adequate oxygenation (PaO<sub>2</sub> &gt;60 mmHg) continues to be a priority.</li><li>Recent study found that, the lowest mean PaO<sub>2</sub> observed to maintain PbtO<sub>2</sub> (Oxygen partial pressure in brain tissue) above the ischemic threshold (20mmHg) was 94 mmHg. The authors' results suggest that the minimal PaO<sub>2</sub> target to ensure adequate cerebral oxygenation during the first few days after TBI should be higher than that suggested in the Brain Trauma Foundation guidelines</li></ul></li></ul><h3>IX. OXYGEN TOXICITY AND COMPLICATIONS</h3><ul><li>Oxygen toxicity — Oxygen toxicity is considered to be a harmful effect of inspired oxygen at pressures greater than atmospheric pressure (i.e., &gt;0.21 inspired fraction of oxygen at sea level).</li><li>Oxygen toxicity can be caused by hyperoxia and hyperoxemia and is generally responsible for parenchymal lung injury, the retinopathy of prematurity and bronchopulmonary dysplasia in infants.</li><li>In general, patients at greatest risk of oxygen toxicity are those who are receiving mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure with a fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO<sub>2</sub>) greater than 0.6 for prolonged durations (e.g., &gt;24 hours).</li><li>Efficient oxygen usage should be:<ul><li><b>Target Saturation Range:</b> Oxygen should be prescribed according to a target saturation range. For most acutely ill patients, the goal is to achieve normal or near-normal oxygen saturation.</li><li><b>Monitoring:</b> Continuous monitoring of oxygen saturation using pulse oximetry is essential. This helps ensure that the patient remains within the target range and allows for adjustments as needed.</li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 41 -->

<ul><li>Controlled Administration: For patients with conditions like COPD, controlled or low-dose oxygen therapy is recommended to avoid complications such as hypercapnia.</li></ul><p><b>X- REFERENCES</b></p><ol><li>Clinical care for severe acute respiratory infection: toolkit, update 2022. <h1>EARLY WARNING SCORE IN HOSPITAL</h1>
<p><i>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. NGETH Sopanha</i></p>
<h2>I- INTRODUCTION</h2>
<p>Patients seldom deteriorate abruptly, even though clinicians may recognize the deterioration suddenly. In early stages, some signs may be subtle, and clinicians may not fully appreciate the severity of the clinical picture. The physiologic deterioration precedes many cardiopulmonary arrests by hours, suggesting that early intervention could prevent the need for resuscitation, admission to the ICU, and other sentinel events.</p>
<h2>II- EARLY RECOGNITION OF PATIENT WHO DETERIORATES IN HOSPITAL</h2>
<p>The NEWS-2 score</p>
<p>Assessment of vital signs correctly frequently plus observation of patient general condition may ensure good patient care. Based on the degree of change from normal range of the vital signs, the score NEWS (National Early Warning Score) categorizes the patient group who need more frequent assessment and escalation of management before they become urgent or critically ill. The NEWS provides the basis for a unified and systematic approach to the first assessment and triage of acutely ill patients, and a simple track-and-trigger system for monitoring clinical progress for all patients in hospitals.</p>
<p>The NEWS is based on a simple aggregate scoring system in which a score is allocated to physiological measurements, already recorded in routine practice, when patients present to, or are being monitored in hospital.</p>
<p>The NEWS-1 issue in 2012, was reviewed and updated in 2017 as NEWS-2</p>
<p>Six simple physiological parameters form the basis of the scoring system:</p>
<ol>
<li>respiration rate</li>
<li>oxygen saturation</li>
<li>systolic blood pressure</li>
<li>pulse rate</li>
<li>level of consciousness or new confusion*</li>
<li>temperature.</li>
</ol>
<p>*The patient has new-onset confusion, disorientation and/or agitation, where previously their mental state was normal – this may be subtle. The patient may respond to questions coherently, but there is some confusion, disorientation and/or agitation. This would score 3 or 4 on the GCS (rather than the normal 5 for verbal response), and scores 3 on the NEWS system.</p>
<p>A score is allocated to each parameter as they are measured, with the magnitude of the score reflecting how extremely the parameter varies from the norm. The score is then aggregated. The score is uplifted by 2 points for people requiring supplemental oxygen to maintain their recommended oxygen saturation.</p>

<ul>
<li>The chart has a dedicated section (SpO2 Scale 2) for use in patients with hypercapnic respiratory failure (usually due to COPD) who have clinically recommended oxygen saturation of 88–92%. (for general patient use scale-1 to score SpO2, use scale 2 only after discussed with doctor)</li>
<li>Sepsis should be considered in any patient with a known infection, signs or symptoms of infection, or in patients at high risk of infection, and a NEWS score of 5 or more.</li>
<li>In identifying patients with sepsis (sepsis-3) outside of ICU, qSOFA_ (three criteria: altered mental status, systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg, and respiratory rate ≥22 breaths per minute. When any 2 were positive) have been proposed. Compared with NEWS-2, qSOFA is more specific but it is less sensitive than NEWS-2. So, when both are positive, it is more certain that patient has sepsis.</li>
<li>Clinical response to the NEWS should be recorded. This will provide a continuous record of actions taken in response to variations in the NEWS and act as a prompt for escalating care if necessary.</li>
</ul>

Higher-dependency unit or ICU<br/>• Clinical care in an environment with monitoring facilities</td></tr></tbody></table><p><b>Note:</b></p><ul><li>A ward-based response typically involves a prompt assessment by a ward nurse to decide on changes to the frequency of monitoring or escalation of clinical care.</li><li>An urgent-based response involves an urgent review by a ward-based doctor to determine the cause and decide on changes to monitoring or escalation of clinical care</li><li>To adapt to our situations, a Registered nurse (RN) should be the head of the nurse-shift.</li></ul><h3>III- EARLY RECOGNITION AND MANAGE THE PATIENTS WHO DETERIORATED IN HOSPITALS</h3><p>(The care that should be provided to all critically ill patients in all hospitals in the world)</p><h4>A. The concept of Essential Emergency and Critical Care (EECC)</h4><p>In hospitals, sometimes patients' conditions may deteriorate and become life threatening while the medical team only manages or transfers the patient to ICU lately. Not as people expected, many factors contributed to this situation: No correct vital signs checked, no vital signs Interval Policy, Understaffed Hospital, Undertrained providers, critical illness not recognized, No Senior Staff Available.</p></div>

<!-- PAGE 45 -->

<div><p>The early stage of critical condition, mostly response well with the simple measures and techniques of management while late management in ICU is often costly, complex, less effective or fails to help.</p><p>Critical illness is often reversible. Identification is time-critical. Early identification of critically ill patients is key. Prompt, time-critical care interventions are crucial to reversing the course of critical illness and saving patient lives.</p><p>Essential Emergency and Critical Care (EECC) was established around 2020, with its initial framework and guidelines developed through a Delphi process—a structured approach to building consensus among healthcare experts worldwide. Over 270 specialists from various regions and backgrounds collaborated on the design of EECC, focusing on practical, low-cost interventions that could be feasibly implemented in all hospitals, including those in low-resource settings. This initiative was partially driven by the need for effective care models during the COVID-19 pandemic, which highlighted critical care gaps globally.</p><p>The framework builds on WHO's Basic Emergency Care principles and aims to provide consistent, essential care that can stabilize critically ill patients, regardless of their specific diagnosis or the availability of specialized intensive care resources. This model is being gradually implemented worldwide, especially in areas where access to advanced critical care is limited, to address preventable mortality among critically ill patients.</p><h3>B. The process of EECC</h3><p>The purpose of EECC is to identify critical illness and provide the timely, lifesaving care patients need to reverse their course of illness. Evaluating the 8 vital signs of EECC is core to this process. Providers must be able to determine normal vital signs. Knowing the normal enables providers to then recognize when vital signs are critically deranged. When patient vital signs are in danger zone, the clinical management starts to stabilize the condition by using adapted basic life support techniques. If conditions are a common problem like post-partum bleeding, anaphylaxis reaction, poisoning, healthcare providers may start the initial measures and follow the EECC protocol.</p><h3>C. The EECC vital signs</h3><p>There are 8 vital signs in EECC. Traditional 5 vital signs include:</p><ol><li>heart rate,</li><li>blood pressure,</li><li>respiratory rate,</li><li>oxygen saturation, and</li><li>temperature.</li></ol><p>EECC includes additional 2 vital assessments:</p><ol><li>level of consciousness</li></ol><p>Level of consciousness can be assessed by GCS or AVPU scale.</p></div>

<!-- PAGE 46 -->

<div>
<p>(7) assessment for abnormal airway sounds.</p>
<p>Snoring, gurgling, or stridor predict airway obstruction and compromised oxygenation.</p>
<p>The additional one from overall patient condition and intuition of health worker</p>
<p>(8) The overall condition of the patient's health (health worker, patient, or guardian concern that condition has worsened). Health worker intuition when a health worker is concerned that a patient is critically ill, then they ARE critically ill, even if all vital signs are ok</p>
<p>All hospital patients should have their (8) vital signs assessed at initial presentation and at a minimum every 24 hours thereafter. EECC recommends that vital signs be reassessed for changes in condition and setting, for example when:</p>
<ul>
<li>When bedside providers, patients, or guardians become concerned the patient's condition has worsened</li>
<li>During and after surgery or anesthesia</li>
<li>During and after transport/transfer of a patient at risk of critical illness</li>
<li>Following treatment or action for re-evaluation</li>
</ul>
<p>Even before vital assessments, providers must start to determine if the patient is experiencing a life-threatening process. This is done by assessing:</p>
<ul>
<li>If the patient is awake (level of consciousness), which can be assessed using AVPU</li>
<li>If the patient is talking (airway) and their breathing is calm, easy and quiet, (breathing).</li>
<li>If the patient is unconscious, providers must quickly determine if there is a palpable pulse (circulation)</li>
</ul>
<p>Airway, breathing and circulation can be remembered by “ABC”.</p>
<p>From data of vital signs measured, classify the degree of derangement, identify danger signs and prompt intervention using VSĐT (Vital signs Direct therapy) table.</p>
<p>Danger signs of Airway:</p>
<ul>
<li>When GCS &lt; 8 or Unresponsive</li>
<li>Abnormal airway sound</li>
</ul>
<p>Danger signs of breathing:</p>
<ul>
<li>Respiratory rate &lt;8 or &gt;30 bpm or</li>
<li>Need supplemental oxygen &gt; 10L/min or FiO<sub>2</sub>= 80-100% or</li>
<li>Saturation (SpO<sub>2</sub>) &lt; 90%</li>
</ul>
<p>Danger signs of Circulation:</p>
<ul>
<li>Heart rate &lt;40 or &gt;130 bpm or</li>
<li>Systolic blood pressure &lt;90 mmHg</li>
</ul>
</div>

<p>Bedside nurse or treatment team should prompt the management without delay or wait for doctor to come.</p>
<p>If a health provider or patient's family remarks that the patient condition is getting worst (= danger sign), whatever vital signs measured, it should prompt to check the patient again or ask doctor to review.</p>
<p>Clinical practice and procedures in VSDT (Should be able to practice by nurse):</p>
<ul>
<li>Protect airway _ see basic life support techniques</li>
<li>Recovery position_ see basic life support techniques</li>
<li>Chin tilt / jaw thrust_ see basic life support techniques</li>
<li>Oro-pharyngeal airway suction_ SOP in Emergency &amp; ICU nursing</li>
<li>Position the patient according to pathology (sit-up, lateral, elevation head of the bed, bed head down.) _ see basic life support techniques.</li>
<li>Use oxygen correctly_ see guideline on oxygen use</li>
<li>IV-line placement, and fluid (Ringer lactate) bolus up to 2L in 2h</li>
</ul>
<p>Continuous Monitoring: Regularly reassess vital signs to ensure the patient's condition is improving</p>
<p>Doctor reviews and take additional measures or transfer the patient</p>
<ul>
<li>Procedure for post-partum hemorrhage</li>
<li>Procedure for coma</li>
<li>Procedure for poisoning</li>
<li>Procedure for anaphylaxis</li>
</ul>
<p>The content of the EECC program includes:</p>
<ul>
<li>40 Clinical Processes: These are specific actions and treatments, such as triage, monitoring, patient positioning, oxygen therapy, and intravenous fluids.</li>
<li>67 Hospital Readiness Requirements: These ensure that hospitals are equipped to provide the necessary care.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 48 -->

<ul><li>COVID-19 Specific Additions: Additional guidelines tailored to the care of critically ill patients with COVID-19.</li></ul><p>Implementing EECC can help reduce preventable deaths and improve patient outcomes. Most of the clinical practices skills needed are included in basic life support, however healthcare providers should be able to regularly refresh their skill, and additional skill can be gained by EECC online training or Institutional organized training.</p><h4>IV- REFERENCES</h4><ol><li>Royal College of Physicians. <h1>SHOCK</h1>
<p>Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. CHHUOY Meng,<br/>
Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha,<br/>
Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy,<br/>
Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya</p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Shock is a life-threatening, generalized form of acute circulatory failure associated with inadequate oxygen utilization by the cells. Circulatory shock leads to cellular and tissue hypoxia resulting in cellular death and dysfunction of vital organs. There is circulatory failure manifested as hypotension (= reduced tissue perfusion); however, it is crucial to recognize that a patient in shock can present hypertensive, normotensive, or hypotensive.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Shock affects about one-third of patients admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU). Distributive shock is the most common type of shock, followed by hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock. Obstructive shock is relatively less common. The most common type of distributive shock is septic shock and has a mortality rate between 40 to 50%.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Four types of shock are recognized: hypovolemic, distributive, cardiogenic and obstructive.</p>
<h3>1. Hypovolemic Shock</h3>

<li>Ruptured ectopic pregnancy</li>
<li>Postpartum hemorrhage</li>
<li>Uterine or vaginal hemorrhage (eg, infection, tumors, lacerations)</li>
</ul>
</td>

<li>Skin losses (eg, heat stroke, burns, dermatologic conditions)</li>
<li>Renal losses (eg, excessive drug-induced or osmotic diuresis, salt-wasting nephropathies, hypoaldosteronism)</li>
<li>Third space losses into the extravascular space or body cavities (eg, postoperative and trauma, intestinal obstruction, crush injury, pancreatitis, cirrhosis)</li>

<h3>4. Obstructive Shock</h3>
<p>Obstructive shock is due to extracardiac cause of cardiac pump failure and often associated with poor right ventricular failure. It is divided into 2 categories:</p>
<ul>
<li>Pulmonary vascular
        <ul>
<li>Pulmonary embolus</li>
<li>Severe pulmonary hypertension</li>
<li>Acute obstruction of pulmonic or tricuspid valve</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Mechanical
        <ul>
<li>Tension pneumothorax / hemothorax (trauma, iatrogenic)</li>
<li>Pericardial tamponade (trauma, viral/bacterial infection, autoimmune...)</li>
<li>Constrictive pericarditis</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h3>
<p>Cellular hypoxia causes cell membrane ion pump dysfunction, intracellular edema, leakage of intracellular contents into the extracellular space, and inadequate regulation of intracellular pH. These processes progress to the systemic level, resulting in acidosis, and</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 51 -->

<div><p>endothelial dysfunction, as well as further stimulation of inflammatory or anti-inflammatory cascades. Compounding this process is further reduction in tissue perfusion from complex humoral and microcirculatory processes that impair regional blood flow. Serum lactate levels have traditionally been used as surrogates for hypoperfusion and tissue hypoxia. Elevations in serum lactate level are useful risk-stratification tools in undifferentiated shock. Four types of shock are recognized:</p><ul><li>Distributive: is characterized by severe peripheral vasodilatation with decreased systemic vascular resistance and altered oxygen extraction (vasodilatory shock). For example, severe sepsis or anaphylaxis.</li><li>Cardiogenic: is due to intracardiac causes of cardiac pump failure that result in reduced cardiac output (CO) such as due to acute myocardial infarction, end-stage cardiomyopathy, advanced valvular heart disease, myocarditis, or cardiac arrhythmias).</li><li>Hypovolemic: is due to reduced intravascular volume from internal or external fluid loss (ie, reduced preload), which, in turn, reduces CO.</li><li>Obstructive: is due to extracardiac causes of cardiac pump failure and often associated with poor right ventricular output (pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade, or tension pneumothorax).</li></ul><img alt="Figure 1 shows four schematic representations of the main types of shock: Distributive shock (Vasodilation), Hypovolemic shock (Loss of plasma or blood volume), Cardiogenic shock (Ventricular failure), and Obstructive shock (Obstruction, Pericardial tamponade)."/><p>Figure 1: Schematic Representations of the four main types of shock (From NEJM.org)</p><h2>V. DIAGNOSIS</h2><p>A diagnosis of shock is based upon a constellation of clinical suspicion, biochemical, and hemodynamic features.</p><h3>a. Clinical Manifestation</h3><p>The clinical findings associated with shock vary according to the etiology and stage of presentation (pre-shock, shock, end-organ dysfunction). A diagnosis of shock is based on clinical, hemodynamic, and biochemical signs, which can broadly be summarized into three components:</p><ol><li>Hypotension:<ul><li>Absolute (eg, systolic blood pressure &lt;90 mmHg; mean arterial pressure &lt;65 mmHg, associated tachycardia (except for patients under beta blockers))</li><li>Relative (eg, a drop in systolic blood pressure &gt;40 mmHg)</li></ul></li><li>Clinical signs of tissue hypoperfusion which are apparent through the three “windows” of the body:<ul><li>Cutaneous (skin that is cold and clammy, with vasoconstriction and cyanosis, findings that are most evident in low-flow states)</li><li>Renal (urine output of &lt;0.5 ml/kg/h)</li><li>Neurologic (altered mental state, which typically includes obtundation, disorientation, and confusion).</li></ul></li></ol></div>

<!-- PAGE 52 -->

<h3>3. Hyperlactatemia (&gt;1.5 mmol/L)</h3>
<p>A focused history should be obtained from the patient (if feasible) and/or patient's relatives (information regarding risk factors, medications, and trend of baseline vital signs including blood pressure, valuable clues regarding the patient's risk for shock and potential etiology). Clinical features and symptoms can vary according to the type and stage of shock. Also, features pertaining to the underlying cause of the shock can be present.</p>
<ul>
<li>Patients with hypovolemic shock can have general features as mentioned above as well as evidence of orthostatic hypotension, pallor, flattened jugular venous pulsations, may have sequelae of chronic liver disease (in case of variceal bleeding).</li>
<li>Patients with septic shock may present with symptoms suggestive of the source of infection (example-skin manifestations of primary infection such as erysipelas, cellulitis, necrotizing soft-tissue infections)</li>
<li>Patients with anaphylactic shock can have hypotension, flushing, urticaria, tachypnea, hoarseness of voice, oral and facial edema, hives, wheeze, inspiratory stridor, and history of exposure to common allergens such as medications or food items the patient is allergic to or insect stings.</li>
<li>Tension pneumothorax should be suspected in a patient with undifferentiated shock who has tachypnea, unilateral pleuritic chest pain, absent or diminished breath sounds, tracheal deviation to the normal side, distended neck veins and also has pertinent risk factors for tension pneumothorax such as recent trauma, mechanical ventilation, underlying cystic lung disease.</li>
<li>In a patient with undifferentiated shock, diagnostic clues to pericardial tamponade as the etiology include dyspnea, the Beck triad (elevated jugular venous pressure, muffled heart sounds, hypotension), pulsus paradoxus, and known risk factors such as trauma, the recent history of pericardial effusion, and thoracic procedures.</li>
<li>Cardiogenic shock should be considered as the etiology if the patient with undifferentiated shock had chest pain suggestive of cardiac origin, narrow pulse pressure, elevated jugular venous pulsations or lung crackles, and significant arrhythmias on EKG.</li>
</ul>
<p><i>Point-of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS)</i> is effective at identifying the cause of shock and identifying appropriate next steps.</p>
<h4>b. Investigation</h4>
<p>Laboratory evaluation:</p>
<ul>
<li>Complete blood count and differential</li>
<li>A complete metabolic panel, including renal and liver function tests</li>
<li>Serum lactate</li>
<li>Blood gas analysis (arterial or venous)</li>
<li>Coagulation studies and D-dimer level</li>
<li>Cardiac enzymes (Troponin-I or -T) and natriuretic peptides (NT-proBNP) [cardiogenic shock]. C-Reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin, urine analysis, blood culture and/or urine culture (before administration of antibiotics) and other microbiology exploration [Septic shock]</li>
</ul>
<p>Imaging:</p>
<ul>
<li>EKG</li>
<li>Chest radiography</li>
<li>Point-of care (POC) ultrasound (if available with trained personnel)</li>
<li>Directed at etiology of shock</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 53 -->

<h2>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h2>
<p>Each class of shock (distributive, cardiogenic, hypovolemic, obstructive) is distinguished from the other by a collection of clinical features supported by etiology found, laboratory, imaging, and hemodynamic findings.</p>
<ol>
<li>Hypovolemic shock
    <ul>
<li>Reduced preload in context of a suspected or known cause.</li>
<li>Hypovolemia displaying signs of reduced skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, a collapsible IVC on imaging.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Distributive shock
    <ul>
<li>Hypotension without clinical and hemodynamic signs of reduced preload (eg, normal skin turgor, normal inferior vena cava on imaging) or fluid overload.</li>
<li>A preserved or hyperdynamic left ventricle is typically observed on echocardiography.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<p><b>a. Septic Shock</b></p>
<p><b>i. Definition</b></p>
<p>Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.</p>
<p>Septic Shock is defined as sepsis that has circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities. Clinically, this includes patients who fulfill the criteria for sepsis who, despite adequate fluid resuscitation, require vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥ 65mmHg and have a lactate &gt; 2mmol/L (&gt;18mg/dL).</p>
<p><b>ii. Evaluation</b></p>
<p>Patients who have sepsis have organ dysfunction that can be identified by using the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA):</p>
