<p>b. Anaphylactic shock</p>
<ul>
<li>Clinical = Diagnostic</li>
<li>Most common (90%) Cutaneous: Urticaria, erythema, pruritus, angioedema, flushing</li>
<li>Danger sign:
        <ul>
<li>Respiratory: stridor, wheezing, dyspnea, increased work of breathing, persistent cough, cyanosis</li>
<li>Cardiovascular: Hypotension, dysrhythmias, collapse, chest pain</li>
<li>Gastrointestinal: Nausea, Vomiting</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>c. Neurogenic Shock</p>
<ul>
<li>Clinical: Hypotension without tachycardia, bradycardia, warm and dry skin</li>
</ul>
<p>3. Cardiogenic shock</p>
<ul>
<li>Hypotension in association with pulmonary edema,</li>
<li>Large dilated ventricles and poor left ventricle function, or valvular or septal abnormalities on echocardiography.</li>
</ul>
<p>4. Obstructive shock</p>
<ul>
<li>Hypotension associated with distended neck veins but usually without clinical signs of fluids overload or reduced preload.</li>
<li>Bedside ultrasonography or echocardiography is useful in this setting to detect pericardial tamponade and pneumothorax.</li>
<li>Clinical:
        <ul>
<li>Pulsus paradoxus (a drop on systolic BP greater than 10 mmHg on inspiration)</li>
<li>Muffled heart tones (cardiac tamponade)</li>
<li>Elevated JVD (depending on volume status)</li>
<li>Unilateral absence of breath sounds (tension pneumothorax)</li>
<li>Tracheal deviation (tension pneumothorax)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2>
<p>Shock is a time-sensitive condition. All patients with shock must be early recognized and managed well without delay. The management of shock comprises of the following principles that include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Recognition of the pattern of shock</li>
<li>Selecting appropriate treatment (resuscitation)</li>
<li>Specific therapy for the underlying problem</li>
<li>Monitoring clinical response.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 55 -->

<div><p>1. Objectives</p><p>The objectives of intervention:</p><ul><li>Restore adequate tissue perfusion</li><li>Prevent worsening or to help recover organ dysfunction (include coagulation disorders) and organ failure.</li><li>Once identified, the cause must be corrected rapidly.</li></ul><p>2. Critical Sign</p><ul><li>Anuria and acute renal failure</li><li>Acidemia further depresses CO (pH &lt;7.2)</li><li>Hypotension becomes severe and unresponsive to therapy</li><li>Hyperlactatemia often worsens</li><li>Restlessness evolves into obtundation and coma.</li></ul><p>3. Mortality risk factor</p><ul><li>Patient-related factors (age, comorbidities, immune status...)</li><li>Shock-related factors (types, duration and severity, underlying causes, MOD...)</li><li>Response to treatment (delayed appropriate treatment or failure to respond to initial treatment)</li></ul><p>4. Outpatient Management</p><p>All patients with shock cannot be managed in the outpatient setting.</p><p>5. First-line treatment</p><p>Initial management (= ABC)</p><ul><li>Airway:<ul><li>Assess the signs of airway obstruction: “see-saw” respiration, central cyanosis, no breath sounds.</li><li>Opening the airway using: Head-tilt chin-lift, Jaw-thrust maneuver, insertion of an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway. Tracheal intubation may be required if those maneuver fails.</li></ul></li><li>Breathing:<ul><li>All patients should receive supplemental oxygen.</li><li>For patients with respiratory distress or who are hemodynamically unstable, noninvasive or invasive mechanical ventilation are typically needed.</li><li>Goal: Arterial oxygen saturation should be restored to &gt;94% and ventilation controlled to maintain a PaCO<sub>2</sub> of 35 to 40 mm Hg.</li></ul></li><li>Circulation:<ul><li>IV access through large-bore peripheral venous lines.</li><li>Central venous access is the preferred route for the long-term administration of vasopressor therapy and in assessing volume status (preload) and monitoring ScvO<sub>2</sub>.</li><li>Passive leg raising above the level of the heart with the patient supine (useful in hypovolemic shock but not in cardiogenic shock).</li><li>Internal bleeding: surgical consultation.</li><li>External hemorrhage: direct compression, wound packing and extremity tourniquets.</li><li>Isotonic Crystalloid solutions:<ul><li>0.9% NaCl, Ringer lactate (use RL for all cases except brain injury that use 0.9% NaCl)</li><li>20 to 40 mL/kg given rapidly (over 10 to 20 minutes)</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 56 -->

<ul><li>Hemorrhagic shock: new concept in early intervention is to stop the bleeding source and early transfusion to minimize crystalloid or colloids use.</li></ul><p>6. Treatment Adjustment</p><p>A. Hypovolemic Shock</p><table border="1"><thead><tr><th>Supportive Treatment</th><th>Etiologic Treatment</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><ul><li>O2: 6 - 10L/min (High flow oxygen mask) - Intubation-Ventilation?</li><li>2 large caliber IV access (14 - 16 G)</li><li>Passive leg raising above the level of the heart with the patient supine.</li><li>Anti-shock pant</li><li>Fluid therapy<ul><li>Crystalloids (RL, SSI)</li><li>Colloids: Gelatins (Gelofusine), Dextrans, Albumin</li></ul></li><li>If no response to fluids (SBP &lt; 80 mmHg and MAP &lt; 60 mmHg): Norepinephrine starts 5 mcg/min IV</li><li>Blood products:<ul><li>Packed red blood cell (PRBC)<ul><li>Objectives, Hemoglobin:<ul><li>&gt; 7g/dl most case</li><li>10g/dl: heart failure or coronary artery disease; traumatic brain injury</li></ul></li></ul></li><li>Platelet transfusion: 1 unit of apheresis platelets, or 6 units of random donor platelets if platelet &lt;50,000/microL</li><li>Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) if PT &lt; 40% or INR &gt; 2</li></ul></li></ul></td><td>Contemporary of the symptomatic treatment:<ul><li>Surgical procedure:<ul><li>goal to achieve hemostasis in aortic aneurysm rupture; gastrointestinal bleeding; open penetrating wound</li></ul></li><li>Medical procedure:<ul><li>Sclerosis of varices</li><li>Embolization endovascular</li></ul></li></ul></td></tr></tbody></table><p>Notes:</p><ul><li>The presence or likelihood of severe, ongoing hemorrhage, Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP) in a 1:1:1 ratio of plasma to platelets to pRBCs is generally used.</li></ul><p>B. Distributive Shock</p><p>i. Septic shock</p><table border="1"><thead><tr><th>Supportive Treatment</th><th>Etiologic Treatment</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><ul><li>Oxygen therapy (6-10L/min) - Intubation - Ventilation</li><li>2 large peripheral IV, Central venous catheter (CVC) if needed</li><li>Measure serum lactate</li><li>Fluid therapy:</li></ul></td><td><ul><li>BLOOD CULTURE prior to antibiotic use</li><li>Empiric antibiotic therapy:<ul><li>IV - dual therapy</li><li>Choice according to clinical context, suspected infectious source</li></ul></li></ul></td></tr></tbody></table>

<div>
<p><b>D. Obstructive Shock</b></p>
<ul>
<li>The goal is to remove the obstruction as quickly as possible.</li>
<li>A cardiac tamponade requires a pericardiocentesis in which a provider inserts a needle or catheter into the pericardium to remove the accumulated fluid.</li>
<li>In a tension pneumothorax, a provider inserts a large bore needle (i.e., 14-gauge) or chest tube into the pulmonary space causing immediate evacuation of air, therefore re-expanding the lung.</li>
<li>A pulmonary embolism large enough to cause shock is treated with a thrombolytic or removed during a surgical embolectomy or fragmented and aspirated through percutaneous mechanical thrombectomy.</li>
</ul>
</div>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<p>Patients often present with combined forms of shock. Examples include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Patients with shock from sepsis or pancreatitis have distributive shock (due to the effects of inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cascades on vascular permeability and peripheral vasodilation); however, they also often have a hypovolemic component (due to decreased oral intake, insensible losses, vomiting, diarrhea) and a cardiogenic component (due to inflammation-related myocardial depression).</li>
<li>Patients with underlying cardiomyopathy may present with hypovolemic shock (from over-diuresis) and cardiogenic shock (from inadequate compensatory tachycardia and/or stroke volume).</li>
<li>Patients with severe traumatic injury may have hemorrhagic shock from blood loss as well as distributive shock from SIRS or, less commonly, fat embolism.</li>
<li>Patients with trauma to the spinal cord can have distributive shock from injury-related autonomic dysfunction and cardiogenic shock from myocardial depression.</li>
<li>Patients with a ruptured left ventricular free wall aneurysm can have cardiogenic shock from primary pump failure, obstructive shock from cardiac tamponade when blood loss is contained by the pericardial sac, and hemorrhagic shock when blood loss is not contained by the pericardial sac.</li>
<li>Patients with septic shock may transition from a distributive (low systemic vascular resistance) shock state to multifactorial shock state after massive volume resuscitation that results in abdominal compartment syndrome and/or acute right heart syndrome.</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<p>Effects of shock are reversible in the early stages and a delay in diagnosis and/or timely initiation of treatment can lead to irreversible changes including multiorgan failure (MOF) and death. Even with treatment, mortality from cardiogenic shock after MI (60 to 65%) and septic shock (30 to 40%) is high. Prognosis depends on the cause, preexisting or complicating illness, time between onset and diagnosis, and promptness and adequacy of therapy.</p>
<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<p>As global tissue hypoxia progresses, shock ensues, followed by the multiorgan dysfunction syndrome (MODS), which is manifested by:</p>
<ul>
<li>Acute renal failure (ARF)</li>
<li>Respiratory failure: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)</li>
<li>Myocardial depression</li>
<li>Liver failure</li>
<li>Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)</li>
<li>Anoxic encephalopathy.</li>
</ul>
<p>Once MODS progresses, in some cases, death is inevitable despite proper eradication of the inciting cause.</p>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<p>For medical professionals:</p>
<ul>
<li>Recognize the patients from early stage of shock (pre-shock, shock)</li>
<li>Rapidly identify the etiology</li>
<li>Early apply the appropriate interventions and therapy to correct the cause of shock and prevent MOF and death.</li>
</ul>
<p>For general population:</p>
<ul>
<li>Alert any serious case without delay (SAMU, hospital, etc.)!!! (Time is life)</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 62 -->

<ul><li>Get regular vaccinations against viral infections that may cause sepsis.</li><li>Avoid any contact with the responsible allergen (anaphylactic shock)</li><li>Practice good hygiene.</li><li>Care for and clean any open or gaping wounds.</li><li>Follow medical advice on managing bacterial infections.</li><li>Treat fungal and parasitic infections as soon as symptoms appear.</li><li>Control diabetes, if relevant.</li><li>Avoid smoking.</li></ul><h2>XII. <h1>HEMORRHAGIC SHOCK</h1>
<p><i>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. NGETH Sopanha</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Hemorrhagic shock refers to a state of hypoperfusion due to significant rapid blood loss. Significant and rapid blood loss results in decreased circulating blood volume and therefore inadequate tissue perfusion. This results in severe, life-threatening systemic hypoxia and cellular dysfunction. Without support, hemorrhage may result in hemodynamic instability, end-organ hypoperfusion, and eventually death.</p>
<p>Shock is a physiologic continuum, there are 3 stages of shock:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Compensated shock (Pre-shock):</b> Patient's physiologic reserve prevents significant alteration in vital signs. Potentially, with timely and appropriate management, deterioration can be prevented, and signs of impending deterioration can be reversed (eg, normalization of heart rate and serum lactate levels).</li>
<li><b>Decompensated shock (Shock):</b> Loss of circulating volume overcomes patient's physiologic reserve, resulting in significant alteration in vital signs. The signs and symptoms of organ dysfunction appear (tachycardia, dyspnea, restlessness, diaphoresis, metabolic acidosis, hypotension, oliguria, and cool, clammy skin)</li>
<li><b>End-organ dysfunction –</b> Progressive shock leads to irreversible organ damage, multiorgan failure (MOF), and death. During this stage, anuria and acute kidney failure develop, acidemia further depresses CO, hypotension becomes severe and recalcitrant to therapy, hyperlactatemia often worsens, and restlessness evolves into obtundation and coma. Death is common in this phase of shock.</li>
</ul>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Hemorrhagic shock in Southeast Asia is a critical public health issue, often resulting from trauma, gastrointestinal bleeding, or ruptured aneurysms.</p>
<p><b>Incidence and Mortality</b></p>
<p><b>High Incidence:</b> Southeast Asia has a high incidence of hemorrhagic shock due to road traffic accidents, natural disasters, and violence.</p>
<p><b>Mortality Rates:</b> Mortality rates vary by country, but hemorrhagic shock remains a leading cause of death in trauma cases.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li>Trauma- penetrating and blunt:
        <ul>
<li>Abdominal:
                <ul>
<li>Splenic injury</li>
<li>Liver injury</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Chest:
                <ul>
<li>Hemothorax</li>
<li>Aorta or great vessel injury</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 64 -->

<ul><li>Pelvis:<ul><li>Pelvic fracture with vascular injury</li></ul></li><li>Vascular malformations:<ul><li>May lead to thoracic, intraperitoneal, or retroperitoneal bleeding</li><li>Aneurysms:<ul><li>Abdominal aortic aneurysm most common</li><li>Mycotic aneurysm secondary to endocarditis</li></ul></li><li>Aortogastric fistula</li><li>Arteriovenous malformations</li></ul></li><li>□ Abortion: Complete, partial, or inevitable</li><li>□ Ectopic pregnancy</li><li>□ Epistaxis</li><li>□ Fractures (especially pelvis and long bones)</li><li>□ GI bleeding</li><li>□ Hemoptyxis</li><li>□ Malignancies</li><li>□ Placenta previa or abruption</li><li>□ Postpartum hemorrhage</li><li>□ Retroperitoneal bleeds</li><li>□ Splenic rupture</li><li>□ Vascular injuries</li></ul><h4>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h4><p>In hemorrhagic shock, blood loss exceeds the body's ability to compensate and provide adequate tissue perfusion and oxygenation.</p><p>Cellular hypoxia occurs as a result of reduced tissue perfusion/oxygen delivery and/or increased oxygen consumption or from inadequate oxygen utilization. Cellular hypoxia, in turn, causes cell membrane ion pump dysfunction, intracellular edema, leakage of intracellular contents into the extracellular space, and inadequate regulation of intracellular pH. These biochemical processes, when unchecked, progress to the systemic level, resulting in acidosis and endothelial dysfunction, as well as further stimulation of inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cascades.</p><p>Compounding this process is a further reduction in tissue perfusion from complex humoral and microcirculatory processes that impair regional blood flow.</p><p>Serum lactate levels, when elevated, have traditionally been used as surrogates for hypoperfusion and tissue hypoxia (note that epinephrine-mediated aerobic glycolysis in skeletal muscle contributes to hyperlactatemia as well).</p><p>A posttraumatic coagulopathy (trauma-induced coagulopathy) may be resulted from dilutional loss of coagulation factors during hemorrhage and fluid resuscitation, increased chemical mediators like activated protein C, disordered fibrinolysis, and posttraumatic platelet and endothelial dysfunction.</p><p><b>Note:</b> Total blood volume (TBV) is about 7% of ideal body weight = 70ml/kg IBW.<br/>Male (height 158.5-168.5cm) whose IBW ~ 60kg, will have TBV= 60 x 70= 4200ml</p><h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4><p>Signs and Symptoms</p><ul><li>□ Class I hemorrhage: Loss of up to 15% of blood volume (up to 630 ml in 60-kg adult).</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 65 -->

<ul><li>HR &lt;100</li><li>SBP normal</li><li>Respiratory rate (RR) 14-20</li><li>Increased or normal pulse pressure</li><li>Slight anxiety</li></ul><ul><li>Class II hemorrhage: Loss of 15-30% of blood volume (630-1260 ml):<ul><li>Tachycardia: HR &gt;100</li><li>SBP normal, or minimally decreased</li><li>Tachypnea: RR 20-30</li><li>Narrowed pulse pressure</li><li>Mild anxiety</li><li>Small decrease in urine output</li></ul></li><li>Class III hemorrhage: Loss of 30-40% of blood volume (1260-1680 ml):<ul><li>Marked tachycardia: HR &gt;120</li><li>Hypotension: SBP decreased</li><li>Marked tachypnea: RR 30-40</li><li>Marked narrowing of pulse pressure</li><li>Significant change in mental status: Confusion</li><li>Delayed capillary refill</li><li>Marked decrease in urine output</li></ul></li><li>Class IV hemorrhage: Loss of &gt;40% of blood volume (&gt;1680 ml):<ul><li>HR &gt;140</li><li>Marked hypotension: SBP decreased</li><li>RR &gt;35</li><li>Very narrow pulse pressure</li><li>Depressed mental status: Confusion, lethargy, loss of consciousness</li><li>Negligible urine output</li><li>Cold and pale skin</li></ul></li></ul><p>Note: Female patient with height of 156.4-166.4cm, has IBW~55kg their total blood volume is 3850ml. Hemorrhage class I, II, III, IV correspond to the volume loss of &lt; 577ml, 577-1155ml, 1155-1540ml, &gt; 1540ml)</p><h3>History</h3><p>Thorough health and past medical history:</p><ul><li>Underlying disease, risk factors, age</li><li>Medications</li><li>Trauma</li></ul><h3>Physical Exam</h3><p>(complete physical exam usually performed after stabilization of A.B.C.)</p><ul><li>Complete physical exam to determine shock class and assess for hemorrhage source</li><li>Vital signs including HR, RR, BP</li><li>Temperature</li><li>Mental status (anxiety, confusion, lethargy, obtundation, coma)</li><li>Pulse character, capillary refill, and skin perfusion</li><li>Pulse pressure</li></ul>

<ul><li>Abdominal exam</li><li>Pelvic/rectal exam for bleeding as indicated</li></ul><p><b>Essential Workup</b></p><ul><li>Thorough history and physical exam</li><li>IV access for resuscitation</li><li>Blood type and crossmatch</li></ul><p><b>Diagnostic Tests and Interpretation</b></p><ul><li>Ultrasound FAST.</li><li>CBC</li><li>Blood type and crossmatch</li><li>Coagulation studies:<ul><li>PT, PTT</li><li>International normalized ratio (INR)</li></ul></li><li>Other measures of tissue hypoperfusion:<ul><li>Base deficit/excess:</li><li>Can assist in determining class of hemorrhage</li><li>Arterial blood gas</li><li>Serum lactate level</li><li>Serum electrolytes</li></ul></li><li>Pregnancy test/β-hCG</li></ul><p><b>Imaging</b></p><ul><li>CXR:<ul><li>Hemothorax:<ul><li>Blunt chest injuries</li><li>Thoracic arteriovenous malformation</li></ul></li><li>Pelvic x-ray for possible occult fracture</li><li>Focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST exam):<ul><li>Abdominal trauma</li><li>Possible abdominal aortic aneurysm</li><li>Nontraumatic intraperitoneal hemorrhage</li><li>Fluid in Morrison pouch implies significant hemorrhage or ascites</li><li>Negative findings do not rule out intraperitoneal hemorrhage</li></ul></li><li>Endovaginal Ultrasound:<ul><li>Positive pregnancy test</li><li>Fluid in the cul-de-sac</li><li>Ectopic pregnancy</li></ul></li><li>Abdominal CT scan (once patient stable):<ul><li>Detects both intraperitoneal and retroperitoneal hemorrhage</li><li>Abdominal aortic aneurysm</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul><p><b>Diagnostic Procedures/Other</b></p><ul><li>Insert Foley catheter:<ul><li>Monitor urine output</li></ul></li><li>Nasogastric tube:<ul><li>For undifferentiated hypovolemic shock to rule out GI hemorrhage</li></ul></li><li>Diagnostic peritoneal lavage:</li></ul>

<ul><li>For unstable trauma patients when US fails to show intraperitoneal hemorrhage</li><li>Endoscopy:<ul><li>In the setting of upper or lower GI bleeding</li></ul></li><li>Angiography:<ul><li>Pelvic fracture</li><li>Retroperitoneal hemorrhage</li><li>Lower GI bleeding</li><li>Embolization therapy for bleeding from arterial sources can be performed</li></ul></li></ul><h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4><ul><li>Cardiac tamponade</li><li>Tension pneumothorax</li><li>Cardiogenic shock</li><li>Sepsis</li><li>Adrenal insufficiency</li><li>Neurogenic shock</li></ul><h4>VII. MANAGEMENT</h4><ol type="a"><li>Objective<p>Treatment should be initiated as soon as shock state is recognized while simultaneously identifying the underlying bleeding source.</p><p>The goal is to restore tissue and organ perfusion and to control the source of hemorrhage to normalize hemodynamic, coagulation, and perfusion parameters.</p></li><li>Critical signs<p>Early recognition and initiate treatment of shock is the key to prevent mortality. Reliance solely on SBP as indicator of shock state can result in delayed recognition</p><p>Massive blood loss may only result in minimal decrease in Hb or Hct initially</p><p>A high index of suspicion is necessary for prompt, accurate diagnosis. Probable mechanisms of hemorrhagic shock must be thoroughly and rapidly examined and treated.</p><ul><li>A narrowed pulse pressure is typically present, and often missed owing to a normal systolic value.</li><li>Anxiety or violent behavior may be a sign of shock and can easily be confused for intoxication or isolated brain injury.</li><li>Decreased mental status should be considered an ominous sign of impending decompensation.</li><li>Hypothermia and / or acidosis a key component of the lethal triad (hypothermia, coagulopathy, acidosis), is an independent predictor of mortality in hemorrhaging patients.</li><li>Acute bleeding in previously normal individual, a hemoglobin &lt; 11 g/dL is associated with a mortality rate of nearly 40%</li><li>Patients with a base deficit (BD) greater than 6 are at higher risk of mortality and the need for massive transfusion.</li></ul></li></ol>

<ul>

<p>c. Mortality risk factors</p>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Very young and very old people</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Underlying illness or injury</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> cardiac arrest (ROSC)</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Craniotomy</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> thoracotomy</li>
</ul>
<p>d. Outpatient management</p>
<p><b>Pre-Hospital</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Minimize further blood loss and provide limited fluid resuscitation and other life-saving measures while rapidly transporting the patient to a facility for definitive care.</li>
<li>Immediate interventions during rapid transport may include:
        <ul>
<li>Bleeding site identification and control (strategies may include direct pressure, tourniquets, hemostatic dressing, and tranexamic acid if possible; use of a pelvic binder for suspected pelvic fracture)</li>
<li>Restrictive fluid resuscitation with crystalloid solutions to a target mean arterial pressure of 50-60 mm Hg in patients without clinical evidence of a traumatic brain injury (TBI); in patients with severe TBI (Glasgow Coma Scale ≤ 8), maintain a mean arterial pressure of ≥ 80 mm Hg.</li>
<li>Hypothermia prevention (such as the removal of wet clothing, increasing the ambient air temperature, and the warming of IV fluids).</li>
<li>Endotracheal intubation or other airway management if indicated in trauma patients.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>e. First line treatment</p>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Every patient who is at risk for hemorrhage should be evaluated by quickly proceeding through the primary survey (A. B. C.), immediate life threats are recognized and treated before a head-to-toe exam and precise diagnosis is made.</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma [FAST] for patients with thoracoabdominal injuries (if feasible) should be the first investigation exam.</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Coagulopathy resulting from hemorrhage or resuscitation efforts must be minimized to reduce additional bleeding risk.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Initial Stabilization/Therapy</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Airway and breathing:
        <ul>
<li>Intubation as indicated by patient's respiratory and mental status</li>
<li>100% oxygen via face mask should be administered</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Circulation:
        <ul>
<li>2 large-bore peripheral IV lines (16G or larger)</li>
<li>Central venous line or venous cutdown (saphenous) may be necessary</li>
<li>Intra-osseous route may be considered</li>
<li>Fluid resuscitation with warmed, isotonic crystalloid fluid - total volume based on patient response to initial fluid bolus (bolus: 1-2L for adult, 20ml/kg</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 69 -->

<div>
<p>pediatric). Target: MAP of 50-60 mm Hg in absence of TBI, and 80-90 mm Hg in cases of severe TBI.</p>
<ul>
<li>Approach is to balance goal of perfusion and risk of rebleeding and may vary with patient:
        <ul>
<li>In blunt trauma, BP maintenance may take precedence to reduce risk of traumatic brain injury</li>
<li>In penetrating trauma with hemorrhage, delayed aggressive fluid resuscitation until definitive control may reduce bleeding risk</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Early transfusion with whole blood or balanced blood products for class III or IV shock:
        <ul>
<li>Type-specific and cross-matched blood preferred when time permits, often 1 hr</li>
<li>Type-specific blood is usually available within 10-15 min</li>
<li>Type O blood can be used in immediate, life-threatening situations (type O Rh-negative blood only for women of child-bearing age)</li>
<li>Massive transfusion protocols for patients requiring &gt;4u pRBC in 1 hr, or &gt; 10 U pRBC / 24 hr</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3><b>Ed Treatment/Procedures</b></h3>
<ul>
<li>Place patient on continuous monitor</li>
<li>NPO status, strict bed rest</li>
<li>Control hemorrhage (direct pressure, pelvic fixation/stabilization, etc.)</li>
<li>Central venous access may be indicated for CVP monitoring, but placement of such lines should not interfere with resuscitation</li>
<li>Continually reassess patient for clinical response/deterioration:
        <ul>
<li>Vital signs, mental status, and urine output</li>
<li>Follow serial blood gas, lactate level, and hemoglobin/hematocrit measurements</li>
<li>Maintain urine output at 50 ml/h</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Response to initial fluid resuscitation is the key to determining subsequent therapy:
        <ul>
<li>Rapid response to fluid indicates minimal (&lt;20%) blood loss</li>
<li>Transient response indicates ongoing hemorrhage or inadequate resuscitation; continue fluid and blood administration and obtain necessary studies and consultations</li>
<li>Minimal or no response to volume resuscitation indicates ongoing severe blood loss; immediate angiography or surgical intervention is warranted</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Use fluids warmed (~39°C) by microwave ovens, fluid warmers</li>
<li>Transfuse whole blood, RBCs, platelets, and other blood products as indicated</li>
<li>Consider autotransfusion devices with tube thoracostomy treatment of large hemothoraces.</li>
<li>Monitor closely for coagulopathy particularly with massive transfusion</li>
<li>Specialty consultation and additional procedures (surgery) as indicated by cause and source of hemorrhagic shock</li>
</ul>
</div>

<ul>
<li>☐ Antifibrinolytic agents: Tranexamic acid should be given as soon as possible (within 3h of injury) to hemorrhaged patients. Dose: 1g bolus over 10min followed by an infusion of 1g over 8h. Do not use through the transfusion line.</li>
<li>☐ Initiate damage control surgery in patients with
        <ul>
<li>the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy,</li>
<li>combined abdominal vascular and pancreatic injuries,</li>
<li>severe injuries and signs of ongoing bleeding or</li>
<li>coagulopathy, and in those in whom definitive repair is not immediately feasible.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>Provide definitive surgical management in all other patients with traumatic hemorrhage.</p>
<ul>
<li>☐ Vasopressors have a limited role and may be used for selected patients in hemorrhagic shock.</li>
<li>☐ The Assessment of Blood Consumption (ABC) score includes four variables:
        <ul>
<li>penetrating mechanism,</li>
<li>SBP ≤90 mm Hg in emergency department</li>
<li>emergency department heart rate ≥120 beats/minute, and</li>
<li>positive fluid on abdominal ultrasonography (FAST)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>Give 1 point to each positive item. Sum the points to get ABC score.<br/>Score ≥ 2, patient is likely to require massive transfusion (≥ 10 units pRBCs)<br/>[sensitivity: 75-90%, specificity: 67-88%]</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 71 -->

<h2>g. Algorithm</h2>
<h3>Hospital management of hemorrhagic shock</h3>
<div>
<p>Patient with hemorrhagic shock being managed in a hospital setting</p>
<ul>
<li>Institute early mechanical thromboprophylaxis</li>
<li>Provide reversal for any patient receiving antithrombotic therapy</li>
</ul>
<p>Is bleeding source evident, or if death imminent if bleeding is not rapidly controlled?</p>
<ul>
<li>No: Institute initial fluid resuscitation as need<br/>Immediately institute further investigations and monitoring studies*<br/>Correct hypocalcemia if present</li>
<li>Yes: Initiate fluid resuscitation, and immediately institute bleeding control procedures such as:<ul><li>Direct pressure/tourniquets</li><li>Packing</li><li>Damage control surgery</li><li>REBOA</li><li>Definitive surgery</li></ul></li>
</ul>
<p>Is there a rapid response and normalization of hemodynamic vital signs without indications of inadequate tissue perfusion and oxygenation, with initial fluid resuscitation?</p>
<ul>
<li>Yes: Provide maintenance fluids<br/>Keep typed and cross-matched blood available<br/>Obtain surgical consultation and evaluation<br/>Provide operative intervention as need</li>
<li>No: Is there a transit response in hemodynamic vital signs to initial fluid resuscitation?</li>
</ul>
<p>Is there a transit response in hemodynamic vital signs to initial fluid resuscitation?</p>
<ul>
<li>Yes: Transfuse blood and blood products<br/>Initiate rapide operative or angiographic bleeding control intervention<br/>Consider initiating a massive transfusion protocol to ensure sufficient blood products</li>
<li>No: Initiate massive transfusion protocol<br/>Provide immediate definitive intervention (operative or angiographic)<br/>Consider cardiac ultrasound to identify the cause of shock, and consider non-hemorrhagic shock or pump failure</li>
</ul>
<p>* Essential serial blood tests include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Lactate and/or base deficit (BD)</li>
<li>Hemoglobin or hematocrit</li>
<li>Coagulation studies (viscoelastic testing or traditional lab)</li>
<li>Ionized calcium in all patients, especially those receiving transfusions</li>
</ul>
<p>REBOA: resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta</p>
</div>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<h4>1. Pediatric Considerations</h4>
<ul>
<li>Children often have greater physiologic reserve than adults and can preserve normal vital signs longer</li>
<li>Systemic responses to blood loss in the pediatric patient include:
        <ul>
<li>Volume loss &lt;25%: Weak, thready pulse and tachycardia; lethargy, irritability, and confusion; cool, clammy skin; decreased urine output/increased urine specific gravity</li>
<li>Volume loss 25--40%: Tachycardia; marked change in consciousness; dulled response to pain; cyanotic, cold extremities with decreased capillary refill; minimal urine output</li>
<li>Volume loss &gt;40%: Hypotension, tachycardia, or bradycardia; comatose; pale, cold skin; no urine output</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h4>2. Geriatric Considerations</h4>
<ul>
<li>Underlying disease, overall deconditioning, and medications may alter responses to hemorrhage and blood loss.</li>
</ul>
<h4>3. Postpartum hemorrhage</h4>
<ul>
<li>In patients with major hemorrhage (blood loss &gt; 1,000 mL and continued bleeding and/or signs of clinical shock), infuse a maximum of 3.5 L of clear fluids (initially 2 L of warmed isotonic crystalloid) while awaiting compatible blood.</li>
<li>Isotonic crystalloids are preferred over colloids for fluid resuscitation</li>
<li>Blood Transfusion
        <ul>
<li>A blood transfusion is indicated in patients with continued bleeding or signs of clinical shock and major postpartum hemorrhage.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>For patients with major postpartum hemorrhage:</p>
<ul>
<li>In the absence of timely laboratory results, a massive transfusion protocol with a fixed ratio of 1:1:1 of packed red blood cells (RBC) to fresh frozen plasma to platelets can be used.</li>
<li>If immediate transfusion is indicated, give emergency type O, RhD-negative blood in the form of red cell concentrate and switch to type-specific red cells as soon as possible.</li>
<li>Consider transfusion of platelets when the platelet count is &lt; 75 × 10<sup>9</sup>/L based on laboratory monitoring</li>
<li>If hemostatic results are unavailable and bleeding continues, infuse fresh frozen plasma 12-15 mL/kg after 4 units of red blood cells until hemostatic test results are available</li>
<li>Consider early fresh frozen plasma if hemostatic results are unavailable and coagulopathy, such as placental abruption or amniotic fluid embolism, is suspected or detection of postpartum hemorrhage has been delayed.</li>
<li>If prothrombin time/activated partial thromboplastin time is &gt; 1.5 times normal and hemorrhage is ongoing, fresh frozen plasma &gt; 15 mg/kg may be needed to correct coagulopathy.</li>
<li>Maintain plasma fibrinogen level &gt; 2 g/L during ongoing postpartum hemorrhage</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 73 -->

<div>
<p>☐ Medication:</p>
<ul>
<li>Oxytocin 10 units intramuscularly or 10-40 units IV in 0.5-1 L normal saline as a continuous infusion [20-40 milliunit/min] (or another uterotonic if IV oxytocin is not available)</li>
<li>Avoid undiluted rapid IV infusion as it may cause hypotension.</li>
<li>Adverse effects include nausea and vomiting.</li>
<li>If oxytocin is not available or for bleeding refractory to oxytocin, alternative uterotonics may be considered. Options include:
        <ul>
<li>Ergot alkaloids
            <ul>
<li>Methylergonovine (Methergine):<br/>0.2 mg intramuscularly every 2-4 hours.</li>
<li>Ergonovine (ergometrine)</li>
<li>Ergometrine/oxytocin</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Misoprostol (Cytotec) [oral/sublingual/rectal]</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>The prognosis of hemorrhagic shock depends on several factors, including the severity of the blood loss, timeliness of medical intervention, and underlying health conditions of the patient</li>
<li>Without intervention, severe hemorrhagic shock presents a classic trimodal distribution of deaths:
        <ul>
<li>Death occurs within minutes of hemorrhage (immediate exsanguination),</li>
<li>Death after 1 to several hours (progressive decompensation),</li>
<li>Death occurs days to weeks later (sepsis and organ failure).</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Among survivors, hemorrhagic shock is associated with poor functional outcomes and significantly increased long-term mortality.</li>
<li>Elevated serum lactate and/or base deficit (BD) at admission is associated with increased mortality and worse outcomes in trauma patients.</li>
<li>Patients in end-stage/refractory shock will have irreversible cellular damage, resulting in multiple organ failure and most likely death.</li>
</ul>
<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Major hemorrhage may lead to a "lethal triad" of coagulopathy, metabolic acidosis, and hypothermia.</li>
<li>Without life-saving interventions, complications of hemorrhagic shock and continued bleeding may include cardiac failure, acute kidney injury, lung damage, and poor cerebral perfusion.</li>
<li>Shock-related hypoperfusion and end-organ damage in the kidneys, liver, intestine, and skeletal muscle may lead to multiorgan failure in survivors.</li>
<li>Patients with multiple-trauma are at high risk for hospital-acquired venous thromboembolism (VTE),</li>
<li>Complications of rapid transfusions of blood products and large amounts of fluids.</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 74 -->

<h2>XI. RECOMMENDATIONS</h2>
<ul>
<li>Initial therapy until blood products are available needs to be differentiated to be effective in terms of hemodynamic stabilization and coagulation. Treatment of acidosis and hypothermia can further reduce bleeding complications.</li>
<li>Early imaging (ultrasonography or contrast-enhanced CT) should be used for detection of free fluid in patients with suspected torso trauma.</li>
<li>CT assessment should be provided for hemodynamically stable patients.</li>
<li>Low initial Hb should be considered an indicator for severe bleeding associated with coagulopathy.</li>
<li>Repeated Hb measurements should be used as a laboratory marker for bleeding, as an initial Hb value in the normal range may mask bleeding.</li>
<li>Serum lactate and/or base deficit measurements are sensitive tests to estimate and monitor the extent of bleeding and shock.</li>
<li>Repeated monitoring of coagulation, using a traditional laboratory determination (prothrombin time [PT], activated partial thromboplastin time [APTT], platelet counts, and fibrinogen) and/or a viscoelastic method, should be provided.</li>
<li>Target systolic blood pressure is 80-90 mm Hg until major bleeding has been stopped in the initial phase following trauma without brain injury.</li>
<li>In patients with severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) (GCS ≤8), mean arterial pressure ≥80 mm Hg should be maintained.</li>
<li>Fluid therapy using isotonic crystalloid solutions should be initiated in the hypotensive patient with bleeding trauma.</li>
<li>Excessive use of 0.9 % NaCl solution should be avoided.</li>
<li>Hypotonic solutions such as lactated Ringer's solution should be avoided in patients with severe head trauma.</li>
<li>Use of colloids should be restricted due to adverse effects on hemostasis.</li>
<li>Target Hb is 7-9 g/dL.</li>
<li>In initial management of patients with expected massive hemorrhage, one of the following strategies should be used: Plasma (FFP or pathogen-inactivated plasma) should be provided at a plasma-to-RBC ratio of at least 1:2 as needed, with fibrinogen concentrate and RBC according to Hb level.</li>
<li>Tranexamic acid should be administered as early as possible to the trauma patient who is bleeding or is at risk of significant hemorrhage, at a loading dose of 1 g infused over 10 minutes, followed by an IV infusion of 1 g over 8 hours.</li>
<li>Tranexamic acid should be administered to the bleeding patient with trauma within 3 hours after injury.</li>
<li>Protocols for treatment of bleeding patients should consider administration of the first dose of tranexamic acid en route to the hospital.</li>
<li>If a plasma-based coagulation resuscitation strategy is used, plasma (FFP or pathogen-inactivated plasma) should be administered to maintain PT and APTT &lt; 1.5 times normal control values.</li>
<li>Plasma transfusion should be avoided in patients without substantial bleeding.</li>
<li>Platelets should be administered to maintain a platelet count above 50 × 10<sup>9</sup>/L.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 75 -->

<ul><li>Platelet count above 100 × 10<sup>9</sup>/L should be maintained in patients with ongoing bleeding and/or TBI.</li><li>Initial dose is 4-8 single platelet units or 1 apheresis pack</li></ul><p>In general, few indications exist to transfer a patient who is in shock to a specialized facility. Ideally, all hospitals and physicians should be prepared to initially treat and stabilize the patient with exsanguinating hemorrhage. After control of the bleeding and reversal of acute shock, patients may be transferred to facilities that can treat additional injuries. The patient should be transferred by an advanced life support unit with the capability of blood transfusion in route.</p><h2>XII. <h1>STROKE SYNDROME IN EMERGENCY</h1>
<p><i>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Stroke is defined as any disease process (non-traumatic) that interrupts blood flow to the brain.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Approximately 80 percent of strokes are due to ischemic cerebral infarction and 20 percent to brain hemorrhage.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<p>There are two main subtypes of stroke: (1) Ischemic stroke, (2) Hemorrhagic stroke. Ischemic stroke may be caused by: Thrombosis, Emboli or Systemic hypoperfusion. Hemorrhagic stroke sub-divided into:</p>
<ul>
<li>Intra cerebral hemorrhage, usually due to chronic hypertension, and vascular disease (amyloidosis), or complications from cocaine or methamphetamines use.</li>
<li>Subarachnoid hemorrhage, most frequently caused by rupture of cerebral arterial-venous malformations or cerebral aneurysm.</li>
</ul>
<p>The transient ischemic attack (TIA): A transient episode of neurological dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia, without acute infarction.</p>
<h2>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h2>
<p>In ischemic stroke, the lower or absence perfusion to a brain territory due to emboli, thrombosis or systemic hypotension may produce an ischemic zone that evolve to necrosis. The center of the ischemic zone, called “ischemic penumbra” usually stays longer and may survive if the reperfusion was achieved early (before 4.5h). The signs and symptoms of ischemic stroke is related to the damaged zone.</p>
<p>In Hemorrhagic stroke, the hematoma may compress underneath brain causes its dysfunction. The hematoma may extend triggering ICP elevation, blood in the ventricle may block CSF absorption and induce hydrocephalus. In subarachnoid bleeding, the coagulation process of hematoma may trigger cerebral vasospasm and secondary brain ischemic. In the process of intracranial problems (hematoma, cerebral edema, hydrocephalus) the ICP tend to increase, the acute treatment of hypertension may vary also the cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) that tend to decrease. CPP = MAP - ICP</p>

<!-- PAGE 77 -->

<h2>V. DIAGNOSIS</h2>
<p>The diagnosis of stroke in the ED rests on the bedrock of a focused, accurate history and physical examination.</p>
<h3>A. Clinic signs &amp; symptoms.</h3>
<p>Signs &amp; symptoms of stroke varied to the location of the lesion (anterior cerebral artery circulation, posterior cerebral artery circulation, middle cerebral artery circulation, watershed infarction).</p>
<h4>a. Ischemic stroke</h4>
<p>The mnemonic BE FAST, is the suspect signs of stroke.</p>
<ul>
<li>B: Sudden Balance impairment</li>
<li>E: Sudden vision loss in one Eye / one field</li>
<li>F: Facial droop (have patient show teeth or smile)</li>
<li>A: Arm drift (patient closes eyes and extends both arms straight out, with palm up for 10")</li>
<li>S: Abnormal Speech</li>
<li>T: Time to call emergency</li>
</ul>
<p>Clinically, the differentiation of an ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke is not accurate. It is necessary to obtain an emergency non-contrast-enhanced CT for all suspected acute stroke upon arrival. The utility of the first brain CT is primarily to exclude intracranial bleeding, abscess, tumor, and other stroke mimics, as well as to detect current contraindications to thrombolytics.</p>
<h3>Physical examination</h3>
<p>Assessment of airway, breathing, and circulation is the top priority.</p>
<p>Next, the goals of examination are to confirm the diagnosis of stroke, exclude stroke mimics and identify co-morbidities.</p>
<h3>B. Investigation</h3>
<h4>Non-contrast-enhanced brain CT imaging</h4>
<div>
<img alt="Two axial non-contrast-enhanced brain CT scans. Image A shows a normal scan. Image B shows early changes consistent with stroke, including basal ganglia hypodensity, loss of the insular ribbon, and slight effacement of the sulci on the left."/>

</div>

<!-- PAGE 78 -->

<div>
<p><b>b. Hemorrhagic stroke</b></p>
<p>Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) classically presents with sudden onset of a headache at its most severe. It occurs 20% of the time during activity associated with elevated blood pressures, such as sexual intercourse, weightlifting, defecation, or coughing. Vomiting, photophobia, nuchal irritation, low-grade fever, and altered mental status all may occur. Focal findings can occur depending on the location of the aneurysm.</p>
<div>
<img alt="Non-contrast head CT scan showing a large subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) from a ruptured berry aneurysm, resulting in blood in all major cisterns, interhemispheric and Sylvian fissures, and both ventricles. Mild obstructive hydrocephalus is also present, visible by the slightly dilated temporal horns (indicated by white arrows)."/>
<p>Shown is the non-contrast head CT of a large SAH from a ruptured berry aneurysm, resulting in blood in all major cisterns, interhemispheric and Sylvian fissures, and both ventricles. Mild obstructive hydrocephalus is also present, as visible by the slightly dilated temporal horns (white arrows).</p>
</div>
<p>Pictures from: textbook of Critical care 8<sup>th</sup> Edition, Jean-Louis Vincent</p>
<p>Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), is intraparenchymal hemorrhage from previously weakened arterioles. The frequent etiology is chronic arterial hypertension, amyloidosis, iatrogenic anticoagulation, vascular malformations and cocaine use.</p>
<div>
<img alt="Four axial CT scans (A, B, C, D) showing common locations of spontaneous hypertensive intracranial hemorrhage. A shows hemorrhage in the thalamus, B in the caudate/putamen, C in the pons, and D in the cerebellum."/>

</div>

<h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<p>Stroke mimics conditions:</p>
<ul>
<li>Seizures/ post tical paralysis (Todd's paralysis)</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 79 -->

<ul><li>Syncope</li><li>Meningitis / encephalitis</li><li>Complicated migraine</li><li>Brain neoplasm or abscess</li><li>Epidural / subdural hematoma</li><li>Subarachnoid hemorrhage</li><li>Hypoglycemia</li><li>Hyponatremia</li><li>Hypertension encephalopathy</li><li>Hyperosmotic coma</li><li>Wernicke's encephalopathy</li><li>Labyrinthitis</li><li>Drug toxicity (Lithium, phenytoin, carbamazepine)</li><li>Bell's palsy</li><li>Ménière's disease</li><li>Demyelinating disease (multiple sclerosis)</li><li>Conversion disorder</li></ul><h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2><ol><li><b>Objectives</b><p>The management of ischemic stroke is time-dependent, different steps need to be done quickly. Find out whether any specific treatment is feasible.</p><ul><li>Eliminate the problems that mimic stroke symptom.</li><li>Differentiate ischemic from hemorrhagic stroke.</li><li>Re-perfusion therapy, if feasible. (Thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy)</li><li>Prevent the expansion of the brain damage, by saving the “ischemic penumbra” and prevent or treat the early complications (re-bleeding, vasospasm, cerebral edema, intracranial hypertension).</li><li>Maintain cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP). In selected patients, surgery or microinvasive procedures is indicated to remove hematoma, drain the hydrocephalus, or to prevent re-bleeding (clipping, stenting, coiling).</li></ul></li><li><b>Severity grading</b><p>In Acute phase of stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic), NIHSS is used to grade the severity of stroke and help decide on treatment modality. After treatment, the severity of handicap was commonly measured by modified Rankin Score.</p></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 80 -->

<h3><b>The National Institutes of Health stroke scale (NIHSS) for Ischemic stroke</b></h3>
<p>It is composed of 11 items. A score of 0 indicates normal function and the higher score indicates impairment with maximum score of 42. Score of more than 25 indicate a severe stroke. (For details, see reference 1).</p>
<p>At the time of presentation, the severity of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is scored by Hunt &amp; Hess scale or The WFNS scale.</p>

<ol>
<li>Risk factors for mortality
        <ul>
<li>Larger size of brain damage or hematoma</li>
<li>Factors contributed to elevation of intracranial pressure (cerebral edema, extending hematoma, cerebral herniation)</li>
<li>Systemic factors contributed to secondary exacerbation (hypotension, hypoxia, hypercapnia, fever, agitation, hyponatremia, cerebral vasospasm, re-bleeding)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Out-patient management
        <p>Only after assessment and treatment in acute phase, that patients who survived with variable handicaps may have outpatient management. The treatment focus on rehabilitation, most importantly during the first 3 months, and the Secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.</p>
</li>
<li>First-line treatment
        <p>The management of Stroke syndrome consisted of early stabilization (<math>\text{SpO}_2 &gt; 94\%</math>, <math>\text{PaCO}_2: 35\text{-}40\text{mmHg}</math>, <math>\text{SBP} &gt; 90\text{mmHg}</math>, treat hypoglycemia, keep glycemia 140-180mg/dl for hyperglycemic patient. Once the patient's condition is stabilized, immediately send the patient for a non-contrast head CT</p>
<ol type="a">
<li>Supportive treatment
                <p>Supportive therapy for patients with Intracerebral vascular diseases (ICVD) should begin upon hospitalization.<br/>Head of the bed elevated to 30 - 45 degree<br/>Keep the patient nothing-per-os (for the first few days).<br/>Treatment of elevated blood pressure in the first 24 hours of an ischemic stroke is reserved for those with malignant hypertension (<math>&gt; 220 \text{ mmHg systolic}</math>, <math>120 \text{ mmHg diastolic}</math>) or other end-organ failure (e.g., congestive heart failure, renal failure, and hypertensive encephalopathy). The blood pressure typically autoregulates spontaneously with bed rest in the first few days after ischemic stroke; if it remains substantially elevated, it should be carefully lowered daily up to 20% of the mean arterial pressure. Subcutaneous heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin therapy should be considered for immobilized patients with ICVD to reduce the risk of deep venous thrombosis. In</p>

Ischemic stroke:</h5><p>Hypertension management in acute ischemic stroke depend on the thrombolysis.</p><ul><li>Is not a candidate for thrombolysis, then permissive hypertension is in order (No intervention unless SBP &gt;220mmHg or DBP &gt;120 mmHg.)</li><li>Is a candidate for thrombolytics, then the target blood pressures are SBP ≤185 mmHg and DBP≤ 110mmHg</li></ul><p>If blood pressure control is needed, use a titratable IV antihypertensive, Labetalol, starting dose is 10 to 20 mg over 1 to 2 min; continuous infusion at 2 mg/min, (titrated to effect) with a target MAP reduction of 10% to 25%.</p><p>Take extreme caution to avoid overcorrection.</p><h4><u>Reperfusion therapy:</u></h4><p>(1) Intravenous Thrombolysis, (2) Mechanical thrombectomy</p><h5>a. Intravenous Thrombolysis</h5><p>Thrombolytic therapy for patients with ICVD is directed at reversing the neurological deficits and preventing progression. The total dose of IV tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) for stroke is 0.9 mg/ kg, given as a 60-minute IV infusion, with 10% of the total dose given as an initial bolus.</p><p>Indication &amp; contra-indication of r-TPA (recombinant tissue plasminogen activator)</p><p>Alteplase®</p><h4><u>Alteplase is Contraindicated in:</u></h4><ul><li>Active internal bleeding</li><li>History of cerebrovascular accident (for MI and PE only)</li><li>Recent (within 3 mo) intracranial or intraspinal injury or trauma</li><li>Intracranial neoplasm, arteriovenous malformation, or aneurysm</li><li>Known bleeding diathesis</li><li>Severe uncontrolled hypertension (systolic BP &gt;185 mmHg or diastolic BP &gt;110 mmHg specifically for stroke indication)</li></ul></div>

1), Have a causative occlusion of the internal carotid artery or proximal middle cerebral artery, Have a NIHSS score of ≥ 6, have a reassuring non-contrast head CT (ASPECT score of ≥ 6), And if they can be treated within 6 h of last known normal.</p>

Subarachnoid hemorrhage:</b></p><ul><li>Reduce the chances of re-bleeding: maintaining the patient's pre-bleed blood pressure (or MAP &lt;130 mmHg if baseline blood pressure is unknown). IV titratable labetalol (10 to 20 mg over 1 to 2 min; continuous infusion dosage at 2 mg/min, titrated to effect).</li><li>Nimodipine (60 mg PO every 4 hours) may decrease vasospasm.</li><li>Emergent neurosurgical consultation is indicated.</li><li>Administer medications and antiemetics as needed.</li><li>Seizure prophylaxis is controversial,</li></ul><p><b>a. General measure:</b></p><ul><li>Strict bed rest in a quiet environment to diminish hemodynamic fluctuations, pain control with titrated doses of opioid analgesics.</li><li>Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis with pneumatic compression stockings.</li><li>Pharmacologic DVT prophylaxis can be added after definitive treatment for the aneurysm.</li><li>GI ulcer prophylaxis and stool softeners.</li><li>Fever should be managed with antipyretics and adequate source control.</li><li>Correct hypoglycemia or Control glycemia at the level ~150mg/dL</li></ul><p><b>b. Specific Measure:</b></p><ul><li>Surgical clipping of the neck of the aneurysm and Endovascular aneurysmal obliteration by metal coils are the options available for aneurysmal repair</li></ul><p><b>C. Intracerebral Hemorrhage:</b></p><ul><li>Management of blood pressure for spontaneous ICH remains controversial. SBP greater than 220 mm Hg, indicate a continuous IV drug infusion and close BP monitoring to lower SBP. The optimal goal blood pressure is uncertain, SBP of 140 to 160 mmHg is a reasonable target. Aggressive reduction can increase renal adverse events.</li><li>Early neurosurgical consultation is indicated for patients with ICH with evidence of increased ICP or in other conditions where surgical intervention may be indicated, (For example, cerebellar stroke). All non-surgical measures to reduced ICP should be considered.</li><li>Rapid reversal of anticoagulation to INR &lt; 1.6 may improve survival.</li><li>Decompressive craniotomy and evacuation for all patients with ICH is not indicated.</li><li>For Supratentorial ICH, surgery is usually avoided and should be considered on an individual basis based on assessment of prognosis with or without surgery.</li></ul><p><u>Measures to reduce intracranial pressure (ICP)</u></p><ul><li>Raise Head of Bed (reduce veinous volume)</li><li>Hyperosmolar (NS 3%, mannitol) [Reduce (remove) some water from brain tissue]</li><li>Hyperventilate (Vasoconstriction, reduce cerebral blood flow)</li><li>Sedation (reduce sympathetic nervous system tone)</li></ul></div>

Treatment adjustment</p><p>In case of patient arrived hospital late, or the criteria for re-perfusion therapy was not fulfilled, the treatment is directed to active-supportive treatment and prevent the factors of secondary aggravating brain damage.</p><p>7. If No, inform &amp; consent and consider transfer to suitable center. The center decision branches into Ischemic stroke - Or TIA - Or Normal, Non-hemorrhagic, SAH, and ICH. <div><p>Priority on arrival is making sure that airway (A), breathing (B), and circulation (C) are OK. Maintain SpO2&gt;94%, if need, administer oxygen by mask. Make sure that patient was not hypovolemic, put a good IV line and RL to keep line open. Patient with GCS≤ 8 need intubation and supported ventilation. Hypotension is the worst factors of exacerbation; moderate hypertension is desirable. Inform-consent form should be completed as soon as stroke is clinically diagnosed to catch the time when patient is eligible for the procedures, and if they refuse the intervention, some investigations exam may be omitted. If consented, consider transfer patient to hospital or center where the specific treatments (Thrombolysis, thrombectomy, clip, neurosurgery) are available, as soon as possible.</p><h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3><h4>1. Ischemic stroke with concomitant myocardial infarction</h4><p>Troponin elevation in acute ischemic stroke is not uncommon (prevalence, 0% to 34%), is associated with multiple disease processes (e.g., acute coronary syndrome, congestive heart failure, renal failure, myocarditis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, atrial fibrillation), and is independently associated with worse all-cause mortality. Troponin elevation in acute stroke is most probably secondary to acute coronary syndrome if other obvious causes are excluded, especially if typical ECG findings for acute coronary syndrome are present. Simultaneous acute ischemic stroke and myocardial infarction can be therapeutically problematic because treating one condition with a procedure may delay a time-dependent indicated procedure for the other. In addition, there are some therapies for acute myocardial infarction (e.g., heparin) that are contraindicated in acute stroke.</p><p>"For patients presenting with concurrent AIS [acute ischemic stroke] and acute MI [myocardial infarction], treatment with IV alteplase at the dose appropriate for cerebral ischemia, followed by percutaneous coronary angioplasty and stenting if indicated is reasonable." (AHA/ASA guidelines, 2018). Obtain emergent neurology and cardiology consults on these patients, but do not delay thrombolysis for stroke if the patient qualifies.</p><h4>2. Transient ischemic attack (TIA)</h4><p>TIA treatment is important, even all symptoms were disappeared. The patient returned to normal but the risk of developing a real stroke is high especially during the first month. Treatment of TIA primarily focuses on prevention of subsequent stroke.</p><ul><li>Anti-platelet agents<br/>Can select among: Aspirin (75-81mg), clopidogrel (75mg), Dipyridamole (75-100mg qid), alone or combined clopidogrel or dipyridamole with aspirin take every day.</li><li>Anticoagulation<br/>The risk of recurrent stroke in the presence of atrial fibrillation without anticoagulation is low, probably &lt;5% over the next 48 hours; moreover, the risk of hemorrhagic transformation of an acute stroke is also greatest in the first 48 hours.<br/>The use of unfractionated heparin, low molecular-weight heparin, or heparinoids for emergent treatment of a specific stroke subtype or TIA cannot be recommended based on available evidence, even in the presence of atrial fibrillation.</li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 87 -->

<ul><li>Carotid artery endarterectomy or stent</li></ul><p>In TIA patients with medically treated high-grade internal carotid artery lesions, The Carotid Revascularization Endarterectomy or carotid stenting should be performed promptly, because surgical benefit is greatest within 2 weeks of the TIA. Carotid stenting may be especially useful in patients &lt;70 years old or in patients with higher surgical risks.</p><h3>IX. EVOLUTION &amp; PROGNOSIS</h3><p>The prognosis of stroke depends on: (1) Type of stroke, (2) Location and size of the stroke, (3) Severity of symptoms, (4) Age and overall health.</p><p>The prognosis of ischemic stroke is generally better than for hemorrhagic stroke. Strokes affecting the speech center or motor cortex, are more likely to cause lasting disabilities. Larger strokes also tend to have a worse prognosis than smaller strokes. People with mild symptoms are more likely to make a good recovery than those with severe symptoms. Prompt diagnosis and treatment of an acute cerebral vascular accidents can improve the chances of a good recovery.</p><p>The recovery aspect of stroke:</p><ul><li>1-3 months: the brain exhibits the most remarkable plasticity and potential for improvement. During this time, most patients undergo intensive rehabilitation in hospitals or specialized centers, focusing on regaining lost function in movement, speech, and cognitive skills. Significant progress is often observed during this phase.</li><li>3-6 months: the rate of recovery slows down but can still be substantial</li><li>6-12 months: The improvement becomes less dramatic,</li><li>1 year and beyond: While some individuals achieve near-complete recovery, others may have permanent disabilities.</li></ul><h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3><p>Acute ischemic stroke may complicate malignant cerebral edema, venous thromboembolism, symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage (post-thrombectomy), angioedema (post-thrombolysis), dysphasia, infection.</p><p>The main complications of SAH:</p><ul><li>Re-bleeding (within the first 24h, particularly within 6h).</li><li>Vasospasm and delay cerebral ischemia (3-4day after rupture, peak at 7-10d and resolves by 14-21d).</li><li>Raise ICP and hydrocephalus (within 3 days of rupture, in 20% of patient)</li></ul><p>Other complication:</p><ul><li>Seizure 20% (mostly at first 24h); risk: thick clot, ICH, prior seizure, middle cerebral artery aneurisms, delayed infarct.</li><li>Hyponatremia (SIADH, and Salt-wasting sd.).</li><li>Cardiac change (neurogenic stunned myocardium).</li><li>Neurogenic pulmonary edema (NPE), usually resolves in 48-72h.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 88 -->

<div>
<p>The early complications of ICH are Intracranial pressure (ICP) elevation causing local neuronal damage, and vasoconstriction mediated by blood breakdown products or neuronal mechanisms causing remote perfusion changes.</p>
<h4>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h4>
<ul>
<li>Primary prevention of cardiovascular disease (pre-stroke): control the chronic hypertension, Diabetes, dyslipidemia; life-style change.</li>
<li>Early seek medical advice when suspect a stroke. Stroke is time-dependent disease.</li>
<li>Do no harm to patient (multiple-transfers, waiting-treatment), “time is brain”</li>
<li>Important of rehabilitation therapy immediately after stroke</li>
<li>Secondary prevention of cardiovascular diseases (post-stroke)</li>
</ul>

<h1>COMA</h1>
<p><i>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Altered mental status and coma are broad clinical categories used to describe disorders of arousal (awake) and content of consciousness (aware). Arousal behaviors include wakefulness and basic alerting. Content of consciousness includes awareness, memory, language, reasoning, spatial relationship integration, emotions, complex attention, and the myriad integration processes that make us human.</p>
<p>Coma is characterized by failure of both arousal and content functions of consciousness. A coma is the most severe of consciousness altered.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>In a study by Keun Tae Kim et al., in South Korea 2022, among patient in ED 80.738 they found 2028 patient (2.51%) had consciousness altered. Most of those patients were in their 70s (546, 26.9%) followed by their 80s (506, 25.0%). The study also found that the etiology of consciousness altered in South Korea ED is as follow:</p>

<h4>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h4>
<p>The function of the brainstem and/or both hemispheres must be impaired for unresponsiveness to occur. Coma can result from</p>
<ul>
<li>deficiency of substrates needed for neuronal function (as with hypoglycemia or hypoxia).</li>
<li>a brainstem disorder such as hemorrhage or</li>
<li>bilateral cortical dysfunction.</li>
<li>Cerebral edema and infection of the brain and/or surrounding</li>
</ul>
<p>Cerebral blood flow is constant at mean arterial pressures of 50 to 100 mm Hg due to the process of cerebral autoregulation. Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is the pressure that maintain the blood flow to the brain. It is the net pressure gradient between mean arterial pressure (MAP) and intracranial pressure (ICP): CPP = MAP- ICP<br/>In extreme uncontrolled elevation of the ICP, cerebral perfusion pressure is diminished which may causes brain ischemia. The Cushing reflex (Hypertension and bradycardia in a comatose patient): may be observed with increased ICP.</p>
<h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<h5>a. Signs &amp; symptoms</h5>
<p>The clinical features of a coma vary with both the depth of coma and the cause. Examination, laboratory procedures, and neuroimaging allow differentiation between structural and metabolic causes of coma in almost all patients in the ED</p>
<ul>
<li>Structural Coma<br/>Patient may have hemiparesis, the eyes may conjugately deviate toward the side of brain lesion.</li>
<li>Toxic-metabolic coma<br/>The diffuse CNS dysfunction is reflected by the lack of focal physical examination findings that point to a specific region of brain dysfunction. Pupillary response is generally preserved in toxic-metabolic coma.<br/>A posterior fossa or infratentorial expanding lesion, such as cerebellar hemorrhage or infarction, may cause abrupt coma, abnormal extensor posturing, loss of pupillary reflexes, and loss of extraocular movements.<br/>A Pseudo coma or psychogenic coma is occasionally encountered.</li>
</ul>
<p>General examination may reveal signs of trauma or suggest other diagnostic possibilities for the unresponsiveness. However, asymmetric findings on examination of cranial nerves through pupillary examination, assessment of corneal reflexes, and testing of oculovestibular reflexes may suggest focal CNS lesions. Asymmetric muscle tone or reflexes raise the suspicion of a focal lesion. The goal of the physician is to rapidly determine if the CNS dysfunction is from diffuse impairment of the brain or if signs point to a focal (and perhaps surgically treatable) region of CNS dysfunction.<br/>Liberal use of CT scanning is encouraged because exceptions to the tentative clinical diagnosis are frequent.</p>
<p>The Glasgow Coma Scale (Table-2) is a widely used clinical scoring system for alterations in consciousness. GCS stratify consciousness altered from 15 (alert) to 3 (deep coma). Typically, a score of 8 or below is indicative of coma.</p>

<h4>b. Investigation</h4>
<p>CT is the neuroimaging procedure of choice. Acute hemorrhage is readily identified, as is midline shift and mass lesions. Consider lumbar puncture if CT scan findings are unremarkable and subarachnoid hemorrhage or CNS infection is suspected. Suspect basilar artery thrombosis in a comatose patient with “normal” results on head CT, in which the only finding may be a hyperdense basilar artery. MRI or cerebral angiography is needed to make the diagnosis of basilar artery thrombosis.</p>
<h3>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h3>
<p>Delirium, dementia, and coma may each affect consciousness, but their clinical presentations are distinct. Prompt and accurate differentiation between the three conditions is essential for appropriate management in the ED setting.</p>
<p><b>Delirium</b>, acute encephalopathy, refer to an abrupt disorder characterized by impairment of attention and cognition. The literature suggests that at least 1 out of 10 elderly ED patients and at least 1 out of 4 elderly hospitalized patients have delirium at the time of admission. Delirium typically develops over days. Disordered attention and acute fluctuating course are the hallmarks of the condition, which may also affect cognition, level of consciousness, language, and perception. Activity levels may be either increased or decreased.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 93 -->

<div><p><b>Dementia</b> is a chronic, major neurocognitive disorder entailing a gradual loss of mental capacity. Executive, social, and cognitive abilities deteriorate, and behavioral problems can develop. The typical course of dementia involves insidious symptom onset. Hallucinations, delusions, repetitive behaviors, depression, and anxiety are all common.</p><table border="1"><tbody><tr><td rowspan="2">Coma</td><td>Awake: No</td><td rowspan="2">Delirium / Dementia</td><td>Awake: Yes</td></tr><tr><td>Aware: No</td><td>Aware: Abnormal / no</td></tr></tbody></table><p>arousal = Awake,<br/>content of consciousness = cognitive function + psychic function = Aware</p><h3>Compare Delirium with Dementia</h3><table><thead><tr><th></th><th><b>Delirium</b></th><th><b>Dementia</b></th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Onset</td><td>Acute (a few h, few days)</td><td>Insidious, many years</td></tr><tr><td>Progress</td><td>Fluctuated during the day</td><td>Aggravated progressively</td></tr><tr><td>Prognosis</td><td>May be recover, known cause &amp; treat</td><td>Not reversible</td></tr><tr><td>Signs &amp; symptoms</td><td>a disturbance in a person's thoughts, mood, and behavior. It causes inattention, distractibility disorganized thinking, and confusion.<br/>→ inattention, or difficulty focusing, shifting, or maintaining attention<br/>In some case, a person may have altered mental status and delirium</td><td>Memory &amp; decision-making disorders<br/>People with dementia may forget recent events, older memories and events, names of familiar people and places.<br/>In some cases, a person may have Dementia + delirium</td></tr></tbody></table><h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2><ol><li><b>Objectives of Management</b><p>Maintain vital function, in the same time, find and correct the possible reversible causes<br/>Treat and prevent the structural and functional derangement caused by coma (elevation ICP, respiratory depression) and treat its cause.</p></li><li><b>Critical signs</b><p>Depth of coma, GCS lower or equal 8, the lower is the more severe<br/>Coma secondary to prolong shock, hypoxia or hypoglycemia<br/>Coma on Cardiac arrest with return of spontaneous circulation post resuscitation (CPR)<br/>Coma which GCS drops abruptly (secondary deterioration of brain injury, herniation)</p></li></ol></div>

<!-- PAGE 94 -->

<h3>3. Mortality risk factor</h3>
<p>Age and medical conditions of patient</p>
<ul>
<li>Coma associated with condition that deteriorates hemodynamic (hypotension/ bleeding)</li>
<li>Coma associated with condition that deteriorates oxygenation (pneumonia, chest trauma)</li>
<li>Systemic factors that exacerbated the secondary brain injury: fever, agitation, hypoxia, hypercapnia, hypotension, hyponatremia.</li>
<li>Localize factors that exacerbated the secondary brain injury: expansion of intracranial hematoma, cerebral edema, intracranial herniation, cerebral vasospasm, Intracranial Pressure elevation.</li>
</ul>
<h3>4. Outpatient management</h3>
<p>All patient with acute loss of consciousness should be evaluated and follow-up in emergency department. Coma is a Medical Emergency. While waiting for, and during the transport, be cautious about aspiration pneumonia (patient may vomit).</p>
<p>Check breathing and pulse. If breathing OR pulse is absent then start first aid CPR. If breathing AND pulse is present then put the patient on recovery position.</p>
<h3>5. First-line treatment</h3>
<p>Treatment of coma involves identification of the cause of the brain failure and initiation of specific therapy directed at the underlying cause.</p>
<p>Attend to airway, ventilation, and circulation. Evaluate and treat for readily reversible causes of coma, such as hypoglycemia and opioid toxicity.</p>
<p>Rapid point-of-care glucose determination can identify the need for dextrose. Give D50% 50ml IV in once or divided in two doses followed by D10% infusion, check glycemic again 10-15min after the bolus. Give Thiamin 100mg IM/IV if suspect vitamin B1 deficiency. In case coma with bradypnea and myosis, suspect opioids overdose, give Naloxone 0.4-2mg IV repeat every 2-3min, or put into IV infusion with rate adjusted to patient response. In patient who is opioids dependent, too quick to reverse may trigger withdrawal syndrome.</p>
<p>The patient suspect to have intracranial hypertension (severe headache, nausea-vomiting, blur vision, secondary altered consciousness, pupillary dilated or unequal) need to be managed immediately:</p>
<ul>
<li>Raise Head of Bed (reduce veinous volume) to 30degree</li>
<li>Hyperosmolar (NS 3%, mannitol) [Reduce (remove) some water from brain tissue]</li>
<li>Hyperventilate (Vasoconstriction, reduce cerebral blood flow)</li>
<li>Sedation (reduce sympathetic nervous system tone)</li>
<li>Control fever / seizure (Reduce cerebral oxygen demand, reduce the cerebral blood flow)</li>
<li>Ventriculostomy [Remove (Reduce volume of CSF)</li>
<li>Intracranial Hematoma removal. (hematoma with midline deviated)</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 95 -->

<h3>6. Treatment adjustment</h3>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Problem</th>
<th>Management</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>In cases of severe facial trauma</td>
<td>Intubation is indicated for airway protection.</td>
</tr>
<tr>

<td>Start vasopressors to avoid cerebral hypoperfusion</td>
</tr>

<td>the cervical spine should be immobilized until it can be cleared</td>

</tr>
<tr>

<tr>

<td>warm the patient with a warming blanket.</td>
</tr>
<tr>

</tr>
<tr>

</tr>
<tr>
<td>Endocrine emergencies, including myxedema coma</td>
<td>should be treated with thyroid hormone and supportive measures to correct hypothermia and hyponatremia</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)</td>
<td>fluids, electrolyte repletion, and insulin</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Infectious cause is suspect</td>

Algorithm Initial management of patient with Coma<br/>(See Fig_3)</p><h3>VIII. SPECIAL CONSIDERATION</h3><h4>1. Head trauma &amp; coma.</h4><p>If trauma is suspected, maintain stabilization of the cervical spine during assessment. If protection of the airway is in doubt or the coma state is likely prolonged, then protect the airway by intubating the patient.</p><h4>2. For children,</h4><p>For children consider ingestions (intoxication), infections, and child abuse in the appropriate clinical setting.</p><h4>3. nonconvulsive status epilepticus or subtle status epilepticus</h4><p>A state of electromechanical dissociation of the brain and body after seizure. If the motor activity of the seizure stops and the patient does not awaken within 30 minutes, then consider nonconvulsive status epilepticus. Obtain neurologic consultation and electroencephalography.</p>

<p>Fig. 3_ Decisional tree of initial management</p>
<div style="text-align: center;">
<h3>Initial management of patient with Coma</h3>
</div>
<img alt="Flowchart titled 'Initial management of patient with Coma'. The process starts with 'Coma' (circle). The first step is 'Airway, Breathing, Circulation' (rectangle). This leads to three decision points:
1. Suspect ICP Elevated*? (diamond). Yes path leads to a list of interventions: Head of bed elevated 30°, Head in neutral position, Minnitol: 0.5-1.0g/kg IV or Hypertonic saline: 3% 1.5-3ml/kg given as bolus infusion over 10-20min, Dexamethasone: 10mg IV (in tumoral edema), Hyperventilation (PaCO₂ ≤ 35mmHg first 24h post brain injury).

The No path from 'Suspect reversible causes?' and the path from 'Intubate + Ventilate' both lead to 'Cause of coma? Specific Treatment' (rectangle)."/>
<p>* Signs &amp; symptoms of elevated ICP: severe headache, nausea-vomiting, blur vision, altered consciousness, pupillary dilated or unequal.</p>
<p>Note: some author recommend head of bed elevation ≥ 45°, HS: 3% dose 2.5-5ml/kg given in 15-20min</p>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<p>The evolution and prognosis of coma is varied to its cause. Toxic and metabolic coma usually has better prognosis than structural coma. However, with the delay of treatment metabolic coma will transform to structural coma, e.g., hypoglycemia. In other condition that coma resulted from severe organ dysfunction, e.g., liver encephalopathy, multi-organs system dysfunction, the prognosis is poor.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 98 -->

<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3><p>Coma with GCS lower than 8 usually had a depressed ventilation; The resulting hypercapnia induced cerebral vasodilatation and elevation of intracranial pressure. In acute phase of head trauma patient often had a vomit that risks aspirated and compromised the airway. Other complications included, cerebral edema, aspiration pneumonia, bed-sore, deep-vein thrombosis infections, long-term handicaps, and complications link to the cause of coma.</p><h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3><p>Acute coma is a medical emergency. Coma may be a sign of cardiac arrested; identify early, the first 10-15min is precious time for cardiorespiratory resuscitation (CPR). Coma patient may lose control on his airway and had high risk of aspiration (airway obstruction, pneumonia), put the patient on recovery position or other preventive measures taken. In poisoning, coma is the latest stage of any poison, treat early may prevent it from happen.</p><h3>XII. REFERENCE</h3><ol><li>M. Kathryn Mutter, J. Stephen Huff, (2020).
