<h1>ALLERGIC REACTION</h1><p>Dr. IM Virya, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Asst. TAING Sovanna, Dr. Pen Phallkun, Dr. Krouch Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara.</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>Allergic reaction is a various conditions caused by hypersensitivity of the immune system to typically harmless substances in the environment.</p><p>It can be classified into different types based on the underlying mechanisms involved. The four main types of allergic reactions are:</p><ol><li>Type I (Immediate Hypersensitivity) Reactions:<ul><li>These reactions occur rapidly, within minutes to hours of exposure to the allergen.</li><li>Examples include allergic rhinitis (hay fever), asthma, food allergies, and anaphylaxis.</li></ul></li><li>Type II (Cytotoxic) Reactions:<ul><li>These reactions involve antibodies targeting and attacking cells within the body, leading to cell destruction.</li><li>Examples include certain drug-induced hemolytic anemia and blood transfusion reactions.</li></ul></li><li>Type III (Immune Complex-Mediated) Reactions:<ul><li>These reactions involve the formation of immune complexes that get deposited in tissues, triggering inflammation and damage.</li><li>Examples include serum sickness and certain autoimmune diseases like lupus.</li></ul></li><li>Type IV (Delayed-Type) Reactions:<ul><li>These reactions typically occur 48-72 hours after exposure to the allergen and involve T-cell activation.</li><li>Examples include contact dermatitis (e.g., poison ivy rash) and certain drug hypersensitivity reactions.</li></ul></li></ol><p>Anaphylaxis is defined as a serious allergic or hypersensitivity reaction that is usually rapid in onset and may cause death.</p><p>The term “anaphylaxis” is derived from the Greek words “ana” (against) and “phylaxis” (protection). Anaphylaxis requires urgent recognition and treatment.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>The incidence and prevalence of anaphylaxis vary worldwide, with differences dependent on a number of variables. Anaphylaxis is likely underreported as well.</p><p>Worldwide incidence: recent studies estimate that the global incidence of anaphylaxis ranges from 50 to 112 episode per 100 000 person-years. Additionally, a population-based analysis found approximately 46 cases of anaphylaxis per 100 000 populations per year.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><ul><li><b>IgE Mediated</b><ol><li>Food Triggers: Most commonly peanuts or other nuts, fish or shellfish, eggs and cow’s milk. Asthma and others atopic diseases are a risk factor for food-based anaphylaxis.</li></ol></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 100 -->

<div>
<p>2. Drug triggers:</p>
<ul>
<li>Antibiotics: Penicillin-related antibiotics and sulphonamides. Reactions are twice as likely to occur after intravenous or intramuscular administration when compared to the oral route.</li>
<li>Other antivirals, antihelminthics and TB medications</li>
<li>Muscle relaxants</li>
<li>Antineoplastic/cytotoxic/immunomodulators.</li>
</ul>
<p>3. Insect venom triggers: Bees, wasps, yellow jackets, hornets and fires ants.<br/>Venoms-allergic patients respond well to immunotherapy</p>
<p>4. Other triggers</p>
<ul>
<li>Latex</li>
<li>Horse derived antitoxins (snake antivenoms)</li>
<li>Helminths</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li><b>Non-IgE Mediated</b>
<ol>
<li>Immune complex: Blood products, immunoglobulins and dextrans</li>
<li>Non-immunological mast cell activators: Radiocontrast media</li>
<li>Modulators of arachidonic acid metabolism: Aspirin and NSAIDs</li>
<li>Idiopathic</li>
<li>Exercise</li>
</ol>
</li>
</ul>
<h4>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h4>
<p>The mechanism responsible for most cases of human anaphylaxis involves immunoglobulin E (IgE). Possible alternative mechanisms remain incompletely understood.</p>
<p>The term "anaphylaxis" has traditionally been reserved for <b>IgE-dependent</b> events, and the term "anaphylactoid reaction" has been used to describe <b>IgE-independent</b> events, although the two reactions are often clinically indistinguishable.</p>
<p>Instead, the World Allergy Organization has proposed that anaphylactic reactions be categorized as <b>immunologic</b> and <b>non-immunologic</b>.</p>
<ul>
<li>Immunologic anaphylaxis is typically described as IgE mediated. The traditional IgE-mediated mechanism of anaphylaxis begins with an antigen binding to an allergen-specific IgE. Antigen-bound IgE in turn binds to the receptor Fc-epsilon-RI on mast cells and/or basophils. This causes these cells to degranulate, releasing a number of inflammatory mediators.</li>
<li>Non-immunologic anaphylaxis being a result of sudden basophil or mast cell degranulation in the absence of immunoglobulins.</li>
</ul>
<h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<h5>1. Clinical features</h5>
<p>Anaphylactic reactions vary in duration and severity but typically are rapid in onset with most occurring within 2 hours of allergen exposure. Clinical presentations depend on the degree of hypersensitivity, the quantity, route, and rate of antigen exposure, as well as the target organ sensitivity and responsiveness. Presentations include a combination of clinical characteristics, affecting an array of organ systems including the skin, respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, cardiovascular, or the central nervous system.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 101 -->

<div>

<p>Anaphylaxis is predominately a clinical diagnosis. Criteria for defining anaphylaxis were developed in 2004 by a panel of experts at the National Institutes of Health, which resulted in the publication of the NIAID/Anaphylaxis Network Definition of Anaphylaxis.</p>
<table border="1">
<caption>Clinical criteria for diagnosis anaphylaxis</caption>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>
<p>1. Acute onset of an illness (minutes to several hours) with involvement of the skin, mucosal tissue, or both (e.g., generalized hives, pruritus or flushing, or swollen lips-tongue-uvula) and at least one of the following:</p>
<ul>
<li>a. Respiratory compromise (e.g., dyspnea, wheeze-bronchospasm, stridor, or hypoxemia)</li>
<li>b. Reduced BP or associated symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (e.g., hypotonia [collapse], syncope, or incontinence)</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>
<p>2. Two or more of the following that occur rapidly after exposure to a likely allergen for that patient (minutes to several hours):</p>
<ul>
<li>a. Involvement of the skin-mucosal tissue (e.g., generalized hives, itch-flush, or swollen lips-tongue-uvula)</li>
<li>b. Respiratory compromise (e.g., dyspnea, wheeze-bronchospasm, stridor, or hypoxemia)</li>
<li>c. Reduced BP or associated symptoms of end-organ dysfunction (e.g., hypotonia [collapse], syncope, or incontinence)</li>
<li>d. Persistent gastrointestinal symptoms (e.g., crampy abdominal pain or vomiting)</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>
<p>3. Reduced BP after exposure to a known allergen for that patient (minutes to hours):</p>
<ul>
<li>a. Infants and children: low systolic BP (age specific) or greater than 30% decrease in systolic BP</li>
<li>b. Adults: systolic BP of &lt;90mmhg or greater than 30% decrease from that person's baseline</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h2>2. Investigation</h2>
<ul>
<li>There are currently no biomarkers or laboratory tests that can resolutely confirm or refute the diagnosis and no biomarker that increases in concentration irrespective of trigger.</li>
<li>Tryptase levels
        <ul>
<li>These are now recommended for patients presenting with anaphylaxis, but this only needs to be done for one episode.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 102 -->

<ul><li>When present, the degree of rise in tryptase does correlate with severity of the symptoms, but a rise may not be found in all patients.</li><li>Skin prick tests and allergen-specific serum IgE levels can be performed by the allergy specialist after 3–4 weeks to avoid false-positive results.</li><li>Challenge or provocation tests can be performed but should be done with caution in a facility that has the resources to manage any subsequent anaphylaxis.</li></ul><h2>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h2><table border="1"><thead><tr><th colspan="2">Differential Diagnosis of Anaphylaxis</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><p>Acute generalized urticarial<br/>Asthma exacerbation<br/>Myocardial infarction<br/>Pulmonary embolus<br/>Syncope<br/>Adverse cutaneous drug reaction<br/>Anxiety/panic attacks</p><p><b>Flush Syndrome</b><br/>Flushing associated with food<br/>Alcohol<br/>MSG<br/>Sulfites<br/>Scombroidosis<br/>Carcinoid tumor Perimenopause<br/>Thyrotoxicosis<br/>Basophilic leukemia<br/>Mastocytosis (systemic mastocytosis and urticaria pigmentosa)<br/>Vasointestinal peptide tumors</p></td><td><p><b>Shock Syndromes</b><br/>Septic shock<br/>Hypovolemic shock<br/>Cardiogenic shock<br/>Distributive shock</p><p><b>Miscellaneous</b><br/>Hypoglycemia<br/>Acquired and HAE<br/>ACE-inhibitor-associated angioedema<br/>Red man syndrome (Vancomycin)<br/>Neurologic disorders (seizure, stroke, autonomic epilepsy)<br/>Vocal cord dysfunction syndrome<br/>Pheochromocytoma</p><p><small>ACE, Angiotensin-converting enzyme; HAE, hereditary angioedema; MSG, monosodium glutamate.</small></p></td></tr></tbody></table><h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2><h3>1. Objectives</h3><p>Prompt recognition and initiation of the appropriate interventions remain key in avoiding adverse outcomes. Treatment delays, even by a few minutes, could potentially lead to hypoxia, circulatory collapse, and even death. It is also important to treat anaphylaxis promptly because it appears to be most responsive to treatment in its early phases, based on the observation that delayed epinephrine injection is associated with fatalities.</p><h3>2. Critical sign</h3><ul><li>Cardiovascular system:<ul><li>Myocardial depression</li><li>Arrhythmias</li><li>Myocardial ischemia</li></ul></li><li>Respiratory system:<ul><li>Bronchospasm</li><li>Laryngeal edema</li><li>Asphyxia</li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 103 -->

<h3>3. Mortality risk factor</h3>
<p>Risk factors for increased anaphylaxis severity and mortality:</p>
<ul>
<li>Very young (under-recognition)</li>
<li>Elderly (Decrease physiologic reserves)</li>
<li>Comorbid conditions
        <ul>
<li>Cardiovascular disease (heart failure, ischemic heart disease, hypertension)</li>
<li>Pulmonary disease (asthma, obstructive airway disease)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Others:
        <ul>
<li>Concurrent use of anti-hypertensive agents, specifically beta-blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors</li>
<li>Concurrent use of cognition-impairing drugs (e.g., alcohol, recreational drugs, sedatives, tranquilizers)</li>
<li>Recent anaphylaxis episode</li>
<li>Upright posture at the onset of symptoms</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>4. Outpatient Management</h3>
<p>The cornerstones of initial management are the following.</p>
<ul>
<li>Removal of the inciting cause, if possible (stop infusion of a suspect medication).</li>
<li>Call for help</li>
<li>Intramuscular (IM) injection of epinephrine at the earliest opportunity, followed by additional epinephrine by IM or intravenous (IV) injection as needed.</li>
<li>Placement of the patient in the supine position with the lower extremities elevated, unless there is prominent upper airway swelling prompting the patient to remain upright (and often leaning forward). If the patient is vomiting, placement of the patient semi recumbent with lower extremities elevated may be preferable. Place pregnant patients on their left side.</li>
<li>Supplemental oxygen.</li>
<li>Volume resuscitation with IV fluids.</li>
</ul>
<h3>5. First line treatment</h3>
<ul>
<li>The first and most important treatment in anaphylaxis is epinephrine. There are no absolute contraindications to epinephrine in the setting of anaphylaxis.</li>
<li><b>Air way</b> – Immediate intubation if evidence of impending airway obstruction from angioedema. Delay may lead to complete obstruction. Intubation can be difficult and should be performed by the most experienced clinician available. Cricothyrotomy may be necessary.</li>
<li><b>IM epinephrine</b>
<ul>
<li>Adult: give epinephrine 0.3 to 0.5 mg IM in the mid-outer thigh. Can repeat every 5 to 15 minutes (or more frequently), as needed. If epinephrine is injected promptly IM, most patients respond to 1, 2, or at most, 3 doses. If symptoms are not responding to epinephrine injections, prepare IV epinephrine for infusion.</li>
<li>Pediatric: 0.01mg/kg (0.01ml/kg of 1:1000 dilution).</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Position</b> – Place patient in recumbent position, if tolerated, and elevated lower extremities</li>
<li><b>Oxygen</b> – Give 8-10l/MN via facemask or up to 100% oxygen, as needed.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 104 -->

<ul><li><b>Normal Saline or Ringer lactate rapid bolus</b> – Rapid infusion of 1 to 2 liters IV or 10-20ml/kg in pediatric. Repeat, as needed. Massive fluid shifts with severe loss of intravascular volume can occur. Monitor urine output.</li></ul><p><b>6. Treatment adjustment</b></p><ul><li><b>Albuterol (salbutamol)</b> – For bronchospasm resistant to IM epinephrine.<ul><li>Adult: 2.5-5mg in 3 mL saline via nebulizer, or 4 to 6 puffs by metered dose inhaler (MDI). Repeat every 20mn as needed.</li><li>Pediatric: 1.25-2.5mg nebulized, or 4-6 puffs from MDI with holding chamber. Repeated every 20mn as needed</li></ul></li><li><b>H1 antihistamine</b> – for relief of urticarial and itching only.<ul><li>Adult: Cetirizine (Zyrtec) 10 mg IV or chlorpheniramine 10mg IM/IV or diphenhydramine (Polaramine) 25 to 50 mg IV/IM/PO.</li><li>Pediatric: Diphenhydramine (Polaramine) 1mg/kg IV/IM/PO.</li></ul></li><li><b>H2 antihistamine</b> – for relief of urticarial and itching only.<ul><li>Adult: Famotidine 20 mg IV or cimetidine 300mg or Ranitidine 50mg IV.</li><li>Pediatric: Ranitidine 0.5mg/kg IV or Cimetidine 4-8mg/kg IV.</li></ul></li><li><b>Glucocorticoid</b> – for prevention of protracted and biphasic reactions.<ul><li>Adult: Methylprednisolone 80-125mg IV or hydrocortisone 250-500mg IV.</li><li>Pediatric: Methylprednisolone 1-2mg/kg IV or hydrocortisone 5-10mg/kg IV.</li></ul></li><li><b>Magnesium sulfate</b> – for treatment of bronchospasm.<ul><li>Adult: 2g IV over 20mn.</li><li>Pediatric: 25-50mg/kg IV.</li></ul></li><li><b>Glucagon</b> – for treatment of patient on beta-blockers with refractory hypotension.<ul><li>Adult: 1mg IV every 5mn until hypotension resolves followed by 5-15 mcg/mn infusion.</li><li>Pediatric: 50mcg/kg every 5mn.</li></ul></li><li><b>Monitoring</b> – Continuous noninvasive hemodynamic monitoring and pulse oximetry monitoring should be performed. Urine output should be monitored in patients receiving IV fluid resuscitation for severe hypotension or shock.</li></ul>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASE</h3>
<h4>1. Urticarial and Angioedema</h4>
<p><b>Urticarial</b> is commonly encountered in the ED. It is characterized by the presence of wheals, angioedema, or both. Urticarial appears as papules or wheals that consist of central swelling with surrounding reflex erythema and is associated with itching or a burning type sensation. These lesions are a result of mediators (predominately histamine) released from mast cells. They tend to occur on the extremities and are usually transient, with skin often returning to its normal appearance within 24 hours. Urticarial can be classified based on its duration, with acute urticarial lasting less than 6 weeks and chronic episodes lasting longer than 6 weeks. There are also several types of inducible urticarial including cold contact, delayed pressure, heat contact, solar, aquagenic, or cholinergic.</p>
<p><b>Angioedema</b> is characterized by edema of the subcutaneous or submucosal tissues, commonly involving the face, mouth, lips, tongue, extremities, or genitalia. It is a result of abrupt vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, allowing fluid to move from the vascular to the interstitial space. As the swelling is located in the deeper layers of the skin, the appearance is often normal in color and patients often complain of pain or a pressure sensation, rather than an itch. Of particular concern is when the tongue, posterior pharynx, or larynx is involved, which could progress to airway obstruction and compromise. Angioedema can be mediated by an allergic mechanism in response to exposure to foods, drugs, or physical stimuli or by a nonallergic mechanism such as Hereditary Angioedema (HAE), acquired angioedema, or ACE-inhibitor-induced angioedema.</p>
<h4>2. Management</h4>
<p>Angioedema with urticarial without airway threatening:</p>
<ul>
<li>H1-Antihistamine: cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine or Diphenhydramine</li>
<li>H2-Antihistamine may also beneficial: Famotidine, Ranitidine or Cimetidine.</li>
<li>Corticosteroids: prednisone as a second-line therapy</li>
<li>Epinephrine: anaphylactic dosing for severe symptoms and no cardiac risk factors.</li>
<li>Avoid exposure to potential triggering agents.</li>
</ul>
<p>Angioedema with airway-threatening:</p>
<ul>
<li>Epinephrine at anaphylactic doses.</li>
<li>Antihistamines</li>
<li>Intubation if situation required and paralytics should be utilized with caution.</li>
<li>Prepared for difficult airway algorithm using alternative measures (fiber optic laryngoscopy, surgical airway).</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Biphasic reaction: reoccurrence of anaphylactic symptoms without re-exposure to the triggering agent within 8 hours to 72 hours.</li>
<li>Prevention by administer corticosteroids but recent studies have failed to show significant effect.</li>
<li>Risk factor for biphasic reactions include
        <ul>
<li>Hypotension</li>
<li>Wide pulse pressure</li>
<li>Unknown trigger</li>
<li>Greater than 1 dose of epinephrine</li>
<li>Cutaneous signs and symptoms, prior anaphylaxis</li>
<li>And delayed epinephrine administration.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 107 -->

<ul><li>Patients should be monitored for a minimum of 6 h after resolution of symptoms. This observation period may need to be longer depending on the presence of any of the following high-risk features:<ul><li>Extremes of age</li><li>Significant co-morbidity</li><li>Severe reaction with slow onset</li><li>Severe asthma</li><li>Likely continued absorption</li><li>History of significant biphasic reaction</li><li>Evening or night presentation</li><li>Difficulty accessing emergency care</li></ul></li><li>Hospitalization should be strongly considered for patients who present with protracted anaphylaxis, hypotension, or airway involvement; receive more than two doses of IM epinephrine; or have poor outpatient social support, or inability to acquire an auto-injectable epinephrine device.</li></ul><h3>X. COMPLICATION</h3><p>The main complications which can occur following an anaphylactic reaction include:</p><ul><li>Wheeze</li><li>Stridor</li><li>Hypoxemia</li><li>Hypotension</li><li>End-organ dysfunction</li><li>Death</li></ul><h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3><p>Anaphylaxis is a potentially life-threatening allergic condition which can present with multiple symptoms.</p><p>Anaphylaxis should be treated with intramuscular epinephrine, supportive management, and adjunct medications as needed. The mainstay of management is avoidance of triggers and to carry an epinephrine auto-injector.</p><p>A prescription for an epinephrine auto-injector should be provided following treatment of anaphylaxis, and training should also be provided regarding its use. Patients should also be assessed and followed by an allergist.</p><h3>XII. REFERENCES</h3><ol><li>Cardona V, Ansotegui IJ, Ebisawa M, et al. World allergy organization anaphylaxis guidance 2020. <h1>GENERAL MANAGEMENT OF POISONING</h1>
<p><i>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Poisoning or intoxication is a serious condition that occurs when a person or an animal is exposed to a substance that can harm their health or even kill them.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>An epidemiological Surveillance report 2011 in Thailand found that the incidence of environmental pesticide poisoning is 3.20 per 100.000 person. The incidence of prescribed drugs poisoning is 3.81 and the intentional ingestion of toxic substances is 5.91 per 100.000. In Singapore, the incidence of alcohol consumption-related ED visit was remarkably increased from 48.7 per 100.000 person (in 2007) to 79.1 per 100.000 person (in 2016).</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Poisoning may be “acute” (occurs a few hours to few days after exposure) or “Chronic” (problems occur after repeated and long-time exposure). In emergencies most of the intoxication cases was acute poisoning. Intoxication or poisoning may be intentional or non-intentional. Intentional poisoning: suicide attempt, self-harm, abuse, misuse. Non-intentional poisoning: error dose, accidental, environmental toxics (air pollution, arsenic in water...), occupational poisoning, food, drink (methanol poisoning), animal bites. Poison can be a drug that is used in clinic (overdose), food, drink, chemical that use in industrial / agricultural works, or household-use, or biologic (mushroom, some fishes). Exposure route may be inhalation, skin contact, mucous membrane contact, ingestion, or injection. Animals or snakebites were also a kind of poisoning in which the poison or venom were injected into the subcutaneous tissue or muscle during the bite.</p>
<h2>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h2>
<p>To initiate the poisoning, the organism is exposed to the toxic chemical. When a toxic level of the chemical is accumulated in the cells of the target tissue or organ, the resultant injury to the cells disrupts their normal structure or function. Symptoms and toxic signs then develop, and, if the toxicity is severe enough, death may result. Different groups of substances may have different mechanisms of toxicity to human. It may be a Systemic poisoning (Cyanide, lead, warfarin, pesticides), specific organ poisoning (paracetamol-liver, gentamycin-kidney, snake Viperidae-venom-hematologic / snake Elapidae-venom- neurologic), local poisoning (caustic, acid, snake Viperidae-venom), some substances may cause endocrine disruption (DDT, Bisphenol A, Dioxins), some other may be cancerogenic (arsenic-skin, Asbestos-lung, tobacco-lung). Substances belonging to a particular pharmaceutical or chemical class often produce a cluster of symptoms and signs, or</p>

<!-- PAGE 109 -->

<div>
<p>“toxidrome”, enabling the identification of potential toxins when a clear history is unavailable.</p>
<h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<p>The diagnosis of poisoning is based on the meticulous history, physical examination and/or toxidrome found in physical exam.</p>
<ol>
<li><b>Signs &amp; symptoms</b><br/>The common toxidrome with signs and symptoms are shown in table_1</li>
<li><b>Laboratory analysis:</b><br/>For clinical use, common laboratory tests were order:
        <ul>
<li>“Basic metabolic panel” for electrolytes (Na, K, Cl, HCO<sub>3</sub>, Calcium) plus glucose, urea, creatinine) and to determine anion gap;</li>
<li>ethanol, acetaminophen (paracetamol), and salicylate concentrations (if overdose is suspected)</li>
<li>transaminases,</li>
<li>serum osmolarity if toxic alcohol is suspected;</li>
<li>blood gas for pH</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<p>The specific toxicology screens in general, are of limited utility and seldom impact care and outcome. False negative and positive results on urine drug screening may be confusing and potentially distract the clinician. It was indicated in some specific cases e.g., in mass poisoning or empoisoning cases or when the exact cause of poisoning was necessary.</p>
<h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<p>In emergency, one should consider a poisoning as a possible cause of unexplained coma / seizure or shock. In practice, patient who was intentionally poisoning usually take more than one drugs or substances. Besides, in intoxication with some products like insecticides, patient may be intoxicated also with the solvent (petroleum, benzene, xylene) of those products. Many compounds medicine has multiple active ingredients, (e.g., Codalgin® = paracetamol + codeine) so overdose of main component may be associated with others.</p>
<p>In the case of Ethanol, sedative hypnotic or opioids, different scenario may happen, patient may enter ED because, experience side-effects / allergic reaction, or present with toxic effects of overdoses, or withdrawal syndrome. In chronic poisoning, it is a challenge to link a clinical feather to a toxic cause, as it may take several years for the symptoms and signs to be uncovered.</p>
</div>

<h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2>
<ol>
<li>Objective of management
        <ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Stabilize the vital signs (Resuscitation)</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Identify the substances, the amount, the route, the time of exposure or the present toxidrome.</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Provide antidote, or antivenom, if available</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Decontamination, and/or enhance the elimination.</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Supportive treatment (hypotension, respiratory failure, renal failure)</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Preventive treatment for recurrence poisoning.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Critical signs
        <p>The severity grading of poisoning depends on whether the poison is stimulant or depressant. Coma and cardiovascular collapse are common in the most severe, grade 4, of stimulant as well as depressant poisoning.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p>Table 2: Severity grade of poisoning, for stimulant and depressant substances</p>
<table border="1">

</tr>
</thead>

</tr>

<ol>
<li>Mortality risk factor
        <p>Multiple factors contributed to the risk of mortality</p>
<ul>
<li>Type of poisoning, intentional (suicide, of empoisoning)</li>
<li>The dose of poison or duration of exposure to the toxic substances</li>
<li>The degree or intensity of toxicity of the exposed substances or toxin</li>
<li>Medical background of intoxicated patient, age group</li>
<li>The delay of management</li>
<li>Availability of supportive /substitutive treatment (Hemodialysis, mechanical ventilation)</li>
<li>Some classical procedures may be harmful (gastric lavage-associated aspiration pneumonia)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 112 -->

<h4>4. Out-patient management</h4>
<p>Only people who exposed to a known non-toxic substance and asymptomatic may be observed at home and contact with emergency personal for any abnormality.</p>
<h4>5. First-line treatment</h4>
<p>In all case, consider the supportive treatment first. The shock state, depressed respiration should be the first measure to be taken. If the poison was identified and it has antidote, it should be administered as soon as possible.</p>
<h4>A. Gastrointestinal decontamination</h4>
<h5>i. Gastric lavage</h5>
<p>If performed because of a potentially life-threatening poison ingestion, an experienced provider should perform the lavage based on the complications that can occur.</p>
<p>Gastric lavage involves a large-bore (36F–40F) orogastric tube passed into the stomach, after which small volumes (200–300 mL) of liquid are alternately administered and aspirated. Comatose patients and those with loss of their protective airway reflexes should have an endotracheal tube placed before this procedure.</p>
<p>Contraindications include loss of protective airway reflexes (unless the patient is endotracheally intubated), ingestion of a corrosive substance or a hydrocarbon, gastrointestinal pathology, and other medical conditions that could be worsened by the use of lavage. Complications of the procedure include aspiration, laryngospasm, hypoxia, hypercapnia, mechanical injury, and fluid and electrolyte imbalances in children.</p>
<h5>ii. Single dose activated charcoal</h5>
<p>Administration of activated charcoal may be considered if a patient has ingested a potentially toxic amount of poison that is known to be adsorbed to charcoal not longer than 1 hour before treatment, as its effectiveness decreases over time. There is no evidence that the administration of activated charcoal improves outcome.</p>
<p>The dose is 1 gram/ kilogram in children or 25 to 50 grams in adults. The minimal dose should be no less than a 10:1 ratio of AC to drug. Same contraindication as gastric lavage.</p>
<h5>iii. Whole-bowel irrigation</h5>
<p>Whole-bowel irrigation consists of administration through a nasogastric tube of an osmotically balanced, polyethylene glycol-based electrolyte solution to decontaminate the entire gastrointestinal tract by physically expelling intraluminal contents. As much as 1500–2000 mL/hr can be administered to an “awake” adult patient.</p>
<p>Whole-bowel irrigation should not be used routinely in the poisoned patient. However, it can be considered for potentially toxic ingestions of sustained-release or enteric-coated drugs and for drugs not likely to be adsorbed to activated charcoal (iron, lithium, potassium) and for the removal of illicit drug packets. Contraindications include bowel</p>

<!-- PAGE 113 -->

<div><p>pathology, unprotected or compromised airway, hemodynamic instability, and intractable vomiting. Complications are nausea, vomiting, and abdominal cramps.</p><p>iv. Multiple-dose activated charcoal</p><p>Multiple-dose activated charcoal decreases the re-absorption blood-enteral, also interrupts the enterohepatic and enterogastric circulation of drugs. Drugs with a prolonged elimination half-life, a small volume of distribution (less than 1 L/kg), and little protein binding are the most amenable to this sort of management. Multiple-dose activated charcoal should be considered if a patient has ingested a life-threatening amount of carbamazepine, dapsone, phenobarbital, quinine, or theophylline. With all of these drugs, data confirm enhanced elimination, although no controlled studies have demonstrated clinical benefit.</p><p>The initial dose of charcoal is 50–100 g, and this treatment is followed every 1, 2, or 4 hours by a dose equivalent to 12.5 g/hr. More frequent, smaller doses may prevent vomiting. Multiple-dose activated charcoal can be continued until the patient improves clinically. Complications include bowel obstruction and vomiting with subsequent aspiration.</p><p>B. Urinary alkalinization</p><p>Urinary alkalinization is the administration of intravenous (IV) sodium bicarbonate to produce urine with a pH ≥7.5. The objective of treatment is pH manipulation, not forced diuresis. Hypokalemia is the most common complication. Alkalemia also can occur. Urinary alkalinization should be considered as first-line treatment in patients with moderately severe salicylate poisoning who do not meet the criteria for hemodialysis. Urinary alkalinization is not recommended as first-line treatment for cases of phenobarbital poisoning, because multiple-dose activated charcoal is superior.</p><p>C. Ipecac and emetics</p><p>There is no role for syrup of ipecac in the hospital setting.</p><p>D. Antidote</p><p>Not all substances have their antidote. Table 2 shows Common antidotes used in Clinical practice. Outside the poison center, only a few are available.</p></div>

<p><b>F. Supportive / substitution treatment</b></p>
<p>Supportive treatment is essential; in many situations it was the only feasible measure in poisoning management. Most of the substances do not have their antidote. The decontamination and enhanced elimination process were useful in limited cases only. Even the antidote is available and administered, it takes time for the organ dysfunction to reverse, during this time supportive measures is also needed. E.g., in cobra-snakebites, patient may have respiratory depressed or arrest while antivenom was administered. It takes a few hours for spontaneous respiration to re-appear. The active supportive treatment consists of maintaining the normal water, electrolytes acid-base equilibrium, a good oxygenation and perfusion; sometimes mechanical ventilation, hemodialysis and pharmacologically cardiac support were needed.</p>
<h4>6. Treatment adjustment</h4>
<p>In general, gastric lavage is not recommended when the patient arrived later than 1 hour after ingested the substances, it should be possible to try in case the patient took a large quantity of substance or/and the substance is known to slow the peristaltic. For the corrosive substance or a hydrocarbon, the gastric lavage is not recommended. For patient whose consciousness is altered, intubation and ventilation support should be done prior to lavage.</p>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASE</h3><h4>1. Poisoning during pregnancy</h4><p>Intoxication during pregnancy can be a serious health concern for both the mother and the baby. Drinking alcohol during pregnancy can cause premature labor, miscarriage, stillbirth, and a range of developmental, physical, mental, and emotional disabilities and disorders in the baby. The effects of intoxication on a developing fetus can vary greatly depending on several factors, including the type of substance used, the amount ingested, and the gestational age of the fetus.</p><ul><li>First trimester of pregnancy: Intoxicants can disrupt organogenesis process, leading to birth defects, developmental delays, and miscarriage.</li><li>Second trimester: growth and development. Exposure to toxins can affect weight, height, and brain development. Risk of cleft palate or other facial malformations</li><li>Third trimester: brain development may interfere by intoxication, risk of premature birth.</li></ul><p>Management of acute poisoning in pregnant women follow the same principle.</p><h4>2. Poisoning in children</h4><p>Children 1-3 years old are prone to acute poisoning. Children's bodies are still developing, and their brains are particularly sensitive to the effects of alcohol and drugs. Even small amounts can cause significant harm. For some substances they are more vulnerable than adult, e.g., lead poisoning. Young children (age 6 months to 7 years) are at the highest risk due to their developing brains and bodies, which readily absorb lead. Effects can range from developmental delays and learning difficulties to behavioral problems, anemia, and even coma in severe cases. Lead poisoning (chronic poisoning) can also affect growth and stature, hearing, and kidney function.</p><h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3><p>The evolution and prognosis of patients who are intoxicated can vary widely, depending on the substance involved, the amount ingested, the patient's overall health, and the timeliness and effectiveness of treatment. With proper management, most intoxication patients gradually improve and regain consciousness. Patient who repeatedly intentional intoxicate should be checked and follow up with psychiatric.</p><h3>X. COMPLICATION</h3><p>In acute poisoning, the complications link to intrinsic effect of substances may consist of, seizures, coma, shock, acute respiratory failure, acute kidney failure, acute liver failure and death. Complications may be link to the supportive procedures like mechanical ventilation or hemodialysis. In chronic exposure to toxic substances, long-term complications may be serious e.g., alcohol may lead to liver cirrhosis or/and liver cancer. Chronic exposure to Lead in small children may develop a learning difficulty, behavioral problems, affect growth and kidney function, anemic and hearing problem.</p>

<!-- PAGE 119 -->

<div><p><b>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</b></p><ul><li>Store chemicals and medications safely.</li><li>Read and follow instructions carefully</li><li>Dispose of old or unused products and dangerous substances responsibly</li><li>Install childproof safety latches</li><li>Educate children about the dangers of poisoning</li><li>Advocate for proper labeling and packaging</li><li>Do not forcing patient to vomit by any mean; do not try to neutralize the toxic effects by forcing patient to swallow the solution (lemon and sugar) especially when his/her mental status was altered.</li></ul><p><b>XII. <h1>PARACETAMOL POISONING</h1><p>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>A disorder characterized by hepatic necrosis following large acetaminophen (or Paracetamol) ingestions.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>In USA, hospitalizations due to acetaminophen toxicity from 1998 to 2011 were 67% due to intentional ingestion, 16% from unintentional ingestion, and 17% unspecified. Of the hospitalizations related to acetaminophen toxicity, 83% were primarily adults and 69% were female (95% CI 0.68–0.69%). From 2008 to 2012, about 49% of unintentional acetaminophen-related poison-control calls were regarding children aged ≤5 years.</p><p>In Thailand, among 184 patients with paracetamol overdosed, had median age 22 (15-76), 79.9% was female. Most overdoses were intended self-poisoning (90.8%) with a median dose of 10.5g (4.5-50). Overall, 15.6% developed severe hepatotoxicity and 3 patient developed acute liver failure.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><p>Paracetamol preparation has many forms:</p><ul><li>Rapid-release form_ onset of action: 10-30min, duration of action: 4-6h; half-life: 2-3h</li><li>Extend-release form_ onset of action: 30-60min, duration of action: 8-12h</li><li>Paracetamol combined formular_ associated with opioids (e.g., Codalgin®) or caffeine (e.g., Kinal®) to increase its strength. Some flu-medicines may include with paracetamol, pseudoephedrine, antiallergic, dextromethorphone in their constituents.</li></ul><p>Mode of poisoning:</p><ul><li>poisoning from a single large dose, or</li><li>prolong-repeat of mild overdose or</li><li>normal therapeutic dose in patients with liver disorders or malnourished alcoholism.</li></ul><h2>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h2><p>In a therapeutic dose and normal people, paracetamol is safe. About 2% of administered dose exit unchanged in urine. About 98% is metabolized in the liver. More than 80% by conjugated with glucuronide or sulfate to form a non-toxic fraction that eliminate by urine. About 8% of administered dose metabolized with cytochrome P450 enzymes to produce N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI). NAPQI is a by-product, toxic to the liver. In normal people, this product existed in a very short time without any harm to the liver. It was combined by liver glutathione to form a non-toxic NAPQI and eliminate in urine. In the situation of toxic overdose, the metabolism pathway with</p>

<!-- PAGE 121 -->

<div>
<p>glucuronide and sulfate is saturated, the CYP450 pathway increased, more NAPQI was produced; when Glutathione is not enough, NAPQI will damage the liver.</p>
<img alt="Diagram illustrating the Normal Metabolism pathway in therapeutic dose of Paracetamol. The diagram shows that 90% of paracetamol is metabolized via Cytochrome P450 into Glucuronide and Sulfate, which are excreted by the kidney. 8% is converted to NAPQI (N-acetyl-p-benzoquinoneimine), which is detoxified by Glutathione. 2% is excreted unchanged by the kidney. The NAPQI pathway is labeled as Hepatotoxic."/>
<p><b>Graphic-1: mechanism of paracetamol intoxication</b></p>
<h3>V. DIAGNOSIS</h3>
<p>Diagnosis of paracetamol poisoning is based on history, clinical signs with blood-paracetamol concentration assessment. Signs and symptoms of paracetamol poisoning develop over the first 24 hours following large ingestions. Symptoms may develop gradually in those with a history of long-term ingestion near supratherapeutic doses</p>
<p>A toxic exposure to acetaminophen is suggested when a patient ≥6 years old ingests:</p>
<ol>
<li>&gt;10 grams or 200 milligrams/kg as a single ingestion,</li>
<li>&gt;10 grams or 200 milligrams/kg over a 24-hour period, or</li>
<li>&gt;6 grams or 150 milligrams/kg per 24-hour period for at least 2 consecutive days.</li>
</ol>
<p>For children &lt;6 years old, ingestion of 200 milligrams/kg or more of acetaminophen as a single ingestion or over an 8-hour period, or of 150 milligrams/kg per 24-hour period for the preceding 48 hours is considered a toxic exposure.</p>
<p>These values are empiric and not validated in human trials, but they are widely used as recommendations for emergency evaluation.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 122 -->

<div>
<p>I. Clinic</p>
<p>Presentation of symptoms varies and is divided into four stages:</p>
<p><b>Stage 1—first 24 hours after ingestion</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Patients may be asymptomatic in the first 8 hours following ingestion.</li>
<li>Symptoms may include nausea, emesis, anorexia, and diaphoresis.</li>
<li>Laboratory results are usually unremarkable at this time.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Stage 2—days 2 to 3 following ingestion</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Typically, less nausea, vomiting, diaphoresis, and malaise than in stage 1; right upper quadrant pain and hepatomegaly may become evident.</li>
<li>Elevated aminotransferases are usually seen.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Stage 3—days 3 to 4 following ingestion</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Stage I symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and malaise reappear.</li>
<li>Severe poisonings may result in jaundice, confusion, somnolence, and coma.</li>
<li>Marked liver enzyme elevations which usually peak at this point; prolonged prothrombin time (PT)/international normalized ratio (INR); typically, negative acetaminophen levels.</li>
<li>Multiorgan failure and death most commonly occur in this stage.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Stage 4—days 5+ after ingestion</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Possible recovery stage in patients with resolving stage 3 symptoms.</li>
<li>recovery may be prolonged but is typically complete and without long-term sequelae.</li>
<li>Laboratory abnormalities typically resolve.</li>
<li>Fulminant hepatic failure occurs in &lt;1% of adults and is very rare in children &lt;6 years of age.</li>
</ul>
<p>2. Investigation</p>
<p>Plasma acetaminophen level is an essential laboratory test that help decide to use antidote early, before the liver injury occurred. Draw plasma acetaminophen levels on all patients ≥ 4 hours after ingestion (levels peak at 4 hours). Draw additional levels at 6 and 8 hours if extended-release form was ingested. Plot the result on the paracetamol nomogram and see if it is above the treatment line? (See Graphic-2) Liver functions test: alanine transaminase (ALT), aspartate transaminase (AST), PT/INR, bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is important, but it usually evident after 24h post ingestion.</p>
<p>Additional labs: electrolytes, glucose, BUN, creatinine, urinalysis, serum alcohol, and salicylate</p>
<p><b>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</b></p>
<p>Consider the presence of co-ingestants, especially alcohol, opiates, and aspirin.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 123 -->

<div>
<p>Other ingested toxins that produce severe acute hepatic injury include mushrooms, products containing yellow phosphorus or carbon tetrachloride. Consider other causes of hepatitis: alcoholic, viral, ischemic</p>
<h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2>
<ol>
<li>Objectives of management
        <ul>
<li>Stabilized the vital signs</li>
<li>Check if patient needs antidote &amp; administer NAC as soon as possible</li>
<li>Supportive treatment</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Critical Signs
        <ul>
<li>Hepatic encephalopathy, fulminant liver failure,</li>
<li>High Transaminase elevation (ALT or SLT) &gt; 1000.</li>
<li>Acute kidney failure, Severe acidosis, bleeding disorders, Coma</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Mortality risk factor
        <ul>
<li>Concurrent poisoning with other substances impacting hepatic metabolism</li>
<li>A psychiatric illness or history of suicide attempts</li>
<li>Regular ingestion of large amounts of alcohol; chronic malnutrition</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Outpatient Management
        <ul>
<li>Behavioral health evaluation for intentional ingestions</li>
<li>Consider hospitalization for toxic ingestions with vital instability and/or laboratory abnormalities (liver function tests).</li>
<li>Consider transfer to a psychiatric facility for intentional ingestions when medically stable.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
</div>

<div><p>4. First-line treatment</p><p>Stabilization of A.B.C is the first priority.</p><p>NAC (N-acetylcysteine) is paracetamol antidote. For severe form of paracetamol poisoning (transaminase levels &gt;1,000 mg/L, severe acidosis, coma/hypotension, or renal failure), additional measure like Hemodialysis, or ECMO is needed. Some patients may need liver transplant to survive.</p><p>A. Gastric decontamination:</p><p>Ipecac and gastric lavage are no longer recommended for routine use at home or in health care facilities.</p><p>Adequate GI decontamination consists of the early administration (&lt; 4h) of active charcoal orally or through a nasogastric tube. More aggressive forms of decontamination, such as gastric lavage or whole-bowel irrigation, are unnecessary because of the rapid GI absorption of paracetamol. Patients who arrived later than 4h, and patients whose airway was not well controlled are not the candidate for active charcoal administration.</p><p>B. Active charcoal:</p><p>Single dose activated charcoal (1 g/kg PO) may be effective if given within 1 to 4 hours of ingestion. Never delay oral NAC for activated charcoal.</p><p>C. Enhanced elimination: no indication</p><p>D. Antidote treatment</p><p>a. <u>N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC)</u></p><p>N-acetyl-cysteine (NAC), detoxify acetaminophen metabolites and replenish glutathione stored in the liver. NAC administration may reduce mortality from 5% to 0.7%. Give NAC when acetaminophen plasma levels measured ≥4 hours after ingestion are at the “treatment line” or higher on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram. In most cases, liver enzymes will be elevated only after 24h.</p><p>Empirically start NAC within 8 hours for suspect case or even while awaiting lab results. It may be effective up to ≥36 hours after ingestion.</p><p>NAC may be given PO or IV, depending on situation and availability. IV NAC has been shown to decrease the length of hospitalization compared to PO NAC.</p><p>Begin with a 200 mg/kg IV dose over 4 hours followed by a 100 mg/kg IV dose over 16 hours. A total of 300 mg/kg IV NAC over a 20-hour period.</p><p>Oral route: oral loading dose of 140 mg/kg and then 70 mg/kg q4h for 17 additional doses (72-hour regimen).</p><p>b. <u>NAC precautions:</u></p><p>Consider a nasogastric tube, if nausea, vomiting with Oral route. Metoclopramide, 1 to 2 mg/kg IV, or ondansetron, 0.15 mg/kg IV may be effective.</p></div>

<!-- PAGE 126 -->

<div><p>IV NAC may cause anaphylactoid reactions, (3–6%) including rash, bronchospasm, pruritus, angioedema, tachycardia, or hypotension. Reactions usually occur with the loading dose. To prevent this, slow or temporarily stop the infusion; may concurrently treat with antihistamines.</p><p><b>E. Second Line</b></p><p>In massive ingestions (levels &gt;1,000 mg/L, severe acidosis, coma/hypotension) or when severe renal failure is present, hemodialysis may improve survival.</p><p>Supportive treatment</p><p><b>5. Treatment adjustment</b></p><p>Metoclopramide, 1 to 2 mg/kg IV, or ondansetron, 0.15 mg/kg IV for nausea or vomiting.</p><p>IV fluids are generally provided for hydration purposes.</p><p>E.g., Nuclear® 600mg tab; patient 60kg, give 14 tab dissolved in water, drink or via NG tube, then 7 tab every 4h for additional 17 doses. Mucomyst® oral come with 200mg packet. Injectable Acetyl cysteine usually available as 6g/30ml solution (200mg/ml).</p><p><b>6. Algorithm (see Graphic 3)</b></p><p><b>VIII. SPECIAL CASE</b></p><ol><li><b>Geriatric Considerations</b><p>There is an increased risk of hepatic damage in frail, elderly patients due to decreased hepatic metabolism and co-ingestion of other hepatotoxic medications. Keep dose of acetaminophen ≤3,000 mg/day in seniors and in patients with liver disease and/or alcohol abuse disorders.</p></li><li><b>Pediatric Considerations</b><p>Hepatic damage after ingestion of toxic acetaminophen doses can be less severe in young children, potentially because they have more stores of glutathione.</p></li><li><b>Pregnancy Considerations</b><p>There is an increased incidence of spontaneous abortion in pregnant patients with acetaminophen poisoning, especially with overdose at an early gestational age. Abortion incidence and possible fetal death is increased if N-acetylcysteine (NAC) treatment is delayed. IV NAC is generally preferred in pregnancy due to greater bioavailability.</p></li></ol></div>

<!-- PAGE 127 -->

<div style="text-align: center;"><b>TREATMENT GUIDELINES FOR PARACETAMOL INGESTION</b></div><div style="text-align: center;"><table border="1" style="width: 100%; text-align: center;"><tbody><tr><td colspan="3"><b>Paracetamol ingestion</b></td></tr><tr><td>&lt;4h from ingestion</td><td>4 – 24h from ingestion</td><td>Unknown or &gt; 24h from ingestion</td></tr><tr><td>Consider GI decontamination<br/>Send &gt; 4h APAP level</td><td></td><td>Consider GI decontamination for unknown ingestion<br/>Sent APAP levels<br/>Sent transaminase, PT<br/>Give 1<sup>st</sup> dose NAC</td></tr><tr><td>Level available &lt;8h<br/>Plot on nomogram</td><td>Level not available until &gt; 8h<br/>Give 1<sup>st</sup> dose NAC (within 8h)</td><td>APAP &gt; 10 microg/ml or transaminase increased</td></tr><tr><td>Toxic: NAC Rx</td><td>Not toxic: symptomatic Rx</td><td>Yes:<br/>Continue NAC<br/>If<br/>pH &lt;7.3<br/>PT &gt; 100<br/>Cr &gt; 3.3<br/>Altered mental status<br/>Refer to liver transplant unit</td></tr><tr><td></td><td></td><td>No:<br/>Supportive Rx</td></tr></tbody></table></div><div style="text-align: center;">Rx: treatment; PT: prothrombin time;<br/>NAC: N-acetylcysteine; APAP: paracetamol</div><div style="text-align: center;">Graphic_3_Guideline for paracetamol ingestion;<br/>(Adapted from Tintinalli, Emergency Medicine. <h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3><p>Complete recovery with early therapy (with NAC) is possible and more likely in stage 4 of toxicity. 10% of adult patients with severe liver complications develop necrosis, hepatic encephalopathy, or require transplant. Hepatic failure is rare in children &lt;6 years of age.</p><h3>X. COMPLICATION</h3><p>Recovery after acute poisoning is complete, and sequelae are rare.</p><h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3><p>In the situation where plasmatic paracetamol level measurement is not available, consider administer NAC early, in the first 8h, based on history and suspect toxic dose.</p><ul><li>10g in adult, as single dose or in 24h, or &gt; 6g per day for 2 consecutive days.</li><li>For children &lt; 6y, ingestion of ≥ 200 milligrams/kg as a single ingestion or over an 8-hour period, or of 150 milligrams/kg per 24-hour period for the preceding 48 hours)</li><li>For people with liver disease (cirrhosis) the maximum dose is lower may be 2-3g/24 depend on the severity of liver disease.</li></ul><p>Outpatient management is adequate for nontoxic accidental ingestions. Transaminase elevation usually occurred from day 2, repeat measurement is necessary to follow up. The elevation of liver enzymes seen on the first few hours after paracetamol ingestion may indicate an anterior liver problem than the paracetamol-acquired one but, in patient with history liver disorders, standard dose of paracetamol can be toxic also. Educate parents/caregivers during well-child visits regarding appropriate OTC dosing and medication storage. Provide anticipatory guidance for caregivers, family, and cohabitants of potentially suicidal patients.</p><h3>XII. REFERENCES</h3><ol><li>Rachel S. Wightman, Lewis S. Nelson, 2020. Acetaminophen. in: Judith E. Tintinalli, Editor-in-Chief Emergency Medicine. A comprehensive Study Guide, 9th edition, Mc Graw Hill; p. 1252-8</li><li>Mark B. Stephens, Grant M. Reed, (2023), Acetaminophen poisoning. In: Frank J. <h1>METHAMPHETAMINES POISONING</h1><p>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya</p><h2>I. AMPHETAMINES &amp; METHAMPHETAMINES</h2><p>Amphetamines were synthesized in 1887 (by Lazăr Edeleanu, a Romanian scientist who was working in Germany), and in 1932, they were marketed medicinally in an inhaler form as a bronchodilator. Methamphetamines (N-methyl amphetamine) were first synthesized in 1883 (Nagai Nagayoshi, a Japanese scientist).</p><p>The crystallized form of methamphetamine was first synthesized in 1919 by scientist Akira Ogata. The use of methamphetamine to enhance physical and intellectual performance began in the 1930s.</p><p>Amphetamines may be used medically in “attention deficit hyperactivity disorders” (ADHD), and narcolepsy. Some derivatives were used as weight-loss treatment. Nowadays, amphetamines have limited therapeutic roles but are widely used as drugs of abuse. Methamphetamines is purely produced as illicit drugs.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>The use of methamphetamine and amphetamine has increased rapidly throughout the world, with more than 34 million users worldwide. East and Southeast Asia and North America remain the two main subregions for methamphetamine trafficking worldwide.</p><p>During the first half of the 2023, Cambodia authorities had arrested 9034 drugs-related suspects. 52% were drug traffickers, manufacturers, possessors, and transporters. A total of 993 kg of illicit drugs, 9kg of dry marijuana and some 326kg of chemical substances used for drug manufacturing were also confiscated. The seized drugs included heroin, ecstasy, cocaine, crystal methamphetamine, methamphetamine pills, cathinone and ketamine, among others*.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><p>Methamphetamines is an illicit street drug with no medical usage. People may expose to it by -smoking, - swallowing, - snorting, - injecting (s/c, IM, IV)- intra rectal, - intravaginal. Methamphetamines enters the brain quicker than other amphetamine drugs, leading to quick and intense effects. When it is used, a chemical, dopamine, is released in the brain, bringing about a sense of well-being. This high is addictive and causes people to crave the drug repeatedly in order to achieve it.</p><p>Physiological adaptation occurs through receptor or coupling down-regulation; this tolerance and an accompanying psychological tolerance (need more and more drug to obtain the same effects) can lead to escalating use of the drug and increased toxicity. Some people may expose by misused amphetamine derivatives as weight-loss medicine. Yama, Yaba, ice (crystal meth.); MDMA (3-4 methylenedioxymethamphetamine, “ecstasy” or “molly”) are common name found in Cambodia.</p>

<!-- PAGE 130 -->

<h4>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4>
<p>Methamphetamine is an indirect sympathomimetic, it increased arousal and decreased fatigue. On cardiovascular system it induced, tachycardia, dysrhythmias, hypertension and/or coronary vasospasm (sympathomimetic toxidrome). Other central effects: movement disorders, schizophrenia, and euphoria, hallucinogenic and anorexic.</p>

<h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<h5>1. Clinic</h5>
<p>Clinicians should consider the diagnosis of methamphetamine intoxication in any diaphoretic patient with hypertension, tachycardia, severe agitation, and psychosis.</p>
<p>Acutely intoxicated patients may become extremely agitated and pose a danger to themselves, other patients, and medical staff. Other symptoms include headache, hyperactivity, toxic psychosis, coma, focal neurologic deficits, or seizures. Some abusers develop stereotyped, compulsive behavior such as cleaning or buttoning shirts.</p>
<p>Psychosis from amphetamines can present as paranoid delusions and perceptual disturbances; these may persist long after the drug has been stopped and can result in homicidal or self-destructive behavior.</p>
<h5>2. Investigation</h5>
<p>Many patients who are admitted users of methamphetamine but are clinically well with normal vital signs do not need any lab testing. However, other methamphetamine users with moderate to severe intoxication can develop several dangerous manifestations and complications. The following tests should be obtained:</p>
<ul>
<li>Basic serum electrolytes (i.e., sodium, chloride, potassium, bicarbonate)</li>
<li>Serum lactate</li>
<li>Creatine phosphokinase (CPK)</li>
<li>Aminotransferases (ALT, AST)</li>
<li>Clotting times (prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time)</li>
<li>Renal function studies (creatinine, BUN)</li>
<li>Urinalysis</li>
</ul>
<h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<p>Other substances overdoses that produce sympathomimetic toxidromes: Cocaine, cathinone, Ecstasy, amphetamine; the clinical presentation of these different agents is largely indistinguishable, especially initially. The treatment of sympathomimetic intoxication is generally the same across different agents.</p>
<p>Medical conditions in which the present symptoms may be of concerned: Chronic stress, anxiety disorders, post-traumatic-stress- disorders (PTSD), hyperthyroidism, heart disease.</p>

<!-- PAGE 131 -->

<h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2>
<ol>
<li>Objective of management
<ul>
<li>Reduce the toxic effects of the drugs.</li>
<li>Reduce morbidity.</li>
<li>Prevent complications.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Critical Signs
<p>hypertension, tachycardia, severely agitated delirium, hyperthermia, metabolic acidosis, seizures and coma.</p>
</li>
<li>Mortality risk factors
<p>Prognostic factors for mortality include:</p>
<ul>
<li>coma,</li>
<li>shock,</li>
<li>body temperature &gt;39°C,</li>
<li>acute renal failure,</li>
<li>metabolic acidosis,</li>
<li>hyperkalemia (K 5.6 to 8.5 mmol/L)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Outpatient management
<p>Methamphetamines overdose without disturbance of vital signs, without critical signs can be managed supportively at home.</p>
</li>
<li>First line treatment
<p>Follow the standard protocol of “General Management of Poisoned Patients”.</p>
<ul>
<li>Decontamination
<p>Gastrointestinal decontamination — Activated charcoal is rarely indicated due to the route of methamphetamine administration (e.g., intranasal, inhalation, injection, intravaginal). If methamphetamine has been ingested, the greatest benefit of activated charcoal occurs if administered within 1 to 2 hours of ingestion. In case of body packing or stuffing, indication may be a whole bowel irrigation, or immediate laparotomy to prevent bowel ischemia from local vasoconstriction.</p>
</li>
<li>Enhanced elimination—Urine acidification, formerly used to promote the elimination of methamphetamine, is no longer recommended. The administration of acidic intravenous fluids may exacerbate life-threatening metabolic acidosis</li>
<li>Antidote: not existed</li>
<li>Supportive treatment: is the main treatment
<ul>
<li><b>Hyperthermia.</b> Antipyretics have no role in the management of acute methamphetamine intoxication. Aggressive sedation, neuromuscular paralysis, and fluid resuscitation are used to control methamphetamine-induced hyperthermia; these measures can be supplemented with external cooling blankets or evaporative cooling techniques. Paralyzed patients at risk for seizures should receive continuous bedside electroencephalography.</li>
<li><b>Rhabdomyolysis:</b> (muscle pain or weakness, dark red or brown urine, abdominal pain) Aggressive IV hydration is the primary treatment for rhabdomyolysis. One method is rapid correction of the fluid deficit with IV</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 132 -->

<div>
<p>crystalloids followed by infusion of 4 mL/kg/h, with the goal of maintaining a minimum urine output of 3 to 4 mL/h (1-2ml/kg/h). Another method is a goal of 200 to 300 mL of urine output each hour. Any isotonic fluids can be used (attention: patient may have hyperkaliemia).</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Seizures</b> are initially treated with benzodiazepines, status epilepticus requires aggressive treatment, propofol or thiopental may be used. Attention of blood pressure falling and / or respiratory depression that necessitate supportive ventilation. Obtain a head CT to identify intracranial pathology as the cause of seizures. Phenytoin should be avoided.</li>
<li><b>Agitation:</b> Lorazepam, 2 milligrams IV, or diazepam 5 milligrams, midazolam 2.5mg IV, can be administered and titrated with repeated doses after 8-10min. May start by double the dose and give IM, then about 10min later, give IV dose (up to 30-50mg with appropriate airway monitoring). If it was not effective enough, use antipsychotics: Haloperidol (5-10mg IM / IV), droperidol or chlorpromazine. Ziprasidone 10mg IM (check ECG for long QT first). Physical restraints should be avoided if possible. Patients who struggle against physical restraints undergo isometric muscle contractions that can be associated with lactic acidosis, hyperthermia, sudden cardiac collapse, and death.</li>
<li><b>Chest pain:</b> Cocaine users with suspected acute coronary syndrome are managed with aspirin and nitroglycerin and IV Diltiazem 5-20mg IV if ST-segment elevation or depression was observed.</li>
<li><b>Dysrhythmia:</b> may response to sedation, cooling and IV fluid rehydration; other anti-dysrhythmia used is a calcium channel blocker, blood alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate (to pH 7.50-7.55), and Lidocaine. If beta-blocker is necessary, use labetalol (alfa and beta-adrenergic antagonist).</li>
<li><b>Hypertension:</b> Severe hypertension not response to sedation should be treated with phentolamine (initial dose, 2.5 to 5.0 mg IV), or nitroglycerine, nicardipine, or sodium nitroprusside, but do not use beta blockers except labetalol.</li>
</ul>
<h2>6. Treatment adjustment</h2>
<p><b>ACUTE WITHDRAWAL</b> After heavy or prolonged use, abrupt discontinuation of methamphetamine can cause a withdrawal syndrome. Symptoms may develop within hours, typically peak within 1 to 2 days, and most often decrease within two weeks. Symptoms of withdrawal are strongest during the first 48 hours, but milder symptoms can last up to 2 weeks.</p>
<p>During the acute withdrawal phase ("the crash"), patients may have dysphoria, anhedonia, fatigue, increased sleep, vivid dreams, insomnia, agitation, anxiety, drug craving, and increased appetite.</p>
<p>A subacute withdrawal phase: may persist for up to three weeks with insomnia, hypersomnia, appetite changes, depression, and possibly suicidal thoughts.</p>
<p><b>Treatments:</b> There is no specific methamphetamine withdrawal medication approved. The combinations of the following drugs, have been used with variable efficacy: benzodiazepines, antidepressants, antipsychotics, riluzole, naltrexone,</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 133 -->

<div>
<p>and behavioral therapy. Some studies found that injectable naltrexone plus oral bupropion was safe and effective.</p>
<h2>7. Algorithm</h2>
<p><b>Graphic-1_ management of methamphetamines poisoning</b></p>
<p>Initial emergent control of psychomotor agitation and hyperthermia is of the highest priority to limit life-threatening sequelae.</p>
<p>Aggressive supportive care with supplemental oxygen, sedation, fluid administration, prevention and treatment of hyperthermia, and close monitoring while addressing the specific myriad complications that can occur.</p>
<img alt="Flowchart titled 'Methamphetamines poisoning'. The initial step is 'Venous access &amp; fluid, give oxygen support'. This leads to four potential complications: Rhabdomyolysis (muscle pain, weakness, brown urine, abdominal pain), Agitation, Hypertension, and Hyperthermia. Each complication is followed by 'Initial ttt' (initial treatment). Rhabdomyolysis leads to 'Fluid resuscitation for hypovolemia. Use RL bolus 1.5-2L in 60min then continue with 4ml/kg/h to get urine 1-2ml/kg/h (Attention to kelemia and heart overload)'. If failed, it leads to '(oliguria, pulmonary edema, hyperkalemia, severe acidosis)' which leads to 'Hemodialysis'. Agitation, Hypertension, and Hyperthermia all lead to 'Initial ttt' which results in 'Diazepam 5mg IV, or start 10mg IM, then IV repeat every 8-10min titrate to sedation or Lorazepam 4mg or Midazolam 2.5mg IV repeat every 8-10min (if seizures may add propofol or thiopental. Phenytoin had minim effects.)'. If this fails, three paths are taken: Haloperidol IM/IV, Droperidol, chlorpromazine, Ziprasidone IM; Nicardipine, Phentolamine, Nitroprusside (use betablocker cautiously) Labetalol; and (No antipyretic) Evaporative cooling, Cooling blanket. If any of these fail, they lead to 'Myorelaxant + intubated + ventilated (no succinyl choline)'. Additional failure conditions are noted: Haloperidol path failure leads to '(Psychomotor agitation, danger to self and others)'; Nicardipine path failure leads to '(End organ damage + Hyperthermia)'; and Cooling blanket path failure leads to '&gt; 38.3°C'."/>
<h2>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h2>
<p><b>Pregnancy and lactation</b> — In utero exposure to methamphetamine is associated with low birth weight and decreased head circumference, among several abnormalities, and may produce withdrawal symptoms in the perinatal period. Amphetamines, including methamphetamine, are excreted into breast milk.</p>
<p><b>Pediatric</b> Although sympathomimetic and neuropsychiatric manifestations of methamphetamine exposure should be similar in a pediatric patient, inadvertent exposure may be difficult to diagnose. The most frequent signs and symptoms noted in pediatric patients exposed to methamphetamine are nonspecific.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 134 -->

<div><p>Asymptomatic children taken from clandestine production sites may also have been exposed to methamphetamine and other chemicals (eg, ephedrine) used to synthesize methamphetamine. These children are particularly vulnerable to child abuse, neglect, serious injury, exposure to toxic chemicals, and malnutrition. The hypersexuality and drug-seeking behaviors of adult methamphetamine users may lead to sexual abuse of such children, or they may be prostituted for money or drugs.</p><h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3><p>Methamphetamine user rapidly became addicted. Addicted people show the “methamphetamine-use disorders” symptoms:</p><ul><li>A compulsive use of the drug despite harmful consequences.</li><li>Taking larger amounts of meth or using it for a longer period than planned</li><li>Unsuccessful attempts to cut down or quit</li><li>Giving up activities due to meth use</li><li>Inability to keep up with responsibilities at home, work.</li></ul><p>The physiologic tolerance process makes the user use higher and higher dose to get the same effects, increase the risk of intoxication.</p><p>It is a chronic brain disease.</p><h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3><p>Long-term use of the drugs can lead to myonecrosis and dilated cardiomyopathy or myocardial infarction. Use of methamphetamine during pregnancy has been associated with intrauterine growth restriction and preterm birth. Incidental injuries from blunt and penetrating trauma are common.</p><p>Complications of methamphetamine use include (substance-induced disorders):</p><ul><li>Rhabdomyolysis</li><li>Acute kidney injury</li><li>Seizures</li><li>Stroke with permanent deficits</li><li>Coma</li><li>Acute coronary ischemia or infarction</li><li>Congestive heart failure (CHF)</li><li>Ventricular arrhythmias</li><li>Psychosis (paranoid delusion, may be dangerous to surrounding)</li><li>Addiction (substance-use disorders)</li><li>Death</li><li>HIV and viral hepatitis</li><li>Periodontal disease</li><li>Skin infections</li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 135 -->

<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<p>Early to have consultation (better, is in the Emergency room, when the vital signs were stable) with psychiatric specialist for continue the treatment. Be aware that Methamphetamine addiction is notoriously difficult to treat successfully.</p>

<h1>ORGANOPHOSPHATE AND CARBAMATE INSECTICIDES POISONING</h1><p>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. NGETH Sopanha</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>Organophosphate insecticides are a class of chemical compounds that are derived from phosphoric acid. They work by inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, which is responsible for breaking down the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. This leads to a buildup of acetylcholine in the nervous system, which can cause a variety of symptoms, including muscle weakness, tremors, convulsions, and even death.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>There are approximately 385 million cases of acute pesticide poisoning each year globally, resulting in around 11,000 deaths. A significant proportion of these cases are due to intentional self-poisoning, particularly in low- and middle-income countries<sup>1</sup>.</p><p>Agricultural workers and individuals in areas with heavy pesticide use are at higher risk of accidental poisoning.</p><p>Older pesticides like DDT and lindane, though banned in many developed countries, are still in use in some developing regions, contributing to ongoing health risks</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><p>In Cambodia, Organophosphates is one group of chemical compounds commonly use as insecticides among other group like pyrazole, thiazole, neonicotinoid, pyrethroids, organochlorines. Organophosphate can be further categorized into several subgroups based on their chemical structure and mode of action:</p><ul><li><b>Phosphates</b>: These include compounds like malathion and parathion, which are commonly used in agriculture</li><li><b>Phosphorothioates</b>: ex. diazinon and chlorpyrifos, (commonly use in Cambodia)</li><li><b>Thiophosphates</b>: phosmet, which is used in both agricultural and residential settings</li><li><b>Dithiophosphates</b>: dicrotophos.</li></ul>
