<p>Carbamate insecticide is another chemical group classified into two main subgroups based on their chemical structure:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Phenolic Carbamates:</b> ex. Carbaryl, pirimicarb, Propoxur, Bendiocarb</li>
<li><b>Oxime Carbamates:</b> Examples of this subgroup include aldicarb and methomyl,</li>
</ul>
<p>The most use carbamate in Cambodia is Propoxur, and Bendiocarb, commonly used to control pests like cockroaches, flies, mosquitoes, and lawn insects.</p>
<h4>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h4>
<h5>Organophosphates (OPs)</h5>
<ul>
<li>Primary toxic mechanism is inactivating acetylcholinesterase (AChE)</li>
<li>OPs cause alkyl phosphorylation of the AChE enzyme. The phosphorylated AChE is inactive. AChE is thereby unable to degrade and hydrolyze acetylcholine into choline and acetic acid. Resulting accumulation of acetylcholine at the synaptic junction throughout the nervous system causes overstimulation of receptors.</li>
<li>Potential locations where cholinergic synaptic transmission can be paralyzed—
        <ul>
<li>Central nervous system</li>
<li>Autonomic ganglia</li>
<li>Parasympathetic nerve endings</li>
<li>Some sympathetic nerve endings (such as sweat glands)</li>
<li>Somatic nerves</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Direct myocardial injury can occur during the acute, early phase in severe OP poisoning</li>
</ul>
<h5>Carbamates</h5>
<ul>
<li>When a carbamate binds to AChE the enzyme undergoes an allosteric change which prevents breakdown of acetylcholine. Carbamates undergo carbamylation of the serine hydroxyl group. The carbamylated AChE is inactive. AChE activity can be spontaneously regenerated.</li>
<li>Clinical signs of toxicity often occur more rapidly than Ops</li>
</ul>
<p>Organophosphates (OPs) and carbamates are highly lipophilic, and therefore readily absorbed across the skin, respiratory, and gastrointestinal mucosa.</p>
<p>Onset and severity of symptoms depends on the specific compound, amount, route of exposure, and rate of metabolic degradation. Symptoms are proportional to the decrease in cholinesterase activity</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 138 -->

<h3>V. DIAGNOSIS (ACUTE POISONING)</h3>
<ul>
<li><b>History</b>
<ul>
<li>Substance(s) involved or suspected (including specific product name when available)</li>
<li>Timing, duration, and mode of exposure (such as inhalation, ingestion, or cutaneous)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Classic symptoms of cholinergic toxicity</b>
<p><b>Muscarinic effects</b></p>
<ul>
<li>SLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Diarrhea, Gastrointestinal upset, Emesis (literature meaning: Sludge = soft, wet soil, muddy deposit)</li>
<li>“3 Killer Bees” Bradycardia, Bronchospasm, Bronchorrhea,</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Nicotinic effects</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Nausea, vomiting, increased salivation, muscle cramping and weakness, headache, dizziness</li>
<li>Can also produce opposing symptoms to muscarinic effects, including mydriasis, tachycardia, and hypertension</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Central nervous system</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Headache, insomnia, giddiness, confusion, dizziness, ataxia, emotional lability, slurred speech, drowsiness, seizures, unconsciousness, coma</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Laboratory</b>
<ul>
<li>RBC and plasma cholinesterase levels to confirm diagnosis:
        <ul>
<li>RBC (true) cholinesterase level is best for synaptic inhibition</li>
<li>Plasma (pseudo)cholinesterase level not as reliable but more timely:
                <ul>
<li>These are markers for poisoning</li>
<li>Depending on the agent and the patient, these levels may vary</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Cholinesterase levels:
                <ul>
<li>Latent exposure: &gt;50% of normal value</li>
<li>Mild exposure: 20–50% of normal value</li>
<li>Moderate exposure: 10–20% of normal value</li>
<li>Severe exposure: &lt;10% of normal value</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Do not wait for cholinesterase results before administering treatment</li>
<li>CBC, electrolytes, glucose, BUN, creatinine</li>
<li>ABG when respiratory symptoms are present</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Imaging</b>
<ul>
<li>CXR if respiratory difficulty is present or suspect pulmonary edema:
        <ul>
<li>Pneumonitis from hydrocarbon aspiration</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>ECG
        <ul>
<li>Dysrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, torsades de pointes, QT prolongation)</li>
<li>Bradycardia</li>
<li>Heart block</li>
<li>ST-T-wave abnormalities</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>CT scan of head for altered mental status when diagnosis is uncertain</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Definitive diagnosis:</b> There is no specific assay readily available to screen for individual agents.</p>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 139 -->

<div><p>Suspecting the diagnosis:</p><ul><li>History of exposure to/contact with a cholinergic agent</li><li>Clinical signs and symptoms of cholinergic toxicity</li><li>Decreased red blood cell cholinesterase activity</li><li>Symptom improvement following atropine or oxime administration</li></ul><h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4><ul><li>Mild to moderate exposure:<ul><li>Gastroenteritis</li><li>Asthma</li><li>Venomous arthropod bite (black widow, scorpion)</li><li>Progressive peripheral neuropathy (Guillain–Barré syndrome)</li><li>Carbon monoxide</li></ul></li><li>Severe exposure:<ul><li>Narcotic overdose</li><li>Coma and miosis:<ul><li>PCP, meprobamate, phenothiazine, clonidine</li><li>Muscarinic-containing mushrooms – cholinergic crisis without nicotinic symptoms</li><li>Nicotine poisoning</li></ul></li></ul></li><li>Metabolic and infectious:<ul><li>Ketoacidosis, sepsis, meningitis, encephalitis</li><li>Hypoglycemia</li><li>Reye syndrome</li></ul></li><li>Neurologic:<ul><li>Cerebrovascular accident</li><li>Subdural or epidural hematoma</li><li>Postictal state</li></ul></li></ul><h4>VII. MANAGEMENT</h4><ol><li>Objectives<ul><li>Maintain stability of vital signs</li><li>Neutralize the toxic effects (on muscarinic, nicotinic and central receptors)</li><li>Prevent or minimize the treatment-related disorders</li><li>Prevent the recurrence intoxication</li></ul></li><li>Critical signs<ul><li>Shock, seizures or coma, difficult breathing or respiratory failure</li></ul></li><li>Mortality risk factors<ul><li>Advanced age</li><li>OP poisoning: elevated lactate, low blood pH, and poor lactate clearance</li><li>Hypoglycemia</li><li>The insecticide of group Ia (Parathion, Methyl parathion, Aldicarb, Metamidophos)</li><li>Delay from accident to emergency care</li></ul></li></ol></div>

<!-- PAGE 140 -->

<h4>4. Outpatient management</h4>
<p>Pre-Hospital (if patient have normal vital signs, and cooperated)</p>
<ul>
<li>Decontamination is initial priority:
        <ul>
<li>Decontaminate, airway, breathing, circulation (DABC)</li>
<li>Remove all clothes (in spillover accident) and store as toxic waste (double bagged)</li>
<li>Protection of health care workers of utmost importance:
                <ul>
<li>Impenetrable gloves (neoprene, nitrile), gowns, eye protection</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Decontaminate skin with soap and water:</li>
<li>Shower or gentle scrubbing ideal if done before entrance into the ED</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Maintain airway and oxygenate</li>
<li>IV access and place on cardiac monitor</li>
</ul>
<h4>5. First line treatment</h4>
<p>Initial Stabilization/Therapy</p>
<ul>
<li>Decontaminate and ABCs:
        <ul>
<li>Decontamination and protection of staff</li>
<li>Maintain airway and oxygenate</li>
<li>For unstable airway, intubate, and ventilate (caution: succinylcholine may produce a long myorelaxant time)</li>
<li>IV access with D5W 0.9% NS</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Altered mental status: Administer thiamine, glucose, or naloxone if suspect alcoholic overdose, hypoglycemia or overdose opioids respectively.</li>
</ul>
<p>ED Treatment/Procedures</p>
<h4>Atropine:</h4>
<ul>
<li>Blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptor sites</li>
<li>No effect on nicotinic receptors</li>
<li>Onset of action is 1–4 min, peaks at 8 min</li>
<li>Goal of therapy/end point:
        <ul>
<li>Drying secretions of tracheobronchial tree</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Administer test dose 1–2 mg IV/IM:
        <ul>
<li>No clinical response: Double dose q5min until muscarinic findings subside</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Dose: 1–4 mg IV q5min (peds: 0.05–0.2 mg/kg)</li>
<li>Common pitfalls in therapy:</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 141 -->

<ul><li>Not giving enough atropine</li><li>Using pupillary findings (mydriasis) as end point of treatment</li><li>Dilated pupils or tachycardia are not contraindications to atropine</li></ul><p><b>Pralidoxime (2-PAM):</b></p><ul><li>Regenerates cholinesterase by reversing the phosphorylation of the enzyme</li><li>Synergistic with atropine – muscarinic signs/symptoms will start to resolve in 10–40 min</li><li>1–2 g (peds: 25–50 mg/kg) dissolved in 0.9% NS over 30 min IV; repeat in 1 hr if necessary, then q6h as needed:<ul><li>Some propose continuous infusion (500 mg/hr) for serum concentration of 4 mg/L</li></ul></li><li>Side effects: Neuromuscular blockade with rapid infusion, respiratory arrest, HTN, nausea/vomiting, dizziness, blurred vision</li><li>End point is resolution of muscle weakness and fasciculations</li><li>Effective before enzyme aging occurs (permanent inactivation of cholinesterase)</li><li>Onset of aging varies among products</li><li>No restriction to its use even if 24–48 hr have passed</li></ul><p><b>Supportive care:</b></p><ul><li>Dermal decontamination: Remove clothes and flush skin with water</li><li>Gastric lavage (early presentation of severe ingestion):<ul><li>Gastric emptying with continuous suction via a nasogastric tube</li><li>Handle contents with care – avoid direct contact to prevent personal exposure</li></ul></li><li>Respiratory difficulty:<ul><li>Frequent oropharyngeal suction</li><li>Treat bronchospasm with atropine, not bronchodilators</li><li>Tachycardia may result from hypoxia (pulmonary secretions and bronchospasm)</li><li>Atropine will dry secretions and paradoxically lower the heart rate</li><li>Intubate and ventilate if necessary</li><li>Avoid succinylcholine; may have prolonged duration as it is metabolized by cholinesterase</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>6. Treatment adjustment</b></p><ul><li>In case of carbamate intoxication, Pralidoxime was usually no need.</li><li>Treat hypovolemia (from gastrointestinal losses) with IV crystalloid</li><li>Treat vomiting with antiemetics such as ondansetron</li><li>Vasopressors: Can be used as an adjunct to treat hypotension</li><li>Diazepam recommended for seizure control. Phenitoine was not effective.</li><li>Prophylaxis with diazepam has been shown to decrease neurocognitive dysfunction after OP poisoning</li></ul>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<h4>Pediatric Considerations</h4>
<ul>
<li>Symptoms are difficult to differentiate in toddlers</li>
<li>Common symptoms: Miosis, salivation, and muscle weakness</li>
<li>Seizure activity in 25% of pediatric cases. Only 3% in adults</li>
</ul>
<h4>Pregnancy Consideration</h4>
<ul>
<li>Organophosphate poisoning during pregnancy can be particularly dangerous due to the potential for both maternal and fetal toxicity.</li>
<li>These toxic effects can be exacerbated in pregnant women due to physiological changes during pregnancy, such as increased cardiac output and decreased plasma cholinesterase levels. Additionally, there is concern that organophosphate exposure may have adverse effects on fetal development, including birth defects and neurodevelopmental problems.</li>
<li>The management of organophosphate poisoning in pregnant patients follows similar principles as in non-pregnant individuals.</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<p>Mortality rate from acute organophosphate (OP) poisoning varies between 10% and 20% and is generally due to respiratory failure.</p>
<h4>X. Complications</h4>
<ul>
<li>Pulmonary: aspiration pneumonitis/pneumonia, respiratory failure</li>
<li>Cardiovascular: arrhythmias, hypotension</li>
<li>Neurological: seizures, muscle fasciculations, paralysis</li>
<li>Delayed sequelae
        <ul>
<li>Intermediate syndrome
                <ul>
<li>Symptom onset typically 1-4 days after OP poisoning</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Delayed polyneuropathy—
                <ul>
<li>Referred to as organophosphate-induced delay peripheral neuropathy (OPIDN)</li>
<li>Onset 7-14 days after large exposures to OP</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Long-term effects</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li><b>Consult with psychologists</b> for mental disorders.</li>
</ul>
<p>Preventing accidental insecticide poisoning involves several essential measures:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Read Labels Carefully:</b> Always read and follow the instructions on the pesticide label. This includes proper application methods, protective equipment, and first aid measures.</li>
<li><b>Use Personal Protective Equipment (PPE):</b> Wear appropriate PPE such as gloves, masks, goggles, and long-sleeved clothing when handling or applying insecticides.</li>
<li><b>Store Safely:</b> Keep insecticides in their original containers, tightly sealed, and stored in a locked cabinet out of reach of children and pets</li>
<li><b>Avoid Mixing Chemicals:</b> Never mix insecticides with other chemicals, as this can create toxic reactions</li>
<li><b>Proper Disposal:</b> Dispose of empty pesticide containers and unused chemicals according to local regulations to prevent accidental exposure.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 144 -->

<ul><li><b>Ventilation:</b> Ensure good ventilation when using insecticides indoors to avoid inhaling harmful fumes.</li><li>In case of accidental exposure or suicidal encounter, <i>early contact with Emergency service</i>.</li></ul><h3>XII. <h1>METHANOL AND ETHYLENE GLYCOL INTOXICATION</h1><p>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth,<br/>Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak,<br/>Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna,<br/>Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. NGETH Sopanha</p><h2>I. INTRODUCTION</h2><p>Methanol is considered toxic alcohol, due to its metabolite, the formic acid. It is not intended for ingestion. Methanol poisoning typically occurs from ingestion of methanol-containing substances that may include denatured alcohol, homemade or illegally produced alcohol, or commercial products. More rarely methanol poisoning may be caused by inhalation or dermal absorption.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>Methanol poisoning outbreaks occur when illegally produced or homemade grain spirits are fortified with methanol due to its low cost. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), outbreaks of methanol poisoning have occurred in various countries, including Cambodia, Czech Republic, Ecuador, Estonia, India, Indonesia, Kenya, Libya, Nicaragua, Norway, Pakistan, Turkey, and Uganda. These outbreaks often result from methanol being added to these drinks, either accidentally or deliberately.</p><p>In Cambodia, methanol intoxication is a sporadic accident, from time to time the outbreaks of methanol poisoning have occurred with a few to many dozens of deaths and many more hospitalized. One of the largest outbreaks was in 2012 involving 49 deaths and 318 persons hospitalized. Many events happened after funeral ceremony in rural area when people often consume illegally produced alcohol.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><p>Common sources of methanol:</p><ul><li>Wood alcohol</li><li>Paint solvents</li><li>Windshield washer fluid</li><li>Inhalational abuse of carburetor cleaners</li><li>Fuel antifreeze solutions</li><li>Formalin (10-12% of it volume is methanol)</li><li>Gasoline (racing car)</li><li>Household cleaners</li><li>Sterno® cans (cooking fuel)</li><li>Moonshine</li><li>Photocopying fluid</li><li>Perfumes</li></ul><h2>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h2><p>Dose toxic</p><ul><li>lethal doses are not well-established and vary from person to person, generally estimated at 1-2 mL/kg of pure methanol. Doses as low as 0.1 mL/kg (6-10 mL in adults) have been reported to cause permanent blindness and death.</li></ul><p>Toxicodynamic</p>

<!-- PAGE 146 -->

<ul><li>Methanol has low toxicity on its own, but is metabolized into toxic products (formic acid)</li><li>First metabolized in liver by alcohol dehydrogenase to produce formaldehyde (slowly) which is then oxidized by aldehyde dehydrogenase to produce formic acid (1- to 2-minute half-life) and does not accumulate most formic acid dissociates into hydrogen cation and formate anion hydrogen cation reduces pH of body fluids, resulting in acidemia.</li><li>Formate accumulates and inhibits cellular functions by disrupting oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria and decreasing production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Decrease in ATP produces effects similar to hypoxia, although tissue oxygenation may be increased with reduced cellular oxygen uptake.</li><li>Formate is toxic to:<ul><li>central nervous system</li><li>basal ganglia and subcortical white matter in untreated patients.</li><li>retinal and optic nerves.<ul><li>Retinal dysfunction occurs at lower formic acid concentrations than optical neuropathy</li><li>Acidosis enhances toxicity by increasing diffusion of undissociated formic acid into cells, especially optic disc and retrolaminar section of optic nerve.</li></ul></li></ul></li><li>Estimated formate elimination half-life is 1-3 hours for low concentrations and 24 hours for high concentrations.</li><li>small amounts of methanol are excreted in urine and eliminated by lungs (due to high vapor pressure)</li></ul><h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4><h5>A. Clinic</h5><ul><li>Clinical presentation is characterized by early, latent, and delayed stages.<ul><li><i>Early stage</i> of methanol intoxication usually presents with similar symptoms as ethanol inebriation, including mild euphoria, drowsiness, gastric symptoms, sedation and central nervous system (CNS) depression, and faint alcoholic odor on breath.</li><li><i>Latent period</i> occurs after inebriation subsides and methanol is slowly metabolized to formic acid, lasting from 6-30 hours. Patients may be asymptomatic or have blurred vision during this period.</li><li><i>Delayed period</i> begins after significant amounts of methanol have been metabolized, formate accumulates, and acidosis worsens. Serious effects of methanol poisoning begin to present. Visual disturbances and central nervous system symptoms (such as seizures) predominate.</li></ul></li><li>Gastrointestinal symptoms may include hemorrhagic gastritis or pancreatitis.</li><li>Hyperpnea (Kussmaul respirations) may be present with severe metabolic acidosis.</li></ul><h5>B. Investigation</h5><ul><li>Confirmed ingestion of methanol-containing substances from patient or witness may facilitate diagnosis.</li><li>Positive serum methanol concentrations can offer definitive diagnosis, but methanol concentrations below limit of detection cannot rule out methanol poisoning. Co-ingestion of ethanol or other substances may affect methanol metabolism and serum methanol levels.</li><li>Routine toxicity evaluations are especially important in patients with incomplete or unknown histories.<ul><li>Measure arterial pH in all patients.</li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 147 -->

<ul><li>Severe metabolic acidosis with increased osmolar or anion gaps suggests methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning.</li><li>Arterial blood gases suggest methanol poisoning if metabolic acidosis is severe.</li><li>Low total carbon dioxide measurements may suggest metabolic acidosis.</li><li>Brain imaging indicated in patients presenting with altered mental status, seizures, coma, or focal neurological abnormalities. Computed tomography is often normal within the first 24 hours of exposure.</li><li>Nonenhanced head computed tomography findings in patients with severe methanol poisoning may include putamen hypodensity or caudate nucleus.</li><li>Calculate anion gap = (Na+) – (Cl– + HCO3–): Normal = 8–12</li><li>Determine serum osmol gap: Osmol gap = measured osmolality – calculated osmolarity</li><li>Calculated osmolarity = 2(Na+) + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8 + ethanol (in mg/dL)/4.6</li></ul><h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4><p>Few conditions other than methanol and ethylene glycol intoxication present with a profound metabolic acidosis (serum bicarbonate less than 8 mEq/L), and most of these conditions present in a characteristic fashion (e.g., status epilepticus, profound shock, ischemic bowel). Other causes of elevated serum osmolar gap or anion gap, including</p><ul><li>diabetic ketoacidosis</li><li>alcoholic ketoacidosis</li><li>multiple organ failure</li><li>chronic kidney failure</li><li>critical illness</li><li>spurious hyponatremia secondary to hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia</li><li>endogenous solutes (such as amino acids during end-stage organ failure)</li><li>exposure to some other substances.</li></ul><p>Methanol and Ethylene glycol poisoning have some similarity as cause of severe metabolic acidosis, neurologic symptoms. Ocular toxicity from methanol is more frequent than from Ethylene glycol. The antidote treatment is the same for the two: Fomepizole or ethanol. The difference is on the toxic metabolite that is formic acid from methanol, and Glycolic acid from ethylene glycol. The onset of symptom of ethylene glycol poisoning is sooner than methanol, and ethylene glycol causes acute renal failure (from calcium depot), more frequent than methanol poisoning. Clinical poisoning of Ethyle glycol has historically been divided into three stages, although timing may vary, and stages may overlap:</p><ul><li>The first or “neurologic” stage typically begins 30 minutes to 12 hours after ingestion due to the intoxicating effects of the ethylene glycol parent compound</li><li>The second or “cardiopulmonary” stage begins 12 to 24 hours after ingestion. Arrhythmia, multiorgan dysfunction, hypocalcemia. Most deaths occur during this stage.</li><li>The third or “renal” stage is often delayed 24 to 72 hours after ingestion. Renal failure, delay neuropathy</li></ul><h4>VII. MANAGEMENT</h4><ol><li>Objectives<ul><li>Block or delay methanol and ethylene glycol metabolism,</li><li>Treat the toxic effects of formic acid glycolic acid</li><li>Facilitate the elimination of formic acid and methanol</li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 148 -->

<ul><li>Prevent and early treatment of acute kidney injury (ethylene glycol)</li></ul><ol><li>Critical signs<ul><li>Rapid and deep respiration (Kussmaul respiration)</li><li>Blurred vision</li><li>seizures</li></ul></li><li>Mortality risk factors<ul><li>Severe metabolic acidosis, pH &lt; 7.2</li><li>Coma</li><li>Acute kidney failure</li><li>High concentration of methanol</li></ul></li><li>Out-patient treatment<ul><li>Transport all possibly ingested substances</li><li>Dermal decontamination of a methanol spill by clothing removal, irrigation with soap and water</li><li>Monitor airway and CNS depression</li></ul></li><li>First line treatment<ul><li><b>Initial Stabilization/Therapy</b></li></ul></li></ol><p>Airway, breathing, and circulation (ABCs)<br/>Dextrose, naloxone, and thiamine for altered mental status and known hypoglycemia, suspect opioids overdose or alcoholism respectively.</p><p>Prevent further methanol absorption:</p><ul><li>Gastric lavage with nasogastric tube: no indication</li><li>Activated charcoal: may be use for co-ingestants.</li></ul><ul><li><b>Ed Treatment/Procedures</b><ul><li>Prevent methanol conversion to toxic metabolites with fomepizole (preferable) or ethanol infusion</li><li>Fomepizole (4-MP, Antizol®):<ul><li>Competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase</li><li>Indications:<ul><li>Intentional methanol ingestion OR</li><li>Accidental methanol ingestion of more than a sip OR</li><li>Altered mental status or visual symptoms associated with unexplained osmol gap &gt;10 mmol/L and/or elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis, bicarbonate &lt;20 mmol/L, serum pH &lt;7.3</li></ul></li><li>Initiate before serum methanol level returns if intentional ingestion or more than a sip OR if serum methanol concentration is &gt;20 mg/dL<ul><li>Fomepizole Loading dose: 15 mg/kg slow infusion over 30 min</li><li>Maintenance dose: 10 mg/kg q12h for 4 doses, then 15 mg/kg q12h until methanol levels reduced &lt;20 mg/dL</li><li>Dosing related to hemodialysis:<ul><li>Do not administer dose at beginning of dialysis if last dose was &lt;6 hr previously</li><li>Administer next dose if last dose was &gt;6 hr previously</li><li>Dose q4h during dialysis</li><li>If time between last dose and end of dialysis was &lt;1 hr from last dose, do not administer new dose</li><li>If time between last dose and end of dialysis was 1–3 hr from last dose, administer 1/2 of next scheduled dose</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul></li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 149 -->

<ul><li>If time between last dose and end of dialysis was &gt;3 hr from last dose, administer next scheduled dose</li><li>Continue until methanol level is &lt;20 mg/dL</li><li>Advantages:<ul><li>No need for continuous infusion</li><li>No inebriation/CNS depression</li><li>Ease of dosing</li><li>No hypoglycemia, no hyponatremia, no hyperosmolality</li><li>No checking serum concentrations</li><li>Reduced nursing care and monitoring</li><li>Occult methanol exposure can often be ruled out before 2nd dose is needed</li></ul></li><li>Disadvantages:<ul><li>Blurry vision</li><li>Transient elevation of liver function tests</li></ul></li><li>Ethanol therapy<ul><li>Not FDA approved for treatment of methanol</li><li>Ethanol has greater affinity than methanol for alcohol dehydrogenase:<ul><li>Slows metabolism to formaldehyde and formic acid by competitive inhibition</li></ul></li><li>Ethanol is the 2nd-choice antidote if fomepizole is not available</li><li>Initiate before methanol level returns if potentially toxic ingestion is highly suspected or confirmed by history:<ul><li>Therapeutic range is 100 mg/dL</li><li>Oral: 50% ethanol solution (100-proof liquor) via nasogastric tube:<ul><li>Loading dose 2 mL/kg</li><li>Maintenance dose 0.5 mL/kg/hr</li><li>Maintenance dose during hemodialysis 1 mL/kg/hr</li></ul></li><li>IV: 10% ethanol in D5W:<ul><li>Loading dose 8 mL/kg over 30–60 min</li><li>Maintenance infusion 2 mL/kg/hr</li><li>Maintenance infusion during hemodialysis 4 mL/kg/hr</li></ul></li></ul></li><li>Continue until methanol level is &lt;20 mg/dL</li><li>Indications for ethanol therapy:<ul><li>Intentional methanol ingestion</li><li>Accidental methanol ingestion of more than a sip OR</li><li>Altered mental status or visual symptoms associated with unexplained osmol gap &gt; 10 mmol/L and or elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis, bicarbonate &lt;20 mmol/L and serum pH &lt;7.3 OR</li><li>Serum methanol concentration &gt;20 mg/dL</li></ul></li><li>Advantages:<ul><li>Easily accessible</li><li>Oral and IV routes</li></ul></li><li>Disadvantages:<ul><li>CNS depression especially in children</li><li>Respiratory depression</li><li>Hyponatremia or hypernatremia</li><li>Hypoglycemia</li><li>Hyperosmolarity</li><li>Continuous infusion</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 150 -->

<ul><li>Frequent lab testing</li><li>Contraindicated in pregnancy</li><li>Pancreatitis</li><li>Gastritis</li></ul><ul><li>Folic acid and folinic acid (leucovorin):<ul><li>Folic acid: Cofactor required for conversion of formic acid to carbon dioxide and water</li><li>Folic acid: 50 mg (or 1–2 mg/kg) IV q4h for 24 hr</li><li>Supplemental folate important in malnourished individuals (alcoholics)</li></ul></li><li>Correct acid–base abnormalities:<ul><li>Sodium bicarbonate for severe acidosis (pH &lt;7.3)</li><li>Sodium bicarbonate: 1–2 mEq/kg in 1 L of D5W with 40 mEq KCl at 250 mL/hr</li><li>The goal of the sodium bicarbonate drip is to maintain a normal serum pH</li><li>Full compensation (mmol) = 0.3 x body weigh x Base deficit</li></ul></li><li>Hemodialysis:<ul><li>Decreases elimination half-life of methanol</li><li>Removes formaldehyde and formic acid</li><li>Indications:<ul><li>Ingestion of &gt;1 mL/kg of 100% methanol OR</li><li>Ophthalmologic manifestations OR</li><li>Severe metabolic acidosis, bicarbonate &lt;20 mmol/L and serum pH &lt;7.3 OR</li><li>Serum methanol level &gt;50 mg/dL alone without above criteria</li></ul></li></ul></li><li>Continue hemodialysis until methanol level approaches &lt;20 mg/dL and the metabolic acidosis has resolved</li></ul><p>6. Treatment adjustment</p><ul><li>Not all patients will have an elevated osmol and anion gap. Early presenters will have an osmol gap only, because methanol is osmotically active, and there are no toxic metabolites yet. Late presenters may have an anion gap only, because the osmotically active parent compound has metabolized to the toxic acidotic metabolites. Patients who are present in between will have a combination of an anion gap and an osmol gap.</li><li>supportive therapy for methanol poisoning includes treatment with<ul><li>IV fluids</li><li>sodium bicarbonate in patients with severe metabolic acidosis. Dose to give (mmol) = 0.3 x body weight (kg) x base deficit</li><li>antiseizure medications in patients with seizures</li><li>Cofactors<ul><li>In a methanol-poisoned patient, administer either leucovorin 50 mg IV or folic acid 50mg IV every six hours.</li><li>In an ethylene glycol-poisoned patient, administer thiamine 100 mg IV and pyridoxine 100 mg IV daily.</li><li>If toxic alcohol poisoning is possible or suspected but the exact alcohol is unknown, especially in the presence of a metabolic acidosis, it is reasonable to empirically administer all three cofactors</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul><p>7. Algorithm</p><p><b>Approach to possible methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning when confirmatory</b></p>

<!-- PAGE 151 -->

<div>
<p><b>toxicologic testing is not available.</b></p>
<p>Note that Fomepizole an intravenous ethanol is not available in most hospital in Cambodia, as well as measurement of blood methanol level, at least until this day (end of 2024).</p>
<h3>Diagnosis algorithm for methanol poisoning without ABGs</h3>
<img alt="Flowchart: Diagnosis algorithm for methanol poisoning without ABGs. Start: Suspect methanol poisoning (based on history and/or clinical features). Decision 1: Awake? Yes path leads to Hyperventilation? RR &gt; 20-25/min*. No path leads to Observe min 24h (If suspect of drinking methanol re-assess every 1-4h). Yes path leads to Visual disturbances?. No path leads to Give RA or RL 1-2L + Dextrose IV + thiamine within 1h. Yes path leads to Consider ethanol or other poisoning / medical condition as causes (Observe, treat symptomatically and directed toward likely cause (e.g. hypoglycemia, intracerebral cause etc.) or If very high suspicion of methanol: poor prognosis. Consider treating as a methanol poisoning). Decision 2 (after Visual disturbances?): No path leads to Give RA or RL 1-2L + Dextrose IV + thiamine within 1h. Yes path leads to Less hyperventilate after 1h of aggressive fluid ++ treatment?. Decision 3 (after Less hyperventilate...): Yes path leads to Suspect methanol poisoning (Give fomepizole / ethanol + bicarbonate + folic acid, Homodialysis (HD)). No path leads to Likely alcoholic / diabetic ketoacidosis: Continue supportive treatment, Observe min 24h after treatment is terminated."/>
<div style="border: 1px solid black; padding: 10px; margin-top: 10px;">
<p>* Always consider other causes of metabolic acidosis</p>
<ul>
<li>Diabetic ketoacidosis: known diabetic? Check blood glucose</li>
<li>Renal failure: known renal failure? Diuresis? Creatinine?</li>
<li>Sepsis: other signs of infection? Fever? WBC? CRP? Etc..</li>
</ul>
<p><i>RA: Ringer acetate, RL: Ringer lactate, ABG: arterial blood gas</i></p>
</div>
<p><i>Adapted from Methanol poisoning-protocol-EMACC-WG / MSF Norway / Oslo University Hospital - 2023</i></p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 152 -->

<h2>Diagnosis algorithm for methanol poisoning with ABGs</h2>
<div>
<p><b>Suspect methanol poisoning</b> (based on history and/or clinical features)</p>
<p>Arterial blood gas (ABG)*</p>
<table border="1">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Normal ABG<br/>No Symptoms</td>
<td>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> &gt;15 or BD&lt;10<br/>pH typically &gt;7.2**</td>
<td>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> 10-15 or BD 10-15<br/>pH typically &gt;7.0-7.2**</td>
<td>HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> &lt;10 or BD&gt;15<br/>pH typically &lt;7.0**</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<ul>
<li>If Normal ABG/No Symptoms: <b>Observe min 24h</b><br/>If suspect of drinking methanol re-assess every 1-4h</li>
<li>If HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> &gt;15 or BD&lt;10 or HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> 10-15 or BD 10-15: <b>Visual disturbances?</b><br/>If coma treat as NO</li>
<li>If HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> &lt;10 or BD&gt;15: <b>Suspect methanol poisoning</b></li>
</ul>
<p>If Visual disturbances? No:</p>
<ul>
<li>Give RA or RL 1-2L + Dextrose IV + thiamine within 1h</li>
</ul>
<p>If Visual disturbances? Yes:</p>
<ul>
<li>Give RA or RL 1-2L + Dextrose IV + thiamine within 1h</li>
</ul>
<p>If Hyperventilation still present? No:</p>
<ul>
<li>Likely alcoholic / diabetic ketoacidosis:
        <ul>
<li>Continue supportive treatment</li>
<li>Observe min 24h after treatment is terminated</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>If Hyperventilation still present? Yes:</p>
<ul>
<li>Suspect methanol poisoning
        <ul>
<li>Give fomepizole / ethanol + bicarbonate + folic acid</li>
<li>Homodialysis (HD)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div>
<p>* Always consider other causes of metabolic acidosis</p>
<ul>
<li>Diabetic ketoacidosis: known diabetic? Check blood glucose</li>
<li>Renal failure: known renal failure? Diuresis? Creatinine?</li>
<li>Sepsis: other signs of infection? Fever? WBC? CRP? Etc..</li>
</ul>
<p>** pH will always depend on degree of hyperventilation. Therefore focus primarily on base deficit (BD) or HCO<sub>3</sub></p>
<p>RA: Ringer acetate, RL: Ringer lactate, BD: base deficit, ABG: arterial blood gas</p>
</div>
<p><i>Adapted from Methanol poisoning-protocol-EMACC-WG / MSF Norway / Oslo University Hospital - 2023</i></p>
<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<p>Unavailability of antidotes (Fomepizole, or ethanol for injection), consider ethanol oral</p>

<!-- PAGE 153 -->

<div><p>(usually not practical), and hemodialysis. Check the alcohol content (%) of spirit to use if medical product 50% was not available. Mind also the ingredients used in that spirit. Severe patients (pH&lt;7.2, visual disturbance, bicarbonate &lt;20 mmol/L) should be transferred to institution where Hemodialysis is available, and early indication should be considered.</p><h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3><p>The prognosis in methanol poisoning correlates with the amount of methanol consumed and the subsequent degree of metabolic acidosis; more severe acidosis confers a poorer prognosis. The prognosis is further dependent on the amount of formic acid that has accumulated in the blood, with a direct correlation existing between the formic acid concentration and morbidity and mortality. Little long-term improvement can be expected in patients with neurologic complications.</p><h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3><ul><li>visual dysfunction (33%-40% of patients reported to have permanent visual sequelae)</li><li>acute pancreatitis</li><li>Parkinson-like extrapyramidal syndrome</li><li>rare neurological complications include<ul><li>transverse myelitis</li><li>pseudobulbar palsy</li><li>cognitive defects</li><li>brain hemorrhage</li></ul></li><li>myoglobinuria is rare but may lead to acute kidney injury</li><li>fatal intracranial hemorrhage reported 46 hours after methanol poisoning from ingesting windshield wiper fluid.</li></ul><h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3><ul><li>Increase public awareness about the dangers of methanol poisoning and the importance of consuming safe alcoholic beverages</li><li>Strengthen regulations and enforcement to prevent the sale of illicit or adulterated alcohol.</li><li>Ensure healthcare facilities are equipped to diagnose and treat methanol poisoning promptly.</li></ul><h3>XII. REFERENCES</h3><ol><li>Kirk L. Cumpston. Methanol poisoning in 5 minutes Emergency Consult, Unbound Medicine platform, 2024, Wolters Kluwer Health Lippincott Williams &amp; Wilkins. Accessed Nov 2024</li><li>DynaMed. Methanol Poisoning. EBSCO Information Services. Accessed November 16, 2024. <a href="https://www.dynamed.com/condition/methanol-poisoning">https://www.dynamed.com/condition/methanol-poisoning</a></li><li>UpToDate. Methanol and Ethylene glycol poisoning. Walters Kluwer. Accessed Nov 2024 <a href="https://www.uptodate.com/contents/methanol-and-ethylene-glycol-poisoning-pharmacology-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis">https://www.uptodate.com/contents/methanol-and-ethylene-glycol-poisoning-pharmacology-clinical-manifestations-and-diagnosis</a></li></ol></div>

<h1>CARDIOPULMONARY ARREST</h1><h2>BASIC AND ADVANCE CARDIAC LIFE SUPPORT</h2><p>Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya</p><h3>I. DEFINITION</h3><p>Cardiac arrest is the cessation of cardiac mechanical activity resulting in the absence of circulating blood flow, confirmed by the absence of a pulse, apnea or agonal breathing (“gasping”) and unconsciousness. Cardiac arrest stops blood from flowing to vital organs, depriving them of oxygen, and, if left untreated, results in death.</p><h3>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h3><p>Cardiac arrest (or cardiocirculatory arrest) in adults is a common syndrome and constitutes an absolute life-threatening emergency. It occurs most often outside the hospital and affects twice as many men as women with an average age of 60 years. The main cause is coronary ischemia through a mechanism of ventricular rhythm disturbance (ventricular fibrillation or tachycardia).</p><h3>III. ETIOLOGY</h3><ul><li>Acute coronary syndrome (40%-77% depending on the study)</li><li>Other cardiac and vascular etiologies<ul><li>Rhythm disorder in ancient ischemic heart disease.</li><li>Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or dilated cardiomyopathy.</li><li>Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia.</li><li>Arrhythmia-conduction disorder<ul><li>Idiopathic ventricular fibrillation (VF)</li><li>Brugada syndrome</li><li>Paroxysmal auriculoventricular (AV) block (elderly +)</li><li>Congenital or drug-induced long QT syndromes</li><li>Congenital short QT syndromes.</li><li>Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome</li></ul></li><li>Congenital cardiopathy (Tetralogy of Fallot)</li><li>Acute myocarditis</li><li>Tamponade.</li><li>Aortic dissection</li><li>Massive pulmonary embolism</li><li>Aneurysm rupture.</li><li>Non-cardiovascular origins (5 to 25%): The most common are toxic, traumatic causes, acute respiratory failure or drowning.</li></ul></li><li>Risk factors associate with atherosclerotic coronary artery disease.<ul><li>Smoking</li><li>Hypercholesterolemia</li><li>High blood pressure</li><li>Diabetes</li><li>Familial histories of coronary artery disease</li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 155 -->

<ul><li><b>In infants and children</b>, cardiac causes of cardiac arrest are less common than in adults. The predominant cause of cardiac arrest in infants and children is respiratory failure due to various respiratory disorders (eg, airway obstruction, drowning, infection, sudden infant death syndrome [SIDS], smoke inhalation).</li></ul><h4>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4><p>We divide in two sections depending on whether respiratory arrest or cardiac arrest occurs first. Respiratory arrest (blood circulation continues, there is no cardiac arrest yet) lead to hypoxia, hypercapnia, and acidosis (muscular hypoxia produces lactic acid) and then, these three conditions cause secondary cardiac arrest. A victim may be in cardiac arrest (absence of pulse) and continue to breathe (agonal breathing).</p><h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4><p>The diagnosis of cardiopulmonary arrest should be rapid (&lt;10 seconds), confirmed by loss of consciousness (coma), apnea or agonal breathing (“gasping”), absence of arterial pulse either in the carotid or femoral artery.</p><img alt="Illustration showing a rescuer performing rescue breaths on an unconscious person lying on their back."/><p>At the moment of high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), blood and radiological investigation may be needed; like blood sugar; serum potassium; EKG (Pulseless ventricular tachycardia (VT); Ventricular fibrillation; Asystole; Pulseless electrical activity (PEA)), Heart ultrasound.</p><p>It is essential to diagnose the signs of aspirations of a foreign body in the respiratory tract, which includes severe stridor, dyspnea, suprasternal and intercostal retractions. It is recommended to do the Heimlich maneuver if we are suspecting aspiration.</p><h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4><ul><li>Coma</li><li>Syncope</li><li>Seizure</li><li>opiate overdose</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 156 -->

<h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2>
<ol>
<li><b>Objective</b>
<ul>
<li>To maintain an open and clear airway (A).</li>
<li>To maintain breathing by external ventilation (B).</li>
<li>To maintain blood circulation by external cardiac massage (C).</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Warning signs of sudden cardiac arrest (But often has no warning)</b>
<ul>
<li>Chest pain,</li>
<li>Sweating,</li>
<li>Shortness of breath,</li>
<li>Palpitation or Dizziness</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Mortality risk factors of cardiac arrest</b>
<ul>
<li>History of cerebrovascular disease</li>
<li>Higher lactate and presence of PEA or asystole.</li>
<li>Being aged 45-60 years old.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Out hospital management of Out hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA)</b>
<p><b>Adult chain of survival</b></p>
<img alt="Diagram illustrating the Adult OHCA Chain of Survival, showing five interconnected red circles with icons representing the steps: Activation of Emergency Response, High-Quality CPR, Defibrillation, Advanced Resuscitation, Post-Cardiac Arrest Care, and Recovery."/>
<p><b>Adult OHCA Chain of Survival</b></p>
<p><b>Basic life support (BLS) for adult</b></p>
<p>BLS for adults focuses on doing several tasks simultaneously. In many situations, more than one person is available to do CPR. This choreographed method includes performing chest compressions, managing the airway, delivering rescue breaths, and using the automatic external defibrillation (AED), all as a team. By coordinating efforts, a team of rescuers can save valuable seconds when time lost equals damage to the heart and brain.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<table border="1">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><b>Danger</b><br/>(Make sure it's safe to help)</td>
<td>Wear personal protective equipment (PPE) (gloves, apron, mask) if available<br/>Look out for blood spills, sharps, electric wire, etc.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Responsiveness</b><br/>(Check the victim for a response)</td>
<td>Tap shoulder. Say 'Hello, hello are you OK?'</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Shout for help</b><br/>(Ask for help and defibrillator)</td>
<td>Emergency! Emergency! Bring the resus trolley and Defibrillator!</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<!-- PAGE 157 -->

<table border="1">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><b>Circulation</b><br/>(Start chest compression)</td>
<td>High quality chest compression<br/>- Middle of chest and lower half of sternum<br/>- Depth: 5-6 cm<br/>- Rate: 100-120/min<br/>- Full recoil after each compression<br/>- Minimize interruption.<br/>- 30 compressions / 2 ventilations<br/>- Each ventilation in 1 second.<br/>Ventilation methods:<ul><li>Bag Valve Mask (BVM)</li><li>Mouth to mask</li><li>Mouth to mouth rescue breathing</li><li>Mouth to nose rescue breathing</li><li>Mouth to stoma</li></ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Defibrillation</b><br/>(Assess for need to shock)</td>
<td>- Attach AED<br/>- Do not interrupt chest compression.<br/>- Follow AED voice prompt.<br/>- Immediately continue CPR</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Airway</b><br/>(Open the airway)</td>
<td>Perform head tilt-chin lift or Jaw thrust (if suspected cervical injury)<br/>Do Heimlich maneuver if we are suspecting a foreign body in the respiratory tract.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Breathing</b><br/>(Assess for normal breathing)</td>
<td>Look for normal breathing in not more than 10 seconds.<br/>Start chest compressions if not breathing or abnormal breathing (gasping) is seen.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Reassessment</b><br/>(Every 5 cycles or 2mn of CPR)</td>
<td>If the patient recovers with normal breathing?</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Recovery position</b></td>
<td>After the victim has normal breathing but is still unresponsive, place the victim in recovery position.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<p>Adult chain of survival</p>

Below the icons is a colored bar labeling the steps: Early Recognition and Prevention, Activation of Emergency Response, High-Quality CPR, Defibrillation, Post-Cardiac Arrest Care, and Recovery."/>

If the individual's chest is rising without using an advanced airway, continue giving CPR without pausing.<br/>- if you are in a hospital or near trained professionals who can efficiently insert and use the airway, consider pausing CPR.</td></tr><tr><td><b>Breathing</b><br/>(Assess for normal breathing)</td><td>- Administer 100% oxygen (SaO2 ≥ 94%).<br/>- High-quality CPR should produce an End-Tidal CO2 (ETCO2) between 10 to 20 mmHg (if &lt; 10 mmHg after 20 minutes of CPR for an intubated individual (Over ventilated), then you may consider stopping resuscitation attempts). Normal partial pressure of CO2 (PaCO2) is between 35 to 40 mmHg.</td></tr><tr><td><b>Circulation</b><br/>(Start chest compression)</td><td>- Evaluate rhythm and pulse<br/>- Defibrillation/cardioversion<br/>- Obtain IV/IO access<br/>- Give rhythm-specific medications<br/>- Give IV/IO fluids if needed</td></tr><tr><td><b>Defibrillation</b><br/>(Assess for need to shock)</td><td>- Identify and treat reversible causes.<br/>- Cardiac rhythm and patient history are the keys to differential diagnosis.<br/>- Assess when to shock versus medicate</td></tr></tbody></table><h3>Airway management</h3><p><b>a) Basic airway adjuncts</b></p><ul><li>Nasopharyngeal airway (NPA) (A)</li><li>Oropharyngeal airway (OPA) (B)</li><li>Suctioning</li></ul><div><img alt="Image A shows Nasopharyngeal airways (NPA) and their insertion into the nasal cavity. <h2>B) Defibrillation</h2>
<h3>i. Patient selection</h3>
<ul>
<li>Shockable rhythms: Ventricular fibrillation (VF) and Pulseless Ventricular tachycardia (VT)</li>
<li>Unshockable rhythms: Asystole or PEA</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Defibrillation</b> is contraindicated for sinus rhythm, conscious patient with a pulse, or when there is danger to the operator or other (e.g., from a wet patient or wet surroundings).</p>
<div>
<img alt="ECG strip showing irregular, chaotic waves characteristic of Ventricular fibrillation."/>
<p>Ventricular fibrillation</p>
</div>
<div>
<img alt="ECG strip showing regular, rapid waves characteristic of Pulseless ventricular tachycardia."/>
<p>Pulseless ventricular tachycardia</p>
</div>
<h3>ii. Equipment</h3>
<p>There are two types of defibrillation's waveforms: monophasic and biphasic. The amount of energy required for successful defibrillation is typically lower with biphasic waveforms.</p>
<p><b>Manual defibrillators</b> require a manual analysis of the patient's cardiac rhythm, as well as manual delivery of the shock through paddles or self-adhesive pads by the operator.</p>
<p><b>Automated external defibrillators (AED)</b> may be fully or semi-automated. Fully automated external defibrillators will analyze the rhythm automatically, and if indicated, charge and deliver the shock, whereas semi-automated external defibrillators will require an operator to manually deliver the shock after analysis and charging.</p>
<h3>iii. Patient positioning and skin preparation</h3>
<p>Ensure that scene is safe for performing defibrillation including water and environmental scene dangers such as traffic. The patient should be in the supine position with ongoing CPR. To avoid skin burns, remove all metallic objects, jewelry, or medication patches (wipe off any residue). If there is excessive chest hair over the areas where the pads or paddles are to be placed, quickly shave the hair off to ensure a good contact with skin. Remove all direct sources of oxygen to avoid fire.</p>
<h4>a) Placement of pads/paddles</h4>
<p>There are several possible positions for the placement of the pads or paddles:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Antero apical position:</b> place one paddle/pad to the right of the upper half of the sternum, just below the patient's right clavicle, and place the other pad just below and to the left of the left nipple. With a female patient, place the</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 161 -->

<div><p>paddle/pad just below and to the left side of the breast. Do not place it over the breast.</p><ul><li><b>Anteroposterior position:</b> Place one pad/paddle at the left lower sternal border and the posterior pad/paddle below the left scapula</li><li>Pacemakers automated implantable cardiac defibrillators, and other implants: such devices are implanted under the skin and palpable on examination. Ensure that the placement of the pads is at least four fingerbreadths away from such devices.</li></ul><p><b>iv. Step-by-step technique</b></p><ul><li><b>Manual defibrillation</b><ol type="a"><li>Prepare the patient and equipment as described earlier. <b>CPR should be ongoing.</b></li><li>If using paddles, attach the <b>rhythm monitoring electrodes</b>. Alternatively, the paddles may be applied to the chest directly in "quick look" mode to read the rhythm.</li><li>If pads are used, the rhythm will be read by the pads, and additional rhythm electrodes are not necessary.</li><li>Interrupt chest compressions only briefly (&lt;10 seconds) to <b>analyze the rhythm</b> manually.</li><li>Confirm that the rhythm is ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, then <b>resume CPR immediately</b>.</li><li>Select the appropriate <b>energy level</b>. For biphasic defibrillators, select according to the manufacturer's recommendation (150 to 200 J for biphasic truncated exponential waveforms and 120 to 200 J for rectilinear biphasic waveforms). If the recommendation is unknown use the maximum energy available. For monophasic defibrillators, begin with an initial 360-J shock. If starting with less than the maximum energy, consider escalation of shock energy for failed shocks or recurrence of fibrillation.</li><li>Ensure that the defibrillator is in <b>unsynchronized mode</b>.</li><li>If using paddles, apply the paddles and <b>charge</b>. CPR should NOT be interrupted during charging. All other personnel may begin to stand clear at this point.</li><li>Call out, "<b>Stand clear,</b>" and ensure that no one is in contact with the patient or trolley. CPR is interrupted only briefly (&lt;10 seconds) at this point.</li><li>With the CPR interrupted, quickly confirm the rhythm remains shockable, then <b>deliver the shock</b>. The operator's eyes should be back on the patient at the time of shock delivery, to ensure safety.</li><li>Resume CPR immediately once the shock has been delivered. Do NOT pause to check the pulse or reanalyze the rhythm at this time.</li><li>Continue management according to the local resuscitation protocol.</li></ol></li><li><b>Automated external defibrillation (AED)</b><ol type="a"><li>Prepare the patient and equipment as described earlier. <b>CPR should be ongoing.</b></li><li><b>Turn on</b> the automated external defibrillator (follow the voice prompts according to your device).</li></ol></li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 162 -->

<div><p>c. Open the package containing the <b>defibrillation pads</b> with the attached cable and connector. With the chest prepared, carefully pull off the protective backing from the pads and apply the pads to the chest, taking care to avoid air pockets. The pads should be placed at least 2 inches away from any automated implantable cardiac defibrillators.</p><p>d. Initiate <b>analysis</b> of the rhythm. This may be automatic or require pressing a button to activate analysis. Ensure that there is no movement of the patient during analysis, including a brief interruption of CPR.</p><p>e. If a shock is advised, the device will <b>automatically charge</b> to a preset energy level. If a semi-automated external defibrillator is used, CPR should immediately resume while charging. All other personnel may begin to stand clear at this point. Note that fully automated defibrillators do not require the operator's input to discharge a shock, and all rescuers should stay clear at the time of charging. Follow the voice prompts of the device.</p><p>f. Call out, "<b>Stand clear,</b>" and ensure that no one is in contact with the patient or trolley. CPR is interrupted only briefly (&lt;10 seconds) at this point.</p><p>g. <b>Deliver the shock.</b></p><p>h. Resume CPR immediately once the shock has been delivered. Do NOT pause to check the pulse or reanalyze the rhythm at this time.</p><p>i. Continue management according to the local resuscitation protocol.</p><p>j. There are increasing numbers of automated external defibrillators that provide CPR "guidance" in the form of metronome beats or active feedback on the correct rate and depth of chest compressions in real time. Achieving optimal CPR quality increases the likelihood of successful defibrillation.</p><p><b>v. Risks and precautions</b></p><p>Electrical energy can terminate an abnormal rhythm, but if inappropriately delivered, it may also induce ventricular fibrillation. This can happen if the electric shock is delivered during the relative refractory period of the cardiac electrical cycle. Movement artifacts or loose leads may resemble ventricular fibrillation and result in an inappropriate shock. New defibrillator technology is available that can filter compression or movement artifacts to "see through" the artifacts to reveal underlying rhythm. However, when using automated external defibrillators, all manufacturers currently still recommend stopping all compressions and patient movement (e.g., during transport) before initiating rhythm analysis.</p></div>

<!-- PAGE 163 -->

<h2>A. Algorithm</h2>
<div style="text-align: center;">
<h3>Adult BLS Algorithm</h3>
</div>
<div>
<p><b>Criteria for high-quality CPR:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Start chest compressions (hard and fast) within 10 seconds</li>
<li>Allow for complete chest recoil between compressions</li>
<li>Minimize interruptions between chest compressions</li>
<li>Assure that the breaths make chest rise</li>
<li>Do not over-ventilate</li>
<li>Assess for shockable rhythm as soon as AED available in witnessed cardiac arrest as it is most likely a shockable rhythm</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div>
<p><b>UNRESPONSIVE WITHOUT NORMAL RESPIRATIONS</b></p>
<p>CALL 119 GET AN AED</p>
<p>Assess pulse: DEFINITE PULSE WITHIN 10 SECONDS</p>
<p>If NO NORMAL BREATHING, HAS PULSE: Administer one breath every 5 to 6 seconds. Assess pulse every two minutes.</p>
<p>If NO BREATHING, OR ONLY GASPING, NO PULSE: Start cycles of 30 compressions and two breaths.</p>
<p>AED/DEFIBRILLATOR ARRIVES</p>
<p>ASSESS FOR SHOCKABLE RHYTHM</p>
<p>If YES, SHOCKABLE: Administer one shock and resume CPR immediately for two minutes.</p>
<p>If NO, NONSHOCKABLE: Resume CPR immediately for two minutes. Assess rhythm every two minutes. Continue steps until ACLS providers arrive or until the person shows signs of return of circulation.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 164 -->

Second dose: 150 mg.</li></ul></div><div><h3>Advanced Airway</h3><ul><li>Endotracheal intubation or supraglottic advanced airway</li><li>Waveform capnography or capnometry to confirm and monitor ET tube placement</li><li>Once advanced airway in place, give 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 breaths/min) with continuous chest compressions</li></ul></div><div><h3>Return of Spontaneous Circulation (ROSC)</h3><ul><li>Pulse and blood pressure</li><li>Abrupt sustained increase in PETCO<sub>2</sub> (typically ≥40 mm Hg)</li><li>Spontaneous arterial pressure waves with intra-arterial monitoring</li></ul></div><div><h3>Reversible Causes</h3><ul><li>Hypovolemia</li><li>Hypoxia</li><li>Hydrogen ion (acidosis)</li><li>Hypo-/hyperkalemia</li><li>Hypothermia</li><li>Tension pneumothorax</li><li>Tamponade, cardiac</li><li>Toxins</li><li>Thrombosis, pulmonary</li><li>Thrombosis, coronary</li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 165 -->

<div>
<h4>H: HYPOVOLEMIA OR HEMORRHAGE</h4>
<p>History of fluid or blood loss may be available. Rectal examination can identify massive lower GI bleeding; nasogastric intubation can identify massive upper GI bleeding; and bedside FAST can diagnose massive intraperitoneal bleeding. Treat with fluids and blood products.</p>
<h4>H: HYPOXIA</h4>
<p>Hypoxia occurs with lack of oxygen and alveolar ventilation. Make sure that the airway adjunct is placed correctly. Check breath sounds at intervals to ensure that the endotracheal tube has not slipped out of the trachea or to identify pneumothorax. Verify the source of oxygen—an oxygen cylinder or the piped oxygen supply.</p>
<h4>H: HYPOTHERMIA</h4>
<p>Treat hypothermia with gradual rewarming with blankets and warm IV fluids. If there is no recovery of consciousness in the hypothermic patient following ROSC, maintain a body core temperature of 33°C until further assessment and decisions can be made.</p>
<h4>H: HYDROGEN ION (ACIDOSIS)</h4>
<p>The acidosis of cardiac arrest is a combination of respiratory and metabolic acidosis. Respiratory acidosis is addressed by early endotracheal intubation and alveolar ventilation. Metabolic acidosis can be somewhat addressed by good-quality CPR. Sodium bicarbonate can be administered for severe metabolic acidosis from prolonged or poor initial resuscitation, at a dose of 1 to 1.5 mEq/kg. Half the initial dose can be readministered after 10 to 15 minutes, depending on pH. However, data currently do not support routine administration of sodium bicarbonate for acidosis, with no controlled studies demonstrating improved hemodynamics with sodium bicarbonate.<sup>62</sup> If administered, ventilatory rate should be increased to counteract the increased CO<sub>2</sub> produced by sodium bicarbonate. Continuous venovenous hemodialysis may be required for severe acidosis.<sup>62</sup></p>
<h4>H: HYPER- OR HYPOKALEMIA, OTHER METABOLIC DISORDERS</h4>
<p>Suspect hyperkalemia in patients on hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis (look for presence of arteriovenous fistula or dialysis catheter). Other metabolic disorders are extremely difficult to confidently identify in cardiac arrest. If hyperkalemia is suspected, administer calcium chloride, sodium bicarbonate, insulin, and glucose. Treat hyperkalemia from suspected digitalis toxicity with IV magnesium sulfate or digoxin-specific Fab fragments (Digibind®).</p>
<hr/>
<h4>T: THROMBOSIS (PULMONARY EMBOLISM)</h4>
<p>Pulmonary embolism causing cardiac arrest requires fibrinolysis or embolectomy. However, the diagnosis is rarely made at time of collapse, and even then, most systems are not geared to make such prompt diagnosis and initiate the necessary procedures for embolectomy. Fibrinolytic agents could be considered during cardiac arrest from suspected pulmonary embolism on a case-by-case basis.<sup>72</sup> A single-center case series of patients with diagnosed pulmonary embolism suffering PEA arrest found that rapid administration of alteplase 50 milligrams IV to be safe and effective, with 20 of 23 patients demonstrating ROSC.<sup>73–75</sup> High-quality compressions should be continued after thrombolytic therapy is administered, with several studies recommending 60 to 90 seconds of compression after the drug is given. Factors suggestive of pulmonary embolism causing cardiac arrest include two of three signs or symptoms (prearrest respiratory distress, altered mental status, or shock); arrest witnessed by a physician or emergency medical technician; and PEA as the first or primary arrest rhythm.</p>
<h4>T: "TABLETS" (DRUG OVERDOSE)</h4>
<p>Drug overdose is rarely identified as a cause of cardiac arrest during the resuscitation process. In the event of antidepressant overdose, administer IV sodium bicarbonate. Lipid emulsion infusion may be useful in cardiac arrest associated with cyclic antidepressants or local anesthetics. β-Blocker or calcium channel-blocker overdose may require high-dose insulin therapy and lipid emulsion infusion.</p>
<h4>T: CARDIAC TAMponade</h4>
<p>Cardiac tamponade is best identified during resuscitation by bedside transthoracic US. This requires brief interruption of chest compressions. Treatment of tamponade causing cardiac arrest is bedside pericardiocentesis.</p>
<h4>T: CORONARY THROMBOSIS</h4>
<p>Acute coronary thrombosis or acute myocardial infarction is one of the most common causes of cardiac arrest. Risk factors are a history of coronary artery disease and initial rhythm of VF/VT.<sup>63–67</sup> Cardiac catheterization after resuscitation is an underused procedure.<sup>67</sup> A 12-lead ECG in the immediate post-cardiac arrest state can identify an ST-segment elevation acute myocardial infarction and allow arrangements for immediate coronary angiography. Myocardial and neurologic function can improve after percutaneous coronary intervention following cardiac arrest.<sup>68</sup> The 2015 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines<sup>1</sup> provide a class I recommendation to activate the cardiac catheterization laboratory in patients with OHCA with ST-segment elevation acute myocardial infarction on ECG. Thus, after ROSC, especially in the face of post-ROSC ECG evidence of acute myocardial infarction, advocate for cardiac catheterization and percutaneous coronary revascularization if available and appropriate. A few case reports describe fibrinolysis during CPR with resultant ROSC and good neurologic outcome.<sup>69</sup> Coronary angiography is reasonable in select patients with suspected cardiac origin of arrest but without ST elevation or in those electrically unstable patients without ST-segment elevation with suspected cardiovascular lesions. The absence of ST-segment elevation on postarrest ECG does not exclude acute coronary thrombus, as approximately one third of patients without ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction on postarrest ECG demonstrate a culprit lesion on angiography.<sup>70</sup> Reports are too few to determine whether thrombolysis together with CPR results in more severe bleeding than thrombolysis without CPR.<sup>71</sup></p>
<h4>T: TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX</h4>
<p>Suspect tension pneumothorax during cardiac resuscitation if breath sounds are unequal on chest auscultation after verifying correct endotracheal tube placement. Treatment is immediate needle decompression.</p>
</div>

<p>Consider mechanical cause:</p>

<li>Agonal rhythm</li>
<li>Acute MI with pump failure</li>

<h3>VIII. Special case</h3>
<h4>1- BLS for children (Age 1 to puberty) and Infant (Newborn to age of 12 months)</h4>

<td>CPR</td>
<td>
<p><b>For Child:</b> Use the heel of one hand on the lower half of the sternum in the middle of the chest. Put your other hand on top of the first hand. Straighten your arms and press straight down. Compressions should be about two inches (5 cm) into the child's chest and at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute.</p>
<p><b>For infant:</b> Place 2 or 3 fingers of one hand on the sternum in the middle of the nipple line. Press straight down. Compressions should be 1.5 inches (4 cm) into the infant's chest (or about 1/3 the diameter of the chest) and at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute.</p>
<ul>
<li>Be sure that between each compression you completely stop pressing on the chest and allow the chest wall to return to its natural position to make CPR less effective.</li>
<li>After 15 compressions, stop compressions and open the airway by tilting the head and lifting the chin or jaw thrust (neck injury is suspect).</li>
<li>Give a breath while watching the chest rise. Repeat while giving a second breath. Breaths should be delivered over one second.</li>
<li>Resume chest compressions. Switch quickly between compressions and rescue breaths to minimize interruptions in chest compressions.</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>

<h4>Pediatric defibrillation</h4>
<p>In the event of ventricular fibrillation, use a weight-based energy dose of 2 to 4 J/kg body weight for monophasic or biphasic devices. For refractory ventricular fibrillation, consider increasing the dose to 4 J/kg. For ventricular tachycardia with a pulse, perform electrical cardioversion with 1 J/kg. This can be progressively increased up to 4 J/kg subsequently if needed.</p>

<!-- PAGE 168 -->

<h2>2- Resuscitation in pregnancy</h2>
<h3>a. Resuscitation step</h3>
<p>The best maternal care provides the best fetal care, so follow general principle of resuscitation when treating the pregnant woman.</p>
<ul>
<li>To accommodate the increase in blood and plasma volume that develops during the pregnancy, make sure that the volume of resuscitation fluids increases by 50% above that required by the non-pregnant patient.</li>
<li>Place 2 large-bore IVs above the diaphragm level and provide rapid infusion of isotonic saline or ringer lactate. Volume must be adequately replaced before considering vasopressor, especially in pregnancy. Select the vasopressor by desired effects in the mother and least harmful effects on the fetus.</li>
<li>Place the patient to full left tilt position.</li>
</ul>
<img alt="A pregnant woman lying on a hospital bed in a medical setting, illustrating the recommended position for resuscitation."/>
<h3>b. Airways changes affecting intubation.</h3>
<p>In the pregnant patient, the incidence of Mallampati class III airways increase making intubation more difficult associated with weight gain in pregnancy, this contributes to the likelihood of a difficult airways.</p>
<h4>Adjunctive airways equipment and patient preparation:</h4>
<ul>
<li>Smaller sized endotracheal tubes</li>
<li>A gum elastic bougie</li>
<li>A short laryngoscope handle, and a stylet readily available.</li>
<li>Pre-oxygenation (&gt;95%)</li>
<li>Pace the patient to supine position manually displace the uterus to the left. Elevate the head and the shoulder with a pillow.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 169 -->

<h3>c. CPR and defibrillation in pregnancy</h3><p>Cardiopulmonary arrest in pregnancy is broken down in 2 categories: Before and after fetal viability. Typically, the onset of fetal viability varies between 22 and 26 weeks. By 20 weeks the uterus fundus is palpable at the umbilicus; Then from the 20 weeks to 32 weeks, the fundus height (in centimeters) approximates the gestation age. If the fundus height is at or below the umbilicus, resuscitation effort should focus on the mother with no modification of CPR. If the uterus fundus is palpable above the umbilicus, one person should provide manual left lateral displacement of the uterus while another is performing CPR.</p><p>According to current advance life support guidelines, Perform defibrillation at recommended adult dose.</p><img alt="A medical professional performing manual left uterine displacement on a pregnant patient lying on a gurney during adult resuscitation."/><p>Manual left uterine displacement by the one-handed technique from the right of the patient during adult resuscitation. [Reproduced with permission from Zelop CM, Einav S, Mhyre JM, et al: Cardiac arrest during pregnancy: ongoing clinical conundrum, Am J Obstet Gynecol. 2018 Jan 2. pii: S0002-9378(17)32806-5. Copyright Elsevier.]</p><h3>d. Pregnancy related cause of maternal cardiopulmonary arrest</h3><table><thead><tr><th colspan="2">Pregnancy-Related Causes of Maternal Cardiopulmonary Arrest</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><strong>Obstetric complications</strong></td><td></td></tr><tr><td><ul><li>Hemorrhage (17.2%)<ul><li>Uterine atony</li><li>Placental abruption</li><li>Placenta previa, accreta, increta, or percreta</li><li>Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy</li></ul></li><li>Severe pregnancy-induced hypertension (15.7%)</li><li>Amniotic fluid embolism</li><li>Idiopathic peripartum cardiomyopathy (8.3%)</li><li>Iatrogenic events</li><li>Failed intubation</li><li>Pulmonary aspiration</li><li>Intravascular local anesthetic overdose (1.6%)</li><li>Drug error, overdose, or allergy</li><li>Hypermagnesemia</li></ul></td><td><strong>Pulmonary embolism (19.6%)</strong><ul><li>Thrombus</li><li>Air</li><li>Fat</li></ul><strong>Stroke (5%)</strong><br/><strong>Trauma</strong><ul><li>Homicide</li><li>Suicide</li><li>Motor vehicle accident</li></ul><strong>Infection or sepsis (12.6%)</strong><br/><strong>Other (19.2%)</strong> (cardiovascular, pulmonary, and neurologic comorbidities)</td></tr></tbody></table>

<td>Sodium bicarbonate</td>
<td>Cardiac arrest unresponsive to other measures; documented preexisting metabolic acidosis</td>
<td>Category C. No studies of risk. Use for hyperkalemia and selected toxic overdoses.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Calcium chloride or gluconate</td>
<td>Cardiac arrest due to hyperkalemia, or as antidote to magnesium toxicity (a potential complication when giving high doses of magnesium for eclampsia)</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Dopamine</td>
<td>Hemodynamically significant hypotension in the absence of hypovolemia</td>
<td>Category C. No teratogenic effects in animals, but sufficient studies in humans are lacking; use only when clearly indicated.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Dobutamine</td>
<td>Short-term inotropic support of patients with depressed myocardial contractility</td>
<td>Category B. Not teratogenic in animal studies.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Norepinephrine</td>
<td>Vasopressor for septic shock after adequate volume replacement</td>
<td>Category C. No animal reproductive studies done. Crosses the placenta.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Amiodarone</td>
<td>Ventricular fibrillation, tachycardia, and supraventricular tachycardia</td>
<td>Category D. Is part of Advanced Cardiac Life Support algorithm in pregnancy; use if benefit outweighs risk; serious fetal adverse effects of congenital goiter and hypothyroidism.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Adenosine</td>
<td>Supraventricular tachycardia</td>
<td>Class C. Multiple case reports of the safe use of adenosine to treat maternal and fetal supraventricular tachycardia.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Magnesium sulfate</td>
<td>Torsades de pointes; prevention or treatment of seizures in severe preeclampsia or eclampsia</td>
<td>Class D. Crosses the placenta, and levels in fetus are similar to the mother. Neonatal neurologic depression may occur with respiratory depression, muscle weakness, and loss of reflexes. Continuous maternal use for &gt;5 days may cause fetal hypocalcemia or bone abnormalities.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Ephedrine</td>
<td>Hypotension related to spinal anesthesia or unresponsive to fluids</td>
<td>Class C. Multiple reports of use during anesthesia-related hypotension in pregnancy. Maintains uterine blood flow. May cause dose-dependent increase in fetal acidosis, tachycardia, and abnormal variability in fetal heart rate (indicative of fetal stress), or an increase in metabolic activity.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Phenylephrine</td>
<td>Hypotension related to spinal anesthesia or unresponsive to fluids</td>
<td>Class C. Superior to ephedrine for management of hypotension after spinal anesthesia with a decrease in fetal acidosis.<sup>14</sup></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Vasopressin</td>
<td>No longer recommended for cardiac arrest</td>
<td>Class C. There are no controlled data in human pregnancy.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3>IX. Evolution and prognosis</h3>
<p>Survival rates vary significantly; favorable factors include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Early and effective bystander-initiated CPR. The American Heart Association (AHA) estimates that the survival rate for cardiac arrest is estimated to be around 50% in cases, where the CPR is administered within 3–5 min. However, this survival decreases by 7–10% with each minute that defibrillation is delayed.</li>
<li>Witnessed arrest.</li>
<li>In-hospital location (particularly a monitored unit)</li>
<li>Initial rhythm of ventricular fibrillation (VF) or ventricular tachycardia (VT)</li>
<li>Early defibrillation of VF or VT</li>
<li>Post resuscitative care, including circulatory support and access to cardiac catheterization.</li>
</ul>
<p>*** Out hospital cardiac arrest (60%-80%)</p>
<h3>X. Complications</h3>
<ul>
<li>Neurologic dysfunction</li>
<li>Brain injury</li>
<li>Disorder of consciousness</li>
<li>Neurocognitive deficits</li>
<li>Changes in quality of life</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 171 -->

<h2>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h2>
<h3>Lifestyle Changes to Prevent a Heart Attack</h3>
<ul>
<li>Stop smoking and limit alcohol.</li>
<li>Choose good nutrition: Vitamin, mineral, fiber, low calories.</li>
<li>Control LDL cholesterol level (&lt;70 mg/dL) and Triglyceride level at the normal value is considered good for your heart health.</li>
<li>Control your blood pressure regularly.</li>
<li>Manage diabetes.</li>
<li>Exercise regularly and weight control</li>
<li>Get enough sleep and reduce stress.</li>
</ul>
