<h1>ACUTE METABOLIC COMPLICATION OF DIABETES MELLITUS, HYPEROSMOLAR HYPERGLYCEMIA STATE</h1><p>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. NGETH Sopanha</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS, also known as hyperosmotic hyperglycemic nonketotic state [HHNK]) are two of the most serious acute complications of diabetes. DKA is characterized by ketoacidosis and hyperglycemia, while HHS usually has more severe hyperglycemia but no ketoacidosis. Each represents an extreme in the spectrum of hyperglycemia.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>Diabetes prevalence has increased significantly worldwide, leading to a higher incidence of diabetes-related complications. This trend is observed across all regions, with low- and middle-income countries experiencing the most rapid rise. Common acute complications include diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS). These conditions are more prevalent in type 1 diabetes but can also occur in type 2 diabetes under certain conditions.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><ul><li>Hyperosmolar state precipitated by factors that:<ul><li>Impair peripheral insulin action</li><li>Increase endogenous or exogenous glucose</li><li>Decrease patient's ability to replace fluid loss</li></ul></li><li>Infection (esp. pneumonia and UTI) most common precipitating factor</li><li>Other precipitating causes include:<ul><li>Inadequate therapy/medication omission</li><li>Sepsis</li><li>Medications/drugs:<ul><li>Diuretics</li><li>β-blockers</li><li>Calcium channel blockers</li><li>Atypical antipsychotics</li><li>Corticosteroids</li><li>Sympathomimetics</li><li>Phenytoin</li><li>Cimetidine</li><li>Amphetamines</li><li>Ethanol</li></ul></li><li>Myocardial infarction</li><li>CVA</li><li>Renal failure</li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 173 -->

<ul><li>Heat stroke</li><li>Pancreatitis</li><li>Appendicitis</li><li>Intestinal obstruction</li><li>Endocrine disorders</li><li>Pregnancy</li><li>Trauma</li><li>Burns</li></ul><h4>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4><p>The pathophysiology that gives rise to HHS requires that three interrelated elements be present: insulin deficiency, renal impairment, and cognitive impairment.</p><ul><li>Relative insulin deficiency is the fundamental defect in HHS. Patients have sufficient insulin to inhibit ketone body formation but not enough to prevent hyperglucagonemia, glycogenolysis, and gluconeogenesis. The resulting hyperglycemia induces osmotic diuresis, with resultant fluid and electrolyte losses.</li><li>Typical patients with HHS are old. Their renal blood flow and GFR are reduced, and they cannot readily excrete a glucose load. When they become hyperglycemic, the glucose is neither metabolized nor excreted. It remains in the extracellular fluid space. The resulting increase in osmolality, together with the decreased GFR, causes still less glucose to be excreted.</li><li>Hyperglycemia leading to hyperosmolality normally activates thirst. The combination of mild diabetes and azotemia does not lead to HHS unless the affected individual does not drink sufficient water to prevent hyperosmolality.</li></ul><p>Together, these three factors produce dehydration and the hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. The severe dehydration that occurs is due to the osmotic diuresis of glucose in the absence of compensatory free water intake. Dehydration, in turn, leads to hemoconcentration, setting the stage for severe prerenal azotemia, thrombosis, and shock.</p><p>Moreover, hyperglycemic crises are proinflammatory states that lead to generation of reactive oxygen species and oxidative stress. Proinflammatory factors returned to near-normal levels within 24 hours of insulin therapy and resolution of hyperglycemia.</p><h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4><h5>1) Clinic</h5><ul><li>History<ul><li>Progression of signs and symptoms typically occur over days to weeks</li><li>Polyuria/polydipsia/weight loss</li><li>Dizziness/weakness/fatigue</li><li>Decline in mental state</li><li>Blurred vision</li><li>Leg cramps</li></ul></li><li>Physical Exam<ul><li>Dehydration</li><li>Tachycardia</li><li>Sunken eyes</li><li>Hypotension</li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 174 -->

<ul><li>Orthostasis</li><li>Dry mucous membranes</li><li>Decreased skin turgor</li><li>Collapsed neck veins</li><li>Coma/lethargy/drowsiness</li><li>Decreased urinary output – late finding</li><li>Seizures/focal neurologic deficits</li><li>Concurrent precipitating medical illness</li></ul><p><b>2) Investigation</b></p><ul><li>Diagnostic criteria:<ul><li>Serum glucose ≥600 mg/dL (usually &gt;1,000 mg/dL)</li><li>Minimal ketosis</li><li>pH ≥7.30, HCO<sub>3</sub> ≥15 mEq/L</li><li>Effective serum osmolality &gt;320 mOsm/kg:</li></ul><p>Serum osmolality = 2 × Na<sup>+</sup> + glucose in mg/dL/18</p><p>BUN not included because it is freely permeable between fluid compartments</p></li><li>Lab<ul><li>Broad testing indicated to evaluate hyperosmolar syndrome and identify precipitating causes</li><li>Electrolytes:<ul><li>K<sup>+</sup> may be elevated even in the presence of total body deficit owing to shift from intracellular space to extracellular space</li><li>Mild anion gap metabolic acidosis owing to lactic acid, β-hydroxybutyric acid, or renal insufficiency</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul><p>Sodium corrected for hyperglycemia:</p><p>Corrected [Na+] = [Na+] + 0.016 × [(glucose in mg/dL) – 100]</p><ul><li>BUN, creatinine:</li><li>Venous blood gas (VBG) or arterial blood gas (ABG)</li><li>Serum ketones, β-hydroxybutyrate, and lactate level if pH &lt;7.3 or significantly elevated anion gap to evaluate mixed acid–base disorder</li><li>Serum osmolality</li><li>CBC, blood culture</li><li>Lipase: 3× upper limit of normal is diagnostic for pancreatitis</li><li>Urinalysis: Check for ketones/glucose, UTI</li><li>Magnesium, calcium, phosphate</li></ul><ul><li>Imaging<ul><li>CXR to evaluate for possible underlying pneumonia</li><li>Head CT: When indicated for altered mental status or with focal neurologic deficit</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</b></p><ul><li>If acidosis or significant anion gap present, must determine cause (i.e., ketosis, DKA, lactic acidosis, [hypoperfusion, sepsis, or postictal], or other causes of metabolic acidosis)</li><li>Alcoholic and fasting ketoacidosis</li><li>Anion gap acidosis</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 175 -->

<ul><li>Metabolic encephalopathy</li><li>Mixed disorder of HHS and DKA present in up to 33% of patients</li><li>Differentiate HHS from DKA</li></ul><table border="1"><thead><tr><th>DKA</th><th>HHS</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td colspan="2"><strong>Precipitant factors</strong></td></tr><tr><td>Noncompliance with insulin treatment</td><td>Noncompliance with treatment</td></tr><tr><td>Infection</td><td>Infection</td></tr><tr><td>New-onset (type1) diabetes</td><td>New-onset (type2) diabetes</td></tr><tr><td>other</td><td>Other (corticoids, excess diuretics, etc..)</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2"><strong>Course of illness</strong></td></tr><tr><td>Rapid (in general &lt; 24hs)</td><td>Insidious (days)</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2"><strong>Clinical finding</strong></td></tr><tr><td>Polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration, hypovolemia</td><td>Polyuria, dehydration, hypovolemia</td></tr><tr><td>Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain</td><td>Depressed mental status up to coma</td></tr><tr><td>Fruity odor of breath, Kussmaul respiration</td><td></td></tr><tr><td colspan="2"><strong>Diagnostic laboratory Criteria</strong></td></tr><tr><td>Blood glucose &gt; 200-500 mg/dL*</td><td>Blood glucose &gt; 540-600 mg/dL*</td></tr><tr><td>AND elevated ketones in blood or urine</td><td>AND serum osmolality &gt; 320mmol/kg</td></tr><tr><td>AND metabolic acidosis<br/>(pH &lt;7.3 and HCO3 &lt; 18 mmol/L)</td><td>No significant ketosis<br/>No metabolic acidosis</td></tr><tr><td colspan="2"><strong>Concomitant Laboratory Abnormalities</strong></td></tr><tr><td>Elevated anion gap</td><td>Variable anion gap</td></tr><tr><td>Low C-peptide</td><td>Normal C-peptide</td></tr><tr><td></td><td>Acute kidney injury</td></tr></tbody></table><p>* For conversion of blood glucose concentrations in mg/dL to mmol/L, divide by 18. The numbers are the highest reported blood glucose cutoff for both diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. In patients at risk—taking sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, pregnancy, excessive alcohol use, decreased caloric intake, chronic liver disease—ketoacidosis may develop in the absence of elevated blood glucose concentrations (euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis).</p><h3>VII. MANAGEMENT</h3><p>The best treatment for HHS is prevention.</p><ol><li>Objectives<ul><li>correction of the fluid and electrolyte abnormalities that are typically present and</li><li>the administration of insulin</li><li>find and treat the triggering cause</li></ul></li><li>Critical Signs<ul><li>Shock</li><li>Coma</li><li>Hypokalemia</li><li>Very high serum osmolality</li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 176 -->

<div>
<p>3) Mortality Risk factors</p>
<ul>
<li>Prognosis is worse for elderly patients and</li>
<li>patients in whom coma and hypotension are found.</li>
</ul>
<p>4) Outpatient management</p>
<ul>
<li>Check glycemia, give water to drink if possible.</li>
<li>HHS is an acute condition and may be life threatening, patient should be checked and treat in hospital.</li>
</ul>
<p>5) First-line treatment</p>
<p><b>Initial Stabilization/Therapy: ABCs:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Secure airway in comatose patients</li>
<li>Cardiac monitor and 18G IV</li>
<li>Naloxone, thiamine, and blood glucose for Altered mental status, when suspect the corresponding cause.</li>
<li>Restore hemodynamic stability with IV fluids 0.9% NS 1–2 L over the first hour.</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>Frequent reassessment of volume and mental status</li>
</ul>
<p>Serum levels of Na<sup>+</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, PO<sub>4</sub><sup>-</sup> do not accurately reflect the total body solute deficits or the intracellular environment. Repeat electrolyte and glucose levels hourly.</p>
<ul>
<li>Search for a precipitating event. Mortality/morbidity of HHS usually secondary to inciting cause</li>
<li>Fluids:
        <ul>
<li>Begin resuscitation with 0.9% NS 1–2 L over 1–2 hr to restore intravascular volume and achieve hemodynamic stability</li>
<li>Fluid loss avg 20–25% body weight or 100–200 mL/kg</li>
<li>Calculate total body water (TBW) deficit using corrected serum sodium:
                <b>Total Body Water deficit = 0.6 × weight (kg) × (1 – 140/corrected Na<sup>+</sup>)</b>
</li>
<li>Average fluid deficit is 8–10 L</li>
<li>Replace 50% of the fluid deficit over the next 12 hr</li>
<li>After initial resuscitation use NSS if serum sodium is low, 1/2 NS if serum sodium is elevated/normal or patient is hyperosmolar.</li>
<li>Add D5 to fluid to when serum glucose is &lt; 250 mg/dL</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Potassium:
        <ul>
<li>Anticipate hypokalemia:</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Total body deficit of ~5–10 mEq/kg body weight (replace over 3 d)</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Begin potassium repletion after urine output is established. Do not start in anuric patients or if initial K<sup>+</sup> level is &gt;5 mEq/L</li>
<li>1g KCl = 13.4 mEq K + 13.4mEqCl = 27mEq</li>
<li>If the initial K<sup>+</sup> is normal (4–5 mEq/L), give 20–30 mEq KCl in the first L of fluids, then give 20 mEq/hr</li>
<li>If the initial K<sup>+</sup> is low (3–4 mEq/L), give 40 mEq in first L</li>
<li>If serum K<sup>+</sup> is &lt;3 mEq/L hold insulin and give 10–20 mEq/hr until K<sup>+</sup> &gt;3.3, then add 40 mEq to each liter</li>
<li>Follow repeat serum K<sup>+</sup> levels q1–2h and adjust treatment accordingly</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Insulin:
        <ul>
<li>No role in the early resuscitation</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 177 -->

<ul><li>Earlier use of insulin may cause rapid correction of hyperglycemia with collapse of the intravascular space, hypotension, and shock or hypokalemia precipitating dysrhythmias</li><li>Some patients will not require insulin</li><li>Use insulin as sole therapy in patients with fluid overload (i.e., acute renal failure)</li><li>Begin only after achieving hemodynamic stability and evaluating for hypokalemia:<ul><li>Do not use unless serum K+ &gt;3.3 mEq/L</li><li>SC/IM insulin not recommended due to erratic absorption</li><li>Titrate drip to optimally decrease serum glucose by 50–90 mg/dL/hr. More rapid correction places the patient at risk for developing cerebral edema</li><li>Decrease drip rate by 1/2 when serum glucose &lt; 250 mg/dL</li><li>Adjust insulin drip to maintain serum glucose between 150–200 mg/dL</li><li>Insulin: Begin with 0.05–0.1 U/kg/hr; modify after assessing clinical response</li></ul></li><li>Phosphate:<ul><li>Routine replacement not recommended</li><li>If serum levels &lt;1 mg/dL, give 20–30 mmol potassium phosphate over 24 hr</li><li>Monitor serum calcium levels closely</li><li>Potassium phosphate IV:<ul><li>Phosphorous serum level &lt;0.5 mg/dL: 0.5 mmol/kg IV infused over 4–6 h</li><li>phosphorous serum level 0.5–1 mg/dL: 0.25 mmol/kg IV infused over 4–6 h</li></ul></li><li>Potassium phosphate PO:<ul><li>Phosphorus 250 mg per tablet and potassium 1.1 mEq per tablet</li></ul></li></ul></li><li>Magnesium:<ul><li>0.35 mEq/kg magnesium in fluids for first 3–4 hr (2.5–3 g MgSO4 in 70 kg patient). Caution in ARF.</li><li>MgSO4 (magnesium sulfate): 50% (5 g/10 mL; dilute to at least 20% before IV use)</li></ul></li><li>Anticoagulation:<ul><li>Arterial thrombosis may complicate hyperosmolar state: Consider SC heparin as prophylaxis</li><li>Remain vigilant to detect thrombotic complications (e.g., MI, pulmonary embolus, mesenteric ischemia).</li></ul></li></ul><p>6) Treatment adjustments</p><p>Insulin used without concomitant vigorous fluid replacement increases the risk of shock.</p><p>7) Algorithm:</p><p>Management of hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) in adult</p>

<h3>Treatment hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) in adult</h3>
<p>* After history and physical exam, obtain capillary glucose and serum or urine ketones (nitroprusside method). Begin 1 liter of 0.9% NaCl over one hour, and draw arterial blood gases, complete blood count with differential, urinalysis, serum glucose, BUN, electrolytes, chemistry profile, and creatinine levels STAT. Obtain electrocardiogram, chest radiograph, and specimens for bacterial cultures, as needed.</p>
<p># If initial serum K is &lt;3.3 mEq/L, hold insulin and give potassium chloride until K is &gt;3.3 mEq/L.</p>
<p>** Serum Na should be corrected for hyperglycemia (for each 100 mg/dL glucose &gt;100 mg/dL, add 2.0 mEq to sodium value for corrected serum sodium value).</p>
<p>@ An alternative IV insulin regimen is to give a continuous intravenous infusion of regular insulin at 0.14 units/kg per hour; at this dose, an initial intravenous bolus is not necessary.</p>
<p><b>HHS diagnostic criteria:</b> Serum glucose &gt;600 mg/dL, arterial pH &gt;7.3, serum bicarbonate &gt;15 mEq/L, and minimal ketonuria and ketonemia. Normal laboratory values vary; check local lab normal ranges for all electrolytes.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 179 -->

<div><p><b>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</b></p><ul><li>Geriatric Considerations: Most commonly seen in elderly type II diabetics who experience a stressful illness that precipitates worsening hyperglycemia and reduced renal function</li><li>In the elderly, 30–40% of cases are associated with the initial presentation of diabetes</li><li>Pediatric Considerations: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic states (HHS) rare in pediatric patients.</li></ul><p><b>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</b></p><p>Overall mortality for HHS is estimated at 5-20% [7] and is usually due to the underlying illness that caused the hyperglycemic crisis. The prognosis is worse for elderly patients and patients in whom coma and hypotension are found. This is in contrast to the mortality rate of DKA, which is estimated to be about 1-5%.</p><p><b>X. Complications</b></p><ul><li>Hypotension (insulin shifts glucose from interstitial compartment to intracellular accompanied by water may precipitate hypotension and shock)</li><li>Cerebral edema (Rapid reduction of glucose concentration is a major contributor to the development of cerebral edema.</li><li>Non cardiogenic pulmonary edema.</li></ul><p><b>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</b></p><ul><li>For diabetic patient, the elderly, the chronically ill, and institutionalized populations are at increased risk for HHS. Any living situation or comorbidity that prevents adequate hydration, including for example immobility, advanced age, debility, dementia, agitation, impaired thirst response, restricted access to water, and restraint use, place these patients at risk.</li><li>Patient education focused on encouraging adherence to blood glucose monitoring and compliance with prescribed medications coupled with adequate follow-up to establish a durable diabetes management regimen.</li><li>Sick days management (many factors lead to hypoglycemia, or hyperglycemia)</li><li>Review with nursing home staff the importance of adequate fluid intake and close monitoring of hydration status in patients with diabetes.</li><li>Avoid medications that interfere with effectiveness of insulin</li></ul><p><b>XII. Irwin and Rippe's Intensive Care Medicine (p. 6376). Wolters Kluwer Health. Kindle Edition.</li><li>Jan Gunst, Greet Van den Berghe, Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, in Jean-Louis Vincent, MD, PhD Textbook of Critical Care, 8<sup>th</sup> edition 2023, Elsevier p. 1086-91</li></ol></div>

<h1>TRAUMATISM IN ADULT</h1><p>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>Traumatism = A morbid condition of a system owing to an injury or a wound.</p><p>Traumatic injuries can range from minor isolated wounds to complex injuries involving multiple organ systems. All trauma patients require a systematic evaluation to maximize outcomes and reduce the risk of undiscovered injuries. Life-threatening injuries must be immediately stabilized before moving along the primary survey. A primary survey should be repeated whenever the patients' status deteriorates.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>According to the World Health Organization (WHO), road traffic injuries accounted for 1.25 million deaths in 2014, and trauma is expected to rise to the third leading cause of disability worldwide by 2030<sup>1</sup>. Over 45 million people globally sustain moderate to severe disability each year due to trauma<sup>2</sup>. Outside areas of armed conflict, penetrating injuries are responsible for fewer than 15 percent of traumatic deaths worldwide. Approximately half of traumatic deaths result from central nervous system (CNS) injury, while a third result from exsanguination.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><p>Variety of causes including:</p><ul><li>Penetrating trauma</li><li>Motor vehicle and motorcycle accidents</li><li>Falls from height.</li><li>Assault (including domestic violence)</li><li>Mass-casualty events (including terrorism)</li><li>Burns</li></ul><p>High-risk patients: Extremes of age, pregnancy, bleeding disorders (including potent antiplatelet or anticoagulant use), GCS &lt;14, abnormal vital signs, dangerous mechanism.</p><h2>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h2><p>Particular mechanisms predispose patients to specific injuries.</p><p>Certain high-risk blunt mechanisms, have been associated with greater morbidity and mortality including:</p><ul><li>pedestrians struck by automobiles,</li><li>motorcycle accident.</li><li>severe motor vehicle accidents, and</li></ul><hr/><p><sup>1</sup>Global Status on Road Safety 2015, World Health Organization, <a href="http://www.who.int/violence_injury_prevention/road_safety_status/2015/">http://www.who.int/violence_injury_prevention/road_safety_status/2015/</a> (Accessed on April 04, 2016)</p><p><sup>2</sup>World Health Organization. Global burden of disease. <a href="http://www.who.int/healthinfo/global_burden_disease/en/">www.who.int/healthinfo/global_burden_disease/en/</a> (Accessed on May 01, 2010)</p>

<!-- PAGE 181 -->

<ul><li>falls greater than 6m.</li></ul><p>Any hypotensive trauma patient is at risk for development of hemorrhagic shock, a common cause of postinjury death.</p><p>Table 1: Classification of the degree of hemorrhage</p><table border="1"><caption>Classification of hemorrhage based on Estimated blood loss at initial presentation.</caption><thead><tr><th></th><th>Class I</th><th>Class II</th><th>Class III</th><th>Class IV</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Blood loss (ml)*</td><td>Up to 750</td><td>750 - 1500</td><td>1500 – 2000</td><td>&gt; 2000</td></tr><tr><td>Blood loss (% blood volume)</td><td>Up to 15</td><td>15 – 30</td><td>30 – 40</td><td>40</td></tr><tr><td>Pulse rate (beats/min)</td><td>&lt; 100</td><td>100 – 120</td><td>120 - 140</td><td>&gt; 140</td></tr><tr><td>Blood pressure</td><td>Normal</td><td>Normal</td><td>Decreased</td><td>Decreased</td></tr><tr><td>Pulse pressure (SBP-DBP)</td><td>Normal or increased</td><td>Decreased</td><td>Decreased</td><td>Decreased</td></tr></tbody></table><p>* Assumes a 70kg patient with a pre-injury circulating blood volume of 5L</p><h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4><p>In general, severely injured patients (especially those with unstable vital signs) with a potential need for acute surgical intervention should be transported immediately to the nearest major trauma center.</p><p>Triage to major trauma center per EMS/SAMU protocol.</p><p>A primary survey should be performed at the scene and upon ED arrival.</p><h5>a. Clinic and investigations</h5><p>The protocol Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) provides a standardized approach to trauma including rapid assessment and treatment. This protocol consists of following steps:</p><ul><li>Preparation</li><li>Triage</li><li>Primary survey (ABCDEs)<ul><li>Resuscitation</li><li>Adjuncts to primary survey &amp; resuscitation (eFAST, blood type, Ht...)</li></ul></li><li>Secondary survey (Head to toe Evaluation)<ul><li>Adjuncts to secondary survey (Xray, CT scan.)</li></ul></li><li>Continued post resuscitation monitoring and reevaluation</li><li>Definitive care (to OR, or ICU.)</li></ul><p>The primary and secondary surveys should be repeated frequently.</p><p>In the actual clinical situation, many of these activities occur in parallel or simultaneously.</p><h4><u>Signs and Symptoms</u></h4><h5>Primary survey (ABCDE):</h5><p>Airway (with cervical spine precautions):</p><ul><li>Assess and stabilize the airway before moving to the next step in the primary survey.</li><li>Maintain C-spine precautions throughout</li><li>Indicators of airway patency: Clear speech or effectively/silently moving air</li><li>Indicators of airway obstruction: Gurgling, stridor, snoring, choking, or no air movement</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 182 -->

<div><p><b>Breathing:</b></p><ul><li>Assess and stabilize breathing before moving to the next step in the primary survey.</li><li>Indicators of effective breathing: Symmetric chest wall rise/fall, equal bilateral breath sounds, normal resp rate, and O2 saturation.</li><li>Indicators of ineffective breathing: Asymmetric or minimal chest movement, unequal breath sounds, abnormal resp rate or O2 saturation</li><li>Tension pneumothorax: Suggested by unilateral decreased breath sounds, tracheal shift (to opposite side), hyper expansion, hyperresonance to percussion, subcutaneous air, hypoxia, and/or hemodynamic compromise</li><li>Hemothorax: Suggested by decreased breath sounds and/or dullness to percussion</li></ul><p><b>Circulation:</b></p><ul><li>Assess and stabilize circulation before moving to the next step in the primary survey.</li><li>Assess HR, BP, pulse quality, and end-organ (e.g., mentation, capillary refill, urine output); when abnormal, assume internal hemorrhage.</li></ul><p><b>Disability:</b></p><ul><li>Assess and stabilize disability before moving to the next step in the primary survey.</li><li>Assess level of consciousness, gross motor and sensory function, pupillary size/reactivity</li><li>Glasgow Coma Scale is commonly used; score of ≤8 indicates severe head injury/coma.</li><li>Spinal cord injuries: Grossly assess for lateralization of motor/sensory deficits.</li><li>Assess brainstem function via pupillary size and reactivity to light.</li></ul><p><b>Exposure:</b></p><ul><li>Undress completely, then warm passively</li></ul><p><b>Secondary survey:</b></p><ul><li>Performed after the primary survey.</li><li>Complete physical exam from head to toe</li><li>“Finger in every orifice”</li></ul><p><u><b>History</b></u></p><p>Key features: Initial clinical presentation, mechanism of injury, suspected injuries, and treatment rendered should be elicited from EMS/SAMU personnel, family, and bystanders.</p><p>Motor vehicles collision (MVCs): Note approximate speed of all vehicles, impact point, location of patient in vehicle, seatbelt use, passenger space intrusion, steering column damage, or extrication by EMS/SAMU.</p><p>AMPLE history: Allergies, medical/surgical issues, past medical, last oral, events leading up to trauma. (Discuss tetanus status if stable)</p><p><u><b>Physical Exam</b></u></p><ul><li>See Signs and Symptoms</li><li>Stabilize simultaneously during assessment.</li></ul><p><b>Essential Workup</b></p><ul><li>Primary and secondary surveys</li><li>Critically ill patients: Activate trauma team, rapid transfusion and lab/imaging standby.</li><li>Point of care (POC) US (e-FAST)</li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 183 -->

<ul><li>Portable radiographs include AP chest, AP pelvis, and lateral cervical spine.</li><li>Computed tomography: Only when hemodynamically stable or adequately stabilized.</li><li>Use evidence-based clinical decision rules (e.g., NEXUS, Canadian) to avoid unnecessary imaging.</li></ul><h3>Diagnostic Tests and Interpretation</h3><p><b>Lab</b></p><ul><li>POC Hgb serially if hemorrhagic shock</li><li>POC glucose if altered mental status.</li><li>Blood type, CBC, coagulations, blood gas, lactate, renal function, lipase, and Urine analysis for major trauma patients</li><li>Pregnancy test in all females of childbearing age</li><li>Consider cardiac enzymes to rule out cardiac injury.</li></ul><p><b>Imaging</b></p><ul><li>Significant chest trauma requires objective evaluation of the lungs, heart, and great vessels with e-FAST, CXR, CT, angiography, and/or thoracotomy.</li><li>Blunt abdominal trauma requires objective evaluation using e-FAST followed by abdominal CT or exploratory-laparotomy:<ul><li>If free fluid on e-FAST</li><li>Hemodynamically stable: CT with IV contrast</li><li>Hemodynamically unstable: Exploratory lap</li></ul></li></ul><p>For head trauma, CT is recommended if prolonged loss of consciousness, amnesia, persistent altered level of consciousness, or severe head ach or vomiting.</p><p>For cervical spine fractures: CT is highly sensitive.</p><p>Pan CT scan, (head, neck, chest, abdomen/pelvis in a single pass with IV contrast) lower missed injury rate but significant radiation exposure</p><ul><li>Suspected spine injuries (with neuro deficits): emergent MRI</li><li>Extremity injuries:<ul><li>Plain films identify most fractures (aside from scaphoid, hip, tibial plateau, talus, etc.)</li><li>Suspected vascular injury: Duplex US or CT angiography.</li></ul></li></ul><h3>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h3><p>Consider medical conditions leading to trauma (e.g., stroke, seizures, dysrhythmias, and suicide attempt)</p><h3>VII. MANAGEMENT</h3><ol><li><b>Objectives</b><br/>Rapid assessment, rapid treatment to maintain vital signs. Treat as early as possible the derangement that may threaten the victim life. Not left behind or overlook any lesion incurred by trauma. Get the definitive treatment early.</li><li><b>Critical signs</b><br/>Trauma with unstable vital signs, altered mental status, combined head-chest trauma, head trauma plus other bleeding lesion. Spinal trauma with neurological signs or cervical spinal lesion.</li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 184 -->

<div>
<p>3- Mortality risk factor</p>
<p>Mechanism of trauma (pedestrian hit by car, high speed motor vehicle accident, fallen from height &gt; 6m, blast injury, penetrating wound, high velocity projectile or fragments etc)</p>
<p>Multiple lesions, age extremities, victims were under anticoagulant treatment, medical condition of victims.</p>
<p>4- Out-patient management</p>
<p>Any patient of remarkable trauma or accidents should be assessed in ER. A presumed minor head injury or minor chest trauma may overlook a progressively develop severe lesions.</p>
<p>5- First line treatment</p>
<p><b>a. Initial Stabilization/Therapy</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Primary survey: Immediately stabilize any serious injuries once identified:
        <ul>
<li>Airway (with cervical spine precautions):
                <ul>
<li>Use jaw thrust, suction, oropharyngeal vs. nasopharyngeal airways, and/or McGill forceps.</li>
<li>Rapid sequence intubation: the preferred technique in major trauma; consider ketamine or etomidate to minimize peri-intubation hypotension.</li>
<li>Video laryngoscopy may allow endotracheal intubation with minimal impact on traumatic brain or unstable cervical spine injuries.</li>
<li>Failed airway: Extra glottic device (e.g., laryngeal mask airway) or cricothyroidotomy.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Breathing:
                <ul>
<li>100% oxygen and respiratory monitoring</li>
<li>Pre-oxygenation: 8 deep breaths or 3 min of tidal volume</li>
<li>Tension pneumothorax: (Diagnosed clinically) emergently decompress with needle thoracostomy followed by tube thoracostomy.</li>
<li>Hemothorax: Tube thoracostomy (28F) is usually indicated, if massive hemothorax consider autotransfusion and thoracotomy in the OR.</li>
<li>Open chest wounds: Cover with a 3-sided adherent dressing and consider tube thoracostomy.</li>
<li>Flail segment, pulmonary contusion, burns: Treat respiratory distress with mechanical ventilation (use low tidal volume + PEEP for lung protection)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Circulation:
                <ul>
<li>Place on a cardiac monitor.</li>
<li>Obtain IV access (ideally 2 large-bore peripheral IVs; alternatives include intraosseous lines, central lines, or venous cut down)</li>
<li>Control external bleeding with direct pressure or tourniquets temporarily.</li>
<li>Crystalloid fluid bolus (10–20 cc/kg) is controversial (e.g., allow permissive hypotension)</li>
<li>Replace lost blood with blood products in 1:1:1 ratio of PRBC, FFP, and platelets. (CE, plasma frais congelé, plaquette)</li>
<li>Treat unstable pelvic fractures with pelvic binding.</li>
<li>Consider giving tranexamic acid (TXA) to all patients with hemorrhagic shock, as part of a massive transfusion protocol.</li>
<li>Pericardial tamponade:
                        <ul>
<li>Stable: Emergent pericardiocentesis window</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 185 -->

<ul><li>Unstable; thoracotomy</li><li>Penetrating chest trauma and witnessed arrest: Consider thoracotomy (if an available surgeon); see “algorithm” below.</li></ul><ul><li>Disability:<ul><li>If Glasgow Coma Scale score of ≤ 8 + head injury: Treat elevated intracranial pressure with mannitol or hypertonic saline, controlled ventilation (ideal PCO<sub>2</sub> 30–35 mm Hg), and elevating head to 30 degrees (while maintaining spine immobilization)</li><li>Intracranial bleeding or spinal cord injury: Obtain neurosurgical consultation; high-dose steroids are generally not recommended.</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>b. Emergency department Treatment/Procedures</b></p><p>Emergency department Treatment/Procedures</p><ul><li>Definitive treatment may require emergent surgery or interventional radiology.</li><li>Prompt stabilization, early recognition of the need for operative intervention, and appropriate surgical consultation are paramount.</li><li>Re-evaluation is key to identify occult/delayed injuries.</li></ul><p><b>Medication</b></p><ul><li>Dictated by need for specific interventions.</li><li>TXA (Tranexamic acid) must be given before transfer/arrival to a trauma center in order to meet the time requirement of early administration. The dose is 1 gram of tranexamic acid IV bolus over 10 minutes, followed by 1 gram IV over 8 hours.</li><li>Consider short-acting, hemodynamically neutral medications.</li><li>Consider prophylactic antibiotics in penetrating trauma.</li><li>Ensure an updated tetanus status.</li></ul><p><b>c. Disposition</b></p><p>Admission Criteria</p><ul><li>Many major trauma patients are routinely admitted for observation, monitoring, and re-evaluation.</li><li>Patients with significant injuries or hemodynamic instability should be admitted to the OR/ICU.</li><li>Patients requiring frequent assessments should be admitted to a monitored setting.</li></ul><p>6- Treatment adjustment _Pearls and pitfalls</p><ul><li>In general, severely injured patients (especially those with unstable vital signs) with a potential need for acute surgical intervention should be transported immediately to the nearest major trauma center.</li><li>The ABCs of trauma remain the standard approach to the initial assessment and treatment in major trauma.</li><li>Life-threatening injuries must be immediately stabilized before moving along the primary survey.</li><li>A primary survey should be repeated whenever the patients’ status deteriorates.</li><li>A high level of suspicion for occult injuries should be maintained, with a low threshold for observation and/or advanced imaging.</li><li>Ensure an updated tetanus status.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 186 -->

<h3>7- Algorithm</h3>
<p>Unless obvious signs of death are present in the field, providers in most emergency medical systems continue to transport patients without pulse or respiration to a hospital once cardiopulmonary resuscitation has been initiated.</p>
<p>For patients in traumatic arrest upon arrival to the ED, a critical decision must be made regarding the appropriate level of intervention and, specifically, the use of emergent thoracotomy.</p>
<p>The strongest recommendation for performing ED thoracotomy can be made for patients with penetrating chest trauma with witnessed signs of life during transport to or in the ED and at least cardiac electrical activity upon arrival. There were no survivors among patients with blunt trauma and no respiration or pulse in the field. ED thoracotomy for this group is not indicated (including in the presence of myocardial electrical activity).</p>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ul>
<li>Elder patients</li>
</ul>
<p>Assume that older patients involved in trauma have sustained a significant injury, even if they appear well. The paradox of elder trauma patients is that their physiology and medical interventions can both mask and exacerbate the severity of injuries. Medications are but one example: beta blockers may mask the effects of shock by suppressing tachycardia, while warfarin and other anticoagulants increase the risk of severe hemorrhage.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 188 -->

<h4>• Victims of crime</h4>
<p>Clinical evaluation and treatment of injuries is the foremost responsibility of the clinician caring for a trauma patient. When possible, caretakers should consider and act on the need to preserve potential evidence if the trauma may be connected to a crime. As examples, placing removed clothing into paper bags, avoiding cutting through holes in clothing created by penetrating injuries, and careful documentation of injuries may all be significant.</p>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<p>There are notable disparities in mortality rates for injured patients around the world. For example, one study looked at the mortality rates for all seriously injured adults (injury severity score of 9 or more) in three cities, in countries at different economic levels. The mortality rate (including both pre-hospital and in hospital deaths) rose from 35% in a high-income setting to 55% in a middle-income setting, to 63% in a low-income setting. Considering only patients who survive to reach the hospital, a similar study demonstrated a six-fold increase in mortality for patients with injuries of moderate severity (injury severity score of 15–24). Such mortality increased from 6% in a hospital in a high-income country to 36% in a rural area of a low-income country.</p>
<p>In addition to an excess mortality, there is a tremendous burden of disability from extremity injuries in many developing countries. By comparison, head and spinal cord injuries contribute a greater percentage of disability in high income countries. Much of the disability from extremity injuries in developing countries should be eminently preventable through inexpensive improvements in orthopedic care and rehabilitation.</p>
<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<p>Complications of trauma management may arise from some special situations.</p>
<p>Common pitfalls and ways to avoid them:</p>
<p><b>Esophageal intubations —</b></p>
<p>Between 0.5 and 6 percent of prehospital intubations are esophageal due to airway difficulty or displacement during transport. Verify the position of all endotracheal tubes either by direct visualization or use of an end-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO<sub>2</sub>) detector.</p>
<p><b>Hemorrhagic shock —</b></p>
<p>Approximately 30 percent of the circulating blood volume may be lost before the onset of hypotension. A transient response to one or more fluid boluses means the patient likely has ongoing hemorrhage and is in a persistent state of shock. A high index of suspicion should be maintained and an aggressive search for the source of ongoing hemorrhage is warranted.</p>
<p><b>Cardiac tamponade —</b></p>
<p>Assume that elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP) in a trauma patient is caused by pericardial tamponade. However, hypovolemic patients with tamponade may not have elevated JVP. Perform the FAST exam early in the circulation evaluation of the unstable patient and begin by looking at the heart.</p>
<p><b>Thoracoabdominal injury —</b></p>
<p>Assume that any penetrating wound of the thorax or abdomen involves both compartments until proven otherwise.</p>
<p><b>Penetrating bowel injury —</b></p>
<p>During the initial resuscitation, injuries caused by low velocity penetrating wounds (typically stab wounds) are easily missed by ultrasound, because there is too little intraperitoneal</p>

<!-- PAGE 189 -->

<div><p>blood to be detected, and by CT, because there is inadequate tissue destruction. For stab wounds, high clinical suspicion may warrant further evaluation by laparoscopy, laparotomy, or diagnostic peritoneal tap despite initially negative imaging studies. Alternatively, a trauma surgeon may opt to perform serial observations of patients with abdominal stab wounds (and some extraperitoneal gunshot wounds) over a 12- to 24-hour period.</p><p>Gunshot wounds typically require therapeutic laparotomy and should be distinguished from the aforementioned stab wounds – these high velocity injuries are associated with a much greater morbidity and mortality than their low velocity counterparts.</p><p>Open book pelvic fractures —</p><p>The unstable pelvis should not be manipulated multiple times; additional manipulation exacerbates hemorrhage. Once suspected, open or unstable pelvic fractures should be stabilized using a pelvic binder, or a sheet if no binder is available. If the patient is hemodynamically stable, computed tomography (CT) imaging is obtained. The unstable patient requires either surgery or angiography.</p><p>Ocular injuries —</p><p>Periorbital swelling and ecchymosis do not preclude performing an ocular examination. Patients with such findings are at higher risk of ocular injury. In addition, injuries such as a globe rupture or retro-orbital hematoma must be diagnosed quickly in order to maximize the opportunity to salvage vision.</p><h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3><p>Improved safety standards and programs to minimize injury from vehicular-related events (motor vehicle, motorcycle, bicycle, pedestrian), working places, falls, violence, sports, and recreation provide best prevention against Traumatic injuries.</p><ul><li>Wear helmet while riding two wheelers.</li><li>Do have access to seat belts and air bags while driving. Take good care of children to avoid injuries.</li><li>Do not drive under the influence of alcohol and drugs.</li><li>Maintain safe living areas for seniors.</li></ul><h3>XII. <h1>INITIAL MANAGEMENT OF HEAD TRAUMA</h1>
<p><i>Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. Pen Phallkun, Dr. Kruoch Sophallida, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Head trauma is a broad term describing an external trauma to the craniofacial area of the body from blunt, penetrating, blast, rotational, or acceleration-deceleration forces. Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is often categorized into mild (Glasgow Coma Scale score, 13–15), moderate (GCS score, 9–12), and severe (GCS score, 3–8), but this actually represents a spectrum of injury. Patients with a presentation GCS score of 13–15 who are stable or improving are unlikely to have CT scan findings that warrant intervention</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>The most common principal mechanisms of injury for all age groups includes falls, being struck by or against an object, and motor-vehicle crashes in the civilian population. Gunshot wounds (GSWs) to the head are particularly lethal; the overall mortality rate is estimated to be 90%, with 70% of deaths occurring at the scene. TBIs in Cambodia are on the rise, 34% occur during 5-9pm and 40% during the weekend; while the vast majority is 74% occur as the result of road traffic accidents of which 81% are motorcycle related. Skull fracture is the most common diagnosis, where frontal lobe hematomas most commonly involved, resulting the ratio of subdural to epidural is 1:1.05<sup>1</sup>.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<p><b>Direct injury.</b> Direct head trauma occurs when the head is struck, or its motion is suddenly arrested, by an object. The resulting damage to the skull and brain depends on the consistency, mass, surface area, and velocity of the object striking the head. Direct injury can also be caused by compression of the head.</p>
<p><b>Indirect injury.</b> In indirect brain injury, the cranial contents are set into motion by forces other than the direct contact of the skull with an object. A common example is an acceleration- deceleration injury in which no direct mechanical impact is sustained, but the cranial contents are set into vigorous motion. As the bridging subdural vessels are strained, subdural hematomas (SDHs) may result.</p>
<p>Besides these two patterns of head injuries, there are more causes such as: penetrant head trauma, scalp wounds, skull fracture (linear fractures, depressed fractures and basilar fractures), extra-axial injury (epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma, traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage, subdural hygroma) and intra-axial injury (diffuse axonal injury, cerebral contusion, intracerebral hematoma and intracerebellar hematoma).</p>
<h2>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Cerebral hemodynamics and increased intracranial pressure</p>
<p><sup>1</sup>Reference: <a href="https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30790736/">https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30790736/</a></p>

<!-- PAGE 191 -->

<div><p>The brain has an extremely high metabolic rate, accounting for approximately 20% of the entire oxygen consumption of the body and requiring approximately 15% of total cardiac output. Hypertension, alkalosis, and hypocarbia promote cerebral vasoconstriction, whereas hypotension, acidosis, and hypercarbia cause cerebral vasodilation. Cerebral Perfusion Pressure (CPP) defines by: CCP = MAP – ICP</p><p>If CPP falls below 40 mm Hg, autoregulation is lost and cerebral blood flow (CBF) declines, resulting in tissue ischemia and altered cerebral metabolism. Avoidance of hypotension or elevation in ICP in the head- injured patient helps ensure that CPP can be maintained. The recommended target CPP value is between 60 and 70 mm Hg.</p><p>Cushing reflex</p><p>Progressive hypertension associated with bradycardia and diminished respiratory effort is a specific response to acute, potentially lethal increases in ICP. This response is called Cushing reflex or Cushing phenomenon, and its occurrence indicates that the ICP has reached life- threatening levels. However, only one- third of cases of life- threatening increased ICP manifest the full triad of hypertension, bradycardia, and respiratory irregularity</p><h3>V. DIAGNOSIS</h3><p><b>Physical examination:</b></p><p>In the setting of head trauma and suspected brain injury, management should be guided by the principles of trauma resuscitation. A primary survey focusing on airway, breathing, and hemorrhage control should be performed expeditiously. After immediate life threats are adequately addressed, a secondary survey should evaluate for underlying head injury, brain injury, and neurologic compromise.</p><p><b>Acute Neurologic Examination:</b></p><p>The goals of the acute neurologic assessment of head trauma patients include detection of life- threatening injuries and identification of neurologic changes in the immediate post-trauma period. An efficient neurologic examination in the emergency setting includes evaluation of mental status, GCS score, pupillary size and responsiveness, and motor strength and symmetry.</p><table><caption>Table 1: Glasgow Coma Scale</caption><thead><tr><th colspan="3">Glasgow Coma Scale</th></tr><tr><th>Response</th><th>Score</th><th>Significance</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td colspan="3"><strong>Eyes opening</strong></td></tr><tr><td>Spontaneously</td><td>4</td><td>Reticular activating system intact; patient may not be aware</td></tr><tr><td>To verbal command</td><td>3</td><td>Opens eyes when told to do so</td></tr><tr><td>To pain</td><td>2</td><td>Opens eyes in response to pain</td></tr><tr><td>No eyes opening</td><td>1</td><td>Does not open eyes to any stimuli</td></tr><tr><td colspan="3"><strong>Verbal Stimuli</strong></td></tr><tr><td>Oriented, converses</td><td>5</td><td>Relatively intact CNS, aware of self and environment</td></tr><tr><td>Disoriented, converses</td><td>4</td><td>Well- articulated, organized, but disoriented</td></tr><tr><td>Inappropriate words</td><td>3</td><td></td></tr><tr><td>Incomprehensible</td><td>2</td><td>Random exclamatory words</td></tr><tr><td>No verbal response</td><td>1</td><td>Moaning, no recognizable words</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

<!-- PAGE 192 -->

<table><thead><tr><th colspan="2"></th><th>No response or intubated</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td colspan="3">Motor response</td></tr><tr><td>Obey verbal commands</td><td>6</td><td>Readily moves limbs when told to</td></tr><tr><td>Localizes to painful stimuli</td><td>5</td><td>Moves limb in an effort to remove painful stimuli</td></tr><tr><td>Flexion withdrawal</td><td>4</td><td>Pulls away from pain in flexion</td></tr><tr><td>Abnormal flexion</td><td>3</td><td>Decorticate rigidity</td></tr><tr><td>Extension</td><td>2</td><td>Decerebrate rigidity</td></tr><tr><td>No motor response</td><td>1</td><td>Hypotonia, flaccid—suggests loss of medullary function or concomitant spinal cord injury</td></tr></tbody></table><p><i>Mild TBI: GCS of 13-15, Moderate TBI: GCS of 9-12 and Severe TBI: GCS of 3-8</i></p><h3>Investigations</h3><p>Laboratory tests: Routine laboratory tests are generally not needed for patients with isolated mild TBI in the acute setting, except for a bedside glucose test in patients with altered mental status and determination of the blood alcohol level in patients suspected of alcohol intoxication and head trauma. Suspicion of systemic pathology as the cause of the head trauma, such as when a diabetic patient sustains an moto vehicle collision (MVC) after losing consciousness from hypoglycemia, warrants directed testing for culprit conditions. Coagulation studies are indicated in patients with coagulopathies (e.g., hemophilia, Von Willebrand disease), suspected liver disease, and those on anticoagulants.</p><h3>Neuroimaging</h3><p>Skull radiography: skull radiography after head trauma has long been replaced by cranial CT, which is the cornerstone of imaging for acute head trauma. Skull radiographs for adults with either mild or severe TBI are not recommended.</p><p>Computed tomography: Noncontrast CT of the head is the diagnostic standard for identifying intracranial injury in the ED. This scan delineates acute intra-axial and extra-axial bleeding, cerebral swelling, ischemic infarction caused by hypoxia after trauma, evidence of increased ICP, and pneumocephalus. It is sensitive for demonstrating mass effect, ventricular size and configuration, bone injuries, and acute hemorrhage, regardless of location (i.e., parenchymal, subarachnoid, subdural, or epidural spaces).</p>

<h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<p>In the context of trauma, conditions presenting with an altered loss of consciousness (LOC) include seizures, intoxication with alcohol or drugs, and systemic trauma resulting in hypoxemia or hypoperfusion. Sedatives or motor function may be altered by neuromuscular blocking agents administered prior to ED arrival. Head trauma may result in confounding injuries to other parts of the head or neck, including skull or facial bone fractures, cervical spine or spinal cord injuries, eye injuries, otolaryngeal injuries, and damage to blood vessels within the neck. LOC can be also caused by stroke, spontaneous acute subdural hematoma, cerebral aneurysms, brain metastasis, hydrocephalus, or Alzheimer disease.</p>
<p>With age, the brain atrophies and creates more space within the cranial vault for blood to accumulate, so older adults can have significant hemorrhage and not show signs of deterioration.</p>
<h4>VII. MANAGEMENT</h4>
<h5><b>Out- of- Hospital Care</b></h5>
<p>The out- of- hospital management of the head- injured patient should focus on preventing or minimizing secondary brain injury specifically on the major systemic insults of hypotension, hypoxia and hypocarbia. Interventions should be aimed at maintenance of oxygenation and prevention of hypocarbia through appropriate airway management, supplemental oxygen as needed, and controlled ventilation. Hypotension should be avoided through directed fluid resuscitation and control of hemorrhage.</p>
<h5><b>Emergency Department Management</b></h5>
<p><b>Airway:</b> The airway should be secured early to protect against aspiration and prevent secondary brain injury as a result of hypoxia or hypercarbia.</p>

<!-- PAGE 194 -->

<div><p>Hypotension: Systemic hypotension has profound implications for neurologic outcomes. As such, fluids or blood transfusion should be delivered to maintain a blood pressure as close to normal as possible, with a SBP of at least 110 mm Hg for those 15 to 49 and over 70 years of age, and at least <b>100 mm Hg</b> for those 50 to 69 years old.</p><p>Brain-directed osmotic therapies should be reserved for patients with signs of transtentorial herniation or progressive neurologic deterioration not attributable to extracranial causes. If there are signs of impending herniation syndrome, such as deepening coma, a newly asymmetric pupil, or other substantially diminishing neurologic parameters, osmotic diuretics, such as mannitol is recommended.</p><p>Hyperventilation: hyperventilation was recommended as a method to reduce ICP. However, this reduction in ICP is accomplished by reducing CBF, which is important in meeting the brain's metabolic demands. A low Paco2, and the resulting lower CBF, may result in cerebral ischemia, whereas high Paco2 levels can result in cerebral hyperemia and high ICP. Normal ventilation is currently the goal for severe TBI patients in the absence of cerebral herniation, and Paco2 should be maintained in the normal range of 35 to 45 mm Hg.</p><p>Cranial decompression: In patients with impending herniation who do not respond to first-line therapies, cranial decompression may temporarily reverse or arrest the herniation syndrome.</p><h3>Algorithm</h3><div><p>Primary survey and resuscitation</p><p>Assess severity of head Injury<br/>Calculate GCS</p><table border="1"><tbody><tr><td>Mild head injury without risk factors*<br/>(GCS=15)</td><td>Mild head injury with other risk factors*<br/>(GCS= 14-15)</td><td>Moderate head injury<br/>(GCS = 9-163)</td><td>Severe head injury<br/>(GCS = 3-8)</td></tr><tr><td><ul><li>Complete secondary survey</li><li>If no other injuries and acting normally, may be discharged</li></ul></td><td><ul><li>Complete secondary survey</li><li>Observe for up to 4 hours post injury</li><li>Treat with simple analgesic</li><li>Consider anti-emetic</li><li>A persistent headache or vomiting requires further observation.</li><li>May be discharged if return to normal conscious state and tolerate oral fluid</li></ul></td><td><ul><li>Consult senior clinician or neurosurgical team</li><li>Urgent CT head +/- cervical spine</li><li>Complete secondary survey</li><li>Ensure early specialist consultation</li></ul></td><td><ul><li>Trauma call</li><li>Consider intubation</li><li>Maintain circulation and cerebral perfusion</li><li>Treat signs of raise intra cranial pressure</li><li>Consult neurosurgical team</li><li>Urgent CT head +/- cervical spine</li><li>Complete secondary survey</li></ul></td></tr></tbody></table></div></div>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<p>Mild Traumatic Brain Injury and Sports- Related Concussion: Athletes with a concussive head injury should be immediately removed from play and not return until they have been evaluated by a health care provider with expertise in concussion management. There should be a gradual stepwise increase in physical activity. Anticoagulated patients: there is a higher incidence of intracranial bleeding in TBI patients on anticoagulants following head trauma, with an incidence of up to 22% in patients. patients taking anticoagulation with intracranial lesions should be managed with reversal of anticoagulation like vitamin K or fresh frozen plasma, where patient with a negative initial head CT scan do not need to have their anticoagulation reversed.</p>
<p>Head trauma in older adult: older patients have increased morbidity and mortality from TBI and have higher rates of intracranial injuries following head trauma The presence of comorbid medical conditions, use of anticoagulants, preexisting cognitive deficits, polypharmacy, alcohol consumption, and unique physiology of the aging brain make it challenging for the emergency clinician to detect brain injury.</p>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<p>The ultimate survival and neurologic outcome of the brain-injured patient depends on the extent of TBI occurring at the time of injury (primary injury) and the subsequent effects of systemic insults (secondary injuries), such as those caused by hypotension and hypoxia. Thus, clinical care of patients with TBI emphasizes early management to minimize the occurrence of secondary brain injury. Emergency clinicians can influence the incidence and severity of primary brain injury through injury prevention programs.</p>
<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<p>The complications of head trauma are divided into two main outcomes:</p>
<p><b>Central Nervous System Infections:</b> meningitis after basilar fractures (caused by variety of microbes but early meningitis within 3 days injury of CSF usually caused by Pneumococci), brain abscess (after penetrant injury) and cranial osteomyelitis.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 196 -->

<div><p>Medical complications: Disseminated intravascular coagulation, respiratory complication and cardiac dysfunction.</p><h4>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h4><p>All patients with moderate to severe head trauma require imaging to determine the extent and nature of the brain injury and necessity of neurosurgical intervention. Neurosurgical consultation should be obtained as soon as possible to help direct the patient's subsequent management.</p><p>In patients with persistent symptoms of headache, confusion, or memory difficulties, delayed MRI may define lesions in the regions related to cognition that cannot be seen on CT. Although not useful in the emergency setting, MRI has prognostic value during subsequent care and assists in directing the future rehabilitation of these patients</p><h4>XII. <h1>INITIAL MANAGEMENT OF CHEST TRAUMA</h1>
<p><i>Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. KRUOCH Sophallida, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak</i></p>
<h2>I. INTRODUCTION</h2>
<p>Chest trauma is any form of injury to the chest including ribs, heart and lungs, great vessels, trachea and esophagus. Chest injuries are potentially life-threatening because of immediate disturbances of cardiorespiratory physiology, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, airway obstruction, and uncontrolled hemorrhage. Care of severe thoracic trauma is multidisciplinary in nature, involving trauma surgeons, cardiothoracic surgeons, and intensivists. Improved understanding of underlying physiologic mechanisms, newer imaging modalities, minimally invasive approaches, and pharmacologic therapies have contributed to decreasing morbidity and mortality in patients with thoracic injuries.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Chest trauma is a major cause of death and disability in Asia. In 2019, an estimated 1.2 million people died from chest trauma worldwide, and Asia accounted for 40% of these deaths. The most common causes of chest trauma in Asia are road traffic accidents, falls, and assaults.</p>
<p>Approximately 75% of patients with thoracic trauma require only simple tube thoracostomy and volume resuscitation, and the initial care and disposition of these patients is usually performed by emergency clinicians.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<p>It is either blunt or penetrating. Blunt chest trauma results from sudden compression or positive pressure inflicted to chest wall. Penetrating trauma occurs when a foreign object penetrates to the chest wall. Injury location and type dictates both assessment and management.</p>
<h2>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Life-threatening injuries are often resulted from chest trauma throughout one or more pathologic mechanisms. There are:</p>
<ul>
<li>Hypoxemia from disrupting of the airway: injury to the lung parenchyma, rib cage and respiratory musculature, massive hemorrhage, collapsed lung, and pneumothorax.</li>
<li>Hypovolemia from massive fluid loss from great vessels, cardiac rupture, or hemothorax.</li>
<li>Cardiac failure from cardiac tamponade, cardiac contusion, or increased intrathoracic pressure.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 198 -->

<div>
<p>Hypoxemia, hypovolemia &amp; cardiac failure</p>
<p>↓</p>
<p>Result in Impaired ventilation and perfusion</p>
<p>↓</p>
<p>Leading to acute respiratory failure &amp; hypovolemic shock and death</p>
</div>
<h3>V. DIAGNOSIS</h3>
<h4>Clinical manifestation</h4>
<ul>
<li><b>Respiratory</b>
<ul>
<li>Dyspnea, respiratory distress</li>
<li>Cough with or without hemoptysis</li>
<li>Cyanosis of mouth, face, nail beds, mucous membrane</li>
<li>Tracheal deviation</li>
<li>Audible air escaping from chest wound</li>
<li>Decreased breath sound on side of injury</li>
<li>Decreased O2 saturation</li>
<li>Frothy secretion</li>
<li>Bruising, abrasion, subcutaneous emphysema</li>
<li>Asymmetric chest movement</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Cardiovascular</b>
<ul>
<li>Tachycardia, decreased blood pressure, narrow pulse pressure</li>
<li>Asymmetric blood pressure values in both arms</li>
<li>Distended neck vein</li>
<li>Muffled heart sound</li>
<li>Chest pain</li>
<li>Dysrhythmia</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h4>Investigation</h4>
<ul>
<li>Assessment of hemodynamic stability and <b>ABC</b> approach (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) before proceeding the secondary survey</li>
<li><b>History taking</b> to assess time and mechanism of the injury</li>
<li><b>Physical examination</b> (head-to-toe examination) to find any signs and symptoms of chest injury:
        <ul>
<li>Abdominal and chest tenderness</li>
<li>Chest wall bruising and swelling</li>
<li>Decreased lung sound, wheezing</li>
<li>Rapid pulse and rapid breathing</li>
<li>Chest crepitation</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 199 -->

<ul><li>Cyanosis and dyspnea</li><li>Imaging<ul><li><b>Chest Radiography:</b> evaluate for pneumothorax, tension pneumothorax, hemothorax, chest wall fractures, and pulmonary contusion.</li><li><b>Focused assessment sonography in trauma (FAST) examination:</b> evaluated for hemothorax, cardiac tamponade and will assist in diagnosis of abdominal injury.</li><li><b>CT of chest, abdomen and pelvic</b> (for stable patients only): higher sensitivity than chest x-ray for detection of acute traumatic chest injuries however, obtaining a chest CT requires transportation out of the ED. Performing with IV contrast, is a rapid and reliable imaging for laceration and contusion.</li><li><b>Pulse oximetry:</b> is helpful to assess adequacy of oxygenation and need for supplemental O2</li><li><b>EKG:</b> An EKG may be helpful in patients with blunt chest to help elucidate a cause of the accident.</li><li><b>CT angiography or MRI</b></li></ul></li><li>Laboratory test: Blood testing, including ABG, does not have much utility in making the diagnosis of any of the conditions listed above.<ul><li>Complete blood count (CBC)</li><li>Type and cross-match</li><li>Arterial blood gas (ABG)</li><li>Cardiac enzymes</li><li>Coagulation profile</li></ul></li></ul><h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4><p>There are two classifications:<br/>Immediate life-threatening injuries (Lethal Six) and Potential life-threatening injuries (Hidden Six)</p><ul><li><b>Immediate life-threatening injuries (Lethal Six)</b><br/>Fetal if they are not recognized and treated immediately<ul><li>Airway obstruction</li><li>Tension pneumothorax</li><li>Open pneumothorax (sucking chest wound)</li><li>Massive hemothorax</li><li>Flail chest</li><li>Cardiac tamponade</li></ul></li><li><b>Potential life-threatening injuries (Hidden Six)</b><ul><li>Cardiac contusion</li><li>Aortic disruption</li><li>Diaphragmatic rupture</li><li>Esophageal injury</li><li>Pulmonary contusion</li><li>Tracheobronchial injuries</li></ul></li></ul>

<h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2>
<p>All trauma patients must be managed as following protocols:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>A (Airway with c-spine protection):</b> Is the patient speaking in full sentences?</li>
<li><b>B (Breathing and Ventilation):</b> Is the breathing labored? Are symmetrical, breath sounds present bilaterally?</li>
<li><b>C (Circulation with hemorrhage control):</b> Are pulses present and symmetric? How does the patient's skin appear? (cold clammy, warm well-perfused)</li>
<li><b>D (Disability):</b> What is their GCS scale? Are they moving all extremities?</li>
<li><b>E (Exposure/Environmental Control):</b> Completely expose the patient. Is rectal tone present? Is there any gross blood per rectum?</li>
</ul>
<h3>Initial intervention:</h3>
<ul>
<li><b>IV</b> – 2 large-bore (minimum 18 Gauge) Antecubital IV</li>
<li><b>O2</b> – Nasal cannula, Face Mask</li>
<li><b>Monitor:</b> Place the patient on a cardiac monitor.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Specific management</h3>
<ul>
<li><b>Hemothorax:</b> is an accumulation of fluid in the pleural space after blunt or penetrating traumatic chest injury. Most commonly finding on clinical examination is the diminution or absent breath sound of affected side.
        <ul>
<li><b>Pleural tapping:</b> removal of pleural fluid</li>
<li><b>Chest tube insertion:</b> to drain excess fluid</li>
<li>Oxygen support</li>
<li>Maintaining of tissue perfusion</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<div style="text-align: center;">
<img alt="Two chest X-rays illustrating Hemothorax. The left image shows normal lung fields. The right image shows a large area of opacity (fluid collection) in the left hemithorax, indicated by arrows."/>
<p>Hemothorax</p>
</div>
<ul>
<li><b>Flail Chest:</b> Loss of stability of chest wall as the result of multiple rib fractures, or combined rib and sternum fractures. It is called paradoxical movement when three or more adjacent ribs are fractured at two points
        <ul>
<li>Stabilize the flail portion of the chest with hands</li>
<li>Apply a pressure dressing and turn the patient on the injured side</li>
<li>Analgésia
                <ul>
<li>Ketamine: 0.1–0.3 mg/kg IV</li>
<li>Fentanyl: (Short-acting): 0.25–2 mcg/kg IV</li>
<li>Morphine: (Intermediate-acting): 0.1 mg/kg IV</li>
<li>Lidocaine: (Topical for chest tubes): &lt;6 mg/kg SQ</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<ul><li>Thoracic epidural analgesia</li><li>Intercostal nerve blocks</li><li>others:<ul><li>Monitored by serial chest Xray daily</li><li>Arterial blood gas analysis</li><li>Pulse oximetry</li><li>Bedside pulmonary function test</li></ul></li></ul><div><img alt="Chest X-ray showing a flail chest, indicated by a red oval highlighting the area of multiple rib fractures."/><p>Flail Chest</p></div><ul><li><b>Rib Fracture:</b> is often a clinical diagnosis, with severe point tenderness, bony crepitus, ecchymosis, and muscle spasm over the rib. Simple rib fracture account for more than 50% for non-penetrating trauma which heal in 3-6 weeks.<ul><li>To control pain<ul><li>Intercostal nerve block</li><li>Ice cover over the fracture site</li><li>Sedation:<ul><li>Ketamine: 1–3 mg/kg IV</li><li>Etomidate: 0.3 mg/kg IV</li><li>Midazolam: 0.05 mg/kg IV</li></ul></li><li>Epidural analgesia</li></ul></li><li>Avoiding excessive activity</li><li>Treating any associated injuries</li><li><b>Surgical fixation:</b> is rarely necessary unless fragments are grossly displaced.</li></ul></li></ul>

<ul>
<li><b>Pneumothorax:</b> accumulation of air in the pleural space, result in 10-15% of chest trauma patients.
        <ul>
<li>Asymptomatic patient with negative initial imaging can be safely observe for 6 hours.</li>
<li>For moderate and large pneumothorax, chest tube should be placed.</li>
<li>In patient with open pneumothorax defect should be covered immediately. Positive-pressure ventilation can then be initiated, if needed, without the fear of producing a tension pneumothorax, and the patient can be prepared for definitive surgical repair.</li>
<li>In tension pneumothorax: needle thoracostomy (2<sup>nd</sup> intercostal space of mid-clavicular line) or tube thoracostomy (5<sup>th</sup> intercostal space of anterior-axillary line)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<h4>Pregnancy consideration:</h4>
<ul>
<li>In pregnant patients, remember to use the least amount of radiation available and to shield the uterus during imaging when possible</li>
<li>Take note of the differences in anatomy of the thoracic cavity in pregnant patients, as well as differences in lab values, intravascular volume, and cardiovascular physiology</li>
</ul>
<h4>Pediatric Considerations</h4>
<ul>
<li>The rib cage is highly elastic in children and can withstand significant forces without overt signs of external trauma and can underestimate even major intrathoracic injuries</li>
<li>Retrospective studies have proposed limiting chest CT in pediatric trauma to patients with a vehicle-related mechanism or an abnormal CXR</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Chest trauma patients can present with several conditions each of which can be acutely life threatening; a majority of these conditions can be clinically diagnosed and treated during the primary survey.</li>
<li>Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, chest x rays are not indicated for making this diagnosis.</li>
<li>Bedside ultrasonography can be extremely useful for diagnosing acute traumatic chest conditions.</li>
<li>Only hemodynamically stable patients should be sent for advanced imaging such as CT scan.</li>
<li>ED thoracotomies are reserved for patients presenting with traumatic arrest secondary to penetrating chest trauma only</li>
</ul>
<h3>X. COMPLICATION</h3>
<ul>
<li>Chest wall injury
        <ul>
<li>Sucking wound and open pneumothorax</li>
<li>Ribs-pain, hemothorax, flail chest, deformed chest, respiratory distress.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Lung injury
        <ul>
<li>Lung contusion, hemopneumothorax</li>
<li>Emphysema thoracis</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Major airway injury (surgical emphysema, massive hemothorax)</li>
<li>Esophageal injury
        <ul>
<li>Mediastinitis, sepsis, septicemia, pneumothorax</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<h1>ACUTE ABDOMINAL SYNDROME</h1>
<p><i>Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Prof. CHHUOY Meng,<br/>Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun,<br/>Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry,<br/>Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha,<br/>Dr. TES Sovannara.</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Acute abdominal syndrome refers to the sudden onset of severe abdominal pain, often signaling a potentially life-threatening condition. This syndrome encompasses a broad range of medical and surgical emergencies that require prompt diagnosis and intervention. The pain may arise from various abdominal organs such as the stomach, intestines, liver, pancreas, kidneys, or reproductive organs.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Acute abdominal syndrome is a common presentation in emergency departments worldwide, representing a significant proportion of emergency medical and surgical admissions. Its epidemiology varies depending on the underlying cause, age group, gender, and geographic location.</p>
<p>The incidence and Prevalence of acute abdominal pain accounts for approximately 5–10% of emergency department visits globally. Appendicitis 7–10%, Cholecystitis about 3–4% and is more prevalent in middle-aged adults, particularly in women, Pancreatitis about 1–2% of cases, with a higher prevalence among individuals with gallstones or alcohol use disorder, Bowel Obstruction around 2–4% of acute abdominal emergencies, more common in older adults.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<ol>
<li>Surgical causes:
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Cause</th>
<th>Diagnostic clue</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Appendicitis (Acute appendicitis)</td>
<td>Common. Laboratory parameters indicating acute inflammation usually increased, but not necessarily yet in the initial phase.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Intestinal obstruction</td>
<td>Surgical scars, hernias, possible malignancy. Initially undulating pain; development of strangulation: a suspicion of this is an indication for surgery.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Perforated peptic ulcer</td>
<td>Acute onset, peritonism. Often the first symptom of peptic ulcer disease. Pain starts in the upper abdomen</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Acute cholecystitis (Cholelithiasis)</td>
<td>Colicky pain in the right costal arch, clear tenderness on palpation, clinical manifestations of an infection. Ultrasonography. Pain becomes constant as the cholecystitis progresses. Often the first symptom of gallstone disease.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</li>
</ol>

<table><tbody><tr><td>Acute pancreatitis (Acute pancreatitis)</td><td>History of alcohol consumption. Consider gallstones as possible etiology. Urine and serum amylase may be normal in chronic or recurrent cases.</td></tr><tr><td>Mesenterial thrombosis</td><td>May be difficult to diagnose on the basis of clinical manifestations; often resembles strangulation. Clear peritonitis is initially absent but the patient is obviously ill. The patient usually has atrial fibrillation or some other cardiovascular disease.</td></tr><tr><td>Complicated diverticulitis of the colon (Diverticulitis and diverticulosis)</td><td>The most common site is the sigmoid colon. Peritonitis or abscess, clear local tenderness, low-grade fever and increased inflammation parameters. Ileus and intestinal bleeding are possible.</td></tr><tr><td>Volvulus</td><td>Sigma is the most common site. Symptoms of intestinal obstruction (risk for perforation!). Plain abdominal X-ray is diagnostic. Volvulus of the caecum develops more slowly.</td></tr><tr><td>Testis torsion</td><td>The testis is tender on palpation. Often pain and tenderness in lower abdomen. Doppler ultrasonography. In an unclear case, explorative surgery should be readily performed.</td></tr></tbody></table><p>2.
