The etiology of acute lower abdominal pain in a young woman is often revealed on laparoscopy.</td></tr><tr><td>Myoma</td><td>Torsion; necrosis; bleeding into the abdominal cavity, infection</td></tr><tr><td>Endometriosis (Endometriosis)</td><td>Menstrual pain</td></tr></tbody></table><p>3. Non-surgical causes for acute abdomen</p><ul><li>☒ Metabolic disorders:</li><li>☒ Infectious causes:</li><li>☒ Referred pain:</li><li>☒ Immunological disorder:</li></ul><p>4. Other Causes</p>

<!-- PAGE 208 -->

<h4>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4>
<p>Acute abdominal syndrome (AAS) encompasses a variety of conditions that lead to severe abdominal pain and can arise from multiple underlying pathophysiological mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for accurate diagnosis and management.</p>
<ol>
<li><b>Inflammation</b>
<ul>
<li>Appendicitis: Inflammation of the appendix due to obstruction (often by fecalith) leads to swelling, necrosis, and potential perforation.</li>
<li>Cholecystitis: Inflammation of the gallbladder typically caused by bile duct obstruction (often by gallstones) results in increased pressure and inflammation.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Mechanical Obstruction</b>
<p>Bowel Obstruction: Can be due to adhesions, hernias, or tumors, leading to distension, ischemia, and potential perforation. Increased intraluminal pressure causes pain and can lead to bowel ischemia.</p>
</li>
<li><b>Ischemia</b>
<p>Mesenteric Ischemia: Reduced blood flow to the intestines (due to embolism or thrombosis) leads to ischemia and can result in tissue necrosis. Symptoms often include severe, sudden abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings.</p>
</li>
<li><b>Perforation</b>
<p>Perforated Viscus: Conditions like peptic ulcers or diverticulitis can lead to perforation, resulting in spillage of intestinal contents into the peritoneal cavity, leading to peritonitis and severe inflammation.</p>
</li>
<li><b>Visceral Pain:</b> the abdominal organs have visceral innervation, and inflammation or injury triggers the release of mediators (like prostaglandins) that activate pain receptors. This can lead to referred pain, where the patient feels discomfort in areas not directly involved.</li>
<li><b>Infection</b>
<p>Conditions like diverticulitis can lead to localized infection, resulting in abscess formation and systemic inflammatory responses. This can progress to sepsis if not addressed promptly.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<ol>
<li><b>History</b>
<p>The history should include a complete description of the patient's pain and associated symptoms. Medical, surgical, and social history should also be sought as this may provide important information.</p>
</li>
<li><b>Physical examination</b>
<p>Before the complete physical examination, take a few moments to gain the patient's trust by explaining what needs to be done, exposing only what needs to be seen, and re-covering exposed parts of the body sequentially. Provide patient privacy. Note the patient's skin (color, temperature, turgor, perfusion status), and perform a targeted heart and lung examination.</p>
<ul>
<li>General examination</li>
<li>Inspection of the abdomen</li>
<li>Palpation of the abdomen</li>
<li>Palpation of the genitals</li>
<li>Auscultation of the abdomen</li>
<li>Touch per rectum</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 209 -->

<h3>3. Symptoms and clinical diagnostic</h3>
<p>Acute abdominal syndrome refers to a collection of symptoms and clinical findings associated with various conditions that cause sudden, severe abdominal pain. These conditions range from surgical emergencies like appendicitis and bowel perforation to medical conditions like pancreatitis and diverticulitis. The clinical presentation and symptoms can vary depending on the underlying cause, but some common features are shared.</p>
<ul>
<li>Severe Abdominal Pain ♦ Nausea and Vomiting ♦ Fever:</li>
<li>Abdominal Distension: typically associated with bowel obstruction or ascites. The abdomen may feel firm and tender upon palpation.</li>
<li>Guarding and Rebound Tenderness:</li>
<li>Altered Bowel Habits: diarrhea or constipation can occur depending on the underlying condition. Diarrhea is common in gastroenteritis, while constipation or obstipation can suggest a bowel obstruction.</li>
<li>Shock Symptoms (Tachycardia, Hypotension): hypovolemic shock or septic shock</li>
<li>Urinary Symptoms: conditions like kidney stones or urinary tract infections can present with lower abdominal pain, sometimes accompanied by hematuria (blood in urine) or dysuria (painful urination).</li>
<li>Referred Pain:</li>
<li>Jaundice may accompany cholecystitis or pancreatitis, indicating possible biliary obstruction or hepatocellular damage.</li>
</ul>
<h3>4. Paraclinical examination</h3>
<p>The choices of paraclinical examination depend on clinical setting (esp. severity of pain, rapidity of onset) and may include complete blood count, serum electrolytes, coagulation parameters, serum glucose, and biochemical tests of liver, kidney, and pancreatic function.</p>
<ul>
<li>Complete Blood count (CBC): Infection: Elevated white blood cell with elevated neutrophilia or with elevated lymphocyte</li>
<li>Biochemistry: Elevated CRP (Infection)</li>
<li>chest x-ray to determine the presence of diseases involving heart, lung, mediastinum, and pleura.</li>
<li>electrocardiogram is helpful to exclude referred pain from cardiac diseases.</li>
<li>plain abdominal radiographs to evaluate bowel displacement, intestinal distention, fluid and gas pattern, free peritoneal air, liver size, and abdominal calcifications.</li>
<li>Abdominal ultrasonography to visualize biliary ducts, gallbladder, liver, pancreas, and kidneys. Optimal utilization of ultrasound depends on the suspected clinical diagnosis and location of pain. For nonlocalized abdominal pain, ultrasound is generally considered to be less sensitive and specific than computed tomography. For right upper quadrant pain, ultrasound of the abdomen is the sole imaging modality assigned to the highest category of appropriateness.</li>
<li>CT to identify masses, abscesses, evidence of inflammation (bowel wall thickening, mesenteric “stranding,” lymphadenopathy, appendicitis), aortic aneurysm; barium contrast radiographs (barium swallow, upper GI series, small-bowel follow-through, barium enema).</li>
<li>Others: upper GI endoscopy, sigmoidoscopy, or colonoscopy; cholangiography (endoscopic, percutaneous, or via MRI), angiography (direct or via CT or MRI), and radionuclide scanning, Arterial blood gas, Liver function test, Kidney function test, Amylase test.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 210 -->

<h2>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h2><p>Acute abdominal syndrome can arise from a wide range of medical, surgical, and gynecological conditions. A comprehensive differential diagnosis is crucial to identifying the underlying cause, as conditions can vary from benign to life-threatening.</p><ul><li>Appendicitis: RLQ pain, presenting with nausea, anorexia, fever, and tenderness at McBurney's point.</li><li>Cholecystitis: RUQ pain, fever, nausea, and a positive Murphy's sign</li><li>Pancreatitis: Epigastric or LUQ pain radiating to the back, associated with nausea, vomiting, and elevated serum lipase/amylase levels.</li><li>Meckel's Diverticulitis: Congenital abnormality causing RLQ pain, often with bleeding or obstruction.</li><li>Hepatitis: RUQ pain, jaundice, and malaise.</li><li>Peptic ulcer disease: Epigastric or RUQ pain, worsened by meals, associated with nausea, and possibly melena (if ulcer bleeds).</li><li>Liver abscess: RUQ pain with fever and malaise, often due to bacterial infection or parasitic disease (e.g., amoebiasis).</li><li>Biliary colic: Intermittent RUQ pain due to gallstones, often postprandial (after meals).</li><li>Ovarian Cyst Rupture or Torsion: Severe RLQ pain in females, sometimes with nausea and vomiting, and possible peritoneal signs.</li><li>Splenic Infarction or Rupture: Acute LUQ pain, often following trauma or related to conditions like sickle cell disease or mononucleosis.</li><li>Gastric Ulcer: Epigastric or LUQ pain, worsened by meals, possibly with hematemesis or melena.</li><li>Diverticulitis: Inflammation of diverticula in the colon, presenting with LLQ pain, fever, and altered bowel habits (constipation or diarrhea).</li><li>Sigmoid Volvulus: Twisting of the sigmoid colon, causing LLQ pain, distension, and constipation.</li><li>Ovarian Pathologies (in females): Conditions like ovarian cysts or ectopic pregnancy.</li><li>Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD): Epigastric or retrosternal burning pain, often after meals, with associated heartburn.</li><li>Peritonitis: Generalized abdominal pain with guarding and rebound tenderness, often secondary to perforation of an organ (e.g., gastric ulcer, appendix).</li><li>Bowel Obstruction: Diffuse crampy pain, abdominal distension, vomiting, and inability to pass gas or stools.</li><li>Mesenteric Ischemia: Severe abdominal pain disproportionate to physical findings, commonly in elderly patients with cardiovascular disease, due to bowel ischemia.</li><li>Renal Colic: Severe, cramping flank pain radiating to the groin, associated with hematuria, caused by kidney stones (nephrolithiasis).</li><li>Pyelonephritis: Infection of the kidney, presenting with fever, flank pain, and dysuria.</li><li>Cystitis: Bladder infection causing suprapubic pain, dysuria, and frequency.</li><li>Ectopic Pregnancy: Lower abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and hemodynamic instability, especially in women of childbearing age.</li><li>Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID): Lower abdominal pain, often bilateral, with fever and vaginal discharge, due to ascending infection from the reproductive tract.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 211 -->

<div>
<p>- Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA) Rupture: Sudden, severe abdominal or back pain, with hypotension and pulsatile abdominal mass, more common in older male.</p>
<h3>VII. MANAGEMENT</h3>
<p>The acute abdomen consists of several intrabdominal processes that require rapid intervention in both diagnosis and treatment. An acute abdomen may present in an obvious or subtle manner, but must always be recognized. Rapid, appropriate testing and concomitant resuscitative therapy are mandatory. If the condition is even possibly surgical, early consultation with a surgeon is mandatory as well.</p>
<p>The management of acute abdominal syndrome (AAS) involves a systematic approach, starting from initial assessment to definitive treatment based on the underlying cause.</p>
<ol>
<li><b>Stabilization and monitoring of the vital signs</b>
<ul>
<li>Intravenous (IV) Fluids: To maintain hydration and electrolyte balance.</li>
<li>Broad-spectrum antibiotics</li>
<li>Pain Management: Analgesics to manage severe pain.</li>
<li>Nausea/Vomiting Management: Anti-emetics as needed.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Surgical Consultation</b>
<ul>
<li>Urgent Referral: If a surgical cause is suspected (e.g., appendicitis, perforation, etc.), consult a surgeon immediately.</li>
<li>Decision for Surgery: Based on imaging results and clinical findings, determine if surgical intervention is necessary.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Specific Treatment Based on Diagnosis</b>
<ul>
<li>Appendicitis: Appendectomy (surgical removal of the appendix).</li>
<li>Cholecystitis: Cholecystectomy (surgical removal of the gallbladder), possibly after stabilization.</li>
<li>Bowel Obstruction: Surgery or conservative management, depending on the cause (e.g., adhesions may be treated surgically, while some cases may resolve with conservative measures).</li>
<li>Diverticulitis: May require antibiotics and dietary modifications, or surgery if complications arise.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Monitoring and Follow-Up</b>
<ul>
<li>Continuous monitoring of vital signs and symptoms.</li>
<li>Re-evaluation of laboratory tests and imaging if the patient's condition does not improve.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<h4>1. Mesenteric Ischemia</h4>
<p>Patient has Severe, sudden-onset diffuse abdominal pain with Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or constipation, shock (hypotension, tachycardia), metabolic acidosis (lactic acidosis), or sepsis. The laboratory test finds the elevated white blood cell (WBC) count, elevated lactatemia and metabolic acidosis. Plain abdominal x-ray (late diagnosis) present pneumatosis intestinalis. CT angiography (CTA) show the vascular occlusion or bowel wall thickening, and identifying bowel infarction. The management: IV fluids to correct hypotension and hypoperfusion, nasogastric tube, pain relief, broad spectrum antibiotic, surgical intervention, anticoagulation and/or vasodilator.</p>
<h4>2. Ectopic Pregnancy</h4>
<p>The female patient has sudden unilateral and lower abdominal pain, amenorrhea 7 weeks, Vaginal bleeding, tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, dizziness and abdominal tenderness. Beta HCG positive. The Transvaginal ultrasound does not find an intrauterine pregnancy and find the free fluids in the pelvis. Management: IV fluids and blood transfusion if necessary and Immediate surgical intervention: Laparoscopy or laparotomy.</p>
<h4>3. Intussusception</h4>
<p>The child has severe and crampy abdominal pain, Stool mixed with mucus and blood, bilious vomiting, asthenia, dry mouth. Palpable abdominal finds the mass as "sausage-shaped" in the right upper quadrant. Abdominal X-ray shows signs of bowel obstruction</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 213 -->

<div><p>and Abdominal ultrasound finds the donut sign on transverse. Management: IV fluids to correct hypovolemia and surgical intervention.</p><h4>4. Necrotizing Enterocolitis (NEC)</h4><p>The child, 15 days, has Vomiting, abdominal distension, and bloody stools, discolor abdomen, Lethargy. Abdominal X-ray finds pneumatosis intestinalis with free air under the diaphragm. Blood tests present the elevated white blood cells, metabolic acidosis, and thrombocytopenia. Management: stop all enteral feeds, initiate parenteral nutrition (IV fluids), Nasogastric decompression, Broad-spectrum antibiotics, and surgical intervention.</p><h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3><ol><li><b>Evolution:</b><br/>Acute abdominal syndrome (AAS) typically progresses in a series of stages, influenced by the underlying cause. With appropriate management (surgical or conservative), symptoms typically improve. Timely intervention is crucial to avoid complications.</li><li><b>Prognosis</b><br/>The prognosis of patients depends on the cause.<br/>The prognosis of AAS varies widely based on the underlying cause and the timeliness of treatment.</li></ol><h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3><p>If left untreated, an acute abdomen may result in the following:<br/>- Sepsis - Fistula - Death<br/>- Necrosis and/or gangrene of bowel.</p><h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3><p>Acute abdomen has many different possible causes, and most of them aren't preventable.</p><p>All patients with an acute abdomen need to be seen by a surgeon. If the patient is stable, imaging studies can be obtained. If the patient is unstable, immediate surgical intervention may be necessary. Early recognition and intervention are essential in managing acute abdominal syndrome. Given its potentially life-threatening causes, timely diagnosis through clinical evaluation and appropriate imaging is critical. Treatment must be tailored to the specific condition, with surgical and non-surgical options available depending on the diagnosis. Multidisciplinary care and close monitoring are often required to ensure favorable patient outcomes.</p><h3>XII. REFERENCES</h3><ol><li>Longstreth, G. F., &amp; Lichter, D. S. (2019). <h1>HYPERKALEMIA</h1>
<p><i>Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara.</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Hyperkalemia is a common electrolyte disorder defined as a plasma potassium (K) concentration &gt;5.5 mEq/L (&gt;5 mmol/L).</p>
<p>Hyperkalemia depresses cardiac conduction and can lead to fatal arrhythmias.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<h3>Incidence</h3>
<p>Incidence is higher in patients of older age, male sex, worse kidney function, comorbidities and use of renin angiotensin-aldosterone system inhibitors.</p>
<h3>Prevalence</h3>
<p>1–10% of hospitalized patients<br/>2–3% in general population but as high as 50% in patients with CKD</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li>Increased load: either endogenous from tissue release or exogenous from a high intake, usually in association with decreased excretion or chronic kidney disease (CKD)</li>
<li>Decreased excretion: due to decreased glomerular filtration rate (GFR) or impaired aldosterone secretion</li>
<li>Cellular redistribution: shifts from intracellular space (majority of K is intracellular) to extracellular space</li>
<li>Pseudohyperkalemia: related to red cell lysis during collection or transport of blood sample, thrombocytosis, or leukocytosis</li>
</ul>
<h2>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li>Pseudohyperkalemia
        <ul>
<li>Hemolysis of red cells in phlebotomy tube (the most common.)</li>
<li>Thrombolysis; thrombocytosis</li>
<li>Leukocytosis (reverse pseudohyperkalemia)</li>
<li>Hereditary spherocytosis</li>
<li>Infectious mononucleosis</li>
<li>Traumatic venipuncture or fist clenching during phlebotomy (spurious result)</li>
<li>Familial pseudohyperkalemia</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Increased K intake
        <ul>
<li>Bananas, potatoes, melons, citrus juice, avocados, red meat, nuts, and dried fruits</li>
<li>Salt substitutes given to chronic kidney patients</li>
<li>Clay ingestion</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Transcellular shift (redistribution)
        <ul>
<li>Metabolic acidosis</li>
<li>Insulin deficiency</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 216 -->

<ul><li>Hyperglycemia (diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state)</li><li>Tissue damage (rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis syndrome, burns, trauma)</li><li>Cocaine abuse</li><li>Exercise with heavy sweating</li><li>Impaired K excretion<ul><li>Renal insufficiency/failure</li><li>Addison disease</li><li>Mineralocorticoid deficiency</li><li>Primary hyporeninemia, primary hypoaldosteronism</li><li>Type IV renal tubular acidosis (hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism)</li><li>Obstructive uropathy</li><li>Cirrhosis</li><li>Congestive heart failure (CHF)</li><li>Sickle cell disease</li><li>Amyloidosis</li><li>Gordon syndrome</li><li>Systemic lupus erythematosus</li></ul></li><li>Medication-induced (numerous)</li><li>Genetics<ul><li>Associated with some inherited diseases and conditions<ul><li>Familial hyperkalemic periodic paralysis</li><li>Congenital adrenal hyperplasia</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul><p><b>Cellular Effects of Hyperkalemia:</b></p><p>Elevated extracellular potassium levels decrease the resting membrane potential, making cells less negative (closer to the threshold potential). This reduced difference between resting and threshold potentials leads to:</p><ul><li>Increased excitability of cells initially, causing symptoms like muscle twitching, cramping, and weakness.</li><li>Prolonged depolarization can eventually lead to cell dysfunction, as the cells become less responsive to stimuli due to inactivation of sodium channels.</li><li>In cardiac tissue, this can cause life-threatening arrhythmias, such as ventricular fibrillation, as well as asystole (cardiac arrest), due to the altered action potential propagation.</li></ul><p><b>V. Diagnosis</b></p><p>Serum K level greater than the normal range (3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L); patients may be asymptomatic until &gt;6 mEq/L.</p><p><b>History</b></p><ul><li>Neuromuscular cramps, myalgias, muscle weakness or paralysis</li><li>Abdominal pain</li><li>Palpitations</li><li>Numbness</li><li>Arrhythmia or cardiac arrest</li></ul><p><b>Physical Exam</b></p><ul><li>Decreased deep tendon reflexes</li><li>Muscle weakness or flaccid paralysis of extremities</li></ul><p><b>Diagnostic Tests &amp; Interpretation</b></p><ul><li>Serum electrolytes</li><li>Renal function: BUN, creatinine</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 217 -->

<ul><li>Urinalysis: K, creatinine, osmoles (to calculate fractional excretion of K and transtubular K gradient; both assess renal handling of K)</li><li>Disorders that may alter lab results</li><li>Acidemia: K shifts from the intracellular to extracellular space</li><li>Insulin deficiency</li><li>Hemolysis of sample</li><li>Cortisol, aldosterone, and renin levels to check for mineralocorticoid deficiency when other causes are ruled out</li></ul><p>Diagnostic Procedures/Other</p><p>ECG abnormalities usually occur when K ≥7 mEq/L.</p><ul><li>Peaked T wave with shortened QT interval in precordial leads (most common, usually earliest ECG change; however, neither sensitive nor specific)</li><li>Lengthening of PR interval, loss of P wave, widened QRS</li><li>Sine wave at very high K &gt;8 mEq/L</li><li>Can eventually lead to arrhythmias including bradycardia, ventricular fibrillation, and asystole</li></ul><div><img alt="A series of five ECG strips illustrating changes associated with potassium levels. 1. Normal ECG: Normal P wave, Normal PR interval, Normal QRS, Normal T wave, U wave shallow if present. 2. Hypokalemia ECG: Slightly peaked P wave, Prolonged PR interval, ST depression, Prominent U wave, Shallow T wave. 3. Hyperkalemia ECG (Serum potassium 6-7 mmol/l): Peaked T wave. 4. Hyperkalemia ECG (Serum potassium 7-8 mmol/l): Flattened P wave, Prolonged PR interval, Further Peaking T wave, ST depression. 5. Hyperkalemia ECG (Serum potassium &gt;9 mmol/l): Sine wave pattern."/></div>

<!-- PAGE 218 -->

<h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<ul>
<li>Acute tubular necrosis</li>
<li>Digitalis toxicity</li>
<li>Hypocalcemia</li>
<li>Tumor lysis syndrome</li>
<li>Congenital adrenal hyperplasia</li>
<li>Burn injuries</li>
<li>Metabolic acidosis</li>
<li>Rhabdomyolysis</li>
</ul>
<h4>VII. MANAGEMENT</h4>
<ol>
<li>Objectives
        <ol type="a">
<li>Prevent or treat the life-threatening effects of hyperkalemia (arrhythmia)</li>
<li>Lower the kalemia to a near normal range</li>
<li>Treat the possible reversible triggering or underlining causes</li>
<li>Prevent the recurrence hyperkalemia if the underlining cause was unable to eliminate</li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>Critical signs
        <ol type="a">
<li>Kalemia 6 mEq/L or higher</li>
<li>Arrythmia</li>
<li>Acidosis</li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>Mortality risk factor
        <ul>
<li>Renal Failure: an inability to excrete potassium effectively.</li>
<li>Diabetes Mellitus: Complications that increase the risk of hyperkalemia.</li>
<li>Adrenal Disease: Addison's disease can affect potassium regulation.</li>
<li>Use of Certain Medications: Medications such as angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), and potassium-sparing diuretics can increase the risk</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Out-patient management
        <ul>
<li>Discontinue any medications that may increase K (e.g., K-sparing diuretics, exogenous K)</li>
<li>Mild hyperkalemia (5.0–5.9 mEq/L): asymptomatic and can be managed with dietary modifications and medication adjustments.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>First line treatment
        <ul>
<li>Stabilize myocardial membranes
                <ul>
<li>initial treatment with calcium gluconate IV 1,000 mg (10 mL of 10% solution) over 2 to 3 minutes</li>
<li>With constant cardiac monitoring. Can repeat after 5 minutes if needed</li>
<li>Effect begins within minutes, but only lasts 30 to 60 minutes and should be used in conjunction with definitive therapies.</li>
<li>Can also use calcium chloride (3 times as concentrated; however, central or deep vein administration is necessary to avoid tissue necrosis.)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>If suspected, stop offending agent and address any reversible causes.</li>
<li>Drive extracellular K into cells.
                <ul>
<li>Nebulized albuterol (at 10 to 20 mg/4 mL saline &gt;10 minutes—4 to 8 times bronchodilation dose) and other β-agonists have an additive effect with insulin and glucose.</li>
<li>Dextrose 50% 1 bottle 50mL (if plasma glucose &lt;250 mg/dL) and insulin 10 U IV may drive K intracellularly but does not decrease total body K and may result in hypoglycemia (close monitoring advised, especially 1 to 2 hours postinjection).</li>
<li>Sodium bicarbonate not routinely recommended but some possible benefits in severe metabolic acidosis.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 219 -->

<ul><li>Remove excess K from body.<ul><li>Cation exchange resins definitive treatment but require several doses and best used with rapidly acting transient therapies above and when dialysis not readily available.<ul><li>Patiromer calcium (Veltassa): 8.4 g PO daily (dose may vary 4.2 to 16.8 g BID in studies). This requires ~7 to 24 hours to lower K. This may be repeated q12h, if necessary.</li><li>Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (Lokelma): 10 mg PO TID for up to 48 hours.</li><li>Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate): 15 g PO or 30 g rectally. This requires 1 to 4 hours to lower K. This may be repeated q6h, if necessary. Enema has faster effect than PO.</li></ul></li><li>Loop diuretics (furosemide): 40 mg IV q12h or continuous infusion; may need to give isotonic fluids as well if patient is euvolemic or hypovolemic prior to furosemide (Lasix)</li><li>Hemodialysis is the definitive therapy when other measures are not effective. This may be required particularly when conditions, such as digitalis toxicity, rhabdomyolysis, ESRD, severe CKD, or acute kidney injury, are present; should watch for post-dialysis rebound.</li><li>Little clinical evidence for the use of diuretics (loop and thiazides), however, can be considered for control of chronic hyperkalemia.</li></ul></li><li>Chronic hyperkalemia treatment<ul><li>Review medication and discontinue those that can be contributing to hyperkalemia.</li><li>Dietary counseling of K-rich food</li><li>Diuretic therapy using thiazide and loop diuretics</li><li>Potassium binder medication can be used. Caution should be taken if Kayexalate is considered:<ul><li>Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) provides a sodium load that may exacerbate fluid overload in patients with cardiac or renal failure.</li><li>Avoid sodium polystyrene sulfonate use in patients who are postoperative or with a bowel obstruction or ileus due to high risk of intestinal necrosis</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul><p>6. Treatment adjustment</p><p>Mineralocorticoid replacement</p><p>If the patient does not have a contraindication (greater than stage 1 HTN, volume overload, history of heart failure) to mineralocorticoid administration then Consider a trial of fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily × 3 to 5 days (in patients with moderately advanced CKD, consider maintaining or increasing diuretics in tandem with the assistance of nephrology consulting service).</p><p>7. Algorithm</p><p>Management of Adults with Hyperkalemia (K&gt; 5.5 mEq/L)</p><p>*All disposition and treatment recommendations should account for local standards of care and should not supersede the clinical judgement of the treating physician</p>

<p><b>History Consistent with hyperkalemia?</b></p>

<li>History of DM, CHF, CDK or</li>

<p><b>Yes</b> → Calcium dosing</p>
<p><b>Calcium dosing</b></p>
<ul>
<li>give 1g IV push Calcium gluconate</li>
<li>Repeat ECG in 5 minutes</li>
<li>If ECG changes persist, may repeat Calcium gluconate x 2</li>
</ul>

<p><b>No</b> → Re-assessment K &lt; 6 mEq/L?</p>
<p><b>Re-assessment K &lt; 6 mEq/L?</b></p>
<p><b>Yes</b> → Disposition</p>
<p><b>Disposition</b></p>
<ul>
<li>* Admit:
        <ul>
<li>Hyperkalemia with unstable vitals</li>
<li>New onset Hyperkalemia</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>* Discharge (consider) Chronic hyperkalemia with:
        <ul>
<li>Stable vitals and EGC and</li>
<li>K eliminated with binder or diuretics and</li>
<li>Closed follow up and</li>
<li>Risk/benefit, shared decision of discharge discussed</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<p><b>No</b> → Treatment Option++:</p>
<p><b>Treatment Option++:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>- K &lt; 6 : Consider Insulin/dextrose + Albuterol ± oral binders ± furosemide/fluids</li>
<li>- K &gt; 6 – 6.5 : Administer Insulin/dextrose + Albuterol ± furosemide/fluids*. Consider oral binders ± Urgent hemodialysis</li>
<li>- K &gt; 6.5 : Administer Insulin/dextrose + Albuterol ± furosemide/fluids*. Consider oral binders. Arrange for immediate hemodialysis</li>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ol>
<li><b>Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS):</b> Hyperkalemia occurs in patients undergoing treatment for cancers like leukemia or lymphoma, where massive tumor cell destruction releases intracellular contents (including potassium) into the bloodstream. This causes hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia, and acute kidney injury. Prophylactic measures (e.g., hydration, allopurinol, or rasburicase) are used to prevent TLS, and acute treatment follows the same principle.</li>
<li><b>Digitalis (Digoxin) Toxicity:</b> Excessive digoxin (digitalis) use can impair cellular potassium homeostasis, leading to hyperkalemia. Digoxin toxicity can also lead to life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias, which are exacerbated by elevated potassium levels. Hyperkalemia in the context of digoxin toxicity is managed with digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Digibind), along with conventional hyperkalemia treatments like insulin/glucose or dialysis in severe cases. @&gt; Rapid administration of calcium in patients with suspected digitalis toxicity may result in fatal dysrhythmia. In the case of digoxin-specific antibody fragments is non-available and myocardial membrane stabilization is need; Calcium should be administered slowly over 20 to 30 minutes in 5% dextrose with extreme caution.</li>
</ol>
<h3>IX. Evolution and prognosis</h3>
<p><b>Evolution of Hyperkalemia:</b></p>
<ol>
<li><b>Acute Hyperkalemia</b> (acute kidney injury, rhabdomyolysis, trauma, or massive hemolysis), the evolution is rapid and if not treated promptly, acute hyperkalemia can lead to ventricular fibrillation, asystole, or death.</li>
<li><b>Chronic Hyperkalemia</b> can evolve more gradually due to impaired renal excretion. If untreated, chronic hyperkalemia can contribute to worsening renal function, recurrent hospitalizations due to cardiovascular issues, or the need for dialysis.</li>
</ol>
<p><b>Prognosis of Hyperkalemia:</b></p>
<p>The prognosis of hyperkalemia depends on several factors, including the underlying cause, the speed at which potassium levels rise, and the effectiveness of treatment:</p>
<ul>
<li>Mild to Moderate Hyperkalemia (Potassium 5.0–6.4 mEq/L): patients have a good prognosis if the underlying cause is treated.</li>
<li>Severe Hyperkalemia (Potassium &gt;6.5 mEq/L): the prognosis depends on how quickly treatment is initiated to stabilize the cardiac membrane and lower serum potassium levels. With timely intervention, patients often recover fully.</li>
</ul>
<h3>X. COMPLICATION</h3>
<ul>
<li>Cardiac arrhythmias,</li>
<li>Muscle weakness and paralysis,</li>
<li>Respiratory failure,</li>
<li>Metabolic acidosis,</li>
<li>Acute or chronic kidney injury,</li>
<li>Neurological effects (confusion, seizures, coma),</li>
<li>Worsening of heart failure and diabetes</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<p>Prevention of hyperkalemia involves a combination of dietary management, careful medication use, and regular monitoring, especially in high-risk populations. The goal is</p>

<!-- PAGE 222 -->

<ul><li>to maintain normal serum potassium levels and</li><li>addressing underlying conditions that may predispose individuals to hyperkalemia.</li></ul><p>In nonhospitalized patients at risk of hyperkalemia with known chronic kidney disease (CKD), heart failure, or diabetes:</p><ul><li>Routinely monitor blood levels (potassium concentration) 2-4 times per year depending on level of kidney function and degree of proteinuria.</li><li>If also taking renin-angiotensin aldosterone system blockers (RAAS), monitor kidney function.</li><li>In patients starting an angiotensin-converting-enzyme (ACE) inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) assess creatinine and electrolytes prior to initiation of ACE inhibitors and ARBs and 1-2 weeks after initiation and every dose titration.</li></ul><h3>XII. <h1 style="text-align: center;">HYPOKALEMIA</h1>
<p style="text-align: center;"><i>Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. IM Virya, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Prof. CHHUOY Meng,<br/>Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun,<br/>Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry,<br/>Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha,<br/>Dr. TES Sovannara.</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Hypokalemia is defined as a serum potassium level less than 3.5 mEq/L (3.5 mmol/L). Potassium is an essential electrolyte that plays a critical role in nerve function, muscle contraction, and maintaining normal heart rhythm. Hypokalemia can result from a variety of causes including insufficient dietary intake, increased potassium loss through the kidneys or gastrointestinal tract, or intracellular potassium shifts.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Hypokalemia affects approximately 1-3% of the general population. The prevalence increases in hospitalized patients (Up to 20% of hospitalized patients may experience hypokalemia, with a higher incidence in patients in intensive care units (ICUs) due to critical illness, medications, and electrolyte imbalances), especially those receiving diuretics or other medications that promote potassium loss.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li><input checked="" type="checkbox"/> Renal losses: Diuretics (thiazides, loop), hyperaldosteronism, renal tubular acidosis, Bartter/Gitelman syndromes, hypomagnesemia. Cushing's syndrome, Liddle syndrome</li>
<li><input checked="" type="checkbox"/> Gastrointestinal losses: Diarrhea, vomiting, nasogastric suction, laxative abuse.</li>
<li><input checked="" type="checkbox"/> Intracellular shifts: Insulin therapy, beta-2 agonists, alkalosis, refeeding syndrome.</li>
<li><input checked="" type="checkbox"/> Inadequate intake: Dietary deficiency, malnutrition, eating disorders.</li>
<li><input checked="" type="checkbox"/> Miscellaneous: Hyperthyroidism, sweating.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 224 -->

<h4>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4>
<h5>1. Inadequate Potassium Intake</h5>
<ul>
<li>Dietary Insufficiency: A diet low in potassium can lead to a decrease in serum potassium levels, particularly if combined with conditions that increase potassium loss.</li>
<li>Increased Requirements: Conditions such as pregnancy, lactation, or intense physical activity can increase potassium requirements, leading to a state of deficiency if intake does not meet these needs.</li>
</ul>
<h5>2. Increased Potassium Loss</h5>
<ul>
<li>Renal Losses
        <ul>
<li>Diuretics: Loop and thiazide diuretics increase urinary potassium excretion by inhibiting sodium reabsorption in the renal tubules, leading to potassium loss.</li>
<li>Hyperaldosteronism: Excess production of aldosterone (primary or secondary) causes increased sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the renal tubules, leading to hypokalemia.</li>
<li>Renal Tubular Disorders: Conditions like renal tubular acidosis (RTA) or Bartter syndrome result in impaired potassium reabsorption in the renal tubules.</li>
<li>Post-obstructive Diuresis: After relief of urinary obstruction, there may be a significant diuresis with increased potassium loss.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Gastrointestinal Losses
        <ul>
<li>Vomiting: Loss of gastric acid leads to a depletion of potassium, especially if prolonged.</li>
<li>Diarrhea: Both osmotic and secretory diarrhea can cause significant potassium loss, especially in cases of chronic diarrhea.</li>
<li>Fistulas or Drainage: Intestinal or biliary fistulas can lead to losses of potassium through the gastrointestinal tract.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h5>3. Shift of Potassium into Cells</h5>
<ul>
<li>Insulin: Insulin promotes the uptake of potassium into cells, particularly after carbohydrate ingestion or in conditions of hyperinsulinemia, leading to transient hypokalemia.</li>
<li>Beta-Agonists: Drugs such as albuterol can stimulate the Na+/K+ ATPase pump, promoting the uptake of potassium into cells and causing a drop in serum potassium levels.</li>
<li>Metabolic Alkalosis: In states of metabolic alkalosis, the increased exchange of hydrogen ions for potassium ions leads to an intracellular shift of potassium.</li>
<li>Stress or Catecholamines: Increased levels of catecholamines (due to stress or conditions like pheochromocytoma) can stimulate potassium entry into cells.</li>
</ul>
<h5>4. Total Body Potassium Deficit</h5>
<ul>
<li>Chronic Diseases: Conditions such as chronic kidney disease, heart failure, and cirrhosis can alter potassium homeostasis, leading to both loss and shift mechanisms.</li>
<li>Inadequate Replacement: In patients with increased potassium losses, failure to adequately replace potassium (either through diet or supplements) leads to a total body potassium deficit.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 226 -->

<h3>5. Effects of Hypokalemia on Cellular Function</h3>
<ul>
<li>Membrane Potential Changes: Hypokalemia leads to hyperpolarization of the cell membrane, making it more difficult for cells to depolarize and fire. This affects muscle cells, neurons, and cardiac cells, leading to symptoms such as weakness, fatigue, and arrhythmias.</li>
<li>Increased Sodium Reabsorption: The kidneys will attempt to compensate for low potassium by increasing sodium reabsorption, leading to increased fluid retention, which can exacerbate conditions like hypertension or heart failure.</li>
</ul>
<h2>V. DIAGNOSIS</h2>
<h3>A. Clinical History and Physical Examination</h3>
<ul>
<li>History: Ask about symptoms like muscle weakness, cramps, fatigue, palpitations, or paralysis, dietary history and medication use.</li>
<li>Physical examination:
        <ul>
<li>Look for signs of muscle weakness, hypotension, or arrhythmias.</li>
<li>Examine for dehydration (dry mucous membranes, hypotension), which may point to GI or renal losses.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Symptoms: Fatigue, muscle weakness, arrhythmias.</li>
</ul>
<h3>B. Serum Potassium Measurement</h3>
<ul>
<li>Confirm hypokalemia: Serum potassium &lt; 3.5 mEq/L.
        <ul>
<li>Mild hypokalemia: 3.0 – 3.5 mEq/L.</li>
<li>Moderate hypokalemia: 2.5 – 3.0 mEq/L.</li>
<li>Severe hypokalemia: &lt; 2.5 mEq/L.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>C. Laboratory Investigations to Determine the Cause</h3>
<ul>
<li>Urinary potassium excretion:
        <ul>
<li>&lt; 20 mEq/L: Suggests extrarenal (GI) losses.</li>
<li>&gt; 20 mEq/L: Indicates renal potassium wasting</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Serum bicarbonate or arterial blood gas (ABG) helps identify the acid-base status</li>
<li>Serum Magnesium: Hypomagnesemia often coexists with hypokalemia, especially in patients on diuretics or with chronic diarrhea.</li>
</ul>
<h3>D. Electrocardiogram (ECG)</h3>
<ul>
<li>Flattened or inverted T waves.</li>
<li>Prominent U waves.</li>
<li>ST-segment depression.</li>
<li>Prolonged QT interval.</li>
<li>Ventricular arrhythmias in severe hypokalemia (e.g., Torsades de Pointes).</li>
</ul>
<h3>E. Further Testing Based on Suspected Cause</h3>
<ul>
<li>Renin and Aldosterone Levels:
        <ul>
<li>These are measured when hyperaldosteronism is suspected.</li>
<li>Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) is associated with low renin and high aldosterone levels.</li>
<li>Secondary hyperaldosteronism (e.g., heart failure, cirrhosis) shows high renin and high aldosterone levels.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 227 -->

<ul><li>Diuretic Screen: If diuretic use is suspected but not reported, a urine diuretic screen may be necessary to detect thiazide or loop diuretics.</li><li>Urine Chloride:<ul><li>Low urine chloride (&lt; 20 mEq/L): Seen in hypokalemia due to vomiting.</li><li>High urine chloride (&gt; 20 mEq/L): Indicates causes like diuretic use or primary hyperaldosteronism.</li></ul></li><li>Genetic Testing: In cases where inherited conditions like Bartter syndrome or Gitelman syndrome are suspected, genetic testing may be considered.</li></ul><h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4><p>The differential diagnosis of hypokalemia is vast. Notable ones include the following:</p><ul><li>Iatrogenic cause: chronic corticosteroid intake, insulin therapy</li><li>Congenital conditions: Bartter syndrome, hypokalemic periodic paralysis</li><li>Renal disorders: RTA, osmotic diuresis</li><li>Gastrointestinal losses: laxative abuse, vomiting</li><li>Poor intake: eating disorders, restrictive diets</li><li>Skin losses: excessive sweating</li><li>Redistribution: alkalosis from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, nonanion-gap acidosis from diabetic ketoacidosis</li><li>Concomitant electrolyte imbalances: hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia.</li></ul><h4>VII. MANAGEMENT</h4><ol><li><b>Objectives</b><ul><li>Reduce potassium loss.</li><li>Replenish stored potassium.</li><li>Evaluate potential toxicities.</li><li>Determine cause.</li></ul></li><li><b>Critical Symptoms and signs</b><ul><li>serum potassium &lt;2.5 mEq/L</li><li>arrhythmias</li></ul></li><li><b>Mortality Risk factors</b><ul><li>the elderly,</li><li>diabetic patients,</li><li>patients with renal insufficiency.</li></ul></li><li><b>Out-patient management</b><ul><li>Nonemergent conditions (serum potassium &gt;2.5 mEq/L, no cardiac manifestations) can be treated as out-patients</li><li>Oral therapy preferred: 40 to 120 mEq/day (40 to 120 mmol/day) in divided doses</li><li>Ensure adequate hydration (100 to 250 mL of water), better if given with or after meal.</li></ul></li><li><b>First-line treatment</b><p><b>General Measures</b></p><ul><li>Manage underlying disease or eliminate causative factor.</li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 228 -->

<ul><li>Discontinue laxative, use potassium-neutral or potassium-sparing diuretics.</li><li>Treat diarrhea and vomiting.</li><li>Use H2 blockers in patients with nasogastric suction.</li><li>Control hyperglycemia if glucosuria is present.</li></ul><p><b>Medication</b></p><ul><li>IV potassium only when oral administration is not feasible (e.g., vomiting, postoperative state).</li><li>Dilution: Potassium must be diluted to avoid hyperkalemia and infusion-related complications. Typically, 10-20 mEq is diluted in 100-250 mL of saline or dextrose solution.</li><li>Rate should not exceed 10 mEq/hr, and concentration should not exceed 40 mEq/L to lessen burning and discomfort at IV site and to avoid phlebitis.</li><li>A central line is recommended for rate &gt;10 mEq/hr; up to 40 mEq in 100 mL can be safely given via central access.</li><li>Potassium chloride (KCl) is suitable for all forms of hypokalemia.</li><li>Potassium bicarbonate or precursor (gluconate, acetate, or citrate) in metabolic acidosis</li><li>Potassium phosphate in phosphate deficiency as in DKA</li></ul><p><b>Precautions</b></p><ul><li>Any form of potassium replacement carries the risk of hyperkalemia.</li><li>Serum potassium should be checked more frequently in groups at higher risk: the elderly, diabetic patients, and patients with renal insufficiency.</li><li>Patients receiving insulin for DKA require more timely and aggressive potassium replacement in order to account for the intracellular shift.</li><li>Dietary potassium is almost entire coupled to phosphate, rather than chloride, and does not correct potassium loss from chloride depletion (e.g., diuretics or vomiting).</li><li>Significant possible interactions: Concomitant administration of potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, triamterene, amiloride, ACE inhibitors) magnifies risk of hyperkalemia.</li></ul><p><b>6. Treatment adjustment</b></p><ul><li>Emergent situations (serum potassium &lt;2.5 mEq/L, arrhythmias)<ul><li>IV replacement—standard infusion rate: 10 mmol/hr; maximum infusion rate: 20 mmol/hr.</li><li>Central line preferred</li></ul></li><li>If patient is hypomagnesemic<ul><li>First, give 4 mL MgSO4 50% (8 mmol) in 10 mL of NaCl 0.9% &gt;20 minutes and then start first 40 mmol KCl infusion followed by magnesium replacement.</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>7. Algorithm for treatment of hypokalemia (next page).</b></p>

<h3>VIII-SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ol>
<li><b>Hypokalemia in Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)</b>
<p>In diabetic ketoacidosis, potassium shifts from the intracellular to the extracellular space due to insulin deficiency and hyperglycemia. Despite normal or elevated serum potassium levels on initial presentation, total body potassium is typically depleted. Potassium supplementation is generally started if the serum potassium is below 5.3 mEq/L, even if levels are within the normal range. Close monitoring of serum potassium is essential, and potassium replacement is continued until the patient is stable and potassium levels normalize.</p>
</li>
<li><b>Hypokalemia in Hyperaldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome)</b>
<p>Primary hyperaldosteronism is a condition where the adrenal glands produce too much aldosterone, leading to increased renal potassium excretion. Common symptoms include hypertension, muscle weakness, and hypokalemia with metabolic alkalosis. Treatment of the underlying condition, such as adrenalectomy in the case of adrenal adenoma or medical therapy with aldosterone antagonists (e.g., spironolactone, eplerenone). Potassium supplementation may be required initially until aldosterone levels are controlled.</p>
</li>
<li><b>Hypokalemia in Refeeding Syndrome</b>
<p>Refeeding syndrome occurs in malnourished patients when they receive high carbohydrate nutrition. It triggers the release of insulin, which causes potassium, phosphate, and magnesium to shift into cells. This can lead to severe hypokalemia, along with other electrolyte imbalances. Careful, slow refeeding with close monitoring of electrolytes, particularly potassium, phosphorus, and magnesium. Potassium supplementation is required, often in significant amounts, to prevent complications.</p>
</li>
<li><b>Hypokalemia in Renal Tubular Acidosis (RTA)</b>
<p>Type 1 RTA (distal) and Type 2 RTA (proximal) can lead to hypokalemia due to impaired acid excretion and subsequent potassium loss in urine. It's often associated with metabolic acidosis. Correction of the underlying acidosis using alkali therapy (bicarbonate or citrate) and potassium supplements. Long-term treatment with potassium citrate is often required to prevent further episodes of hypokalemia and acidosis.</p>
</li>
<li><b>Hypokalemia in Cushing's Syndrome</b>
<p>Cushing's syndrome involves excessive production of cortisol, which has mineralocorticoid activity and can lead to hypokalemia by increasing renal potassium loss. It associated features include central obesity, hypertension, and glucose intolerance. Treatment focuses on addressing the underlying cause of cortisol excess, such as adrenal or pituitary tumors. Potassium supplementation and spironolactone may be used to control hypokalemia until the condition is treated.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<h3>IX- EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<p>The evolution and prognosis of hypokalemia depend on the severity of potassium depletion, the underlying cause, the speed of onset, and whether effective treatment is provided. Most hypokalemia will correct with replacement after 24 to 72 hours.</p>

<!-- PAGE 231 -->

<div><p>If the primary cause is eliminated, hypokalemia will likely resolve with no further treatment needed. Associated with higher morbidity and mortality because of cardiac arrhythmias Complication.</p><h4>X- COMPLICATION</h4><ul><li>Hyperkalemia during the course of treatment</li><li>Increased risk of digoxin toxicity</li><li>Increased risk of arrhythmias by increasing myocyte's resting potential and in turn its refractory period.</li></ul><h4>XI- PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h4><p>Preventing hypokalemia involves a combination of dietary measures, careful medication management, and monitoring of at-risk patients. Dietary (Fruit, vegetables or legumes are rich in potassium such as Bananas, oranges, apricots, avocados, leafy greens, potatoes, tomatoes, Lentils, beans, and peas).</p><h4>VIII. <h1>HYPERNATREMIA</h1><p>Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Prof. CHHUOY Meng,<br/>Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun,<br/>Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry,<br/>Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha,<br/>Dr. TES Sovannara</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>Hypernatremia is a condition characterized by an elevated concentration of sodium in the blood, typically defined as a serum sodium level greater than 145 mEq/L.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>Hypernatremia occurs in approximately 1-3% of hospitalized patients, and 9% in ICU patients frequently linked to mechanical ventilation and diuretic use. The mortality rate from hypernatremia is high, especially among elderly patients. Hypernatremia will not develop in patients with intact thirst mechanisms who are able to access water.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><ol><li>Water Loss: Hypovolemic hypernatremia:<ul><li>Insensible Water Loss: Water loss through skin (sweating) or respiratory tract</li><li>Gastrointestinal Loss: Excessive loss of water via vomiting or diarrhea</li><li>Renal Losses: Increased urine output due to:<ul><li>Diabetes Insipidus (DI)</li><li>Diuretics: Loop diuretics or osmotic diuretics</li><li>Hypodipsia/Adipsia</li><li>Burns or severe skin damage</li></ul></li></ul></li><li>Sodium Gain (Absolute Hypernatremia): Hypervolemic Hypernatremia<ul><li>Hypertonic Saline Administration</li><li>Sodium Bicarbonate Administration</li><li>Salt Poisoning (Salt Ingestion)</li><li>Mineralocorticoid Excess</li></ul></li><li>Isovolemic Hypernatremia:<ul><li>Hypothalamic Diabetes Insipidus (DI): Head trauma, Tumor, Infection, Cerebrovascular disease, Granulomatous diseases</li><li>Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus: Congenital, Drug (Lithium), Obstructive uropathy, Chronic tubulointerstitial disease, Electrolyte disorders (hypercalcemia, potassium depletion)</li></ul></li></ol><p>Etiology of Hypernatremia in Neonates:</p><ul><li>Inadequate Breastfeeding (Breastfeeding-associated Hypernatremia):</li><li>Formula Feeding Errors: Improper preparation of formula (e.g., using too little water) can lead to an excessive sodium load and dehydration in formula-fed infants.</li><li>Excessive Insensible Water Loss:<ul><li>preterm infants: higher surface area-to-body weight ratio</li><li>fever, high environmental temperature, or use of radiant warmers or phototherapy</li></ul></li><li>Diabetes Insipidus (DI):</li><li>Excessive Sodium Intake: Hypertonic saline administration during resuscitation or inappropriate intravenous fluid therapy.</li></ul><h2>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h2>

<!-- PAGE 233 -->

<ul><li>Due to the powerful effect of the thirst mechanism, hypernatremia typically occurs only in patients who cannot readily access water such as infants, intubated patients, and those with altered mental status or patients with hypodipsia.</li><li>Water loss out of proportion to salt loss is the most common cause of hypernatremia. The following conditions lead to excessive water loss:<ul><li>Transdermal loss<ul><li>Burns or excessive sweating (e.g., fever, infants under radiant heaters, heat exposure, extreme exercise)</li></ul></li><li>Urinary loss<ul><li>Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (DI) (congenital or due to renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, medication-related, e.g., lithium)</li><li>Central Diabetes insipidus (DI) (due to head trauma, stroke, meningitis)</li><li>Osmotic diuresis: glucose, urea, and mannitol</li><li>Post-acute tubular necrosis (ATN) diuresis</li></ul></li><li>Gastrointestinal loss<ul><li>Osmotic diarrhea: lactulose, malabsorption, and some types of infectious diarrhea</li><li>Enterocutaneous fistula.</li><li>Vomiting, NG suction</li></ul></li></ul></li><li>Disorders of the thirst mechanism can result in hypernatremia due to reduced water intake (e.g., intracranial lesions, primary hypodipsia, chronic volume expansion in mineralocorticoid excess).</li><li>Excess Na (increase in total body Na) less commonly leads to hypernatremia. The following condition may result in excessive total body Na:<ul><li>IV infusion of hypertonic NaCl or NaHCO3 during treatment of brain injury, metabolic acidosis, or hyperkalemia</li><li>Sea water ingestion</li><li>Excessive use of NaHCO3 antacid</li><li>Incorrect infant formula preparation, tube feeding</li><li>Excessive Na in dialysate solutions</li></ul></li><li>With acute hypernatremia, the rapid decrease in brain volume can cause rupture of the cerebral veins, leading to focal intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhages and possibly irreversible neurologic damage.</li><li>Neonates are more vulnerable to the effects of hypernatremia due to their immature kidneys and limited ability to concentrate urine.</li></ul><h2>V. DIAGNOSIS</h2><ol><li>Clinical History and Physical Examination:<p>History</p><ul><li>History of conditions leading to water loss or impaired thirst: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, polyuria, fever, heat exposure, extreme exercise, brain injury</li><li>Neurologic symptoms are common:<ul><li>Mild: thirst, anorexia</li><li>Moderate: altered mental status, myalgia, muscle weakness, twitching, lethargy, irritability</li><li>Severe: seizure (especially if rapid development of hypernatremia), coma</li></ul></li><li>Severity of symptoms correlate with rapidity of the increase in Na as well as the degree of hypernatremia.</li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 234 -->

<ul><li>Severe symptoms are likely to occur with sudden increases in plasma Na levels or at concentrations &gt;160 mEq/L.</li></ul><p><b>Physical Exam</b></p><ul><li>Signs of water or volume loss: tachycardia, hypotension, orthostatic hypotension, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor</li><li>Neurologic abnormalities: lethargy, weakness, tremor, focal deficits (in cases of intracerebral bleeding/lesion), confusion, coma, seizures</li></ul><p><b>2. Laboratory tests</b></p><ul><li>Serum Electrolytes, BUN/Creatinine, Glucose, CBC</li><li>Serum and Urine Osmolality:<ul><li>Normal serum osmolality is 275-295 mOsm/kg</li><li>High Urine Osmolality (&gt;800 mOsm/kg): Suggests water loss through non-renal mechanisms</li><li>Low Urine Osmolality (&lt;300 mOsm/kg): Suggests inappropriate water loss through the kidneys, such as in diabetes insipidus or diuretic use.</li></ul></li><li>Urine Sodium Concentration:<ul><li>Low Urine Sodium (&lt;20 mEq/L): hypovolemic hypernatremia</li><li>High Urine Sodium (&gt;100 mEq/L): hypervolemic hypernatremia</li></ul></li><li>Assessment of Volume Status:</li><li>Specific Tests for Underlying Causes:<ul><li>Water Deprivation Test: in central DI: an increase in urine osmolality after administration of desmopressin (ADH analog), while in nephrogenic DI, urine osmolality remains low.</li><li>ADH (vasopressin) Levels.</li></ul></li><li>Imaging (If Necessary): Chest x-ray, Brain imaging (CT or MRI)</li></ul><p><b>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</b></p><ul><li>Diabetes Insipidus</li><li>Hyperosmotic coma</li><li>Salt ingestion</li><li>Hypertonic dehydration</li><li>Hypothyroidism</li><li>Cushing syndrome.</li></ul><p><b>VII. MANAGEMENT</b></p><ol><li><b>Objectives</b><ul><li>The treatment of hypernatremia involves treating the underlying cause and correcting the water deficit.</li><li>Determine the duration of hypernatremia because speed of correction depends on symptom severity and rate of development of hypernatremia.</li><li>Avoid rapid correction of chronic hypernatremia to prevent development of cerebral edema (goal rate is 10 mEq/L in 24 hours).</li></ul></li><li><b>Critical signs</b><ul><li>Serum sodium &gt; 155mEq/L</li><li>Hypotension</li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 235 -->

<ul><li>Neurologic abnormalities: lethargy, weakness, tremor, focal deficits (in cases of intracerebral bleeding/lesion), confusion, coma, seizures.</li></ul><ol><li>Mortality Risk factors<ul><li>Rapid development of hypernatremia (&lt;48h)</li><li>CNS thrombosis / hemorrhage, seizure</li><li>Chronic hypernatremia: &gt;2 days duration has higher mortality.</li><li>Serum Na &gt;180 mEq/L (&gt;180 mmol/L): often results in residual CNS damage</li></ul></li><li>Out-patient treatment</li><li>First-line treatment<ul><li>Acute hyponatremia: relatively uncommon, may occur in acute DI, severe hyperglycemia, or salt ingestion<ul><li>D5W infusion at 3 to 6 mL/kg/hr to lower the serum Na by 1 to 2 mEq/L/hr</li><li>Check serum Na every 1 to 2 hours to confirm correction at desired rate.</li><li>When serum Na decreases to 145 mEq/L, reduce D5W infusion to 1 mL/kg/hr until serum Na normalizes.</li><li>Aim to correct hypernatremia in 24 to 48 hours.</li></ul></li><li>Chronic hypernatremia (&gt;48 hours): Avoid rapid correction to prevent development of cerebral edema.<ul><li>D5W infusion at 1.35 mL/kg/hr</li><li>Check serum Na every 4 to 6 hours to determine correction at desired rate.</li><li>Correct at maximum of 0.5 mEq/L/hr or 10 to 12 mEq/L/day.</li><li>Often need to adjust infusion rate to account for ongoing water losses</li><li>Hypernatremia with hypovolemia: Correct severe volume depletion with isotonic IV fluids first and then address hypernatremia:<ul><li>Once hemodynamically stable, can correct hypovolemia and hypernatremia simultaneously with 0.45% saline as every 2 mL of this solution will provide 1 mL of saline and 1 mL of water.</li><li>Water Deficit (L)= Total Body Water × (Natremia (Lab) – 140)/140</li><li>Total body water (TBW) = 0.6 × body weight (kg) for men.<br/>0.5 × body weight (kg) for women.<br/>0.45 × body weight (kg) for elderly individuals.</li></ul></li><li>Hypernatremia with hypervolemia: can treat hypervolemia with diuretics while simultaneously correcting hypernatremia<ul><li>Concomitant diuretic treatment will increase urinary water losses and may necessitate increased water repletion.</li></ul></li><li>Consider oral water repletion for mild hypernatremia.</li><li>Euvolemic Hypernatremia: Free Water Replacement: Give oral water if the patient can drink. If oral intake is not feasible, administer 5% dextrose in water (D5W) intravenously.</li><li>High infusion rates of D5W may cause hyperglycemia.</li><li>Hyperglycemia-induced osmotic diuresis will increase urinary water losses and necessitate increased water repletion.</li></ul></li></ul></li><li>Treatment adjustment<ul><li>Dialysis can be considered if acute kidney injury and conventional treatment has failed.</li><li>May use medication in treatment of diabetes insipidus (DI)</li><li>Central DI</li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 236 -->

<ul><li>Desmopressin acetate (DDAVP): Use parenteral form for acute symptomatic patients and use intranasal or oral form for chronic therapy.</li><li>Free water replacement: may use 2.5% dextrose in water if giving large volumes of water in DI to avoid glycosuria</li><li>May consider sulfonylureas/thiazide diuretics for chronic but not acute treatment</li><li>Nephrogenic DI<ul><li>Treat with diuretics and Non-Steroid Anti-Inflammatory drugs.</li><li>Lithium-induced nephrogenic DI: hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg PO BID or indomethacin 50 mg PO TID, or amiloride hydrochloride 5 to 10 mg PO BID</li></ul></li></ul>

<h2>7. Algorithm</h2>
<h3>Algorithm for the treatment of hypernatremia</h3>
<div>
<p><b>Hypernatremia</b></p>
<p>Onset ?</p>
<ul>
<li>Acute (&lt;48h)</li>
<li>Chronic (&gt;48h or unknown)</li>
</ul>
<table>

<tr>
<td style="vertical-align: top;">
<b>Rapid correction</b>
<p>Decrease in (Na<sup>+</sup>) 1-2 mmol/L/h<br/>Target goal of sodium: 145 mmol/l/within 24h</p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top;">
<b>Slow correction</b>
<p>Decrease in (Na<sup>+</sup>) &lt;0.5mmol/L/h<br/>Target goal of sodium: 6-11 mmol/l/day</p>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Assess volume status</p>
<table>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="vertical-align: top;">
<b>Hypovolemia</b>
<p><b>Correction of Volume deficit</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Initial fluid resuscitation with balanced crystalloid (NSS/LR) until hypovolemia improves</li>
<li>Treatment of the underlying cause of losses (insulin, relief of obstruction, removal of osmotic diuretics etc.)</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Correction of water deficit</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Calculate water deficit</li>
<li>Administer 0.45% saline, 5% Dextrose or oral hydration to replace the water deficit and ongoing losses</li>
</ul>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top;">
<b>Euvolemia</b>
<p><b>Correction of water deficit</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Calculate water deficit</li>
<li>Administer 0.45% saline, 5% Dextrose, or oral hydration to replace the water deficit and ongoing losses</li>
<li>In central DI with severe losses: Desmopressin</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Long-term therapy</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Central DI</li>
<li>Nephrogenic DI: discontinue offending agents and begin thiazide, amiloride, or NSAIDs</li>
</ul>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top;">
<b>Hyervolemia</b>
<p><b>Removal of Sodium</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Discontinue offending agents</li>
<li>Free water replacement (IV D5%) + loop diuretics</li>
<li>Hemodialysis as need for renal failure</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 238 -->

<h3>SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ul>
<li>Geriatric Considerations
        <ul>
<li>Most commonly affected group due to impaired renal concentrating ability and reduced thirst mechanism.</li>
<li>Consider neglect if underlying etiology is dehydration alone</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Pregnancy Considerations
        <ul>
<li>May encounter transient DI of pregnancy</li>
<li>Vasopressin and desmopressin are category B drugs in pregnancy</li>
<li>Hydration status much more difficult to evaluate accurately by exam</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<p>The progression and prognosis of hypernatremia involves several key phases, influenced by the underlying cause, the speed of development, and clinical management. Neonates and elderly patients are at higher risk for complications, can further complicate the prognosis and recovery. Mortality rates of 42-75% have been reported for acutely evolving hypernatremia and 10-60% for chronic hypernatremia</p>
<h3>X. COMPLICATION</h3>
<p>The complications of hypernatremia can be severe and life-threatening, especially in vulnerable populations such as neonates, the elderly, and individuals with underlying health conditions.</p>
<ul>
<li>subarachnoid or subdural hemorrhage due to the rupture of bridging veins and dural sinus thrombosis. It can lead to permanent brain damage or death.</li>
<li>Rapid correction of chronic hypernatremia may cause cerebral edema, seizure, and permanent brain damage.</li>
<li>Acute kidney injury (AKI),</li>
<li>Cardiovascular Issues (hypertension and increased cardiac workload),</li>
<li>thromboembolic Events (the hypercoagulable state).</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<ul>
<li>Early Breastfeeding Support (newborn)</li>
<li>Treatment/prevention of underlying cause</li>
<li>Properly prepare infant formula and never add salt to any commercial infant formula.</li>
<li>Keep patients well hydrated.</li>
<li>Frequent neurologic checks during acute correction of hypernatremia</li>
<li>Daily weight, electrolytes, and blood glucose for a period immediately after correction</li>
<li>Avoid rapid correction of chronic hypernatremia to prevent development of cerebral edema (goal rate is 10 mEq/L in 24 hours).</li>
<li>Monitor serum Na and adjust water repletion to achieve desired rate of correction as available formulas for calculating water deficit and estimating ongoing water losses have limited accuracy.</li>
</ul>

<h1>HYponatremia</h1>
<p><i>Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. IM Virya, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Prof. CHHUOY Meng,<br/>Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun,<br/>Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. SOEU Khemry,<br/>Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha,<br/>Dr. TES Sovannara,</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Hyponatremia, defined as a serum sodium concentration of less than 135 mmol/L, is one of the most common electrolyte disorders encountered in clinical practice. Sodium is an essential electrolyte that helps regulate water balance and is critical for proper muscle and nerve function. Normal serum sodium levels range from about 135 to 145 milliequivalents per liter (mEq/L).</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>The prevalence in the general population is estimated at around 5 - 15%. Hyponatremia occurs in up to 15 - 30% of hospitalized patients in Intensive Care Unit (ICU). Prevalence may reach up to 20 - 30% in elderly hospitalized patients.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li>Hypovolemic Hyponatremia related to fluid losses (diarrhea, vomiting, diuretic use).</li>
<li>Euvolemic Hyponatremia associated with the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH), hypothyroidism, or medications.</li>
<li>Hypervolemic Hyponatremia is seen in conditions like heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome where there is fluid retention.</li>
</ul>
<h2>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h2>
<ol>
<li>Water Retention Mediated by Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH):
        <ul>
<li>ADH Secretion: The most common mechanism in hyponatremia involves inappropriate secretion or enhanced sensitivity to ADH (also called vasopressin). ADH promotes water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts, reducing the excretion of free water. This leads to dilution of sodium in the blood.</li>
<li>Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone Secretion (SIADH): This is the classic example where excessive ADH release occurs despite normal or increased blood volume, leading to water retention and dilutional hyponatremia. SIADH can be caused by various factors such as malignancies (especially small cell lung cancer), central nervous system disorders (stroke, trauma), pulmonary diseases, and certain medications (SSRIs, antipsychotics).</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Renal Water Handling:
        <ul>
<li>Dilutional Hyponatremia: When the kidney's ability to excrete free water is impaired (often due to the action of ADH), the excess water dilutes serum sodium levels. This is the hallmark of many cases of hyponatremia, especially euvolemic forms.</li>
<li>Hypovolemic Hyponatremia: In cases where sodium and water are both lost (e.g., gastrointestinal losses, diuretic use, or adrenal insufficiency), hypovolemia (low blood volume) stimulates ADH secretion and thirst. The kidneys then conserve both water and sodium, but because more water than sodium is retained, hyponatremia occurs.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 242 -->

<div><p>3. Volume Status and Hyponatremia:</p><ul><li>Hypovolemic Hyponatremia: Decreased total body water and sodium with a relatively greater loss of sodium. Conditions like dehydration, blood loss, or severe diarrhea can cause this form. The body compensates by activating ADH, leading to water retention and dilution of sodium.</li><li>Euvolemic Hyponatremia: Characterized by a normal extracellular fluid volume but dilutional low sodium levels, as seen in SIADH.</li><li>Hypervolemic Hyponatremia: Increased total body water and sodium, with a greater increase in water relative to sodium. This is commonly seen in conditions like heart failure, cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome. In these conditions, effective circulating volume is reduced, stimulating ADH release and further water retention.</li></ul><p>4. Sodium and Osmolality Imbalance:</p><p>Hyponatremia reflects a reduction in plasma osmolality, causing water to move into cells, leading to cellular swelling. In the brain, this swelling can result in neurological symptoms ranging from mild confusion to seizures or coma. Rapid correction of hyponatremia can cause osmotic demyelination, especially in chronic cases.</p><p>Plasma Osmolality = 2Na<sup>+</sup> + Glycemia + Blood urea (280 – 295 mOsm/L)</p><p>5. Medications:</p><p>Some medications can impair renal water excretion, leading to hyponatremia. These include diuretics (especially thiazides), antidepressants (SSRIs), antiepileptics (carbamazepine), and chemotherapy agents.</p><p>6. Thirst Mechanism:</p><p>Excessive intake of free water without adequate sodium intake can also dilute serum sodium, especially in patients with impaired renal water excretion, such as those with SIADH or heart failure.</p><h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4><ol><li>Clinical History and Physical Examination: To evaluate symptoms and volume status</li><li>Classify by Duration:<ul><li>Acute Hyponatremia: Onset within &lt;48 hours, more symptomatic.</li><li>Chronic Hyponatremia: Develops over &gt;48 hours, often less symptomatic but still dangerous.</li></ul></li><li>Evaluate Serum Osmolality:<ul><li>Low Osmolality (&lt; 280 mOsm/kg): True hyponatremia, also called hypotonic hyponatremia.</li><li>Normal Osmolality (280–295 mOsm/kg): Pseudohyponatremia (e.g., due to hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia).</li><li>High Osmolality (&gt;295 mOsm/kg): Hypertonic hyponatremia (e.g., due to hyperglycemia).</li></ul></li><li>Determine Volume Status (Hypotonic Hyponatremia):<ul><li>Hypovolemic Hyponatremia (loss of both sodium and water):<ul><li>Causes: Diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea, burns, Addison's disease.</li><li>Urine sodium &lt;20 mEq/L (extrarenal loss) or &gt;20 mEq/L (renal loss).</li></ul></li><li>Euvolemic Hyponatremia (normal body fluid but low sodium):<ul><li>Causes: SIADH, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, polydipsia.</li><li>Urine sodium &gt;20 mEq/L.</li></ul></li><li>Hypervolemic Hyponatremia (excess water retention):<ul><li>Causes: Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome.</li></ul></li></ul></li></ol></div>

<!-- PAGE 243 -->

<ul><li>Urine sodium typically &lt;20 mEq/L.</li><li>Urine Sodium:<ul><li>Low (&lt; 20 mEq/L): Extrarenal losses (GI losses, third-spacing).</li><li>High (&gt; 20 mEq/L): Renal causes (SIADH, diuretics, renal failure).</li></ul></li><li>Urine Osmolality:<ul><li>Uosm = 1.25 x urea in mmol/L + 1.1 x Na in mmol/L + 67 x Glucose in mmol/L</li><li>Low (&lt; 100 mOsm/kg): Suggests polydipsia or beer potomania.</li><li>High (&gt; 100 mOsm/kg): Suggests SIADH or adrenal insufficiency.</li></ul></li><li>Specific Testing for Underlying Conditions:<ul><li>Check for malignancies, pulmonary, CNS diseases, or drugs that cause SIADH.</li><li>Adrenal and Thyroid Function: Rule out adrenal insufficiency or hypothyroidism.</li></ul></li><li>Imaging Studies: If SIADH is suspected, imaging of the chest or brain might be necessary to rule out tumors or lung pathology.</li></ul><h3>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h3><p>True hyponatremia is associated with hypo osmolality. Conditions causing hyperosmolar hyponatremia and iso-osmolar hyponatremia (pseudo-hyponatremia) should be differentiated first.</p><ul><li>Hyperglycemia</li><li>Mannitol overdose</li><li>Hyperlipidemia</li><li>Hyperproteinemia</li></ul><ul><li>Differential Diagnosis for Hypo-Osmolar Hyponatremia<ul><li>Gastroenteritis</li><li>Diuretic use</li><li>Congestive heart failure</li><li>Liver failure</li><li>Psychogenic polydipsia</li><li>Adrenal crisis</li><li>Renal causes</li><li>SIADH</li><li>Hypothyroidism</li></ul></li><li>Postoperative or Trauma-Related Hyponatremia: Post-surgical patients, especially neurosurgical cases, are at risk of developing SIADH.</li></ul><h3>VII. MANAGEMENT</h3><ol><li>Objectives<ul><li>Classify hyponatremia according to severity, symptomatology, and type of hyponatremia associated with volemia and serum osmolarity.</li><li>Early treatment or prevention of cerebral edema</li><li>Prevent the complications neurologic secondary to rapid increase in natremia. Increase natremia not more than 10mEq/L in first 24h.</li><li>Treat the underlying causes.</li></ul></li><li>Critical signs &amp; symptoms<ul><li>Natremia &lt; 125 mEq/L</li><li>Rapid installation hyponatremia (&lt;48h)</li><li>Mental disturbance</li></ul></li><li>Mortality risk factors<ul><li>Cerebral edema with increase ICP</li><li>Seizures</li><li>Hypovolemic shock</li><li>Pathologies that induce SIADH</li></ul></li><li>Out-patient management<ul><li>Admission is mandatory if the patient is symptomatic or has acute hyponatremia (developing over &lt;48 hours), which increases the risk of cerebral edema.</li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 244 -->

<ul><li>Admission is advised if patient is asymptomatic and has a serum Na+ &lt;125 mEq/dL.</li></ul><p>5. First line therapy</p><h3>General Measures</h3><ul><li>Assess all medications that patients are taking.</li><li>Institute seizure precautions.</li><li>Institute fluid restriction for hypervolemic patients.</li><li>Fluid resuscitation in hypovolemic patients.</li><li>Indications for 3% hypertonic saline versus normal saline solution include: acute hyponatremia, symptomatic hyponatremia, association with intracranial pathology already at risk for cerebral edema.</li></ul><h3>Medication</h3><ul><li>Treatment is tailored to etiology, degree of hyponatremia, onset, and symptomatology; some general principles apply:<ul><li>Expected change in serum Na+ with selected infusate: ΔNa = [(infusate Na<sup>+</sup> + infusate K<sup>-</sup> - serum Na<sup>+</sup>) / (TBW + 1)] TBW = a coefficient × weight (kg)</li></ul></li><li>The coefficient for children and men: 0.6, women and elderly men: 0.5, elderly women: 0.45</li><li><i>Asymptomatic</i>, euvolemic patients can be treated with fluid restriction; etiology must be addressed.</li><li><b>Severe hyponatremia (&lt;125 mEq/L)</b> 3% hypertonic saline should be given.<ul><li>Done as a 100 to 150 mL bolus, with the goal of increasing the serum Na<sup>+</sup> 2 to 3 mEq/L. The bolus may be given twice if symptoms have not resolved.</li><li>Done as a continuous infusion of 3% to increase the serum Na<sup>+</sup> 6 to 8 mEq/L, with the goal to not exceed correction of 10 to 12 mEq/L in the first 24 hours.</li><li>Desmopressin can also be considered, given 1 to 2 µg every 4 to 6 hours.</li><li>Serum Na<sup>+</sup> should be checked every 2 hours. The infusion rate and fluids should be changed to isotonic saline when appropriate.</li><li>In patients who do not respond to the aforementioned approach, consider the use of vasopressin V2-receptor antagonists, such as tolvaptan or conivaptan. This class of medications should not be in used in patients with liver disease.</li><li><i>For mild to moderate hyponatremia</i>, use isotonic saline solution (0.9%).</li><li>In patients with <i>severe hyponatremia (euvolemic and hypervolemic state)</i> who do not respond to the aforementioned approach, consider the use of vasopressin V2-receptor antagonists, such as tolvaptan or conivaptan. This class of medications should not be in used in patients with liver disease</li><li>Patients with <i>hypervolemic hyponatremia</i> caused by cirrhosis, heart failure, or kidney disease benefit from restriction of sodium and fluids, diuretic therapy, and management of the underlying etiology.</li><li>Treat underlying etiology.</li><li><i>Chronic hyponatremia</i> resulting from SIADH: demeclocycline (inhibits ADH action at the collecting duct) if fluid restriction alone is not effective<ul><li>Contraindications: drug allergy, pregnancy, children &lt;8 years old; caution in renal and hepatic disease</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul>

<p>☐ In doses of 600 to 1,200 mg/day, the drug produces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.</p>
<p>☐ Significant possible interactions: oral anticoagulants, oral contraceptives, penicillin</p>
<p><b>6. Treatment adjustments</b></p>
<p>☐ In case of overcorrection, re-lower Na<sup>+</sup> concentration. Begin with infusion of 3 mL/kg of 5% dextrose in water over 1 hour. Repeat Na<sup>+</sup> measurement. Be cautious, dextrose infusion rates &gt;250 to 300 mL/hr can cause significant hyperglycemia in both diabetic and nondiabetic patients and may lead to osmotic diuresis and subsequent free water loss with increased serum Na<sup>+</sup> concentration. Consider 2 to 4 µg IV desmopressin every 8 hours to prevent overcorrection.</p>
<p>☐ Rapid correction of severe symptomatic hyponatremia has been associated with central pontine myelinolysis. This results in irreversible injury. Symptoms are apparent 2 to 6 days after injury and include seizure, coma, spastic paraparesis, dysarthria, and dysphagia. Patients at increased risk are those with Na<sup>+</sup> &lt;105 mEq/L, alcoholism, hypokalemia, and malnutrition. MRI may not be positive until 4 weeks after symptom onset.</p>
<p>☐ Caution: If severe, consider hypertonic saline (3% Na<sup>+</sup> chloride) with central line access, exercise extreme caution, and monitor serum Na<sup>+</sup> as frequently as every 1 to 2 hours.</p>

<h2>Treatment of Severe Symptomatic Hyponatremia</h2>
<p>Serum sodium &lt; 125 mEq per L with severe symptoms (e.g., seizures, mental status changes)</p>
<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between;">
<div>
<p>Infuse 3% saline (1 to 2 mL per kg per hour) with goal of increasing serum sodium level by 6 to 8 mEq per L (not to exceed 10 to 12 mEq per L in the first 24 hours or 18 mEq per L in 48 hours)</p>
<p>Consider desmopressin, 1 to 2 mcg every four to six hours</p>
</div>
<div>
<p>Give single intravenous bolus of 100 to 150 mL 3% saline with goal of increasing serum sodium level by 2 to 3 mEq per L; check sodium level every 20 minutes until symptoms resolve; may repeat bolus twice if symptoms do not resolve</p>
</div>
</div>
<p>Symptom resolution</p>
<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between;">
<div>
<p>Check serum sodium level every two hours; adjust infusion rate and switch to isotonic saline</p>
</div>
<div>
<p>Determine underlying cause (see Table 1)</p>
</div>
</div>
<p><b>Figure 2.</b> Algorithm for the treatment of severe symptomatic hyponatremia.</p>
