<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<p><b>Geriatric Considerations</b></p>
<p>Elderly patients have a decreased renal mass placing them at risk for decreased urinary concentration and decreased response to antidiuretic hormone. Presenting symptoms may be frequent falls and gait disturbances. Clinicians should also consider the impact of comorbidities and acute disease.</p>
<p><b>Pediatric Considerations</b></p>
<p>Children are at increased risk of brain herniation from cerebral edema.</p>
<p><b>Pregnancy Considerations</b></p>
<p>Conivaptan and tolvaptan are class C drugs in pregnancy</p>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>In hospitalized patients, hyponatremia is associated with an elevated risk of adverse clinical outcomes and higher mortality.</li>
<li>Recently, in community-dwelling, middle-aged, and elderly adults, mild hyponatremia has been shown to be an independent predictor of death.</li>
<li>Associated with poor prognosis in patients with acute pulmonary embolism</li>
<li>Associated with poor prognosis in patients with liver cirrhosis and those waiting for liver transplant; it is associated with significant postoperative risk and short-term graft loss.</li>
</ul>
<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Occult tumor may be present if SIADH is identified.</li>
<li>Hypervolemia if isotonic saline solution is used</li>
<li>Osmotic demyelination (central pontine and extrapontine irreversible myelinolysis) if the Na<sup>+</sup> is corrected too quickly.</li>
<li>Hyponatremia is the cause of 30% new-onset seizures in intensive care settings.</li>
<li>Can cause hyponatremic encephalopathy and brain herniation if severe and untreated, especially in young women and children.</li>
<li>Chronic hyponatremia is associated with increased risk of osteoporosis, attention deficit, gait disturbances, falls, and fractures.</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<ul>
<li>Preventing hyponatremia involves identifying at-risk individuals, managing underlying conditions, and implementing strategies to maintain appropriate sodium levels to avoid complication.</li>
<li>Specific recommendations vary based on the cause and severity of the condition, but the focus is on monitoring, avoiding precipitating factors, and correcting sodium imbalances cautiously.</li>
</ul>

<h1>SEPSIS AND SEPTIC SHOCK, EMPIRICAL ANTIBIOTHERAPY</h1><p>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. PEN Phallkum, Dr. NGETH Sopanha</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction due to dysregulated host response to infection, and organ dysfunction is defined as an acute change in total Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of 2 points or greater secondary to the infection cause.</p><p>Septic shock is a subset of sepsis with circulatory and metabolic/cellular dysfunction associated with a higher risk of mortality. In the clinical setting, septic shock is characterized by hypotension requiring vasoactive drugs to maintain a mean arterial pressure of greater than 65 mm Hg along with a serum lactate level of greater than 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation.</p><p>SOFA (sequential organ failure assessment) variables:</p><ul><li>Respiration: PaO<sub>2</sub>/FiO<sub>2</sub> ratio</li><li>Central nervous system: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score</li><li>Cardiovascular: mean arterial pressure (MAP), vasopressor administration with type and rate of infusion</li><li>Renal: serum creatinine, urine output</li><li>Liver: bilirubin</li><li>Coagulation: platelet count</li></ul><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>In 2017, there were an estimated 49 million cases of sepsis and 11 million sepsis-related deaths worldwide. This accounts for approximately 20% of all annual deaths globally. Sepsis affects people of all ages, but children under 5 years old are particularly vulnerable, with an estimated 20 million cases occurring in this age group.</p><p>Regional Disparities: While sepsis is a global health concern, the burden is disproportionately higher in lower-middle-income countries (LMICs). These countries face challenges in early diagnosis, timely treatment, and access to appropriate healthcare resources, contributing to higher mortality rates.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><p>Causative organisms (most commonly bacterial)</p><ul><li>Gram-positive bacteria (most common): Staphylococcus sp., Streptococcus sp., Enterococcus sp.</li><li>Gram-negative: Escherichia coli, Klebsiella sp., Proteus sp., Pseudomonas sp., and anaerobic bacteria</li><li>Fungi: Candida sp.</li><li>Causative organism not identified in 1/3 of cases</li><li>Nosocomial infections in 50% of cases</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 250 -->

<div>
<p>Although an infection can originate anywhere, the lung is the most common source of infection (40%), followed by the abdomen (20%), indwelling venous and arterial catheters and primary bacteraemia (15%), and the urinary tract (10%).</p>
<h4>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h4>
<p>Complex pathophysiology.</p>
<p>Multifactorial: Widespread endothelial dysfunction, complement activation, and activation of coagulation cascade led to tissue hypoperfusion, early hemodynamic changes, and organ dysfunction. An imbalance between proinflammatory and anti-inflammatory mediators leads to relative immunosuppression.</p>
<h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<p><b>History:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Past medical, surgical, social, occupational, and travel history to identify risk factors and potential source</li>
</ul>
<p><b>General symptoms</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Fever, chills, rigors, myalgias</li>
<li>Mental status changes: restlessness, agitation, confusion, delirium, lethargy, stupor, coma</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Specific symptoms (relative to primary source)</b></p>
<ul>
<li><b>Respiratory:</b> cough, sputum production, dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain</li>
<li><b>Urinary:</b> dysuria, frequency, urgency, flank pain</li>
<li><b>Intra-abdominal:</b> nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal pain</li>
<li><b>CNS:</b> stiff neck, headache, photophobia, focal neurologic signs</li>
<li><b>Skin/soft tissue:</b> erythema, edema, purulent discharge</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Physical Exam</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Assess vital signs: hyper-/hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension.</li>
<li>Signs of poor perfusion: central venous hypoxia, delayed capillary refill, cyanosis, mottled skin, altered mental status, oliguria/anuria</li>
<li>Signs of target organ involvement</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Investigation:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Complete blood count (CBC) with differential, comprehensive metabolic profile, coagulation studies, serum lactate, arterial blood gas, urinalysis</li>
<li>Peripheral blood cultures from two different sites (if possible) prior to antibiotic administration. It is important to not delay starting antibiotic therapy because positive blood cultures are not required for diagnosis; 50% of blood cultures are negative in severe sepsis/septic shock.</li>
<li>Cultures from potential sites of infection, including indwelling catheters if present.</li>
<li>Radiographic studies targeted at suspected source</li>
<li>Common findings: leukocytosis/leukopenia, bandemia (&gt;10%), hyperglycemia, metabolic acidosis, mild hyperbilirubinemia, hypoxemia, respiratory alkalosis, proteinuria</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 251 -->

<div>
<ul>
<li>☐ Findings associated with severe disease: anemia, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, azotemia, hypoglycemia, acidosis.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Diagnostic Procedures/Other</b></p>
<ul>
<li>☐ Aspiration, biopsy, and/or drainage of potentially infected body sites (pleural cavity, peritoneal cavity, biliary tree, CSF, abscess); interventional radiology techniques to aid in specimen collection as needed.</li>
<li>☐ Echocardiogram if concern for endocarditis</li>
</ul>
<p><b>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</b></p>
<ul>
<li>☐ Bacteremia without sepsis</li>
<li>☐ Viral, rickettsial, spirochetal, and protozoal diseases</li>
<li>☐ Collagen vascular diseases, vasculitis, pancreatitis, myocardial infarction, CHF, pulmonary embolism, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), thyrotoxicosis, adrenal insufficiency, poisoning, drug reaction.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>VII. MANAGEMENT</b></p>
<ol>
<li><b>Objectives</b><br/>The treatment of patients with septic shock has the following major goals:
        <ul>
<li>☐ Start adequate antibiotic therapy (proper dosage and spectrum) as early as possible</li>
<li>☐ Identify the source of infection, and treat with antimicrobial therapy, surgery, or both (source control)</li>
<li>☐ Resuscitate the patient, using supportive measures to correct hypoxia, hypotension, and impaired tissue oxygenation (hypoperfusion)</li>
<li>☐ Maintain adequate organ system function by maintaining blood flow and arterial pressure, guided by cardiovascular monitoring, and interrupt the progression to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) by appropriate antibiotics and surgical debridement, as needed</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Critical signs</b><br/>Score NEWS-2 ≥ 5 indicate possible severe sepsis</li>
</ol>
</div>

<p><i>SpO2 scale-2 is used for patient with chronic respiratory failure (high PaCO2)</i></p>
<p>The (Quick Sequential [Sepsis-related] Organ Failure Assessment) qSOFA ≥ 2</p>
<p>The qSOFA score is a bedside tool used to quickly identify patients at risk of poor outcomes from sepsis. Use qSOFA alone, to screen for sepsis is not recommended.</p>
<table border="1">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>1</td>
<td>Altered mental status: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score &lt; 15</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>2</td>
<td>Respiratory rate: ≥ 22 breaths per minute</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>3</td>
<td>Systolic blood pressure: ≤ 100 mm Hg</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>A qSOFA score of 2 or more indicates a higher risk of mortality and the need for urgent medical evaluation and intervention</p>
<ol>
<li>Mortality Risk factor
<ul>
<li>High Predisposition: Elderly or immunocompromised patients.</li>
<li>Severe Infection: A widespread infection or resistant infection.</li>
<li>Intense Response: High levels of inflammation markers and severe immune response.</li>
<li>Extensive Organ dysfunction: Multiple organ failure (e.g., lungs, kidneys, heart).</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Outpatient management</li>
<li>First-line treatment
<ul>
<li>Early venous access, administration of IV fluids, and antibiotics</li>
<li>Secure airway and correct hypoxemia when indicated.</li>
<li>Volume resuscitation with crystalloids at 30 ml/kg within 3 hours of presentation</li>
<li>Empiric antibiotic therapy targeted to suspected organism/source within 1 hour of presentation.</li>
<li>Vasopressors for refractory hypotension</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 253 -->

<div><p>Targets to measure clinical response are:</p><ul><li>Central venous oxyhemoglobin saturation (ScvO2) ≥ 70%</li><li>Central venous pressure (CVP) alone should not be used to guide resuscitation. Instead, use dynamic variables including passive leg raises, stroke volume variation, or pulse pressure variation to predict response to resuscitation.</li><li>MAP ≥ 65 mm Hg</li><li>Urine output ≥ 0.5 ml/kg/hr</li></ul><ul><li>Identify and eliminate source of infection and any septic foci.<ul><li>Early surgical consultation for acute abdomen, empyema, necrotizing fasciitis</li><li>interventional radiology consultation for image-guided drainage</li></ul></li><li>Transfuse pRBCs, platelets, and/or fresh frozen plasma for coagulopathic complications or in association with planned procedures.</li><li>Transfuse pRBC if Hgb &lt;7.0 in absence of tissue hypoperfusion, myocardial ischemia, severe hypoxemia, or acute hemorrhage.</li><li>Only transfuses fresh frozen plasma if active hemorrhage or planned procedures.</li><li>Prophylactic platelet transfusion if:<ul><li>&lt;10,000/mm<sup>3</sup> in the absence of bleeding,</li><li>&lt;20,000/ mm<sup>3</sup> with significant risk of bleeding, and</li><li>&lt;50,000/ mm<sup>3</sup> for actively bleeding patients</li></ul></li><li>Stress ulcer and deep venous thrombosis (DVT) prophylaxis</li><li>Glucose control (≤ 180 mg/dL)</li></ul><p>Fluid management</p><ul><li>Initial therapy: 30 ml/kg of crystalloids (Ringer lactate)</li><li>Albumin administration is safe and equally effective compared to crystalloids for patients requiring large volume resuscitation</li></ul><p>Initiate broad-spectrum antibiotic within an hour of diagnosis</p><h4>Empirical antibiotherapy</h4><p>Choose antibiotic based on organs-system suspected to be the primary cause of infection and the microbial epidemiology, antibiotic sensitivity data of the local institution. Follow protocolized recommendation of your hospital. In general, the antibiotic choose should be:</p><ul><li>Adult (Pseudomonas not suspected):<ul><li>vancomycin (loading dose 25 mg/kg) + gram-negative coverage (3rd-generation cephalosporin, β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor [piperacillin/tazobactam 3.375 g IV q6h] or carbapenem)</li></ul></li><li>Adult (Pseudomonas suspected):<ul><li>vancomycin (Recommended loading dose for complicated infections in seriously ill patients is 25 to 30 mg/kg based on actual body weight.)</li><li>Vancomycin (to cover MRSA) plus at least one of the following:<ul><li>A 3rd generation Cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) or</li><li>A combination Beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam, ticarcillin clavulanate), or</li><li>A Carbapenem (e.g., imipenem or meropenem)</li></ul></li></ul></li><li>If pseudomonas is a possible cause, consider Vancomycin plus:<ul><li>An Antipseudomonal cephalosporin (e.g., ceftazidime, cefepime), or</li></ul></li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 254 -->

<ul><li>An Antipseudomonal carbapenem (e.g., imipenem, meropenem), or</li><li>An Antipseudomonal combination beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor (e.g., piperacillin tazobactam, ticarcillin-clavulanate), or</li><li>An Antipseudomonal Fluoroquinolone (e.g., ciprofloxacin), or</li><li>Monobactam (e.g., aztreonam)</li></ul><ul><li>Non-immunocompromised child: 3rd-generation cephalosporin</li><li>Neonate (&lt;7 days old): ampicillin and gentamicin</li><li>Alternatives to vancomycin include linezolid or daptomycin.</li><li>If Burkholderia pseudomallei (Melioidosis) is suspected<ul><li>Regular contact with soil and water is a risk factor.</li><li>Increased risk with diabetes, COPD, alcoholism, chronic renal disease, thalassemia, malignancy, and immunosuppression.</li><li>Classic presentations include pneumonia and multiple abscesses. Sepsis, intra-abdominal infection, septic shock are also frequent.</li></ul></li></ul><p>Preferred, initial IV induction phase:</p><ul><li>Ceftazidime 50 mg/kg (2 g max) IV q6-8h or</li><li>Meropenem 25 mg/kg (1 g max) q8h<ul><li>Dose 2g IV q 8h for adult CNS infections</li></ul></li><li>Duration: 10-14d minimum IV minimum; however, relapse rates can exceed 5%.</li></ul><ul><li>Consider narrowing antibiotic regimen at 48 to 72 hours based on culture results.</li></ul><p>Anticipate antibiotic course in general to last 7 to 10 days.</p><p>Antifungals are not routinely given. Risk factors for fungal infections include long-term antibiotic use, Total parenteral nutrition (TPN), and GI surgery.</p><h2>6. Treatment adjustments</h2><h3>Corticosteroids and sepsis</h3><p>Low dose of hydrocortisone was indicated in CIRCI. The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis dysfunction in critically ill patients is termed “critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency” (CIRCI)</p><ul><li>Do not administer corticosteroids to treat sepsis when shock is not present</li><li>Steroids should not be administered to patients with septic shock unless hemodynamic stability cannot be achieved with fluid resuscitation and vasopressor agents.</li><li>When indicated, for patients with septic shock, administer<ul><li>hydrocortisone 200 mg/day IV in 4 divided doses or</li><li>as a 100-mg bolus followed by continuous infusion at 10 mg/hr (240 mg/d);</li><li>in patients with early severe ARDS, the optimal initial treatment regimen is continuous infusion of methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day</li></ul></li><li>A regimen of 7 days or longer should be used in patients with septic shock before tapering, and</li><li>A regimen of 14 days or longer should be used in patients with early acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) before tapering</li><li>Do not use dexamethasone therapy for septic shock or ARDS</li></ul><h3>Vasopressors</h3>

<!-- PAGE 255 -->

<ul><li>Norepinephrine 0.01 to 3.30 µg/kg/min as initial vasopressor of choice</li><li>Vasopressin 0.03 U/min as an adjunct to norepinephrine to raise BP or decrease norepinephrine requirement.</li><li>Low-dose dopamine for renal protection is not recommended</li><li>Inotropic therapy with dobutamine may benefit patients with myocardial dysfunction or ongoing hypoperfusion if intravascular volume is adequate</li></ul><p>Use of IV immunoglobulins (IVig) has no survival benefit based on high-quality studies. Intermittent hemodialysis or continuous veno-venous hemofiltration (CVVHF) for renal failure when indicated</p><p>7. Graphic:</p><p>The three aspects of Septic shock treatment</p><h4>Treatment of Septic Shock</h4><div><p>Hemodynamic stabilization</p><ul><li>Fluids</li><li>Vasoactive agents</li></ul><p>Infection control</p><ul><li>Antibiotic</li><li>Source control</li></ul><p>Modulation of the septic response</p><ul><li>Corticosteroids<br/>in severe septic shock or CIRCI<br/>(when fluid + vasopressor drug<br/>is needed to stabilize<br/>hemodynamic)</li><li>Low dose vasopressin<br/>(when noradrenaline alone failed to<br/>raise BP, or to reduce the<br/>noradrenaline dose to maintain<br/>hemodynamic)</li></ul></div><p><i>CIRCI: Critical Illness-Related Corticosteroid Insufficiency, BP: blood pressor</i></p><h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3><h4>Pediatric Considerations</h4><ul><li>Sepsis is diagnosed with suspected or proven infection in addition to meeting at least 2 SIRS criteria.</li><li>SIRS in pediatric population requires that abnormality in temperature or WBC be present.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 256 -->

<div>
<p>□ Drug metabolism is reduced in children with sepsis. Monitor drug toxicity labs to prevent adverse effects.</p>
<h4>Geriatric Considerations</h4>
<p>Altered mental status may be presenting signs of infection.</p>
<h4>Pregnancy Considerations</h4>
<p>β-lactam antibiotics, macrolides, and metronidazole generally are considered safe.</p>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<p>Sepsis has a high mortality rate. Estimates range from 10 to 52 percent with rates increasing linearly according to the disease severity of sepsis. Following discharge from the hospital, sepsis carries an increased risk of death as well as an increased risk of further sepsis and recurrent hospital admissions.</p>
<ul>
<li>□ Overall mortality risk ≥ 10% if the SOFA ≥ 2, approximately 40% in septic shock</li>
<li>□ SOFA &gt; 15 associated with &gt;90% mortality.</li>
<li>□ Poor prognostic factors include cirrhosis, immunosuppression (HIV/AIDS, cancer)</li>
</ul>
<h3>X. COMPLICATION</h3>
<ul>
<li>□ GI hemorrhage,</li>
<li>□ DIC,</li>
<li>□ Hyperglycemia,</li>
<li>□ De novo embolic foci of infection,</li>
<li>□ ARDS,</li>
<li>□ Multiorgan failure, death</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<ul>
<li>□ <b>Vaccination:</b> pneumococcal vaccine in children and adults ≥ 65 years or immunocompromised. Hemophilus influenzae type B (infants, young children), influenza, meningococcal vaccine</li>
<li>□ y-Globulin for hypo- or agammaglobulinemia</li>
<li>□ Regular hand washing, sterile technique for vascular and indwelling catheter placement</li>
<li>□ Antibiotic prophylaxis for recommended surgical procedures</li>
<li>□ Prompt extubation for patients on mechanical ventilation as soon as clinically appropriate.</li>
</ul>

<h1>SEVERE ACUTE RESPIRATORY INFECTION (SARI) AND INFLUENZA</h1><p>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda,<br/>Prof. Ass TAING Sovanna, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. PHY Sopheak,<br/>Dr. NGETH Sopanha, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha,<br/>Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya</p><h2>I. CASE DEFINITION</h2><p>Patients with acute respiratory infection who have history of fever (or measured fever of = 38 °C), cough and onset within the last 10 days (symptoms within 10 days) and require hospitalization.</p><table border="1"><thead><tr><th>Clinical syndrome</th><th>Definition</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Influenza-like infection (ILI)</td><td>Acute onset within the last 10 days following respiratory symptoms, measured fever of ≥ 38 °C and cough.</td></tr><tr><td>Acute respiratory infection (ARI)</td><td>Sudden onset of respiratory infection symptoms (cough, sore throat, shortness of breath, or coryza).</td></tr><tr><td>Severe acute respiratory infection (SARI)</td><td>Acute respiratory infection with a history of fever or measured fever of ≥ 38 °C and cough with onset within the last 10 days and requires overnight hospitalization.</td></tr></tbody></table><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>The pathogens that may cause SARI include a wide spectrum of community-acquired pathogens, including respiratory viruses, bacteria and other less common micro-organisms. In addition to the common viral and bacterial pathogens, an emerging respiratory virus may result in SARI and lead to a public health emergency of international concern.</p><p>Worldwide, the annual epidemics of SARI are estimated to result in 3 to 5 million cases of severe illness, and 290 000 to 650 000 respiratory deaths. This estimate does not take in account deaths from other diseases such as cardiovascular disease, which can be influenza-related. Emerging respiratory viruses include: zoonotic influenza viruses, such as avian influenza, and coronaviruses, such as MERS-CoV and SARS-CoV-2, a new subtype of influenza A virus may also have pandemic potential.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><h3>Viral pathogens</h3><p>Common viral pathogens</p><ul><li><input type="checkbox"/> Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)</li><li><input type="checkbox"/> Parainfluenza virus</li><li><input type="checkbox"/> Rhinoviruses</li><li><input type="checkbox"/> Adenovirus, enterovirus (EV-D68)</li><li><input type="checkbox"/> Human metapneumovirus</li><li><input type="checkbox"/> Bocavirus</li><li><input type="checkbox"/> Seasonal influenza, known subtype</li></ul><p>Less common viral pathogens</p>

<!-- PAGE 258 -->

<div>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Varicella zoster</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Measles</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Hantavirus</li>
</ul>
<p>Virus that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern</p>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> SARS</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> SARS-CoV-2</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> MERS</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> New subtypes of influenza</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Other zoonotic viral infections</li>
</ul>
<p>If immunosuppressed (i.e. people living with HIV)</p>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Cytomegalovirus,</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Herpes simplex viruses</li>
</ul>
<h3>Bacterial pathogens</h3>
<p>Most common bacterial pathogens</p>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Streptococcus pneumoniae</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Haemophilus influenzae</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Moraxella catarrhalis</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Legionella pneumophila, non-pneumophila Legionella</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Chlamydia pneumonia</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Mycoplasma pneumoniae</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Klebsiella pneumonia</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Staphylococcus aureus</li>
</ul>
<p>Less common, unless at risk or in high-prevalence geographic area</p>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Mycobacterium tuberculosis</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Burkholderia pseudomallei</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Rickettsial infections</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Coxiella burnetti (Q fever)</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Leptospira spp.</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Chlamydia psittaci</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Bordetella pertussis</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Salmonella sp.</li>
</ul>
<p>Resistant pathogens</p>
<p>Risk factors for multidrug-resistant pathogens: intravenous antimicrobial therapy within &lt; 90 days. Resistant pathogens include:</p>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA)</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Non-fermenters such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Extended spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) producers such as E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterobacter</li>
</ul>
<p>The rate of co-infection among these pathogens is unknown. Therefore, a positive diagnostic test for another infection does not exclude the need for other micro-organism testing.</p>
<h3>Influenza viruses and acute severe viral syndromes</h3>
<p>Influenza viruses are single-stranded RNA viruses of the family Orthomyxoviridae that are classified by their matrix protein composition. Three influenza types can infect humans: influenza A, influenza B, and influenza C. The influenza A virus is divided into specific subtypes based upon two major antigenic proteins on its surface: hemagglutinin (HA) [1 to 16] and</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 259 -->

<div><p>neuraminidase (NA) [1 to 9]. Influenza A can replicate in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract of some avian species without causing symptoms, but infection and symptoms may occur in other bird species, mammals, and humans. It is the only subtype with pandemic potential. Influenza B almost exclusively infects humans. Influenza C affects humans, dogs, and pigs but seldom causes severe illness or epidemics in humans.</p><p>Depending on the origin host, humans can be infected with avian, swine and other zoonotic influenza viruses: such as avian influenza virus subtypes A(H5N1), A(H7N9) and A(H9N2), and swine influenza virus subtypes A(H1N1), A(H1N2) and A(H3N2). Human infections are rare and primarily acquired through direct contact with infected animals or contaminated environments; all these animal influenza type A viruses are distinct from human influenza viruses and have not acquired the ability of sustained transmission among humans. Any new influenza virus is considered to have the potential to cause a pandemic if:</p><ul><li>the virus has demonstrated the capacity to infect a human; and</li><li>the haemagglutinin (HA) gene or protein is not a variant or mutated form of those – A(H1) or A(H3) – circulating widely in the human population.</li></ul><h4>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4><p>Influenza virus has a particular predilection for respiratory epithelial cells. Infected cells undergo abrupt cessation of protein synthesis and subsequent apoptosis. Viral particles are released infecting nearby cells. Local immune cells are also infected, causing measurable deficiencies in immune function, increasing the likelihood of secondary complications. Lung histopathology of fatally infected patients reveals a diffuse alveolar filling process, with early hyaline membrane formation, and occasionally focal areas of hemorrhage. The alveolar lining is thickened, with lymphocytic infiltrates and, occasionally, early fibrosis.</p><h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4><p>Avian, swine and other zoonotic influenza virus infections in humans may cause disease ranging from mild upper respiratory tract infection (fever and cough), early sputum production and rapid progression to severe pneumonia, sepsis with shock, ARDS, and even death. Conjunctivitis, gastrointestinal symptoms, encephalitis and encephalopathy have also been reported to varying degrees depending on subtype.</p><h5>Clinical presentation</h5><p>Signs and symptoms of complicated ARI (SARI)</p><ul><li><b>Respiratory distress:</b> fast breathing, shortness of breath, accessory muscle use, cyanosis.<br/>– In children: central cyanosis, severe distress, grunting, severe chest indrawing or danger signs of lethargy, convulsions or inability to breastfeed or drink.</li><li><b>Cardiovascular distress:</b><br/>– Adult: low blood pressure (SBP &lt; 100); delayed capillary refill (&gt; 3 sec &lt; 65 years or &gt; 4.5 sec in older people); fast and weak pulse.<br/>– Child: delayed capillary refill (&gt; 3 sec); fast and weak pulse; or cool extremities or hypotension.</li><li><b>Neurologic distress:</b> alteration in mental status such as coma, lethargy, confusion, seizures, agitation.</li><li><b>Dehydration:</b></li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 260 -->

<ul><li>In children: diarrhea plus any two of the following signs: lethargy, sunken eyes, very slow skin pinch, unable to drink or drinks poorly.<ul><li>Persistent fever that is not responding after 3 days.</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>Investigation</b></p><ul><li>CBC with differential (Decreased leukocyte, platelet, and lymphocyte counts are associated with increased mortality.)</li><li>Liver profile</li><li>Chemical profile</li><li>Blood culture</li><li>Chest x-ray (CXR): initial foci of consolidation. After 7 days, patchy lobar and interstitial infiltrates develop. Pleural effusions with cavitation are less common.</li><li>Lab confirmation of H5N1 is case by case:<ul><li>Positive influenza A/H5 (Asian lineage) virus real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (rRT-PCR).</li><li>Antigen detection tests: Rapid influenza diagnostic tests (RIDT) and immunofluorescence assay tests have low sensitivity to detect H5N1.</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</b></p><ul><li>Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)</li><li>Pneumonia</li><li>SARI caused by different organisms</li></ul><p><b>VII. MANAGEMENT</b></p><ol><li>Objectives<ul><li>Identify and treat severe / critical cases, as soon as possible</li><li>Early provide antiviral as indicated</li><li>Minimize spread through droplet precaution and contact precautions.</li><li>Supportive treatment as indicated (ventilation, fluid, vasopressor, diuretic, prone position)</li><li>Minimize complications of treatment (mechanical ventilation)</li></ul></li><li>Critical Sign<ul><li>Requires life sustaining treatment (mechanical ventilation, hemodialysis, pressor support...)</li><li>Acute respiratory distress Syndrome (ARDS)</li><li>Sepsis</li><li>Septic shock</li><li>Acute thrombosis (pulmonary thromboembolism, acute coronary syndrome, acute stroke...)</li></ul></li><li>Mortality risk factor<ul><li>Risk factors associated with severe disease:<ul><li>Age more than 60 years (increasing with age).</li><li>Underlying noncommunicable diseases (NCDs): diabetes, hypertension, cardiac disease, chronic lung disease, cerebrovascular disease, dementia, mental disorders, chronic kidney disease, immunosuppression (including HIV), obesity and cancer.</li></ul></li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 261 -->

<div>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> In pregnant or recently pregnant: women &gt; 35 years old, obesity, with chronic medical conditions or pregnancy specific disorders (e.g. gestational diabetes and pre-eclampsia/eclampsia).</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Smoking.</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Young children (&lt; 59 months).</li>
</ul>
<p><b>4. Outpatient Management</b></p>
<p>Patient with non-complicate influenza-like infection (ILI) and non-complicate acute respiratory infection (ARI) may have supportive treatment at home. However, people who have risk factors associated with severe disease (above) should have medical check and advice. In adults, the CURB-65 score is a validated tool that, when combined with clinical judgments can be used to predict mortality and aid in determining admission for adult patients with pneumonia.</p>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>CURB-65 score:<br/>one point for each feature present</th>
<th>Total points</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Confusion</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Urea &gt; 7mmol/l</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>RR ≥ 30/min</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Blood pressure (SBP &lt; 90 or DBP ≤ 60mmHg)</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Age ≥ 65 ys</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Score 0 – 1: low severity, risk of death &lt; 3%, consider home-base care</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Score 2 – 3: Moderate severity, risk of death 3 – 15%, consider hospitalization</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Score 4 – 5: High severity, risk of death &gt; 15%, consider ICU</li>
</ul>
<p>Patients should be admitted to ICU based on severity of clinical condition and resource availability. In hospitals where oxygen therapy is only available in the ICU, admit all SARI patients to the ICU. In hospitals where oxygen therapy can also be delivered on wards, admit less severe SARI patients to wards but with increased monitoring.</p>
<p><b>5. First-line treatment</b></p>
<p>Give oxygen to patients who have dyspnea. Target SpO2: 94-96%</p>
<p>Option for oxygenation support:</p>
<ul>
<li>Standard oxygen therapy: use nasal cannula, simple mask, venturi mask, or mask with oxygen reservoir bag.</li>
<li>High Flow nasal canula (HFNC): need specific machine, some ICU-ventilator have this function</li>
<li>Non-invasive ventilation (NIV): use ICU-ventilator, or standalone CPAP machine</li>
<li>Mechanical ventilation: ICU-ventilator. Patient needs to be intubated.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Antiviral drugs</b></p>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Mild to moderate cases: oseltamivir (Tamiflu) 75 mg PO BID for 5 days</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Severe cases: oseltamivir (Tamiflu) 150 mg BID for 7 to 10 days</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Postexposure prophylaxis: oseltamivir (Tamiflu) 75 mg PO once a day for 7 to 10 days</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Monitor for resistance; some H5N1 and H7N9 viruses show resistance to oseltamivir.</li>
</ul>
<p>Almost all patients with severe influenza in the ICU will have deficits in oxygenation, leading to acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and requiring ventilatory support. Shock and renal failure are also common.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 262 -->

<h4>Antibacterial drugs</h4>
<p>Secondary bacterial pneumonia was common in severe influenza. The most important adjunctive pharmacologic treatment in critically ill patients with influenza is empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover possible secondary bacterial pneumonia or influenza-bacterial coinfection. Antibiotics should be selected according to local antibiograms to cover the most common pathogens involved, namely <i>S. pneumoniae</i>, <i>S. aureus</i> (including methicillin-resistant <i>S. aureus</i> [MRSA]), <i>S. pyogenes</i>, and occasionally, gram-negative bacteria.</p>
<h4>6. Treatment adjustment</h4>
<h5>ARDS,</h5>
<p>if PaO<sub>2</sub>/FiO<sub>2</sub> &gt; 200, it may response with NIV.</p>
<p>the severe ARDS (PaO<sub>2</sub>/FiO<sub>2</sub> &lt; 150, usually need mechanical ventilation. Use lung protective strategy with high PEEP. Control mode ventilation with appropriate sedation and use of neuromuscular blockade to avoid ventilatory desynchrony and high airway pressures are often needed.</p>
<h5>Septic shock</h5>
<p>Septic shock is common in critically ill patients with influenza and typically results in refractory hypotension and need for moderate to high doses of vasopressors. For fluid resuscitation, the patient should receive at least 30 mL/kg of crystalloid via bolus dosing. Avoid volume overload by judicious use of diuretics.</p>
<h5>Acute kidney injury</h5>
<p>The development of AKI often necessitates renal replacement therapy (hemodialysis) to correct bicarbonate deficiencies to allow for increased tolerability of hypercapnia when poor lung compliance prohibits effective ventilation.</p>

</li>

</li>
<li>Implement droplet and contact isolation</li>
</ul>

<p>The flowchart branches into two main paths:</p>
<ol>

        <ul>

<ul>

</ul>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>High probability case</b> (from NAAT (+) result):

                <ul>

                        <ul>

<li>If No alternative etiology recovered: Continue antibiotics for 5days* if CAP confirmed or suspected</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>

<p>Reassess antibacterials based on culture / clinic</p>
<ul>
<li>Tailor antibacterials to pathogen and continue for 5days if indicated* OR D/c antibacterials (if low suspicion for bacterial CAP)</li>
</ul>

<p>* A longer course may be needed if CAP is complicated by meningitis, endocarditis, or other deep-seated infection; suspected or proven MRSA or P. aeruginosa pneumonia may require a 7-day treatment course; less common specific pneumonia pathogens may require longer courses (e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Burkholderia pseudomallei).</p>

<div>
<p>** Because of prolonged viral shedding with primary influenza pneumonia, treatment durations longer than 5 days may be warranted, particularly for ARDS, immunocompromised, and/or severely ill patients, to a maximum of 10 days.</p>
<p>*** Results of most NAAT testing are highly sensitive and very highly specific. If influenza is highly suspected clinically during times of high influenza activity and NAAT results are negative, the NPV remains low, and a negative NAAT may reflect a false-negative result. If symptoms present &gt;4 days, diagnostic yield is lower and may also result in a false-negative.</p>
<p>CAP, Community-acquired pneumonia; d/c; discontinue; ILI, influenza-like illness; NAAT, nucleic acid amplification test; NP, nasopharyngeal.</p>

        <ul>

                <ul>

<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<p>Most hospitalized patients have risk factors. However, approximately half of hospitalized patients during pandemic years might otherwise be healthy. Whereas most patients with influenza do not develop critical illness, 11%–19% of patients hospitalized with laboratory-confirmed influenza require treatment in the ICU. Those who develop critical illness often deteriorate rapidly, and severe illness may be protracted. For patients requiring mechanical ventilation, the mean duration is approximately 5–12 days. Many patients are difficult to oxygenate, leading to increased length of ICU stay and excess mortality. H5N1 human disease: among more than 1000 cases since 2013 in 21 countries; mortality rate of 40–61%. Mean age 16 yrs; rare deaths in people &gt;40 yrs.</p>
<h3>X. Complications</h3>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Secondary bacterial pneumonia, ARDS</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Sepsis, septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Myocarditis, dysrhythmia, myocardial infarction</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 265 -->

<div>
<p><input type="checkbox"/> Acute kidney injury</p>
<p><input type="checkbox"/> Encephalitis</p>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<p>Influenza is transmitted from person-to-person primarily through large-particle respiratory droplets; thus, patients with suspected influenza should be instructed to use appropriate hand hygiene, cough etiquette, and be given a face mask to wear upon entry into healthcare facilities. Patients who must be transported outside of the room should wear a mask if tolerated, or when necessary, an oxygen delivery system that limits the spread of aerosols (mask over cannula of HFNC).</p>
<p>Influenza vaccination is the best way to prevent or mitigate the severity of influenza illness, and in the absence of contraindications, is recommended annually, particularly those with risks for severe disease and for HCP. Vaccination and postexposure chemoprophylaxis are recommended for close contacts who are at very high risk of influenza complications.</p>
<p>Healthcare personnel (HCP) should apply droplet precautions by wearing standard surgical tie masks and use appropriate hand hygiene. HCPs should also consider contact precautions with gloves when anticipating contact with bodily fluids or touch with contaminated surfaces. Protective eyewear is recommended when providing direct care in close proximity to the patient. Ill HCPs with fever and respiratory symptoms should be instructed not to work until fever has dissipated for &gt;24 hours.</p>

<h2>I. OVERVIEW</h2>
<p>In Cambodia, among more than 86 known species, 17 species were known to be venomous. There are 11 species of important clinical interests. There are 2 main families of venomous snake in Cambodia. The Elapidae, has short and fixed front fang round eyes. Look from above; their head are mostly trapezoid form. This family includes cobras, king cobra, krait and sea snake, their venom contains mostly neurotoxic effect. The Viperidae has long and moveable fang, their eyes are oval, look from above; their head are mostly triangle. Some of species in this family has thermo-sensor organ. It counts pit vipers, Russell's viper. Their venom is mostly hematotoxic and myotoxic.</p>

EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>It is generally recognized that the epidemiology of snakebite in the South-Est Asia Region has not been adequately studied and that the published data, based almost exclusively on hospital return to the ministry of health, therefore misleading. One reason is that many snakebite victims are treated not in hospital but by traditional healers. The incidence of snakebite varies diurnally and seasonally. It is highest during agricultural activities and seasoning rains. Male are more often bitten than female.</p><p>WHO classified venomous snakes in 2 categories:</p>

<!-- PAGE 269 -->

<div>
<p>① Category 1: Highest medical importance – highly venomous snakes which are common or widespread and cause numerous snakebites, resulting in high levels of morbidity disability or mortality</p>
<p>② Category 2: secondary medical importance – highly venomous snake capable of causing morbidity, morbidity, disability or death, but for which exact epidemiological or clinical data are lacking or are less frequently implicated because of their behavior, habitat preferences or occurrence in areas remote to large human, populations</p>

<td rowspan="2">Category 2</td>
<td>Viperidae</td>
<td>- Malayan pit viper<br/>- Russell's viper</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Elapidae</td>
<td>- Banded krait<br/>- Red-headed krait,<br/>- king cobra.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3>III. ETIOLOGY</h3>
<p>Most often, snake bite is an occupational disease. People get bite at work on the rice field (cobra, Malayan pit viper, Russell's viper) on rubber/palm plantation (Malayan pit viper, green pit viper). The other jobs that predisposing people to snake bite are hunting, fishing, and fishing farming, catching and handling snakes for food, displaying and performing with snakes (cobra). Sometime the bite is the result of trodden upon sleeping snake.</p>
<h3>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h3>
<p>Snakebite may cause “clinical syndrome” that is specific and non-specific. The bites may accompany by a varying degree of envenoming or no envenoming at all. Clinical patterns are related to venom of causal snake.</p>
<p>Composition and antigenicity of snake venoms is more than 90% of snake venom (dry weight) is protein. Each venom contains more than a hundred different proteins:</p>
<ul>
<li>Enzymes (constituting 80-90% of viperid and 25-70% of elapid venom):
        <ul>
<li>Snake venom metalloproteases (SVMPS) damage basement membranes, causing endothelial cell damage and spontaneous systemic bleeding.</li>
<li>Procoagulant enzymes stimulate blood clotting with formation of fibrin on blood, causing platelet aggregation, anticoagulation and hemorrhage.</li>
<li>Phospholipases A2 damage mitochondria, red blood cells, leucocytes, platelets, peripheral nerve ending, skeletal muscle, vascular endothelium and other membranes, producing presynaptic neurotoxic activity, cardiotoxicity, myotoxicity, necrosis, hypotension, hemolysis, anti-coagulation, hemorrhage, plasma leakage and auto pharmacological release of histamine and other autacoids.</li>
<li>Acetylcholinesterase may cause fasciculation.</li>
<li>Hyaluronidase: increasing permeability but can also contribute to damage cell tissue.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Non-enzymatic polypeptide toxins: postsynaptic (②) neurotoxin and presynaptic (②) neurotoxin damage nerve ending irreparably.</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 270 -->

<ul><li>Non-toxic proteins such as growth factor.</li></ul><h2>V. DIAGNOSIS</h2><h3>1. Clinic presentation</h3><p>Victim of snakebite may present with general nonspecific symptoms, specific symptoms for some types of snake venom, and sometimes, the consequences of disorders related to venom (anemia, renal failure, hypovolemic/cardiogenic shock, compartment syndrome...)</p><ul><li>Local symptoms and sign:<ul><li>Fang marks</li><li>Local pain</li><li>Local bleeding</li><li>Bruising</li><li>Lymphangitis (raised red lines tracking up the bitten limb)</li><li>Lymph node enlargement</li><li>Inflammation (swelling, redness, heat)</li><li>Blistering</li><li>Local infection</li><li>Abscess formation</li><li>Necrosis</li></ul></li><li>Generalized(systemic) signs and symptoms<ul><li>Syndrome related to Viperidae<p>Most of the species in the Viperidae family have venom that contains enzymes that interfere with blood clot and coagulation that produce hematologic disorder (i.e. ecchymosis, bleeding from the fang marks, bleeding from the cut wound, internal bleeding, increase the amount of menses...). Bleeding with or without hemolysis may be severe and lead to hemorrhagic shock and acute renal failure. Locally, pain is often severe, inflammation is important and rapidly expand, the blister may color black (Malayan pit viper, Russell's viper). Muscle tissue necrosis expand in depth and in surface with hyperkalemia and rhabdomyolysis.</p></li><li>Syndrome related to Elapidae<p>Most of the Elapidae snake venom contains neurotoxins that cause muscular paralysis (neurologic disorder). The death may result from respiratory muscle paralysis and respiratory arrest. The muscular group in the face is the first to be affected by neurotoxin, follow by neck and truck, when the respiratory muscle paralysis occurred. Ptosis or heavy eyelid is often the first sign of neurotoxin envenoming. Patient was looked like sleep; people has remarked that when that victim falls asleep, he will die.</p><p>All species in genres naja had neurotoxin alpha, the genre krait (Malayan krait, banded krait, red head krait, and sea snake) had neurotoxin alpha and neurotoxin beta. Disorders caused by neurotoxin beta, may be non-reversible or left neurologic sequelae after antivenom therapy. Other neurologic sign and symptoms are drowsiness, paraesthesiae, abnormalities of taste and smell, aphonia, regurgitation through the nose, difficulty in swallowing secretions, respiratory and generalized flaccid paralysis.</p></li></ul></li><li>Clinical syndrome<ul><li>Syndrome 1: local sign (swelling etc.) with bleeding/clotting disturbances = Viperidae (all species)</li><li>Syndrome 2: local sign (swelling etc.) with bleeding/clotting disturbances, shock or acute kidney injury, dark brown urine bilateral ptosis, external ophthalmoplegia, fascial paralysis = Russell's viper, with conjunctival edema (chemosis) and acute pituitary insufficiency = Russell's viper and Malayan viper</li><li>Syndrome 3: local sign (swelling etc.) with paralysis = cobra or king cobra</li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 271 -->

<div>
<ul>
<li>Syndrome 4: paralysis with minimal or no local sign:
        <ul>
<li>bitten on land while sleeping on the ground with/without abdominal pain = krait</li>
<li>bitten in the sea = sea snake</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Syndrome 5: paralysis with dark brown urine and acute kidney injury:
        <ul>
<li>bitten on land (with bleeding/clotting disturbance) = Russell's viper</li>
<li>bitten on land while sleeping indoor = krait</li>
<li>bitten in the sea (no bleeding/clotting disturbance) = sea snake</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p><b>2. Investigation and laboratory tests</b></p>
<ul>
<li>The 20-minute whole blood clotting test “20WBCT” or whole blood clotting test at 20 min. Positive test means that patient had been bitten by snake that mostly is in Viperidae family.</li>
</ul>
<p>Place 2 mL of freshly sampled venous blood in a small, new or heat cleaned, dry, glass vessel. Leave undisturbed for 20 minutes at ambient temperature. Tip the vessel once. If the blood is still liquid (unclothed) and runs out, the patient has hypofibrinogenemia (“uncoagulable blood”) as a result of venom-induced consumption coagulopathy.</p>
<p style="text-align: center;">Clotting time using test tube method</p>
<img alt="Diagram illustrating the 20WBCT procedure. A test tube containing 2ml of blood is shown next to a clock indicating 20 minutes. An arrow points to two outcomes: 'Clot formed' (blood solidified) and 'No Clotting' (blood remains liquid)."/>
<ul>
<li>Other blood test help confirm envenoming: high hematocrit (plasmatic lose), anemia, low hematocrit (blood lose), acute leukocytosis (systemic envenoming), low platelet (coagulation abnormality), high potassium (rhabdomyolysis), abnormal liver function tests (systemic envenoming), respiratory acidosis (Arterial blood gas “ABG”. Low function of respiratory muscle), high BUN, creatinine (acute renal failure).</li>
<li>Other investigation: urine examination, chest X-ray, whole abdominal ultrasound, ECG, heart ultrasound, brain CT scan.</li>
<li>Normally there is no need to wait for lab test results to start antivenom therapy, if clinical signs and symptoms are matched with envenoming or when the 20WBCT was positive.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Anaphylaxis</li>
<li>Deep venous thrombosis</li>
<li>Extremity vascular trauma</li>
<li>Scorpion envenomation</li>
<li>Septic shock</li>
<li>Serum sickness</li>
<li>Wasp stings</li>
<li>Wound infection</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 272 -->

<h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2>
<ol>
<li>Objective
    <ul>
<li>Reassure the snakebite victim</li>
<li>Preserve life and prevent complication</li>
<li>Control distressing or dangerous early symptoms of envenoming</li>
<li>Arrange the transport of the patient to a place where they can receive medical care or more facility.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Critical sign
    <p>Indication or criteria for antivenom treatment: antivenom treatment is recommended if and when a patient with proven or suspected snakebite develops one or more the following signs:</p>
<ol type="a">
<li>Systemic envenoming:
        <ul>
<li>Hemostatic abnormalities</li>
<li>Neurotoxic signs</li>
<li>Cardiovascular abnormalities</li>
<li>Acute kidney injury</li>
<li>Hemoglobin-/myoglobinuria: dark brown urine, rhabdomyolysis</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Local envenoming:
        <ul>
<li>Local swelling involving more than half of the bitten limb</li>
<li>Rapid extension of swelling</li>
<li>Development of an enlarged tender lymph node draining the bitten limb.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>Mortality risk factor
    <p>Factors identified as distributing to a fatal outcome included</p>
<ul>
<li>Availability, the right antivenom and dose of antivenom.</li>
<li>Delayed hospital treatment: transportation problem.</li>
<li>Inadequate of supported treatment: mechanic ventilation, hemodynamic treatment, renal replacement therapy.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Outpatient management
    <ul>
<li>All envenomed patients should be managed in hospital</li>
<li>The traditional measure (tourniquet, cut the wound, suction on the wound, local application of 'medicine', burning point) are not effective and in some case, it may be dangerous.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>First-line treatment
    <ol type="A">
<li>First aid
        <ul>
<li>Reassure the victim who may be very anxious</li>
<li>Immobilize the whole of the patient's body by lying him/her down in a comfortable and safe position</li>
<li>Apply pressure-pad immobilization, pressure-bandage immobilization</li>
<li>Avoid any interference with the bite wound.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Treatment in hospital
        <ul>
<li>Rapid primary clinical assessment and resuscitation</li>
<li>Airway potency, respiratory movements, arterial pulse and level of consciousness must be immediately checked. Conditions that need immediate assessment and management are: shock syndrome from direct venom effect, or secondary to hypovolemia (bleeding), or by arrhythmia secondary to hyperkaliemia (Rhabdomyolysis). Respiratory arrest, central acute respiratory failure (Elapidae). Sudden deterioration and systemic toxic pattern immediately after removing the tight tourniquet and compressed bandage.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 273 -->

<h3>C. Medication</h3>
<ul>
<li>Actually (2011), the available anti-venom are the 2 polyvalent anti venoms made in Thailand.
        <ul>
<li>"TRC Neuro-polyvalent snake" can cover the venoms of neurotoxic Elapidae and</li>
<li>"TRC Hemato-polyvalent snake" can cover the venoms of hematotoxic Viperidae</li>
<li>Normal saline solution is added in 1 vial to make a 10mL solution. The total amount of anti-venom solution needed can be administrated in slow IV injection (max. 2mL/minute) or by IV infusion diluted in about 5mL isotonic fluids per Kg body weight (i.e. about 250mL of isotonic saline or 5% dextrose in case of an adult patient) and infuse in 30-60 minutes.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>The route of administration is intravenously</li>
<li>No test needed prior to injection, but be prepared the emergency treatment of anaphylactic reactions (adrenaline, bag-valve mask, infusion set, anti-histamine, corticoid)</li>
<li>The initial dose is usually empiric and varies with species and with the clinical severity</li>
<li>Guide to initial dosage for some antivenoms for treating bites by medically-important snakes in South-East Asia region, based on clinical experience, rather than antivenoms' recommendation.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 274 -->

<div>
<p>6. Treatment adjustment</p>
<ol type="A">
<li>Antivenom treatment can be expected to neutralize free circulating venom, prevent progression of envenoming and allow recovery. However, these processes take time and the severely envenomed patient may require life support system such as reduction of pain, treatment of shock, assisted ventilation and renal dialysis until the severely damaged organs and tissue have had time to recover.</li>
<li>Treatment of the bitten part
        <ul>
<li>Wound management: wound dressing.</li>
<li>Bacterial infection: gentamicin with benzyl penicillin, amoxicillin or cephalosporin plus a single dose only of gentamicin plus metronidazole and tetanus prophylaxis.</li>
<li>Compartmental syndromes and fasciotomy: fasciotomy should not be contemplated until hemostatic abnormalities have been corrected, otherwise the patient may bleed to death.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<p>7. Algorithm: Recognize species via clinical/symptoms</p>
<img alt="Flowchart for Snakebite diagnosis. Start: Snakebite. Question 1: Is blood incoagulable? If Yes, Question 2: Is there evidence of renal impairment? If Yes, Russell's viper. If No, Malayan pit viper. If No (from Q1), Question 3: Is neurotoxicity present? If Yes, Question 4: Is neurotoxicity the only clinical effect? If Yes, King cobra and cobra. If No, Krait. If No (from Q3), Question 5: Are the local effects very severe? If Yes, Green pit viper. If No, Big eye pit viper or Vogel's pit viper."/>
<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<p>In case antivenom reaction</p>
<ul>
<li>Epinephrine (Adrenaline) is given intramuscularly in an initial dose of 0,5 mg for adult, 0,01 mg/kg body weight for child, can be repeated every 5-10 minutes if the reaction persists or the symptoms become worse</li>
<li>Additional treatment: inhaled short acting β<sub>2</sub> agonist bronchodilator such as salbutamol or terbutaline, antihistamine anti-H1 blocker such as chlorphenamine maleate (adult 10mg, children 0,2 mg/Kg by intravenous injection), intravenous hydrocortisone (adult 100 mg, children 2mg/kg)</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 275 -->

<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3><p>Observation of the response to antivenom, in general the patient feel better quickly, spontaneous systemic bleeding usually stops within 15-30 minutes, blood coagulability (as measured by 20WBCT) is usually restored in 3-9 hours, in shocked patient blood pressure may increase within the first 30-60 minutes and arrhythmia, bradycardia may resolve, neurotoxic envenoming may begin to improve as early as 30 minutes after antivenom but may take several times.</p><p>Criteria for giving more antivenom include a persistence or recurrence of blood incoagulability after 6 hours or of bleeding after 1-2 hours, deteriorating neurotoxic or cardiovascular signs after 1 hours.</p><p>The reversibility of toxic effect depends on time of treatment, correct choice of antivenoms, sufficient doses given. Effects against hematologic disorder (viperidae) still exist even 1 week after bite. Toxic effects may be reserved in a few hours or few days.</p><h3>X. COMPLICATION</h3><ul><li>At the site of the bite, loss of tissue: surgical debridement, necrotic areas, amputation, malignant transformation</li><li>Chronic kidney disease (renal failure)</li><li>Chronic neurological deficit</li><li>Abnormalities of electrophysiological test can persist for over 12 months following elapid bites.</li><li>Delayed psychological morbidities: depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)</li></ul><h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3><ul><li>Be prepared to protect again snake bite when working in the field, sleeping, or walking in the forest.</li><li>Community education reduces the risk of snakebite. Involve all the community workers, traditional healers, villagers. Distribute leaflets, banners, posters, video clips, displayed in hospital or clinic waiting areas and disseminate them via the radio, TV and social network.</li><li>Be informed of signs and symptoms of envenoming and seeking medical care immediately when they got it.</li><li>The difficulty to open the eyes (looks like sleepy) after snake bite is alarming sign of respiratory arrest, and should prompt patient to go to hospital</li><li>Bleeding disorder, purpura, ecchymoses, can be treated medically, if left longer it may kill the patient.</li></ul><h3>XII. REFERENCES</h3><ol><li>Clinical practice guideline for medicine, Cambodia, 2013, snakebite, p.60-67</li><li>Guideline for management of snakebite, 2<sup>nd</sup> edition, 2016, WHO regional office South-Est Asia</li><li>David J Williams, Simon D Jensen, Mark O'Shea, editors. Snakebite management in Cambodia 2009.</li><li>Guideline for the management of snakebite South-East Asia region, WHO 2005, p.61</li><li><a href="https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/168828-differential">https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/168828-differential</a></li><li>Malaysian guideline, management of snakebite</li></ol>

<h1>MASSIVE BLOOD TRANSFUSION</h1>
<p><i>Prof. CHHUOY Meng, Prof. CHHOR Nareth, Dr. SOEU Khemry, Dr. IM Sothy, Dr. HUN Vanasola, Dr. LY Chhuong, Dr. RA Vannak, Dr. OEUR Sovanratha, Dr. KROUCH Sophallyda, Dr. TES Sovannara, Dr. THEANG Pheakdey, Dr. IM Virya, Asst. Prof. TAING Sovanna, Dr. PHY Sopheak, Dr. PEN Phallkun, Dr. NGETH Sopanha</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Common definitions for massive transfusion in adults include:</p>
<ul>
<li>transfusion of ≥ 10 red blood cell (RBC) units within 24 hours or</li>
<li>transfusion of &gt; 4 RBC units in 1 hour with anticipated need for further blood product transfusion or</li>
<li>replacement of &gt; 50% of total blood volume (TBV) by blood products within 3 hours (remember that a female height 160cm has TBV = 70 x54 ~ 3780 ml)</li>
</ul>
<p>Common definitions for massive transfusion in children and adolescents include</p>
<ul>
<li>transfusion of &gt; 100% of TBV within 24 hours</li>
<li>transfusion support to replace ongoing hemorrhage of &gt; 10% TBV/minute</li>
<li>replacement of &gt; 50% TBV by blood products within 3 hours.</li>
</ul>
<p>The general estimate TBV for pediatric patients is about 80 ml per kg of body weight. Here's a quick breakdown:</p>
<ul>
<li>Neonates (0-28 days): Approximately 85-90 ml per kg</li>
<li>Infants (1 month to 1 year): Approximately 75-80 ml per kg</li>
<li>Children (over 1 year): Approximately 70-80 ml per kg)</li>
</ul>
<h2>II. INDICATION</h2>
<p>massive transfusion may be implemented in both trauma and non-trauma clinical settings</p>
<ul>
<li>Common trauma events leading to massive bleeding include:
        <ul>
<li>penetrating trauma such as knife or gunshot wound</li>
<li>blunt trauma to chest or abdomen</li>
<li>suicide attempts</li>
<li>amputations</li>
<li>bone fractures that result in further injury to internal organs and blood vessels</li>
<li>shearing of existing injury from sudden rotation and violent extension and flexion</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Non-trauma settings for massive bleeding include
        <ul>
<li>obstetric hemorrhage</li>
<li>gastrointestinal bleeding</li>
<li>surgical complications</li>
<li>vascular emergencies, such as ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 277 -->

<h3>III. BLOOD PRODUCTS IN CLINICAL USE</h3>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Component</th>
<th>Content</th>
<th>Indication and dose</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Whole blood (1 unit = 500 mL) *</td>
<td>RBCs, platelets, plasma</td>
<td>Rarely required.<br/>May be appropriate when massive bleeding requires transfusion of more than 5 to 7 units of RBCs (increasingly used in early trauma management).</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>RBCs in additive solution (1 unit = 350 mL), [pRBC]</td>
<td>RBCs</td>
<td>Anemia, bleeding.<br/>The increase in hemoglobin from 1 unit of RBCs will be approximately 1 g/dL; the increase in hematocrit will be approximately 3 percentage points.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Fresh Frozen plasma (FFP) or other plasma product<br/>(1 unit = 200 to 300 mL)</td>
<td>All soluble plasma proteins and clotting factors</td>
<td>Bleeding or expected bleeding (e.g., emergency surgery) in individuals with deficiencies of multiple coagulation factors (e.g., DIC, liver disease, massive transfusion, anticoagulation with warfarin or warfarin overdose if not corrected by vitamin K and/or PCC, depending on the clinical setting).<br/>Bleeding in individuals with isolated factor deficiencies (most often factor V) if a factor concentrates or recombinant factor is not available.<br/>Therapeutic plasma exchange in TTP (as a source of ADAMTS13).<br/>In the rare event that FFP is used to replace a clotting factor, the dose is 10 to 20 mL/kg. This dose will raise the level of any factor, including fibrinogen, by close to 30%, which is typically sufficient for hemostasis.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cryoprecipitate, also called "cryo" (1 unit = 10 to 20 mL)</td>
<td>Fibrinogen; factors VIII and XIII; VWF</td>
<td>Bleeding patients with acquired hypofibrinogenemia, which may be due to cardiac surgery, liver transplant, postpartum hemorrhage, or trauma with massive transfusion.<br/>DIC.<br/>Uremia if DDAVP (desmopressin) is ineffective. The increase in plasma fibrinogen from 1 unit of Cryoprecipitate per 10 kg body weight will be approximately 50 mg/dL.<br/>Cryoprecipitate is generally provided in pools containing 5 units, and most patients receive 1 to 2 pools.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<p>DIC: disseminated intravascular coagulation; FFP: Fresh Frozen Plasma; PCC: prothrombin complex concentrate; RBCs: red blood cells; TTP: thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura; VWF: von Willebrand factor.</p>

<h4>IV. EFFECTS OF MASSIVE HEMORRHAGE (OTHER THAN HYPOVOLEMIA)</h4>
<p>Changes Occurring as a Result of Massive Hemorrhage</p>
<ul>
<li>the lethal triad in trauma includes coagulopathy, acidosis, and hypothermia
        <ul>
<li>acute coagulopathy of trauma-shock
                <ul>
<li>also known as trauma-induced coagulopathy, acute traumatic coagulopathy, acute coagulopathy of trauma, trauma-associated coagulopathy.</li>
<li>may occur within 30 minutes of severe injury - prior to red blood cell (RBC) transfusion and fluid resuscitation</li>
<li>tissue injury from trauma or surgery leads to local and subsequent systemic release of tissue factor leading to initiation of coagulation pathway and massive disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)</li>
<li>hypoperfusion due to massive hemorrhage leads to expression of thrombomodulin in endothelial cells and formation of thrombin-thrombomodulin complex, resulting in
                        <ul>
<li>activation of protein C, leading to inactivation of factor Va and VIIIa, and enhancement of fibrinolysis by consumption of plasminogen activator inhibitor and increase in plasmin formation</li>
<li>inactivation of thrombin-activatable inhibitor (TAFI), leading to further hyperfibrinolysis</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>The acute coagulopathy of trauma shock is a disease entity similar to or same as DIC with fibrinolytic phenotype, with possible exception that trauma-shock uniquely activates the thrombomodulin and protein C pathway.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>acidosis
                <ul>
<li>initial appearance may indicate tissue hypoperfusion further contributes to coagulopathy due to:
                        <ul>
<li>change in platelet shape at pH &lt; 7.4</li>
<li>inhibition of thrombin generation at pH &lt; 7.1</li>
<li>acceleration of fibrinolysis</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>hypothermia
                <ul>
<li>defined as core body temperature &lt; 35 degrees C</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 279 -->

<ul><li>may occur in patients having trauma or elective surgery as a result of abnormal thermoregulatory control due to general anesthesia and opening of body cavities</li><li>effects include abnormal platelet function and coagulopathy, enzyme inhibition, and fibrinolysis</li></ul><ul><li>Exacerbation of Coagulopathy as a Result of Massive Transfusion<ul><li>dilution of clotting factors and platelets due to transfusion of red blood cell (RBC) units</li><li>acidosis may occur due to normal saline administration and toxicity from citrate present as anticoagulant in stored blood products</li><li>hypothermia as a result of administration of fluids below body temperature</li><li>hypocalcemia from citrate in storage solution that contributes to decrease in platelet-related activities</li><li>severity of coagulopathy is modified by patient-related factors including<ul><li>age</li><li>comorbidities</li><li>inflammation</li><li>genetic background</li><li>premedication (especially oral anticoagulants)</li><li>pre-hospital admission fluid administration</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul><h4>V. EVALUATION</h4><p>Findings commonly associated with bleeding patients requiring future massive transfusions include ≥ 1 or more of the following:</p><ul><li>INR &gt; 1.5</li><li>systolic blood pressure &lt; 90 mm Hg</li><li>hemoglobin (Hb) &lt; 11 g/dL (&lt; 110 g/L)</li><li>Base deficit (BD) ≥ 6 mEq/L (≥ 6 mmol/L)</li><li>positive focused assessment for the sonography (FAST) of trauma</li><li>heart rate ≥ 120 beats/minute</li></ul><p>Routine assays include hematocrit (Hct), Hb, platelet count, and assays for coagulopathy (including prothrombin time [PT], activated thromboplastin time [aPTT], INR, and fibrinogen measurement).</p><p>Viscoelastic hemostatic assays, including thromboelastography and rotational thromboelastometry, are emergency room or bedside point-of-care assays that use whole blood within minutes of collection, and therefore have shorter turn-around time compared to routine assays.</p><p>Complications of massive transfusion include transfusion-related lung injury (TRALI), transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO), transfusion reactions, and electrolyte abnormalities</p><h4>VI. MANAGEMENT</h4><ul><li>The ultimate goal of massive transfusion is to maintain sufficient circulation and hemostasis in patients with massive hemorrhage.</li><li>In an emergency, provide group O red blood cell (RBC) and AB plasma until patient blood type is determined and patients can receive crossmatched RBC and AB-compatible plasma.</li><li>Massive transfusion protocol (MTP) should be implemented to optimize management and delivery of blood products.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 280 -->

<h2>VII. MASSIVE BLOOD TRANSFUSION (MBT) PROTOCOL</h2>
<p>MTPs may involve predetermined ratio-driven transfusion or goal-directed transfusion protocols or combination of both, but most current MTPs use ratio-driven transfusion protocol followed by goal-directed strategy as laboratory information becomes available.</p>
<h3>General Concepts</h3>
<ul>
<li>massive transfusion protocol (MTP) should facilitate communication between departments and services to deliver rapid clinical care</li>
<li>MTPs may involve ratio-driven transfusion or goal-directed transfusion protocols or combination of both, but most current MTPs use ratio-driven transfusion protocol</li>
<li>MTPs should include
        <ul>
<li>timing and personnel involved in the activation of MTP notification of start and stop of protocol to transfusion service and laboratory</li>
<li>definition of laboratory testing parameters used to predict need for massive transfusion blood product preparation and delivery, including predetermined transfusion packages</li>
<li>patient identification protocol to avoid ABO incompatible transfusion errors</li>
<li>other patient care needs (for example, blood warmers)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>American College of Surgeons Trauma Improvement Program (ACS TQIP) recommendations
        <ul>
<li>during early stages of resuscitation, transfuse universal red blood cell (RBC) and plasma in a ratio between 1:1 and 2:1</li>
<li>once laboratory data are available, use goal-directed resuscitation</li>
<li>transfusion may be discontinued or downgraded to goal-oriented transfusion if bleeding is under control</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Task Force of Advanced Bleeding Care in Trauma recommendations
        <ul>
<li>for initial management of patients with expected massive hemorrhage 1 of 2 following
                <ul>
<li>strategies should be considered
                        <ul>
<li>fresh frozen plasma (FFP) in a plasma:RBC ratio of at least 1:2 as needed</li>
<li>Fibrinogen concentrate and RBC</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>switch to goal-directed strategy as laboratory information becomes available; goals for various blood components
                <ul>
<li>transfuse RBC to maintain Hb &gt; 7-9 g/dL (70-90 g/L) (ABC-T Grade 1C)</li>
<li>FFP
                        <ul>
<li>transfuse FFP to maintain prothrombin time (PT) and activated thromboplastin time (aPTT) &lt; 1.5 × normal control or if viscoelastic hemostatic assay results suggest coagulation factor deficiency</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>avoid use of FFP in patients without major bleeding or for treatment of hypofibrinogenemia
                        <ul>
<li>administer fibrinogen or cryoprecipitate if significant bleeding associated with viscoelastic signs of functional fibrinogen deficiency or plasma fibrinogen level &lt; 150 mg/dL (1.5 g/L)</li>
<li>transfuse platelets to maintain platelet count &gt; 50 × 10<sup>9</sup>/L or &gt; 100 × 10<sup>9</sup>/L in patients with ongoing bleeding or traumatic brain injury.</li>
<li>coagulation factor concentrates</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 281 -->

<ul><li>if used, treat based on routine laboratory coagulation testing and/or viscoelastic evidence of functional coagulation factor deficiency.</li><li>prothrombin complex concentrate may be indicated for bleeding patients with delayed initiation of coagulation as evidenced by viscoelastic monitoring.</li><li>consider monitoring factor FXIII activity and if deficient, supplement in patients who are bleeding</li></ul><p><b>Ratio-driven Transfusion</b></p><ul><li>uses predetermined ratio of red blood cells (RBCs), plasma, and platelets</li><li>administration of fixed ratio of RBC to plasma to platelets at 1:1:1 (initially proposed by the United State military and subsequently used in both military and civilian settings, with rationale that is more closely resembles whole blood)</li><li>more commonly incorporated in MTPs than goal-directed transfusion</li><li>treats coagulopathy early in resuscitation (&lt; 6 hours of admission) while decreasing use of crystalloids and RBCs</li><li>no delay in preparation and delivery of blood products</li><li>may be discontinued or downgraded to goal-oriented transfusion if bleeding is under control</li></ul><p><b>Goal-directed Transfusion</b></p><ul><li>uses laboratory results and clinical findings to guide blood product administration choices, volumes, and timing until target test values are achieved.</li><li>requires use of laboratory tests that are timely and provide enough information on patient coagulation profile.</li><li>viscoelastic hemostatic assays such as thromboelastography (TEG) or rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) results may be helpful in guiding transfusion</li></ul><p><b>Special Populations</b></p><p><b>Obstetric Hemorrhage</b></p><ul><li>for patients with major obstetric hemorrhage, consider ratio-driven transfusion (for example, 6:4:1 ratio of RBC to plasma to platelet units)</li><li>hyperfibrinolysis is common; monitor closely for fibrinogen level and consider early transfusion of fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate</li><li>tranexamic acid administration may decrease blood loss at the time of cesarean section and risk of progression to severe obstetric hemorrhage</li><li>fibrinogen level &lt; 200 mg/dL independently associated with severe bleeding</li></ul><p><b>Pediatric Patients</b></p><ul><li>having pediatric patient-specific MTP may be beneficial but could be logistically difficult to create in institutions without free-standing children's hospital</li><li>data on successful management of massive transfusion in children and neonates is limited, and optimal transfusion protocol is not clear.</li></ul><p><b>Patients in Surgical Settings</b></p><ul><li>American Society of Anesthesiologists suggests use of MTP implemented by individual institution.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 282 -->

<ul><li>consider that patients having cardiac surgery may have had preoperative administration of anticoagulants or antiplatelets, and on-pump heparin that may also contribute to impaired hemostasis.</li></ul><p><b>Patients in Combat Settings</b></p><ul><li>administration of fixed ratio of RBC to plasma to platelet at 1:1:1 initially proposed by the United States military and continues to be used in both military and civilian settings</li><li>administration of fresh whole blood is used in cases when apheresis platelet products are not available<ul><li>transfusion-transmitted infections and transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease may be a concern</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>Monitoring</b></p><ul><li>termination of transfusion with blood products if further transfusion is futile</li><li>discontinuation of ratio-driven massive transfusion or downgrade to goal-oriented transfusion if either<ul><li>surgical bleeding has been controlled</li><li>radiographic or physiologic indication of bleeding control after angioembolization</li></ul></li><li>discontinuation of goal-oriented blood product transfusions based on laboratory test values (including routine laboratory tests and/or viscoelastic hemostatic assays) if patient is not actively bleeding and still in the acute resuscitation phase.</li></ul><p><b>Guide to Laboratory Target Values for Goal-Directed Transfusion*</b></p><table border="1"><thead><tr><th>Test</th><th>ABC-T target Value</th><th>ACS TQIP Target Values</th><th>Case transfusion</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Hemoglobin level</td><td>≥7-9g/dL</td><td>≥ 10g/dL</td><td>RBCs</td></tr><tr><td>Prothrombin time</td><td>&lt;1.5xNormal</td><td>&lt; 18seconds</td><td>Plasma</td></tr><tr><td>Activated partial thromboplastin time</td><td>&lt;1.5xNormal</td><td>&lt; 35seconds</td><td>Plasma</td></tr><tr><td>Platelet count</td><td>&gt;50x10<sup>9</sup> or &gt;100x10<sup>9</sup> if ongoing bleeding and/or TBI</td><td>&gt;150x10<sup>9</sup>/L</td><td>Platelets</td></tr><tr><td>Fibrinogen level</td><td>≥150 mg/dL</td><td>&gt; 180 mg/dL</td><td>Cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate</td></tr></tbody></table><p>* ACS TQIP: American College of Surgeons Trauma Quality Improvement Program, ABC-T, Task force for Advanced Bleeding Cared in Trauma</p><p><b>VIII. COMPLICATIONS OF MBT</b></p><ol><li>complications arising from rapid transfusion of large volume of fluids during massive transfusion include:<ul><li>exacerbation of coagulopathy</li><li>metabolic complications—<ul><li>complications due to citrate in blood product storage solution include<ul><li>hypocalcemia - neonates and patients with liver disease may be at higher risk</li><li>acidosis may be more severe and difficult to treat in patients with liver failure who cannot metabolize citrate to bicarbonate or process lactate</li><li>metabolic alkalosis occurs as a result of increase in blood pH as citrate is metabolized to bicarbonate.</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 283 -->

<ul><li>hypomagnesemia - due to transfusion of magnesium poor solutions in addition to citrate overload</li><li>hyperkalemia<ul><li>due to increase in potassium concentration as a result of red blood cell (RBC) membrane (adenosine triphosphatase) ATPase pump inactivation and hemolysis of RBCs in storage and/or irradiation</li><li>neonates, patients with cardiac and renal insufficiency and tissue injury at higher risk</li></ul></li><li>hypokalemia due to<ul><li>restoration of RBC membrane ATPase pump and potassium uptake by RBCs</li><li>release of aldosterone, antidiuretic hormone, and catecholamines</li><li>co-transfusion of low potassium solutions such as platelets, plasma, and crystalloids</li></ul></li><li>hypothermia<ul><li>due to rapid infusion of blood products in cold storage</li><li>infants and neonates at higher risk</li></ul></li><li>transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) - acute lung injury that occurs within 6 hours of transfusion and not related to other causes of acute lung injury or acute respiratory distress syndrome</li><li>transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)<ul><li>hydrostatic pulmonary edema</li><li>patients with cardiac disease and infants at higher risk</li></ul></li></ul><p>2. Other complications arising from transfusion of blood products include</p><ul><li>allergic reaction</li><li>hemolytic transfusion reaction (acute and delayed)</li><li>febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction</li><li>transfusion-related immunomodulation</li><li>transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease</li><li>posttransfusion purpura</li><li>infection</li><li>air embolism</li></ul><h3>IX. PROGNOSIS</h3><ul><li>Mortality reported in<ul><li>39% of patients having ≥ 10 red blood cell (RBC) units during hospital stay (2.6% of all patients with trauma)</li><li>57% of patients having ≥ 50 units of blood products in first 24 hours (0.6% of all patients with trauma)</li></ul></li></ul><h3>X. Accessed December 27, 2024. <a href="https://www.dynamed.com/procedure/massive-transfusion">https://www.dynamed.com/procedure/massive-transfusion</a></li><li>UpToDate. Massive Blood transfusion. Wolters Kluwer online platform. Accessed December 27, 2024. <a href="https://www.uptodate.com/contents/massive-blood-transfusion">https://www.uptodate.com/contents/massive-blood-transfusion</a></li></ol>
