<h1>ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME</h1>
<h2>ST-ELEVATION MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION(STEMI)</h2>
<p>Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong,<br/>
Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline,<br/>
Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay,<br/>
Prof. SOK Chour</p>
<h3>I. DEFINITION</h3>
<p>ACS is the clinical spectrum of unstable ischemic heart disease ranging from unstable angina (UA), Non-ST segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) to STEMI depending upon the degree and acuteness of coronary occlusion.</p>
<p>STEMI is ACS with persistent ST-segment elevation or new left bundle-branch block.</p>

<h3>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h3>
<ul>
<li>Most recent data from WHO in 2019, ischemic heart disease (IHD) was the principal cause of death (62,22 per 100 000 population) in Cambodia.</li>
<li>In Cambodia:
        <ul>
<li>Mean age: 59,71 years</li>
<li>Female: 26,3%</li>
<li>In-hospital mortality: 11,14% (PCI: 4,7% vs non-PCI: 15,73%)</li>
<li>Primary PCI rate: 78%</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>III. ETIOLOGY</h3>
<p>Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) cause by the rupture or erosion of atherosclerotic plaques in the coronary arteries, leading to the formation of blood clots that block blood flow partially or completely.</p>
<h3>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h3>
<p>STEMI reflects transmural necrosis caused by acute thrombotic occlusion and longer duration of a coronary artery.</p>

<!-- PAGE 286 -->

ACS can also arise from Non-atherosclerotic causes, including Coronary vasospasm, Spontaneous coronary artery dissection, Myocardial bridging, Stress-induced Cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo Syndrome), and Coronary artery embolism."/>
<p>Fig. 2 Mechanism physiopathology of acute coronary syndrome</p>
<h3>V. DIAGNOSIS</h3>
<ol>
<li>Clinical
        <ul>
<li>Symptom:
                <ul>
<li>Chest pain Ischemic-type (Angina): retro-sternal, intense, at rest, longer (&gt;30min), irradiate to jaw and neck, trinitro-resistant.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Physical finding:
                <ul>
<li>Vital sings: BP, HR, SpO2</li>
<li>Heart sounds: Third heart sound (LV dysfunction), Systolic murmur (mechanical complication)</li>
<li>Lung: rales (heart failure)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Investigation
        <ul>
<li>ECG: ST segment elevation &gt; 2mm in 2 contiguous leads or a new onset LBBB in the resting ECG</li>
<li>Cardiac Biomarkers- should not delay to wait for results for reperfusion therapy</li>
<li>Echocardiography-if available</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2>
<ol>
<li>Objectives
<p><b>"Time is muscle"</b>- Every patient with STEMI should have the occluded artery reopened (reperfusion therapy) as soon as possible after the onset of symptoms.</p>
<p>Primary goal of STEMI management is to reduce the risk of death and the extent of permanent cardiac injury associated with MI.</p>
</li>
<li>Critical sign
<ul>
<li>Shock (cool extremities, altered mental status, moist skin, weak pulse)</li>
<li>Heart failure (orthopnea, jugular venous distension, pulmonary edema)</li>
<li>Cardiac arrhythmia (sustained ventricular tachyarrhythmia, bradyarrhythmia)</li>
<li>High bleeding risk patient (elderly, CKD with eGFR&lt;30ml/min, cirrhosis, cancer, previous stroke, previous bleeding transfusion &lt;6months, long-term oral anticoagulation)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Mortality risk factor
<ul>
<li><b>Killip classification:</b> Using physical examination and the development of heart failure to predict and stratify risk of mortality</li>
</ul>

<div>
<p>4.Outpatient Management:</p>
<p>All STEMI patient is recommended to hospitalization. 5.First-line treatment</p>
<p><b>A. STEMI &lt;12hours:</b></p>
<p><i>i. Pre-hospital:</i></p>
<ul>
<li>Antalgic: Morphine 5-10mg SC or IV</li>
<li>On-going chest pain: Nitroglycerine sublingually or oral spay</li>
<li>Transfer with Emergency medical services (EMS) by full monitoring: oximeter, scope vital signs monitor</li>
<li>Aspirin 250mg-500mg IV or PO (absence contraindicated)</li>
<li>Thrombolysis: (see details in iii.a)</li>
</ul>
<p><i>ii. Arrival Cardiac Care Unit (CCU):</i></p>
<ul>
<li>Strictly bed rest</li>
<li>Monitoring with ECG 18 derivations</li>
<li>G5% 500ml + 2gKCL/24h</li>
<li>Blood test: CBC, groupage rhesus, electrolytes, glycemia, cardiac enzyme (CK-MB &amp; Troponin T or I), Creatinine, BUN, PT, cholesterol, triglyceride</li>
<li>Chest x-ray and echocardiography on bedside</li>
<li>Clopidogrel 75mg: 6cp PO then 1cp daily after PCI
<ul>
<li>Or Ticagrelor 90mg: 2 cp then 1cp twice daily after PCI</li>
<li>Or Prasugrel 10mg: 6 cp then 1 cp daily after PCI</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Anticoagulant:
<ul>
<li>Heparin: 60IU/kg (max. 4000 IU) i.v bolus then continues infusion: 400IU/kg/24H (max. 24.000IU). ACT monitoring 4 after with target treatment &gt;250ms or ACT 2 times upper normal value.</li>
<li>Or LWMH: Enoxaparin: 1mg(100IU)/Kg s.c, 2 times/day</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Nitroglycerine: if present LV dysfunction signs (stop if SBP &lt; 100mmHg)</li>
<li>Betablocker: for all patient if no contraindication</li>
<li>ACE-Is/ARBs: for all patient if no contraindication</li>
<li>High dose Statins: for all patient if no contraindication</li>
</ul>
<p><b>iii. Reperfusion strategies:</b></p>
<p>a. Timing to determine choice of reperfusion:</p>
<table border="1">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Onset of symptoms</td>
<td colspan="3">Patient with symptoms of ACS and ECG consistent with STEMI</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>FMC Location</td>
<td>PCI Centre</td>
<td>Non-PCI Centre</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td rowspan="2">Determine therapeutic strategy</td>
<td>PPCI strategy</td>
<td>PCI possible in &lt;120min<br/>Yes<br/>PPCI strategy</td>
<td>No<br/>Fibrinolytic strategy</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Aim: &lt; 60min to wire crossing</td>
<td>Aim: &lt; 90min to wire crossing<br/>Immediate transfer to PCI Centre for primary PCI</td>
<td>Aim: &lt; 10min to lytic bolus<br/>Immediate transfer to PCI Centre after fibrinolysis</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Fig. 3 Timing of choosing reperfusion treatment</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 289 -->

<div>
<p>b. Indication Primary PCI:</p>
<p><b>“Every STEMI &lt;12h patients need emergency transfer to be performed primary PCI”</b></p>
<ul>
<li>STEMI &lt; 12hours</li>
<li>STEMI post-thrombolysis</li>
<li>STEMI with shock state or post cardiac arrest and return of spontaneous circulation</li>
<li>STEMI with contraindication thrombolysis</li>
</ul>
<p>c. Indication Thrombolysis:</p>
<p>c.1. Indication:</p>
<ul>
<li>STEMI &lt; 12hours with
        <ul>
<li>Door to Balloon time &gt; 120min if transferred from non-PCI center</li>
<li>Door to Balloon time &gt; 90min in PCI center</li>
<li>No contraindications to thrombolysis</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>c.2. Choice of Fibrinolysis Agents:</p>
<ul>
<li>Streptokinase: 1,5M IU in 90min</li>
<li>rt-PA: Actilyse: 15mg i.v bolus then 0.75mg/kg in 30min then 0.5mg/kg in 60min</li>
<li>Tenectaplaste: Metalysé: i.v bolus unique in 10s</li>
</ul>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Body weight</th>
<th>Single IV bolus over 5 s</th>
<th>Volume TNK to be administered</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>&lt;60 kg</td>
<td>30 mg</td>
<td>6</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>60 to &lt; 70 kg</td>
<td>35 mg</td>
<td>7</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>70 to &lt;80 kg</td>
<td>40 mg</td>
<td>8</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>80 to &lt;90 kg</td>
<td>45 mg</td>
<td>9</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>&gt;90 kg</td>
<td>50 mg</td>
<td>10</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td colspan="3">In patient &gt; 75years of age, the dose should be reduced by 50%</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>c.3. Contraindication to Thrombolysis:</p>
<div style="border: 1px solid black; padding: 10px;">
<p><b>Absolute</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Previous intracranial hemorrhage or stroke of unknown origin at any time</li>
<li>Ischemic stroke in the preceding 6 months</li>
<li>Central nervous system damage or neoplasms, or arteriovenous malformation</li>
<li>Recent major trauma/ surgery/head injury (within the preceding month)</li>
<li>Gastrointestinal bleeding within the past month</li>
<li>Known bleeding disorder (excluding menstrual)</li>
<li>Aortic dissection</li>
<li>Non-compressible punctures in the past 24h (e.g. liver biopsy, lumbar puncture)</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div style="border: 1px solid black; padding: 10px;">
<p><b>Relative</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Transient ischemic attack in the preceding 6 months</li>
<li>Oral anticoagulant therapy</li>
<li>Pregnancy or within 1-week post-partum</li>
<li>Refractory hypertension (systolic blood pressure &gt; 180mmHg and/or diastolic blood pressure &gt;110mmHg)</li>
<li>Advanced liver disease</li>
<li>Infective endocarditis</li>
<li>Active peptic ulcer</li>
<li>Prolonged or traumatic resuscitation</li>
</ul>
</div>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 290 -->

<div>
<p>c.4. Results of Thrombolysis :</p>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Successful Fibrinolysis</th>
<th>Failed Fibrinolysis</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Resolution chest pain</li>
<li>Early return ST elevation &gt; 50% within 60-90min of initiation of fibrinolysis</li>
<li>Early peaking of CK-MB levels</li>
<li>Restoration +/- maintenance of hemodynamic +/- electrical stability</li>
</ul>
</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Continuing chest pain</li>
<li>Persistent hyper-acute ECG changes (&lt;50% resolution of ST elevation)</li>
<li>Hemodynamic and electrical instability</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>

</tr>

<p><b>B. STEMI &gt; 12hours:</b></p>
<p><i>i. Hospitalization in Cardiac Care Unit (CCU):</i></p>
<ul>
<li>Strictly bed rest</li>
<li>Monitoring with ECG 18 derivations</li>
<li>G5% 500ml + 2gKCL/24h</li>
<li>Blood test: CBC, groupage rhesus, electrolytes, glycemia, cardiac enzyme (CK-MB &amp; Troponin T or I), Creatinine, BUN, PT, cholesterol, triglyceride</li>
<li>Chest x-ray and echocardiography on bedside</li>
<li>Aspirin 250mg i.v or PO</li>
<li>Anticoagulant:
<ul>
<li>Heparin: 400IU/kg/24H (max. 24.000IU) continues i.v, ACT monitoring 4 after with target treatment &gt;250ms or ACT 2 times upper normal value.</li>
<li>Or LWMH: Enoxaparin: 1mg(100IU)/Kg s.c, 2 times/day</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Nitroglycerine: if present LV dysfunction signs (stop if SBP &lt; 100mmHg)</li>
<li>Betablocker: for all patient if no contraindication</li>
<li>ACE-Is: for all patient if no contraindication</li>
<li>High dose Statins: for all patient if no contraindication</li>
</ul>
<p><i>ii. Reperfusion indication:</i></p>
<ul>
<li>Delayed PCI indicated:
<ul>
<li>Ongoing symptoms suggestive of ischemia</li>
<li>Hemodynamic instability</li>
<li>Life-threatening arrhythmia</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>STEMI &gt; 12hours with asymptomatic and stable, PCI (Delayed selective PCI) is indicated depending on age, risk strategy and viable myocardium via non-invasive ischemia test.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>6. Treatment adjustment</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Nitroglycerine can't use in case: inferior AMI +/- RV infarction, Low SBP &lt; 90mmHg, severe bradycardia &lt;50bpm, tachycardia &gt;100bpm</li>
<li>Pulmonary edema: Furosemide</li>
<li>Malaise: Atropine + vascular filling</li>
<li>Shock: Norepinephrine, Dobutamine or Dopamine</li>
</ul>
</div>

<h2>7. Algorithm</h2>
<div style="text-align: center;">
<h3>Management of STEMI patients</h3>
</div>
<div style="display: flex; align-items: flex-start;">
<div style="writing-mode: vertical-rl; text-orientation: mixed; margin-right: 10px;">
<p>ECG<br/>Cardiac biomarkers<br/>Concomitant initial management<br/>Assessment for reperfusion<br/>Onset of symptoms<br/>Location<br/>Transfers duration<br/>Preferred option<br/>Subsequent Management<br/>Concomitant therapy</p>
</div>
<div style="border: 1px solid black; padding: 5px;">
<p>Chest pain / Chest pain equivalent</p>
<p>↓</p>
<p>Continuous ECG monitoring<br/>Nitroglycerine sublingual or spray<br/>Aspirin<br/>Clopidogrel<br/>Analgesic<br/>Oxygen if SpO<sub>2</sub>&lt;95%</p>
<p>↓</p>
<p>Decision based on Onset of symptoms:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>&lt;12 hours:</b>
<ul>
<li>PCI-center → Primary PCI</li>
<li>Non-PCI center → Decision based on Transfers duration:
                <ul>
<li>&lt;120 min → Primary PCI</li>
<li>&gt;120 min → Fibrinolysis</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>&gt;12 hours:</b>
<ul>
<li>Medical treatment +/- Antithrombotic</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>↓</p>
<p>From Medical treatment +/- Antithrombotic:</p>
<ul>
<li>Symptomatic → Hemodynamic instable / Ongoing chest pain → Delayed PCI</li>
<li>Asymptomatic → Ischemic test: Myocardial viable? → Selective PCI</li>
</ul>
<p>↓</p>
<p>Success: Pharmaco-invasive (PCI: 3-24H)<br/>Failed: Rescue PCI (1-3H)</p>
<p>↓</p>
<p>Dual anti-platelet therapy (DAPT)<br/>High-dose Statins<br/>B-blockers<br/>ACE/ARBs<br/>MRA</p>
</div>
</div>
<h2>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h2>
<ul>
<li>STEMI in elderly: may have atypical symptoms or may present with confusion or altered mental status. Special consideration in managing STEMI in elderly include careful assessment of symptoms, monitoring complication and adjusting treatment plans base on individual patient factors.</li>
<li>STEMI in Women: may present with atypical symptoms such as fatigue, shortness of breath, or chest discomfort. They may have higher risk of complication and worse outcomes compared to men.</li>
<li>STEMI in diabetic patients: may have more extensive coronary artery disease and higher risk of complication. Special in managing include aggressive blood sugar control, close monitoring for complications and individualized treatment.</li>
<li>STEMI with cardiogenic shock: is life-threatening co-condition. Special in managing include immediate revascularization with PCI, aggressive hemodynamic support with medications and mechanical devices and close monitoring in an intensive care unit.</li>
<li>STEMI with concurrent conditions: STEMI can occur in patients with other conditions such as renal failure, liver disease, or bleeding disorders. Special in managing include careful assessment of risks and benefits of reperfusion therapy, close monitoring for complications, and coordination with specialists in managing the underlying conditions.</li>
</ul>
<h2>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h2>
<ul>
<li>Early reperfusion of STEMI gives good outcome for short and longtime prognosis.</li>
<li>Without reperfusion treatment, survivors of STEMI face a substantial excess risk of further cardiovascular events, including death, recurrent MI, heart failure, arrhythmia, angina and stroke.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 292 -->

<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Arrhythmia: ventricular arrhythmia, Atrial fibrillation, heart block</li>
<li>Heart failure</li>
<li>Cardiogenic shock</li>
<li>Mechanical complications: ventricular septal rupture, papillary muscle rupture, free wall rupture</li>
<li>Thrombo-embolic events</li>
<li>Post-infarction angina</li>
<li>Post-infarction syndrome (pericarditis post infarction)</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<ul>
<li>All high-risk cardiovascular patient shall be screen for coronary artery disease (CAD) annually.</li>
<li>Lifestyle modification and managing risk factors can help prevent CAD and reduce risk of STEMI.</li>
<li>Cardiac rehabilitation after STEMI can help improve cardiovascular health, manage risk factors, and promote lifestyle modification.</li>
<li>Regular follow-up with a specialist provider is crucial for ongoing management and assessment of cardiovascular health.</li>
</ul>

<h1>ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME (ACS)</h1><h2>NON-ST ELEVATION MYOCARDIAL INFARCTION (NSTEMI)</h2><p>Dr. KHUON Rithy Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</p><h3>I. DEFINITION</h3><p>Acute coronary syndromes (ACS) encompass a spectrum of conditions that include patients presenting with recent changes in clinical symptoms or signs, with or without changes on 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) and with or without acute elevations in cardiac troponin (cTn) concentrations.</p><p>NSTEMI is one type of ACS with characterize by acute chest pain (or chest pain-equivalent signs/symptoms) but without persistent ST-segment elevation (or ST-segment elevation equivalents) on ECG. The majority of patients in this category who subsequently display a typical rise and fall in cardiac troponin levels</p><h3>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h3><p>Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is the most common cause of mortality and morbidity worldwide, with a substantial portion of this burden borne by low- and middle-income countries. ACS is often the first clinical manifestation of CVD.</p><p>In 2019, there were an estimated 5.8 million new cases of ischemic heart disease in the 57 countries. The median age-standardized incidence estimate per 100 000 people was 293.3 (interquartile ratio 195.8–529.5). Ischemic heart disease is the most common cause of CVD death, accounting for 38% of all CVD deaths in females and 44% in males.</p><h3>III. ETIOLOGY</h3><p>Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) cause by the rupture or erosion of atherosclerotic plaques in the coronary arteries, leading to the formation of blood clots that block blood flow partially or completely</p><h3>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h3><p>The underlying pathology of ACS is a mismatch between myocardial oxygen supply and demand. UA, NSTEMI, and STEMI all represent consequences of thrombotic vessel occlusion and varying degrees of this mismatch. Plaque rupture is the most common underlying source of thrombotic occlusion in ACS. Plaque erosion with an intact fibrous cap is the etiology in up to one-third of patients with ACS, typically, women, younger patients, and smokers. Additionally, vasoconstriction at the level of the culprit plaque or of the microcirculation may also cause ACS.</p><div><p>M. Smit et al. / Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia 00 (2019) 1–12</p><img alt="Flowchart illustrating the pathophysiology of myocardial ischemia. 'Pathophysiology of myocardial ischemia' leads to 'Acute coronary syndrome' and 'VO₂ DO₂ mismatch'. 'Acute coronary syndrome' further branches into three conditions: 1. Unstable angina (Unstable plaque), 2. NSTEMI (Unstable plaque with thrombus), and 3. STEMI (Unstable plaque with occluding thrombus). Stable angina is associated with a stable fixed plaque."/></div>

<!-- PAGE 294 -->

<div>
<p>Fig. 1 Mechanism physiopathology of acute coronary syndrome</p>
<h2>V. DIAGNOSIS</h2>
<h3>1. Clinical presentation</h3>
<ul>
<li>Chest pain Ischemic-type (Angina): retro-sternal, intense, at rest, longer (&gt;30min), irradiate to jaw and neck, trinitro-resistant.</li>
<li>Acute chest discomfort: Pain, Pressure, tightness, Heaviness or burning. It can radiate from the chest to the neck, jaw, back and sometime both arms. Other symptoms include:
        <ul>
<li>Shortness of breath</li>
<li>Nausea or vomiting</li>
<li>Feeling faint</li>
<li>Sweating, weakness and fatigue.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>2. Physical examination and history taking</h3>
<ul>
<li>It is crucial to take a focused medical history and accurately characterize the presenting symptoms in order to manage the patient via the appropriate care pathway as soon as possible.</li>
</ul>
<p>Vital sign and EKG are recommended at first medical contact (FMC)</p>
<ul>
<li>Focused physical examination should include checking for the presence of all major pulses, measurement of blood pressure in both arms, auscultation of the heart and lungs, and assessing for signs of HF or circulatory compromise</li>
</ul>
<h3>3. Investigation and risk stratification</h3>
<ul>
<li>It is recommended to base the diagnosis and initial short-term risk stratification of ACS on a combination of clinical history, symptoms, vital signs, other physical findings, EKG and hs-cTn.</li>
<li>12 lead EKG with in 10mn at FMC:
        <ul>
<li>These patients may exhibit other ECG alterations, including transient ST-segment elevation, persistent or transient ST-segment depression, and T wave abnormalities, including hyperacute T waves, T wave inversion, biphasic T waves, flat T waves, and pseudo-normalization of T waves. Alternatively, the ECG may be normal</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<img alt="ECG trace showing three consecutive beats. The first beat shows a normal QRS complex. The second beat shows an inverted T wave. The third beat shows ST segment depression."/>
<p>Normal, Inverted T waves, or ST depression</p>
<ul>
<li>High sensitive cardiac troponine (hs-cTn): is recommended in all patients with suspected ACS
        <ul>
<li>European Society of Cardiology 0 h/1 h and 0 h/2 h algorithms</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Echocardiography:
        <ul>
<li>should not result in relevant delays in transfer to the cardiac catheterization laboratory if there is suspicion of an acute coronary artery occlusion</li>
<li>can be useful to identify signs suggestive of ongoing ischaemia or prior MI.</li>
<li>can also be useful to suggest alternative etiologies associated with chest pain.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Coronary CT angiography:
        <ul>
<li>Routine, early CCTA in patients with suspected ACS is not recommended.</li>
<li>Diagnostic tool of choice for ruling out alternative potentially life-threatening differential diagnoses of ACS, like PE or aortic dissection.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2>
<ol>
<li>Objectives
        <ul>
<li>The goal of initial management is to restore the coronary flow on time and prevent any complication of NSTEMI-ACS (<i>TIME IS MUSCLE</i>)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Critical Sign
        <ul>
<li>Hemodynamic instability or Cardiogenic Shock.</li>
<li>Recurrent or ongoing chest pain refractory to medical treatment.</li>
<li>Acute HF presumed secondary to ongoing myocardial ischemia•</li>
<li>Life-threatening arrhythmias or cardiac arrest after presentation.</li>
<li>Mechanical complications.</li>
<li>Recurrent dynamic ECG changes suggestive of ischemia (particularly with intermittent ST-segment elevation).</li>
</ul>

<td>1</td>
<td>3</td>
<td>5</td>
<td>13</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Recent (&lt;24H) severe angina</td>
<td>1</td>
<td>4</td>
<td>7</td>
<td>20</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Increase cardiac markers</td>
<td>1</td>
<td>5</td>

</tr>
<tr>
<td>ST-deviation &gt; 0.5mm</td>
<td>1</td>
<td>6/7</td>
<td>19</td>
<td>41</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</li>
<li><b>Grace Score:</b> provides the most accurate stratification of risk both on admission and at discharge (<a href="http://www.gracescore.org/WebSite/default.aspx?ReturnUrl=%2f">http://www.gracescore.org/WebSite/default.aspx?ReturnUrl=%2f</a>)

<h4>4. Outpatient Management</h4>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Clinical Presentation</th>
<th>Unit</th>
<th>Rhythm Monitoring</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Unstable Angina</td>
<td>Regular ward or discharge</td>
<td>None</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>NSTEMI at low Risk (a)</td>
<td>Intermediate care unit or coronary care unit</td>
<td>≤ 24H</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>NSTEMI at intermediate to high risk (b)</td>
<td>Intensive/Coronary care units or intermediate care unit</td>
<td>&gt; 24H</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>(a) If none of the following criteria: hemodynamically unstable, major arrhythmias, LVEF &lt; 40%, Failed reperfusion, additional critical coronary stenoses of major vessels or complications related to percutaneous revascularization</p>
<p>(b) If one or more of the above criteria are present</p>
<h4>5. First-line treatment</h4>
<h5>A. Acute Pharmacotherapy</h5>
<ol>
<li>Oxygen: SpO2 &lt; 90% or Hypoxia sign</li>
<li>Strictly bed rest Monitoring EKG and Vital sign</li>
<li>G5% 500ml/24h</li>
<li>Antiplatelet Table 3 antiplatelet in NSTEM-ACS</li>
<li>Anticoagulant Table 4 anticoagulant in NSTEM-ACS</li>
<li>Nitrate: sublingual NTG (0.3mg to 0.4mg) every 5 minutes for up to 3 doses, after which IV NTG should be administered if needed.</li>
</ol>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 297 -->

<div>
<p>7. <b>Pain relieves</b> Intravenous opioids (e.g. morphine 5–10 mg) should be considered for the relief of severe chest pain.</p>
<p>8. <b>Betablocker</b> Should be considered when no signs of acute HF, a systolic blood pressure (SBP) &gt;120 mmHg, and without other contraindications.</p>
<p>9.</p>
<p>10. <b>ACE or ARB</b> If no contre-indication</p>
<p>11. <b>Hight dose statin</b> For all patient if no contre-indication</p>
<p>12. <b>Furosemide</b> If presence congestive sign</p>
<p>13. <b>Norepinephrine, Dobutamine or Dopamine:</b> In shock state</p>
<p>B. Reperfusion indication:</p>
<ul>
<li>Immediate invasive (&lt;2H): very high-risk patient</li>
<li>Early invasive (&lt;24H): high risk patient</li>
<li>Invasive &lt; 72H: intermediate risk patient</li>
<li>Stress test with coronary CTA (if available) for low-risk patient.</li>
</ul>

<h2>6. Treatment adjustment</h2>
<ul>
<li>Cardiac rehabilitation</li>
<li>Lifestyle modification: smoking cessation, dietary changes, exercise and weigh management</li>
<li>Medical therapy maintenance (ensure adherence)
        <ul>
<li>Antithrombotic therapy</li>
<li>Lipid-lowering therapy</li>
<li>Reach and sustain risk factor treatment targets
                <ul>
<li>Systolic BP under 130mmHg</li>
<li>LDL &lt; 55mg/dL or &lt; 1.4mmol/L</li>
<li>HbA1C: &lt; 7%</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Regular follow up</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 299 -->

<h2>7. Algorithm</h2>
<div>
<p><b>Symptoms of acute coronary syndrome</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Obtain serial EKG, Serial Troponin and Chest X-ray</li>
<li>Focused history and physical exam</li>
<li>Assess vitals</li>
<li>Obtain IV access</li>
</ul>
<p>Obtain serial EKG, Serial Troponin and Chest X-ray leads to:</p>
<ul>
<li>ST depression</li>
<li>T wave inversion</li>
<li>Normal</li>
</ul>
<p>ST depression and T wave inversion lead to <b>NSTEMI (troponin +)</b>.</p>
<p>Normal leads to <b>Unstable Angina (troponin -)</b>.</p>
<p><b>Immediate medical therapy upon diagnosis of NSTEMI/UA</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Aspirin 250mg (Load)</li>
<li>P2YQ12 inhibitor load (Consider delaying if coronary anatomy not known and early invasive management planned)</li>
<li>Anticoagulant</li>
</ul>
<p>This leads to risk stratification:</p>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Very High risk</th>
<th>High risk</th>
<th>Intermediate risk</th>
<th>Low risk</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>↓</td>
<td>↓</td>
<td>↓</td>
<td>↓</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Immediate Invasive (&lt;2H)</td>
<td>Early Invasive (&lt;2H)</td>
<td>Delayed Invasive (&lt;72H)</td>
<td>Ischemia-guided strategy</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Ischemia-guided strategy leads to Stress test or Cardiac CTA.</p>
<p>Optimize medical therapy leads to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Refractory angina</li>
<li>Cardiogenic shock</li>
<li>Heart Failure</li>
<li>VT/VF</li>
<li>Rise in troponin</li>
<li>EKG change</li>
</ul>
<p>Inducible ischemia or critical stenosis leads to PCI or CABG.</p>
<p><b>Optimize medical therapy</b></p>
<ul>
<li>DAPT for 1 year followed by lifelong Aspirin monotherapy</li>
<li>Beta blockers: within 24h if no contra-indication</li>
<li>ACE/ARB: within 24H if no contra-indication</li>
<li>Aldosterone antagonist if no contra-indication</li>
<li>High-intensity statin (goal LDL reduction 50%)</li>
<li>Smoking cessation</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 300 -->

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ul>
<li>ACS in elderly: may have atypical symptoms or may present with confusion or altered mental status.</li>
</ul>
<p>Special consideration in managing STEMI in elderly include careful assessment of symptoms, monitoring complication and adjusting treatment plans base on individual patient factors.</p>
<ul>
<li>CS in Women: may present with atypical symptoms such as fatigue, shortness of breath, or chest discomfort. They may have higher risk of complication and worse outcomes compared to men.</li>
<li>ACS in diabetic patients: may have more extensive coronary artery disease and higher risk of complication. Special in managing include aggressive blood sugar control, close monitoring for complications and individualized treatment.</li>
<li>ACS with cardiogenic shock: is life-threatening co-condition. Special in managing include immediate revascularization with PCI, aggressive hemodynamic support with medications and mechanical devices and close monitoring in an intensive care unit.</li>
<li>ACS with concurrent conditions: STEMI can occur in patients with other conditions such as renal failure, liver disease, or bleeding disorders. Special in managing include careful assessment of risks and benefits of reperfusion therapy, close monitoring for complications, and coordination with specialists in managing the underlying conditions.</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Short term prognosis can be vary significantly based on risk factors, age, comorbidities, and the initial clinical response. In general, NSTEMI has a better immediate outcome than STEMI, but it can still result in complications.</li>
<li>The long-term prognosis can be influenced by various factors, including the severity of coronary artery disease, the presence of left ventricular dysfunction and adherence to medical therapy post-discharge.</li>
</ul>
<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Arrhythmia: ventricular arrhythmia, Atrial fibrillation, heart block</li>
<li>Heart failure</li>
<li>Cardiogenic shock</li>
<li>Mechanical complications: ventricular septal rupture, papillary muscle rupture, free wall rupture</li>
<li>Thrombo-embolic events</li>
<li>Post-infarction angina</li>
<li>Post-infarction syndrome (pericarditis post infarction)</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<ul>
<li>All high-risk cardiovascular patient shall be screen for coronary artery disease (CAD) annually.</li>
<li>Lifestyle modification and managing risk factors can help prevent CAD and reduce risk of STEMI.</li>
<li>Cardiac rehabilitation after STEMI can help improve cardiovascular health, manage risk factors, and promote lifestyle modification.</li>
<li>Regular follow-up with a specialist provider is crucial for ongoing management and assessment of cardiovascular health.</li>
</ul>

<h1>CHRONIC CORONARY SYNDROME</h1>
<p>Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION ET CLASSIFICATION:</h2>
<table border="1">
<caption><b>Chronic coronary syndrome categories according to the ESC Guidelines:</b></caption>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Category</th>
<th>Description</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>1</td>
<td>Patients with suspected CAD and “stable” angina symptoms*</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>2</td>
<td>Patient with new onset of heart failure or left ventricular dysfunction and suspected CAD</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>3</td>
<td>Asymptomatic and symptomatic patients &lt;1 year after an ACS or recent revascularisation</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>4</td>
<td>Patients &gt; 1 year after initial angina diagnosis or revascularisation</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>5</td>
<td>Patients with angina and suspected vasospastic or microvascular disease</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>6</td>
<td>Asymptomatic patients in whom CAD is detected at screening</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>* including dyspnoea as angina equivalent. ACS: acute coronary syndrome, CAD: coronary artery disease, ESC European Society of Cardiology.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY:</h2>
<ul>
<li>CCD is a heterogeneous group of conditions that includes obstructive and nonobstructive CAD with or without previous myocardial infarction (MI) or revascularization, ischemic heart disease diagnosed only by noninvasive testing, and chronic angina syndromes with varying underlying causes.</li>
<li>Approximately 20.1 million persons (7.2%) in the United States live with CCD, 11.1 million Americans (4.1%) have chronic stable angina pectoris, and approximately one-quarter (n=200 000) of all MIs in the United States occur among the 8.8 million persons with CCD who have had a previous MI.</li>
</ul>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY:</h2>
<p>Chronic coronary syndrome referred to as stable ischemic heart disease (SIHD), based on a classic history of angina pectoris in the presence of either risk factors for or known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.</p>
<h2>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY:</h2>
<ul>
<li>Multiple pathophysiologic mechanisms may cause CCS.</li>
<li>The most common is atherosclerotic epicardial coronary artery obstruction.</li>
<li>However, as many as one-third of patients may have no significant epicardial disease and often have microvascular disease as the underlying pathophysiology.</li>
</ul>
<h2>V. DIAGNOSIS:</h2>
<ol>
<li>Clinic:
        <ul>
<li>Angina is the main symptom.</li>
<li>Angina pectoris is characterized by substernal discomfort, heaviness, or a pressure-like feeling, which may radiate to the jaw, shoulder, back, or arm and which typically lasts several minutes.</li>
<li>Physical examination is often unrevealing in patients with stable angina.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Investigation:</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 303 -->

<div>
<p>*Six steps to diagnosing CAD (adapted from ESC Guideline 2019):</p>
<p><b>Step 1</b> Assess symptoms and signs to distinguish between typical and atypical symptoms</p>
<p><b>Step 2</b> Assess quality of life and comorbidities. Apply guideline-based risk-factor modification based on commonly applied risk charts e.g. SCORE.</p>
<p><b>Step 3</b> Basic testing including troponin assays should be considered. 12 lead ECG and TTE is recommended. CMR may be considered in patients with strong suspicion of CAD where TTE is within normal limits.</p>
<p><b>Step 4</b> The clinical likelihood of obstructive CAD is estimated. A new phrase has been coined for the guideline entitled “clinical likelihood of CAD” and is underpinned by the improved PTP score.<sup>3</sup> PTP &lt;15% corresponds to &lt;1% annual risk of cardiovascular death or MI.<sup>4</sup> Therefore, routine testing in these patients can safely be deferred reducing unnecessary procedures and costs. The data on which the PTP in the previous guideline was based has since been updated based on a pooled analysis of 3 cohort studies and has highlighted that the presence of obstructive disease amongst patients with suspected CAD is lower than once thought.</p>
<p><b>Step 5</b> Offer diagnostic testing to selected patients screened via steps 1-4 to establish the diagnosis of CAD. This includes the options of invasive and non-invasive imaging depending on the risk. The choice of test also depends on the PTP of CAD with modalities such as CTCA more effective in low clinical probability situations.</p>
<p><b>Step 6</b> Once a diagnosis of obstructive CAD has been confirmed, patients undergo risk stratification to guide subsequent therapeutic interventions. The event risk is determined by clinician judgement and depends on the investigation modality used to determine CAD.</p>
<h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS:</h4>
<p>The differential diagnosis includes myocardial infarction, valvular disease (especially aortic valve stenosis), aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, inflammatory myocardial and/or pericardial conditions, chest wall syndrome, psychogenic causes, respiratory tract infections, and esophageal conditions.</p>
<h4>VII. MANAGEMENT:</h4>
<ol>
<li>Objective:<br/>To reduce angina symptom and exercised-induced ischemia and prevent cardiovascular events.</li>
<li>Critical Sign:<br/>Signs related to the complication of CCS (see complications section).</li>
<li>Mortality Risk Factors: no consensus data.</li>
<li>Outpatient Management:<br/>Most of CCS patients do not require hospitalization.</li>
<li>First-line Treatment: (see algorithm)</li>
<li>Treatment Adjustment: (see algorithm)</li>
</ol>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 304 -->

<div>
<p>7. Algorithm:</p>
<ul>
<li>Lifestyle Management:<br/>Smoking cessation, healthy diet (fruits and vegetables), Physical activities (30-60min a day), Healthy weight (Keep BMI&lt;25kg/m2), influenza vaccination</li>
<li>Pharmacological Management</li>
</ul>
<p>i. <u><b>Anti-ischemic drugs:</b></u></p>
<ul>
<li>1st line drugs: Beta-blockers (Bisoprolol, Metoprolol...), Calcium channel blockers.</li>
<li>2nd line drugs: Ranolazine (Rancard), Trimetazidine (Vastarel), Ivabradine, Nicorandil.</li>
<li>Respond to anti-ischemic therapy should be reassessed after 2-4 weeks of treatment.</li>
</ul>
<p>ii. <u><b>Prevention of Cardiovascular events:</b></u></p>
<ul>
<li>Anti-thrombotic therapy (Aspirin, clopidogrel): low dose aspirin 75-100mg 1tab/day.</li>
<li>Statins and other lipid-lowering drugs (rosuvastatin, atorvastatin, ezetimibe...)</li>
<li>ACE inhibitor/ARBs: if patients have hypertension, heart failure.</li>
</ul>
<table border="1">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td></td>
<td>Standard Therapy</td>
<td>High HR (&gt;80bpm)</td>
<td>Low HR (&lt;50bpm)</td>
<td>Heart Failure</td>
<td>Low BP</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>1<sup>st</sup> step</td>
<td>BB or CCB</td>
<td>BB or non-DHP-CCB</td>
<td>DHP-CCB</td>
<td>BB</td>
<td>Low-dose BB or Low dose non DHP-CCB</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>2<sup>nd</sup> step</td>
<td>BB+DHP-CCB</td>
<td>BB and non DHP-CCB</td>
<td>LAN</td>
<td>Add LAN or Ivabradine</td>
<td>Add low-dose LAN</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>3<sup>rd</sup> step</td>
<td>Add 2<sup>nd</sup> line drug</td>
<td>Add Ivabradine</td>
<td>DHP-CCB +LAN</td>
<td>Add another 2<sup>nd</sup> line drug</td>
<td>Add Ivabradine, ranolazine, or Trimetazidine</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>4<sup>th</sup> step</td>
<td colspan="5">Add nicorandil, ranolazine, or Trimetazidine</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>*BB: beta-blocker, BP: Blood Pressure, CCB: Calcium Channel Blocker, DHP-CCB: Dihydropyridine-Calcium Channel Blocker, HR: Heart Rate, LAN: Long-action Nitrate</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Revascularization:</b><br/>Revascularization with either coronary artery bypass graft surgery (CABG) or percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI), as opposed to continuing medical therapy without revascularization, is indicated in two groups of stable patients:
        <ul>
<li>Patients with specific high-risk anatomy for which revascularization has a proven survival benefit.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 305 -->

<ul><li>Patients who want revascularization for improved quality of life compared with medical therapy, such as those who are not tolerating medical therapy well or who want to increase their activity level.</li></ul><p><b>VIII. SPECIAL CASES:</b></p><ul><li>Individuals over the age of 65 years represent a growing proportion of patients with CSS, however, recognition of disease can be more challenging in this population due to a higher prevalence of atypical symptoms, including exertional dyspnea or silent myocardial ischemia.</li><li>The approach to the management of angina in older adults is essentially the same as for younger patients.</li></ul><p><b>IX. EVOLUTION AND PRONOSIS:</b></p><p>According to CLARIFY registry, in patient with CSS, resolution of angina within 1 year with conservative management predicted outcomes similar to lack of angina, whereas persistence or occurrence was associated with worse outcomes.</p><p><b>X. COMPLICATION:</b></p><ul><li>Acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina or MI),</li><li>Congestive heart failure,</li><li>Cardiac arrhythmias, or sudden death.</li></ul><p><b>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION:</b></p><p>We recommend that all patients with CCS receive education and counseling about issues such as medication compliance, control of risk factors, and regular exercise. In addition, there are several medical therapies which can reduce the risk of cardiovascular events and disease progression.</p><p><b>XII. REFERENCE</b></p><ol><li><a href="https://www.uptodate.com/contents/chronic-coronary-syndrome-overview-of-care">https://www.uptodate.com/contents/chronic-coronary-syndrome-overview-of-care</a></li><li>Ford TJ, Corcoran D, Berry C. Stable coronary syndromes: pathophysiology, diagnostic advances and therapeutic need. <h1>EMERGENCY TACHY-ARRHYTHMIA</h1>
<p><i>Dr. Sok Sorkhan, Dr. Khmao Pichmanil, Dr. Kiry Samnang, Dr. San Samrany, Dr. Lim Eaksrong, Dr. Sreng Dina, Asst. Prof. Suy Sovannara, Dr. Men Sengleap, Dr. Phouy Sonaroth, Dr. Theng Youdaline, Dr. Saing Leang, Dr. Lim Sivutha, Dr. Sok Phang, Asst. Prof. Chan Sokha, Ass Prof. Chhun Lay, Prof. Sok Chour</i></p>
<h2>I. INTRODUCTION</h2>
<p>Arrhythmias (cardiac arrhythmias or dysrhythmias) are irregularities in the heartbeat and the electrical impulses may be too fast, too slow or erratic, spans from a relatively benign condition to life-threatening emergencies.</p>
<p>2 types: Tachy-arrhythmia: HR &gt; 100bpm (at resting) and Brady-arrhythmia: HR &lt; 60bpm (at resting)</p>
<h2>II. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Tachycardia is when the heart beats too fast, at a rate of more than 100 beats per minute, when at rest. This can depend on age, health status and physical condition.</p>
<h2>III. CLASSIFICATION</h2>
<div>
<p>Tachycardia</p>
<ul>
<li>Narrow complex
        <ul>
<li>Regular
                <ul>
<li>Atrial tachycardia</li>
<li>Atrial flutter</li>
<li>AVRT</li>
<li>AVNRT</li>
<li>Junctional tachycardia</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Irregular
                <ul>
<li>AF with RVR</li>
<li>Multifocal atrial tachycardia</li>
<li>Atrial flutter with variable AV block</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Broad complex
        <ul>
<li>Monomorphic
                <ul>
<li>Regular
                        <ul>
<li>Monomorphic VT</li>
<li>SVT* with aberrancy</li>
<li>Sinus tachycardia with aberrancy**</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Irregular
                        <ul>
<li>AF with aberrancy</li>
<li>Multifocal atrial tachycardia with aberrancy</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Polymorphic
                <ul>
<li>Polymorphic VT</li>
<li>Torsades de pointes</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<p><b>AF:</b> atrial fibrillation, <b>AV:</b> atrioventricular, <b>AVNRT:</b> atrioventricular nodal re-entry tachycardia, <b>AVRT:</b> atrioventricular re-entry tachycardia, <b>SVT:</b> supraventricular tachycardia, <b>VT:</b> ventricular tachycardia, <b>SVT*:</b> any cause of regular tachycardia originating from above the ventricle, <b>Aberrancy**:</b> any form of abnormal conduction of the electrical impulse (i.e., left bundle branch block)</p>
<h2>IV. PIDERMIIOLOGY</h2>
<p>For SVT: prevalence is 2.25/1000 persons, incidence is 35/100 000 person-years. Women have a risk of developing SVT that is two times greater than that of men, and persons aged &gt; 65 years or have more than five times the risk of developing SVT than younger individuals. [1]</p>

<!-- PAGE 307 -->

<div>
<p>For SCD by ventricular arrhythmia: low incidence during infancy and childhood (1 per 100 000 person years), 25–27 the incidence is approximately 50 per 100 000 person years in middle-aged individuals (in the fifth to sixth decades of life). [2]</p>
<h4>IV. ETIOLOGIES AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4>
<p>Causes of tachyarrhythmia: [6]</p>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Cardiac</th>
<th>Extra-cardiac</th>
<th>Drug-induced</th>

<tr>
<td>Coronary artery disease<br/>Acute myocardial ischemia<br/>Chronic myocardial ischemia<br/>Cardiomyopathy (dilative,<br/>hypertrophic-obstructive, restrictive)<br/>Inflammatory heart disease<br/>Myocarditis<br/>Pericarditis<br/>Congenital heart disease in adult<br/>Acquired valvular disease<br/>Cardiac neoplasm<br/>Hypertrophy (arterial hypertension)<br/>Channelopathies</td>
<td>Electrolyte disturbances<br/>Toxic (alcohol)<br/>Hemochromatosis<br/>Renal diseases<br/>Hypo- and hyperthyroidism<br/>Autoimmune diseases<br/>Neoplasm<br/>Inflammatory diseases<br/>(sarcoidosis, amyloidosis)</td>
<td>Antiarrhythmic<br/>(Ex.: Digitalis)<br/>Antidepressives<br/>Bronchodilators<br/>Antineoplastic agents<br/>Inotropes<br/>Stimulants<br/>Opioids</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>3 Mechanisms of tachyarrhythmia: [1,2]</p>
<ul>
<li>Abnormal automaticity: When cells outside the normal conduction system generate spontaneous impulse.</li>
<li>Triggered activity: high levels of intracellular calcium, which can lead to spontaneous calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.</li>
<li>Re-entry: A conduction disturbance.</li>
</ul>

<h2>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h2>
<p>Differential diagnosis for tachycardia depends on the type of tachycardia, such as wide QRS complex tachycardia or regular, narrow-QRS tachycardias.</p>
<div>
<img alt="Flowchart titled 'Differential diagnosis for tachycardia'. The chart is divided into two main sections: Narrow QRS tachycardias (SVTs) and Wide complex tachycardias. The initial step is Tachycardia, which branches based on QRS duration (&lt; 120 ms or &gt;= 120 ms). The Narrow QRS section (SVTs) further branches based on rhythm (Irregular or Regular). Irregular rhythm leads to questions about P waves. Regular rhythm leads to a question about atrial rate (AFI &gt; ventricular rate?). The flowchart details various SVT types like Multifocal atrial tachycardia, Atrial flutter/tachycardia with variable AV block, Atrial fibrillation, AVNRT, AVRT, and Focal atrial tachycardia. The Wide QRS section includes Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, Atrial flutter/focal atrial tachycardia/AVNRT with aberrant conduction, AVRT, Ventricular tachycardia (VT), and Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia (PMT)."/>
<p><b>Figure 1. Differential diagnosis for tachycardia</b></p>
</div>
<h3>1- Narrow QRS tachycardia [1]</h3>
<p><b>A. Haemodynamically unstable patients:</b> Synchronized DC cardioversion</p>
<p><b>B. Haemodynamically stable patients:</b></p>
<ul>
<li><b>Vagal manoeuvres in the supine position with leg elevation</b></li>
<li><b>Medications:</b>
<ul>
<li>Adenosine (6-18 mg i.v. bolus with normal saline flush) if vagal manoeuvre fail (Except pre-excited Atrial fibrillation)</li>
<li>Verapamil (0.075-0.15 mg/kg i.v. (average 5-10 mg) over 2 min) or diltiazem (i.v.) (0.25 mg/kg (average 20 mg) over 2 mi) or Beta-blockers (i.v. esmolol (0.5 mg/kg i.v. bolus or 0.05-0.3 mg/kg/min infusion) or metoprolol (2.5-15 mg given i.v. in 2.5 mg boluses) if vagal maneuvers and adenosine fail</li>
<li>Synchronized direct-current cardioversion if drug therapy fails to convert or control the tachycardia)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Catheter Ablation</b></li>
</ul>
<h3>2- Wide QRS tachycardia [2,3]</h3>
<p><b>A. Treatment of reversible conditions</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Withdrawal of offending agents is recommended whenever drug-induced arrhythmias</li>
<li>Investigation for reversible causes (e.g. electrolyte imbalances, ischemia, hypoxemia, fever)</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 309 -->

<div>
<p><b>B. Hemodynamically unstable patients:</b> Synchronized DC cardioversion</p>
<p><b>C. Hemodynamically stable patients:</b> Medication therapy or Synchronized DC cardioversion if drug therapy fails to convert or control the tachycardia</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Medications therapy:</b>
<ul>
<li>Acebutolol PO 200–1200 mg daily or up to 600 mg bid</li>
<li>Amiodarone IV: 300 mg bolus for VF/pulseless VT arrest; 150-mg bolus for stable VT; 1 mg/min x 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min x 18 h, PO: 400 mg q8 to 12 h for 1–2 wk, then 300–400 mg daily; reduce dose to 200 mg daily if possible</li>
<li>Atenolol PO: 25–100 mg qd or bid,</li>
<li>Bisoprolol PO: 2.5–10 mg once daily</li>
<li>Carvedilol PO: 3.125–25 mg q 12 h</li>
<li>Diltiazem IV: 5–10 mg qd: 15–30 min Extended release: PO: 120–360 mg/day</li>
<li>Esmolol IV: 0.5 mg/kg bolus, 0.05mg/kg/min</li>
<li>Flecainide PO: 50–200 mg q 12 h</li>
<li>Lidocaine IV: 1 mg/kg bolus, 1–3mg/min or 1–1.5 mg/kg. Repeat 0.5–0.75 mg/kg bolus every 5–10 min (max cumulative dose 3 mg/kg). Maintenance infusion is 1–4 mg/min although one could start at 0.5 mg/min</li>
<li>Metoprolol IV: 5 mg q 5 min up to 3 doses, PO: 25–100 mg Extended release qd or q 12 h</li>
<li>Sotalol IV: 75 mg q 12h, PO: 80–120 mg q 12 h, may increase dose every 3d; max 320 mg/d</li>
<li>Procainamide IV: loading dose 10–17mg/kg at 20–50mg/min and Maintenance dose: 1–4mg/min, PO (SR preparation): 500–1250 mg q 6 h</li>
<li><b>Verapamil is not recommended in wide QRS complex tachycardia of unknown etiology</b></li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Administration of potassium and magnesium</b> has been proposed as helpful adjuncts in the prevention of ventricular arrhythmias</li>
<li><b>Implanted cardioverted defibrillator (ICD)</b> (for secondary prevention)</li>
<li><b>Catheter ablation</b></li>
<li><b>Surgical ablation</b></li>
<li><b>Autonomic modulation:</b> interruption of sympathetic outflow to the heart, pharmacological beta blockade, or through stimulation of the parasympathetic pathway</li>
</ul>
<p><b>3- Algorithm</b></p>
<img alt="Flowchart titled 'Narrow QRS tachycardia'. The flow starts with 'Narrow QRS tachycardia', leading to a decision point: 'Haemodynamic instability'. If 'Yes', the next step is 'Synchronized cardioversion (I B)'. If 'No', the next step is 'Vagal manoeuvres (I B)'. If 'Vagal manoeuvres' are ineffective, the next step is 'i.v. adenosine (I B)'. If 'i.v. adenosine' is ineffective, the next step is 'i.v. verapamil or diltiazem (IIaB)' OR 'i.v. beta-blocker (IIaC)'. If either of these is ineffective, the final step is 'Synchronized cardioversion (I B)'."/>
<p>Figure 2. Acute management for narrow QRS complex tachycardia [1]</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 310 -->

<div>
<p>Acute management of a patient with regular wide QRS complex tachycardia</p>
<p>Cardioversion/defibrillation/ALS (Class I)</p>
<p>Haemodynamically tolerated</p>
<p>History, physical examination, 12-lead ECG</p>
<p>Adenosine or vagal manoeuvres if SVT likely<sup>a</sup> (Class IIa)</p>
<p>Known or suspicion of structural heart disease</p>
<p>Idiopathic VT</p>
<p>Known fascicular VT</p>
<p>Known outflow tract VT</p>
<p>Other type or uncertain</p>
<p>Anaesthetic risk for cardioversion<sup>b</sup></p>
<p>Verapamil (Class I)</p>
<p>Beta-blockers (Class I)</p>
<p>Procainamide (Class IIa)</p>
<p>Flecainide<br/>Ajmaline<br/>Sotalol<br/>Amiodarone<sup>c</sup> (Class IIb)</p>
<p>Procainamide (Class IIa)</p>
<p>Amiodarone (Class IIb)</p>
<p>Cardioversion (Class I)</p>
</div>
<p><b>Figure 3.</b> Acute management for regular wide QRS complex tachycardia [1]</p>

<!-- PAGE 311 -->

<div>
<p><b>Initial assessment and support</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Maintain patent airway; assist breathing as necessary</li>
<li>Administer oxygen</li>
<li>Cardiac monitor to identify rhythm; monitor pulse, blood pressure, and oximetry</li>
<li>IV/IO access</li>
<li>12-Lead ECG if available</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Probable sinus tachycardia if</b></p>
<ul>
<li>P waves present/normal</li>
<li>Variable RR interval</li>
<li>Infant rate usually &lt;220/min</li>
<li>Child rate usually &lt;180/min</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Search for and treat cause.</b></p>
<p><b>Evaluate rhythm with 12-lead ECG or monitor.</b></p>
<p><b>Cardiopulmonary compromise?</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Acutely altered mental status</li>
<li>Signs of shock</li>
<li>Hypotension</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Doses/Details</b></p>
<p><b>Synchronized cardioversion</b></p>
<p>Begin with 0.5-1 J/kg; if not effective, increase to 2 J/kg. Sedate if needed, but don't delay cardioversion.</p>
<p><b>Drug Therapy</b></p>
<p><b>Adenosine IV/IO dose</b></p>
<ul>
<li>First dose: 0.1 mg/kg rapid bolus (maximum: 6 mg)</li>
<li>Second dose: 0.2 mg/kg rapid bolus (maximum second dose: 12 mg)</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Evaluate QRS duration.</b></p>
<p><b>Narrow (&lt;=0.09 sec)</b></p>
<p><b>Probable supraventricular tachycardia</b></p>
<ul>
<li>P waves absent/abnormal</li>
<li>RR interval not variable</li>
<li>Infant rate usually ≥220/min</li>
<li>Child rate usually ≥180/min</li>
<li>History of abrupt rate change</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>If IV/IO access is present, give adenosine <b>or</b></li>
<li>If IV/IO access is not available, or if adenosine is ineffective, perform synchronized cardioversion</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Wide (&gt;0.09 sec)</b></p>
<p><b>Possible ventricular tachycardia</b></p>
<p><b>Synchronized cardioversion</b></p>
<p>Expert consultation is advised before additional drug therapies.</p>
<p><b>No Cardiopulmonary compromise?</b></p>
<p><b>Narrow (&lt;=0.09 sec)</b></p>
<p><b>Probable supraventricular tachycardia</b></p>
<ul>
<li>P waves absent/abnormal</li>
<li>RR interval not variable</li>
<li>Infant rate usually ≥220/min</li>
<li>Child rate usually ≥180/min</li>
<li>History of abrupt rate change</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Consider vagal maneuvers.</b></p>
<p><b>If IV/IO access is present, give adenosine.</b></p>
<p><b>Wide (&gt;0.09 sec)</b></p>
<p><b>Possible ventricular tachycardia</b></p>
<p><b>If rhythm is regular and QRS monomorphic, consider adenosine.</b></p>
<p><b>Expert consultation is recommended.</b></p>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<p><b>Case 1:</b> A 48-year-old woman had a history of palpitations for 5 years. Her episodes started and stopped suddenly, lasted 1 to 2 minutes, and were associated with lightheadedness. She came to a local emergency room with a prolonged episode: ECG showed a narrow QRS tachycardia (by report; no ECG available) that was terminated with adenosine. She was treated with oral diltiazem and metoprolol but continued to have supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) episodes. She had a normal physical exam; non-invasive evaluation showed no structural heart disease. She was referred for catheter ablation of her SVT. [4]</p>
</div>

<p><b>Case 2:</b> The patient was a 28-year-old woman referred for management of palpitations for the last 2 years. Episodes began after birth of the eighth child and often worsened when she was upset. Ambulatory recorder showed sustained ventricular tachycardia originated from right ventricular outflow tract (having a left bundle branch block (LBBB) and right-inferior axis with a precordial R-wave transition at V3 and smooth R-wave contours in inferior leads). Metoprolol was ineffective at controlling her symptoms</p>

<h2>IX. OMPPLICATIONS</h2>
<p>The common complications include sudden cardiac death, syncope, stroke, heart failure, hypotension and/or shock.</p>

<h1>EMERGENCY BRADYCARDIA</h1>
<p>Dr. Khmao Pichmanil, Dr. Sok Sorkhan, Dr. Kiry Samnang, Dr. San Samrany, Dr. Lim Eaksrong, Dr. Sreng Dina, Asst. Prof. Suy Sovannara, Dr. Men Sengleap, Dr. Phouy Sonaroth, Dr. Theng Youdaline, Dr. Saing Leang, Dr. Lim Sivutha, Dr. Sok Phang, Asst. Prof. Chan Sokha, Asst. Prof. Chhun Lay, Prof. Sok Chour</p>
<h2>I. INTRODUCTION</h2>
<p>Bradycardia spans from a relatively benign condition to life-threatening emergencies. Bradycardia is a frequent finding in clinical practice and its significance is dependent on underlying cause and clinical presentation. The goal of initial management is stabilization by increasing the ventricular rate.</p>
<h2>II. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>A normal heart rate is normally between 60 to 100 beats per minute (bpm). An emergency bradycardia is defined as a heart rate &lt; 50 bpm with one of these conditions: (1) hemodynamic compromised, (2) severe slow heart rate &lt; 35-40 bpm, (3) ventricular tachyarrhythmias, (4) acute heart failure, (5) acutely altered mental status.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGIES AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h2>
<p>The causes of bradycardia can be separated into primary or secondary (Table 1). The primary or intrinsic etiologies are relatively rare in the acute setting and occur more often in the elderly patients. Secondary or extrinsic etiologies are more frequently seen in the acute care and are more likely to be reversible with medical therapy.</p>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Primary</th>
<th>Secondary</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Idiopathic (ageing) degeneration<br/>Ischemic heart disease<br/>Myocarditis, Endocarditis<br/>Infiltrative disease: sarcoidosis, amyloidosis<br/>Congenital disease<br/>Surgical trauma: valve replacement</td>
<td>Acute myocardial infarction<br/>Medications: digoxin, betablocker overdose...<br/>Hypokalemia, hyperkalemia<br/>Hypothyroidism<br/>Hypoxia<br/>Hypothermia<br/>Acidosis<br/>Physical training (athletes, sports)<br/>Vagal tone</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Table 1: The above causes can involve the sinus node and atrio-ventricular node (AV node) or distal His bundle-Purkinje system results in sick sinus syndrome and different degree of AV block at the nodal level or infra-nodal level, respectively.</p>
<h2>IV. DIAGNOSTIC</h2>
<p><b>1- Clinical signs and symptoms</b></p>
<p>Bradycardia may present as fatigue, dizziness, syncope, pre-syncope, shortness of breath, chest pain, palpitations, cardiac arrest. Assessment for signs of hypoperfusion or hemodynamic compromised such as cyanosis, altered mental status, pallor will help guide management.</p>
<p><b>2- Investigations</b></p>
<p>A 12-lead standard ECG has the most diagnostic value. Prolonged Holter monitoring is also helpful for intermittent bradycardia event. Serologic finding such as potassium, BUN, Creatinine, thyroid function test (TSH, fT4, fT3) will reveal common secondary causes of bradycardia. Serum cardiac markers, such as troponin, BNP or NT-proBNP are requested to assess myocardial ischemia or injury as a cause of bradycardia. Chest radiograph may reveal</p>

<!-- PAGE 316 -->

<div><p>enlarged cardiac silhouette (pericardial effusion or cardiomegaly). <i>Cardiac ultrasound</i> can identify structural heart disease.</p><h4>V. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4><p>Premature ventricular complex bigeminy, blocked premature atrial complex.</p><h4>VI. MANAGEMENT</h4><ol><li><b>Objectives</b><br/><i>The goal of initial management is stabilization by increase the ventricular rate through one of the following: (1) pharmacological intervention and/or (2) non-pharmacological intervention.<sup>2,5</sup> The physicians need to assess and determine the underlying causes of bradycardia.</i></li><li><b>Critical sign</b><br/>(1) hemodynamic compromised, (2) severe slow heart rate &lt; 35-40 bpm, (3) ventricular tachyarrhythmias, (4) acute heart failure, (5) acutely altered mental status.</li><li><b>Mortality risk factors</b><br/>Family history of sudden cardiac death, history of syncope, preexistent heart failure, associated cardiovascular and non-cardiovascular comorbidities.</li><li><b>Outpatient management</b><br/>Bradycardia patient with above critical signs are recommended to hospitalization for further investigation and appropriate management.</li><li><b>Treatment</b><ol type="A"><li><b>Pharmacological intervention</b><ul><li><b>Atropine:</b> first-line drug for unstable and acute symptomatic bradycardia<ul><li>Dosage: 1<sup>st</sup> dose 1mg IV bolus, repeat every 3 to 5 min and maximal dose is 3 mg, dose lower than 0.5 mg is not recommended</li></ul></li><li>Alternative drugs: Dopamine, Epinephrine and Isoproterenol<ul><li>Dosage of Dopamine: IV infusion 5 to 20 mcg/kg/min and titrate to patient response</li><li>Dosage of Epinephrine: IV infusion 2 to 10 mcg/min and titrate to patient response</li><li>Dosage of Isoproterenol: IV infusion 2 to 10 mcg/min and titrate to patient response</li></ul></li><li>Pharmacological intervention should not delay implementation of external pacing for patients with poor perfusion</li></ul></li><li><b>Non-pharmacological intervention#</b><ul><li><b>Transcutaneous cardiac pacing</b><ul><li>Technique: places pads on the patient chest and connects the ECG leads. Turn the pacer on with pacing rate to &gt; 30 bpm above intrinsic rhythm and set 70 mA. Start pacing, once pacing captured, set current at 5-10 mA above the threshold.</li><li>Complication: severe discomfort and failure to pace and capture.</li></ul></li><li><b>Temporary transvenous cardiac pacing</b><ul><li>Technique: equipped with fluoroscopy (usually in Cath-Lab). The site chosen is usually on femoral, subclavian or internal jugular vein. Venous sheath is inserted by Seldinger technique. Temporary pacing lead insertion into the appropriate pacing cardiac chamber (apical RV) and ensuring accurate lead placement.</li><li>Complication: thrombophlebitis, infection, cardiac perforation.</li></ul></li></ul></li></ol></li></ol></div>

<!-- PAGE 317 -->

<h2>VII. SPECIAL CASES</h2>
<p><b>Case #1:</b> A 74-year-old female with history of hypertension presented multiple episodes of syncope and was admitted at a referral hospital. Her blood pressure was 85/50 mm Hg, heart rate was 36 bpm and SpO2 was 96%. There, physician did a complete clinical examination and lab test which showed no findings of secondary causes. The ECG (Fig. 1) showed complete AV block with ventricular rate 37 bpm. Atropine and Dopamine IV were given based on the algorithm but there was no clinical response. The patient was transferred to a heart center in Phnom Penh where the electrophysiologist performed transvenous pacing and subsequently permanent pacemaker was successfully implanted (Fig. 2).</p>
<img alt="ECG strip showing complete AV dissociation with a regular ventricular rate of 37 bpm. The atrial rate is faster than the ventricular rate, and there is no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes."/>
<p><b>Figure (1).</b> Complete AV dissociation with heart rate 37 bpm suggested complete atrioventricular block.</p>
<img alt="ECG strip showing normal sinus rhythm with a paced ventricular rate. A pacing spike precedes each QRS complex following a normal P wave, indicating successful permanent pacemaker implantation."/>
<p><b>Figure (2).</b> Restoration of normal heart rate and AV conduction after permanent pacemaker implantation. Pacing spike preceded each QRS complexes following normal P wave.</p>

<!-- PAGE 318 -->

<div>
<p><b>Case #2:</b> A 53-year-old female with history of diabetes, hypertension and chronic kidney disease presented fatigue, dizziness and vomiting. Blood pressure was 95/62 mm Hg, heart rate was 38 bpm and SpO<sub>2</sub> was 92%. The ECG (Fig. 3) showed escape junctional rhythm with heart rate 39 bpm and peaked T wave and shortened QTc. She was found to have severe hyperkalemia (K<sup>+</sup> 7 mmol/L) due to her underlying CKD. Management and correction of hyperkalemia to normal potassium level (K<sup>+</sup> 4.5 mmol/L) resolved the bradycardia (Fig. 4).</p>
<img alt="ECG strip showing an escape junctional rhythm with a heart rate of approximately 39 bpm. The QRS complexes are narrow, and there is a prominent peaked T wave, consistent with hyperkalemia."/>
<p>Figure (3). Escape junctional rhythm, peaked T wave and shortened QTc consistent with hyperkalemia.</p>
<img alt="ECG strip showing a sinus rhythm after potassium level correction. The heart rate is regular and faster than in Figure 3. The T waves are no longer peaked, indicating normalization of the ECG."/>
<p>Figure (4). ECG normalized after potassium level correction.</p>
<h3>VIII. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<p>The common complications include sudden cardiac death, syncope, trauma secondary to fall after syncope, worsening of heart failure, hypotension and/or shock, ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation, death.</p>

<h1>PULMONARY EMBOLISM</h1><p>Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil,<br/>Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap,<br/>Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha,<br/>Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>Pulmonary embolism (PE) refers to obstruction of the pulmonary artery or one of its branches by thrombus.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>PE incidence varies by region, but it is typically estimated at 39 – 115 cases per 100.000 person-years. Incidence increase with age, particularly in people over 60 years old. PE is slightly more common in women, especially those on hormonal therapies, during pregnancy or in post-partum period.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><p>Pulmonary embolism (PE) is typically caused by thrombus formation, most often originating from deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in the legs. The etiology involves three primary factors – <b>Venous stasis</b>, <b>endothelial injury</b>, and <b>hypercoagulability</b> (Virchow's triad). Common triggers include prolong immobility, surgery, trauma, malignancy, hormonal influences (e.g. pregnancy, oral contraceptives), and genetic thrombophilias (e.g Factor V Leiden).</p><h2>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h2><p>PE occurs when a blood clot, usually from a deep venous thrombosis (DVT) in the legs, travels to the lungs and blocks a pulmonary artery. This obstruction reduces blood flow to the lungs, impairing oxygen exchange, and increase pulmonary artery pressure. Large clots can cause right heart strain, reduce cardiac output, and potentially lead to shock or sudden cardiac death.</p><h2>V. DIAGNOSIS</h2><ol><li>Initial assessment:<ul><li>Clinical History and symptoms: assess for dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, hemoptysis and risk factors (e.g. recent surgery, immobilization, cancer)</li><li>Physical examination to assess vital signs, signs of DVT and signs of right heart failure</li></ul></li><li>Risk stratification:<ul><li>Use <b>Modified Wells scoring system</b> (see Annex 1) or <b>Revised Geneva scoring system</b> (see Annex 2) to assess pre-test probability of PE</li></ul></li><li>D-dimer testing:<ul><li>If low/intermediate pre-test probability: Perform D-dimer blood test</li><li>If D-dimer is negative, PE can be ruled out</li><li>If D-dimer is positive, proceed to Imaging</li></ul></li><li>Imaging:<ul><li>CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA): Gold standard imaging technique to visualize and confirm the presence of thrombi.</li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 320 -->

<ul><li>Ventilation-Perfusion (V/Q) scan: used when CTPA is contraindicated (e.g. renal impairment, contrast allergy)</li><li>Compression ultrasound of the legs: perform if DVT is suspected, especially when symptoms of DVT are present</li></ul><p>5. Echocardiography:</p><ul><li>For <b>hemodynamically unstable patients</b>, bedside echocardiography can identify right heart strain suggestive of PE</li></ul><p>6. Additional laboratory tests:</p><ul><li>Arterial blood gas (ABG): show hypoxemia, hypocapnia and respiratory alkalosis.</li><li>Cardiac markers: Elevated troponins and brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) can indicate RV dysfunction and are associated with worse prognosis.</li></ul><h3>Diagnostic Algorithm for patient with suspected PE without hemodynamic instability</h3><div><p>Suspected PE in a patient without haemodynamic instability<sup>a</sup></p><p>Assess clinical probability of PE<br/>Clinical judgement or prediction rule<sup>b</sup></p><table><tbody><tr><td>Low or intermediate clinical probability,<br/>or PE unlikely</td><td>High clinical probability<br/>or PE likely</td></tr></tbody></table><p>D-dimer test</p><table><tbody><tr><td>Negative</td><td>Positive</td></tr></tbody></table><p>CTPA</p><table><tbody><tr><td>No PE</td><td>PE confirmed<sup>d</sup></td></tr></tbody></table><p>Treatment<sup>c</sup></p><p>CTPA</p><table><tbody><tr><td>No PE</td><td>PE confirmed<sup>d</sup></td></tr></tbody></table><p>No treatment<sup>c</sup> or investigate further<sup>e</sup></p><p>Treatment<sup>c</sup></p></div>

<!-- PAGE 321 -->

<h2>Diagnostic Algorithm for patient with suspected high-risk PE with hemodynamic instability</h2>
<div>
<p><b>Suspected PE in a patient with haemodynamic instability<sup>a</sup></b></p>
<p>↓</p>
<p><b>Bedside TTE<sup>b</sup></b></p>
<p>↓</p>
<p><b>RV dysfunction?<sup>c</sup></b></p>
<ul>
<li>If No: <b>Search for other causes of shock or instability</b></li>
<li>If Yes:
        <ul>
<li>CTPA immediately available and feasible?
                <ul>
<li>If No<sup>d</sup>: <b>Treatment of high-risk PE<sup>a</sup></b></li>
<li>If Yes:
                        <ul>
<li><b>CTPA</b>
<ul>
<li>If Positive: <b>Treatment of high-risk PE<sup>a</sup></b></li>
<li>If Negative: <b>Search for other causes of shock or instability</b></li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<h3>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h3>
<p>The differential diagnosis of pulmonary embolism (PE) includes conditions with similar symptoms such as <b>myocardial infarction</b>, <b>pneumonia</b>, <b>pleuritis</b>, <b>pneumothorax</b>, <b>congestive heart failure</b>, and <b>pericarditis</b>. Theses can present with chest pain, dyspnea, or tachycardia, mimicking PE. Careful evaluation of clinical history, risk factors and diagnostic imaging is essential to differentiate PE from these conditions.</p>
<h3>VII. MANAGEMENT</h3>
<ol>
<li>Initial assessment:
        <ul>
<li>Stabilization: assess airway, breathing and circulation (ABCs)</li>
<li>Vital sign monitoring: monitor HR, BP and oxygen saturation.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Risk stratification:
        <ul>
<li>Classify PE as <b>low</b>, <b>intermediate</b> or <b>high risk</b> based on clinical presentation and hemodynamic stability</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Anticoagulation therapy
        <ul>
<li>Immediate treatment: <u>Start anticoagulation as soon as PE is suspected</u>
<ul>
<li>Unfractionated Heparin (UFH): for high-risk patients</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 322 -->

<div>
<table border="1">
<caption><b>Key points about UFH for PE treatment</b></caption>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><b>Administration</b></td>
<td>IV bolus followed by continuous infusion</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Dosing protocol</b></td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Initial bolus: 80 units/kg (usually 5000 – 10000 units)</li>
<li>Continuous infusion: 18 units/kg/h, adjusted based on aPTT results (target: 1.5 – 2.5 times normal value)</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Monitoring</b></td>
<td>aPTT measured every 6 hours initially to ensure target level</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Reversal (antidote)</b></td>
<td>Protamine sulfate</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<ul>
<li><b>Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH):</b> For stable patients</li>
</ul>
<table border="1">
<caption><b>Key points about LMWH for PE treatment</b></caption>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><b>Administration</b></td>
<td>Subcutaneous injection (S/C)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>LMWH</b></td>
<td>Enoxaparin (Lovenox®) 20mg, 40 mg, 60 mg</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Dosing protocol</b></td>
<td>1 mg/kg twice daily</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Monitoring</b></td>
<td>Anti-factor Xa</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Duration</b></td>
<td>LMWH is often used for the initial phase (5 – 10 days). After that, patients are transitioned to oral anticoagulants such as warfarin or direct oral anticoagulant.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<ul>
<li><b>Direct Oral Anticoagulant (DOACs):</b> consider for outpatient management once PE is confirmed, based on guidelines</li>
</ul>
<table border="1">
<caption><b>Key points about DOAC for PE treatment</b></caption>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><b>DOAC Agents</b></td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Apixaban</li>
<li>Rivaroxaban</li>
<li>Dabigatran</li>
<li>Edoxaban</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Dosing protocol</b></td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Apixaban: <b>initial dose 10 mg twice daily for 7 days</b>, then 5 mg twice daily</li>
<li>Rivaroxaban: <b>initial dose 15 mg twice daily for 21 days</b>, then 20 mg once daily</li>
<li>Dabigatran: initial treatment with parenteral anticoagulation (e.g LMWH) for 5 – 10 days, then switch to 150 mg twice daily</li>
<li>Edoxaban: initial treatment with parenteral anticoagulation (e.g LMWH) for 5 – 10 days, then switch to 60 mg once daily</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<ul>
<li><b>VKA (Vitamin K antagonists): second-line therapy.</b> VKA are often considered when DOACs are contra-indicated or unsuitable, such as
        <ul>
<li>In patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR &lt; 30 ml/min)</li>
<li>In patients on certain medications that interact with DOACs, reducing their efficacy or increase bleeding</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 323 -->

<div>
<table border="1">
<caption><b>Key points about VKA for PE treatment</b></caption>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><b>Overlap with heparin</b></td>
<td>UFH or LMWH is used for at least 5 days until the INR reaches the therapeutic range (2 – 3) for 2 consecutive days</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Agents</b></td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Wafarin (COUMADINE®)</li>

</ul>
</td>

</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Reversal agent</b></td>
<td>Vitamin K</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>4. Thrombolytic therapy</p>
<ul>
<li>Indication: for patients with massive PE or those who are hemodynamically unstable (e.g hypotension)</li>
</ul>
<table border="1">
<caption><b>Key points about thrombolytic therapy for PE</b></caption>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><b>Agent</b></td>
<td>Alteplase (tPA)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Administration</b></td>
<td>IV infusion</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Dosing protocol</b></td>
<td>100 mg infusion over 2 hours</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>5. Mechanical Intervention</p>
<ul>
<li>Inferior Vena Cava (IVC) Filter: consider for patients with contraindication to anticoagulant or recurrent PE despite adequate treatment</li>
</ul>
<p>6. Monitoring and Supportive Care</p>
<ul>
<li>Monitoring: complications (bleeding, recurrent PE)</li>
<li>Supportive Care: administer fluids or vasopressors if necessary for hemodynamic support.</li>
</ul>
<p>7. Long term management:</p>
<ul>
<li>Anticoagulation duration:
        <ul>
<li>Provoked PE: 3 – 6 months of anticoagulation</li>
<li>Unprovoked PE: extended anticoagulation based on individual risk factors (e.g cancer, thrombophilia)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ul>
<li><b>Massive PE:</b> Hemodynamically unstable, requires immediate thrombolytics or surgical embolectomy</li>
<li><b>Pregnancy-Related PE:</b> due to physiological changes and venous stasis. Use Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) for treatment and avoid warfarin in pregnancy</li>
<li><b>Cancer-Related PE:</b> increased risk in cancer patients, long-term anticoagulation recommended using LMWH or DOACs</li>
<li><b>Pediatric PE:</b> Less common, often linked to congenital heart disease or surgery, management follow specific pediatric guidelines.</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<p>Without treatment, PE can result in severe complications and high mortality rate. Prognosis improve significantly with timely intervention, reducing mortality rates. Long-term outcomes may include chronic issues like pulmonary hypertension, but many patients recover well with appropriate management.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 324 -->

<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Right heart failure: due to increased pulmonary pressure</li>
<li>Hypoxia: from impaired oxygen change</li>
<li>Pulmonary Hypertension: develop from unresolved clot</li>
<li>Recurrent PE</li>
<li>Post-thrombotic syndrome: in case of DVT leading to PE.</li>
<li>Death: untreated or severe PE can lead to sudden cardiac death</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<p>Preventing PE involves assessing risk factors and implementing strategies such as pharmacologic prophylaxis (e.g. LMWH, DOACs) and mechanical measures (e.g. compression stockings). Early mobilization post-surgery and patient education on PE symptoms are crucial.</p>

<h1>ACUTE PULMONARY EDEMA</h1>
<p>Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Monghak, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. KHUON Rithy, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Acute pulmonary edema refers to clinical syndrome of new or worsening symptoms and/or signs of heart failure, leading to an unplanned hospital admission or an emergency department visit.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li>Prevalence of heart failure in the population is 2% in Europe and 4% in Southeast Asia.</li>
<li>Incidence of new cases per 100,000 per year: 219 in USA, 130 in UK, 70 in china</li>
<li>Main challenges of heart failure hospitalization:
        <ul>
<li>1-4% of total hospital admission</li>
<li>&gt; 9/10 patients hospitalized due to worsening chronic heart failure</li>
<li>Average length of hospital stay: 5-10 days</li>
<li>¼ or 24% patients are re-hospitalized within 30-days post discharge period,</li>
</ul>
<p><b>20% die within 6 months</b></p>
</li>
<li>In-hospital mortality (+++):<b>4.8% in Asia pacific</b></li>
</ul>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Table. 1 Etiology of acute heart failure</p>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Cardiovascular</th>
<th>Non-Cardiovascular</th>
<th>Patient-related or iatrogenic</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Acute coronary syndromes</li>
<li>Tachycardia (i.e., Afib)</li>
<li>Bradycardia (i.e. 3rd degree AVB)</li>
<li>Uncontrolled hypertension or hypertensive crisis</li>
<li>Myocarditis</li>
<li>Acute pulmonary embolism</li>
<li>Acute valvular regurgitation (i.e. endocarditis, MI)</li>
<li>Aortic dissection</li>
<li>Cardiac tamponade</li>
</ul>
</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Infections and febrile states</li>
<li>COPD exacerbation or asthma</li>
<li>Renal dysfunction</li>
<li>Anemia</li>
<li>Hyperthyroidism</li>
<li>Hypothyroidism</li>
<li>Strenuous exercise</li>
<li>Emotional stress</li>
<li>Pregnancy (peripartum cardiomyopathy)</li>
</ul>
</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Poor compliance with medication</li>
<li>Increased salt or fluid intake</li>
<li>Surgery</li>
<li>Drugs (i.e. NSAID, Thiazolidinediones)</li>
<li>Alcohol abuse</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h2>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h2>
<p>There are two main types of congestion:</p>
<ol>
<li>Peripheral congestion: progressive increase in body weight, peripheral edema, jugular distension, hepatomegaly, ascites and renal venous stasis.</li>
<li>Pulmonary congestion: worsening dyspnea, pulmonary rales and B-line at lung ultrasound.</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 327 -->

<div>
<img alt="Diagram illustrating the pathophysiology of acute heart failure. A central heart icon is connected by arrows to various organs and systems showing resulting effects: Kidneys (Renal Dysfunction, ↑ RAAS, Sodium Retention, AKI); Splanchnic Vasconstriction, Fluid Redistribution, Endothelial dysfunction; Peripheral Hypoperfusion, Cold Extremities; Pulmonary Edema, ↓ PaO₂; Cerebral Hypoperfusion, Altered Mental Status; Visceral Congestion, Liver Dysfunction; Intestinal Ischemia, Systemic Inflammation; and ↓ Coronary Flow, ↓ CO, ↑ CVP, ↑ RAP."/>
<p><b>Fig. 1 Pathophysiology of acute heart failure.</b></p>
<p>RASS, renin angiotensin aldosterone system; AKI, acute kidney injury; CO, cardiac output; CVP, central venous pressure; RAP, right atrial pressure</p>
<h3>V. DIAGNOSIS</h3>
<h4>1. Clinical</h4>
<ul>
<li>Symptom:
        <ul>
<li>Dyspnea: paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, reduced exercise tolerance, orthopnea<br/>! Evaluation dyspnea severity classification.</li>
<li>Congestion: lower extremity swelling, ankle swelling, abdominal fullness, hepatic congestion</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Physical finding:
        <ul>
<li>Vital sings: BP, HR, SpO2, Temperature, RR</li>
<li>Heart sounds: Third heart sound (LV dysfunction), Murmur, Jugular venous distension</li>
<li>Lung: rales (heart failure)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<table border="1">
<caption>Table. 2 NYHA Classification</caption>
<thead>
<tr>
<th colspan="2">New York Heart Association Dyspnea Classification</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>I</td>
<td>Cardiac disease, but no symptoms and no limitation in ordinary physical activity</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>II</td>
<td>Mild symptoms and slight limitation during ordinary activity</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>III</td>
<td>Significant limitation in activity due to symptoms, comfortable only at rest</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>IV</td>
<td>Severe limitations. Symptoms event while at rest</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h4>2. Investigation: <i>Treatment should not be delayed while waiting for the results!</i></h4>
<ul>
<li>Laboratory: complete blood count, chemistries, TSH, ABG, BNP if available, D-dimer if suspicion PE</li>
<li>Imaging: ECG, chest X-ray, Echocardiography &amp; lung ultrasound-if available</li>
</ul>
<h4>3. Four major Clinical hemodynamics profiles of acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF):</h4>
<ul>
<li>Acute decompensated heart failure</li>
<li>Acute pulmonary edema</li>
<li>Cardiogenic shock</li>
<li>Isolated right ventricular failure</li>
</ul>
</div>
