<h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2>
<ol>
<li>Objectives
        <ul>
<li>Improve symptoms, congestion and low-output symptoms</li>
<li>Restore normal oxygenation</li>
<li>Optimize volume status</li>
<li>Identifying etiology and precipitating factors</li>
<li>Initiating and optimizing oral therapy, minimizing side effects</li>
<li>Educating patients and considering a disease management program</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Critical sign
        <ul>
<li>Respiratory distress: RR &gt;35/min, SpO2 &lt; 90%, PaO2 &lt; 75mmHg, PaCO2 &gt; 45mmHg</li>
<li>Hemodynamic instable: low/high BP (&lt;85/&gt;140mmHg), Severe arrhythmias, HR &lt;60/min or &gt; 130/min</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Mortality risk factor
        <ul>
<li>Patient intubated or likely to require respiratory support/intubation, includes
                <ul>
<li>SpO2&lt;90% despite supplement oxygen</li>
<li>Using accessory muscles and respiratory rate &gt;25 breaths/min</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Signs and symptoms of hypoperfusion and/or SBP &lt; 90mmHg</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

First-line treatment</p><ol type="i"><li><b>Basic Assessment</b><ul><li>Positioning: head of bed elevated</li><li>O2 10 L/min → SpO2 ≥95%</li><li>Furosemide: 40-60mg i.v. (equal or 2 times to oral dose)</li><li>Morphine: 2mg i.v. if severe anxiety or distress</li><li>Digoxine: 0.25-0.5mg i.v. if rapid Afib (HR&gt;110/min)</li></ul></li><li><b>Adequate perfusion</b><ul><li><b>Wet Cold</b> (SBP &lt;90mmHg):<ul><li>Inotrope drug: Dobutamine= 3-5μg/kg/min</li><li>Vasopressor: Norepinephrine= 0.2-0.5μg/kg/min</li><li>Add Diuretic when perfusion corrected</li></ul></li><li><b>Wet Warm</b> (SBP: elevated or normal): Vasodilatators:<ul><li>Nitroglycerine spray 400μg sublingual, repeat 5-10 min</li><li>Nitroglycerine i.v. continuously 1mg/ml(10mg in 20ml)<ul><li>Start 1mg/h, check BP after 5 and 10min</li><li>Increase 0.5mg/h if need (SBP &gt;100mmHg), check BP 5 and 10min after each increase in dosing</li><li>Check BP every 20min once drip rate is reach (max 2.5mg/h, or drop SBP ≥40mmHg from initial BP)</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul></li><li><b>Reassessed~15-30min after:</b><ul><li>Sufficient respiratory + Ventilation</li><li>Release dyspnea + Symptoms</li><li>Normalization: BP, HR, urinary output<ul><li><b>Goals:</b></li><li>SpO2 : 94-98%</li><li>pCO2 &lt; 45mmHg, paO2 &gt; 70mmHg</li><li>SBP: 100-120/60,</li><li>HR: 60-100/min + regular</li><li>Urinary output &gt;0.5ml/kg/h</li></ul></li></ul></li></ol><p>6. Treatment adjustment</p><ul><li>SBP &lt;85mmHg: Increase dose Inotropes and Add Vasopressor</li><li>Respiratory distress (SpO2 &lt;90% with O2, RR&gt;25/min): CPAP or intubation</li><li>Urine output &lt; 20ml/h:<ul><li>Bladder catheter</li><li>Double dose diuretic= 80-120mg i.v bolus or 100mg/6H continuously</li><li>Combined diuretic= Bumetanide (Burinex), 2mg i.v, repeat every 20min (max 30mg/day)</li><li>Low-dose dopamine= 3μg/kg/min</li><li>Dialysis/ultrafiltration</li></ul></li></ul>

<div style="text-align: center;">
<h3>Acute Heart Failure</h3>
</div>
<table border="1" style="width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse;">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 50%;">
<b>Decompensation- factors triggering:</b>
<ul>
<li>Acute coronary syndrome</li>
<li>Tachyarrhythmia (Afib, VT)</li>
<li>Excessive rise BP</li>
<li>Infection (e.g. pneumonia, sepsis..)</li>
<li>Non-adherence to salt/fluid intake or medications</li>
<li>Toxic substance (alcohol, recreational drugs)</li>
<li>Drugs (NSAIDs, Corticosteroids...)</li>
<li>Exacerbation COPD</li>
<li>Surgery and perioperative complications</li>
<li>Metabolic/hormonal derangements (Thyroid dysfunction, diabetic ketosis, pregnancy and peripartum related..)</li>
</ul>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 50%;">
<b>De novo-Identification of acute aetiology:</b>
<ul>
<li>C acute <b>Coronary</b> syndrome</li>
<li>H <b>Hypertension</b> emergency</li>
<li>A <b>Arrhythmia</b></li>
<li>M acute <b>Mechanical</b> cause*</li>
<li>P <b>Pulmonary</b> embolism</li>
</ul>
<p>*myocardial rupture complicating ACS, chest trauma, acute native or prosthetic valve incompetence secondary to endocarditis, aortic dissection or thrombosis</p>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div style="text-align: center;">
<p><b>Congestion</b></p>
</div>
<div style="text-align: center;">
<p><b>Basic Assessment:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Positioning: head of bed elevated</li>
<li>O<sub>2</sub> 10l/min → SpO<sub>2</sub> ≥95%</li>
<li>Furosemide: 40-60mg i.v. (equal or 2 times to oral dose)</li>
<li>Morphine: 2mg i.v. if severe anxiety or distress</li>
<li>Digoxine: 0.25-0.5mg if rapid Afib (HR&gt;110/min)</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div style="text-align: center;">
<p><b>Adequate perfusion</b></p>
</div>
<table border="1" style="width: 100%; border-collapse: collapse;">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 50%;">
<p><b>Wet Cold (SBP &lt;90mmHg)</b></p>
<ol>
<li>Inotrope drug:
                <ul>
<li>Dobutamine= 3-5µg/kg/min</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Vasopressor:
                <ul>
<li>Norepinephrine= 0.2-0.5µg/kg/min</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Add Diuretic when perfusion corrected</li>
</ol>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 50%;">
<p><b>Wet Warm (SBP: elevated or normal)</b></p>
<p><b>Vasodilators:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Nitroglycerine spray 400µg sublingual, repeat 5-10 min</li>
<li>Nitroglycerine i.v. continuously 1mg/ml(10mg in 20ml)
                <ul>
<li>Start 1mg/h, check BP after 5 and 10min</li>
<li>Increase 0.5mg/h if need (SBP &gt;100mmHg), check BP 5 and 10min after each increase in dosing</li>
<li>Check BP every 20min once drip rate is reach (max 2.5mg/h, or drop SBP ≥40mmHg from initial BP)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<div style="text-align: center;">

<ul>

<li>SBP: 100-120/60,</li>
<li>HR: 60-100/min + regular</li>
<li>Urinary output &gt;0.5ml/kg/h</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<p><b>Yes</b></p>

<p><b>15min</b></p>
<p><b>Respiratory failure (PCO<sub>2</sub>&gt;50mmHg, PaO<sub>2</sub>&lt;60mmHg, pH&lt;7.35, RR&gt;35/min)</b></p>

<li>Double dose diuretic= 80-120mg i.v bolus or 100mg/6H continuously</li>
<li>Combined diuretic= Bumetanide(Burinex), 2mg i.v, repeat every 20min (max 30mg/day)</li>
<li>Low-dose dopamine= 3µg/kg/min</li>
<li>Dialysis/ultrafiltration</li>
</ol>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>Fig. 3 Acute Pulmonary Edema Management Algorithms</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 332 -->

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ul>
<li>Acute right heart failure: secondary to pulmonary embolism, right ventricular infarction or pulmonary hypertension. Management challenges; focus on optimizing preload, reducing afterload and addressing the underlying cause (e.g., anticoagulant for PE)</li>
<li>Flash Pulmonary Edema: sudden onset of severe pulmonary congestion. Management: requires rapid afterload reduction; IV nitroglycerine, diuretics and oxygenation support.</li>
<li>Acute heart failure with acute coronary syndrome: acute MI triggers heart failure. Management requires balancing treatment for both ACS and AHF, revascularization and careful fluid management.</li>
<li>Heart failure with pregnancy: peripartum cardiomyopathy is a notable cause, management focuses on balancing maternal and fetal health.</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Key predictors of poor prognosis: advanced age, low SBP, High heart rate, sings of hypoperfusion with high comorbidities (diabetes, CKD, COPD or malignancy).</li>
<li>Prognosis for Acute pulmonary edema remains worse with significant mortality and morbidity risks:
<ul>
<li>In-hospital mortality: 4-12%, higher in cardiogenic shock, sepsis or severe comorbidities</li>
<li>30-days readmission rates: 20-25%</li>
<li>1-year mortality: 20-40%</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Hemodynamic: cardiogenic shock, arrhythmia</li>
<li>Respiratory: Acute respiratory failure</li>
<li>Renal: Acute kidney injury (AKI), worsening renal function (Cardiorenal Syndrome)</li>
<li>Neurological: stroke, delirium</li>
<li>Metabolic and electrolyte: Hyponatremia, hyperkalemia or hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<ul>
<li>Primary prevention: manage risk factor of heart disease; blood pressure, lipid levels, treat diabetes, lifestyle changed &amp; screening for asymptomatic HF.</li>
<li>Secondary prevention: optimized guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), prevent decompensation, regular follow-up and patient education.</li>
</ul>

<h1>HYPERTENSION</h1>
<p>Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>High blood pressure is actually a leading risk factor for heart disease and early death. It's sometimes called the &lt;silent killer&gt;. High blood pressure is also called hypertension, when the systolic blood pressure is ≥140 mmHg and/or the diastolic blood pressure is ≥90 mmHg.</p>

<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Recent estimates have suggested the number of patients with hypertension in Cambodia could increase to 26% among 30-79 years in both sexes (WHO 2019).</p>
<h2>III. AETIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Over 90% of all cases of hypertension are of unknown aetiology (essential hypertension). One of the described risk factors for the development of essential hypertension is:</p>
<ul>
<li>Age</li>
<li>Family history</li>
<li>Being overweight or obese</li>
<li>Sedentary lifestyle (lack of exercise)</li>
<li>Using tobacco of any kind</li>
<li>Too much salt (sodium) in the diet</li>
<li>Excessive alcohol intake</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 334 -->

<h4>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4>
<p>There are various mechanisms described for the development of hypertension, which include increased salt absorption resulting in volume expansion, an impaired response of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), and increased activation of the sympathetic nervous system. These changes lead to the development of increased total peripheral resistance and increased afterload, which in turn leads to the development of hypertension.</p>
<h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<div>
<p>Elevated BP readings (home, office, or pharmacy)</p>
<p>Hypertension visit 1<br/>History, physical examination,<br/>and diagnostic tests</p>
<p>BP<br/>≥ 180/110 mm Hg</p>
<p>Hypertension</p>
<p>AOBP ≥ 135/85 mm Hg<br/>OBPM ≥ 140/90 mm Hg</p>
<p>No hypertension<br/>(Annual BP measurement recommended)</p>
<p>YES</p>
<p>OBPM<br/>Visit 2-3<br/>SBP ≥ 140 mm Hg or DBP ≥ 90 mm Hg<br/>If possible, confirm with home or ambulatory BP monitoring</p>
<p>Hypertension</p>
</div>
<h4>BP Measuring Technique</h4>
<ul>
<li>Don't smoke, exercise, drink caffeinated beverages or alcohol within 30mn of measurement</li>
<li>Take at least 2 readings at 1 min interval</li>
<li>Rest in a chair for at least 5mn with your left arm resting comfortably on a flat surface at heart level</li>
<li>Sit calmly and don't talk</li>
<li>Place the bottom of the cuff above the bend of the elbow</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 335 -->

<h3>Sign and symptom</h3>
<p>What are the signs and symptoms of high blood pressure? Usually none. That's why many people don't realize they have high blood pressure.</p>
<p>In some cases, people with more severe high blood pressure may have:</p>
<ul>
<li>Severe headaches</li>
<li>Vision changes</li>
<li>Nausea/vomiting</li>
<li>Nosebleeds</li>
<li>Confusion</li>
</ul>
<h3>Investigations</h3>
<ul>
<li>Laboratory tests: FBC, electrolytes, renal function, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid profile, uric acid, urines test</li>
<li>ECG</li>
<li>Heart ultrasound if available</li>
</ul>
<h3>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h3>
<p>Secondary hypertension should always be sought for as the differential, especially if the patient is at extremes of age (young or older).</p>
<p>Adrenal tumor, coarctation of the aorta, renal artery stenosis and kidney disease should always be kept in the differential.</p>

<h3>Antihypertensive recommendations based on patient co-morbidities and characteristics</h3>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Co-morbidity or characteristic</th>
<th>Potentially Beneficial</th>
<th>Avoid</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td rowspan="2">Chronic kidney disease</td>
<td>• ACE inhibitors or ARBs<br/>• Calcium channel blockers<br/>• Loop diuretics (if eGFR&lt;30ml/min/1.73m<sup>2</sup>)</td>
<td>• High salt intake<br/>• Theazides in patients with more than mild renal impairment</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Diabetes</td>
<td>• Beta-blockers<br/>• High dose thiazide diuretics (low doses are acceptable)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Heart failure or asymptomatic left ventricular dysfunction</td>
<td>• Type 1 -ACE inhibitors or ARBs then thiazide (or thiazide-like) diuretic or calcium channel blocker<br/>• Type 2 -ACE inhibitors<br/>• Beta-blockers (dose adjustments may be required for patients with renal dysfunction)</td>
<td>• Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g. diltiazem, verapamil)<br/>• Beta-blockers in uncontrolled heart failure</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Acute myocardial infarction</td>
<td>• Beta-blockers without intrinsic sympathomimetic activity, e.g. carvedilol<br/>• ACE inhibitors or ARBs</td>
<td>• No specific cautions</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Atrial fibrillation</td>
<td>• Beta-blockers<br/>• Rate limiting calcium channel blocker, e.g. diltiazem<br/>• ACE inhibitors or ARBs</td>
<td>• No specific cautions</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Angina</td>
<td>• Beta-blockers<br/>• Calcium channel blockers<br/>• ACE inhibitors or ARBs</td>
<td>• No specific caution</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Cerebrovascular disease, i.e. stroke</td>
<td>• ACE inhibitors or ARBs<br/>• Calcium channel blockers<br/>• Low-dose thiazide diuretics</td>
<td>• Beta-blockers<br/>• Thiazide diuretics in very elderly patients or those with poor daily fluid intake as they could contribute to hypoperfusion</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Asthma/COPD</td>
<td>• No specific recommendations</td>
<td>• Beta-blockers, however, low-dose bisoprolol (or metoprolol) can be used if required in patients with asthma/COPD and heart failure</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Gout</td>
<td>• Losartan (has a uricosuric effect)</td>
<td>• Thiazide diuretics</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Pregnancy</td>
<td>• Labetalol<br/>• Nifedipine<br/>• Methylldopa</td>
<td>• ACE inhibitors and ARBs</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

</ul>
</div>

</ul>
</div>

</div>

</ul>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<p>Hypertensive emergencies are a heterogeneous group of acute hypertensive disorders which require rapid recognition and treatment with the appropriate therapy to avoid progressive organ dysfunction.</p>
<p>A hypertensive emergency is defined by a blood pressure value above 200/120 mmHg with or without target organ damage.</p>

<!-- PAGE 340 -->

<h2>Management of hypertensive emergencies</h2>
<div>
<p><b>Severe blood pressure elevation</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Acute hypertension-mediated organ damage present → <b>Hypertensive emergency</b> → <b>Hospitalization</b></li>
<li>No acute hypertension-mediated organ damage present → <b>Uncontrolled hypertension</b> → Adjust treatment without hospitalization; secure follow-up to reach target blood pressure</li>
</ul>
<p>Hospitalization leads to:</p>
<ul>
<li>Acute hypertensive microangiopathy</li>
<li>Intracranial hemorrhage and stroke</li>
<li>Encephalopathy</li>
<li>Acute coronary artery disease, acute heart failure</li>
<li>Acute aortic diseases</li>
<li>Severe preeclampsia/HELLP syndrome, eclampsia</li>
</ul>
</div>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Clinical presentation</th>
<th>Timing</th>
<th>Target blood pressure</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Acute aortic diseases</td>
<td>Immediate</td>
<td>Systolic BP &lt;120 mmHg and heart rate &lt;60 beats per min</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema</td>
<td>Immediate</td>
<td>Systolic BP &lt;140 mmHg</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Acute coronary artery disease</td>
<td>Immediate</td>
<td>Systolic BP &lt;140 mmHg</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Severe preeclampsia/HELLP syndrome, eclampsia</td>
<td>Immediate</td>
<td>Systolic BP &lt;160 mmHg and diastolic BP&lt;105 mmHg</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Hypertensive encephalopathy</td>
<td>Immediate</td>
<td>Mean arterial pressure -20-25%</td>
</tr>
<tr>

</tr>

<td>Mean arterial pressure -15%</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Acute ischaemic stroke and a BP &gt;220/120 mmHg</td>
<td>1h</td>
<td>Mean arterial pressure -15%</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Malignant hypertension with or without TMA and/or acute kidney injury</td>
<td>Several hours</td>
<td>Mean arterial pressure-20-25%</td>
</tr>

<!-- PAGE 343 -->

<div><p><b>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</b></p><p>Untreated high blood pressure increases a person's risk of developing heart disease, stroke or kidney failure at an early stage.</p><p><b>X. COMPLICATION</b></p><p>Complications of hypertension account for 9.4 million deaths caused by CVD worldwide every year:</p><ul><li>At least 45% of deaths due to heart disease</li><li>51% of deaths due to stroke</li><li>It contributes to about <b>1000 deaths</b> a day</li></ul><ul><li>Heart: LV hypertrophy, heart failure, coronary artery disease</li><li>Brain: ischemic or haemorrhage stroke</li><li>Retina: haemorrhages or exudates, papilledema</li><li>Kidney: microalbuminuria, chronic kidney disease</li><li>Peripheral vasculature: aortic aneurysm, peripheral artery disease</li></ul><p><b>XI. PREVENTION</b></p><p>The best approach to the primary prevention of HTN is a combination of lifestyle changes:</p><ul><li>Don't smoke</li><li>Weight reduction</li><li>Restriction sodium intake</li><li>Physical activity</li><li>Alcohol consumption with moderation</li><li>Eat a healthy diet</li></ul><p><b>XII. REFERENCE</b></p><ol><li>J Clin Hypertens. 2021; 23:422-434</li><li>2020 ISG Global HTN Practice Guidelines</li><li>2010 Royal College of Physicians of London</li><li>Training of Trainer Curriculum for HTN and Diabetes Management in PHC-2022, MoH, Cambodia</li><li>Canadian Journal of Cardiology 36 (2020) 596-624</li><li>Lancet. 2012; 380 (9859): 2224-60</li><li>Robert Lowes, September 5, 2012, theheart.org</li><li><a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK539859/#:~:text=Differential%20Diagnosis&amp;text=Hyperaldosteronism%20coarctation%20of%20the%20aorta,be%20kept%20in%20the%20differential">https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK539859/#:~:text=Differential%20Diagnosis&amp;text=Hyperaldosteronism%20coarctation%20of%20the%20aorta,be%20kept%20in%20the%20differential</a></li><li><a href="https://academic.oup.com/esc/book/35489/chapter/312429354">https://academic.oup.com/esc/book/35489/chapter/312429354</a></li></ol><p><b>Abbreviation:</b></p><p>ABPM: ambulatory BP measurement<br/>ACEi: angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors AOBP: automated office BP<br/>ARB: angiotensin receptor blockers BP: blood pressure</p></div>

<h1>CHRONIC HEART FAILURE</h1>
<p>Asst. Prof. CHHUN Lay Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof CHAN Sokha, Prof. SOK Chour</p>
<h2>I. DEFINITIONS</h2>
<ol>
<li>Heart failure occurs “The situation when the heart is incapable of maintaining a cardiac output adequate to accommodate metabolic requirements and the venous return.”</li>
<li>HF is a clinical syndrome in which patients have the following features:
        <ul>
<li>+ <b>Symptom typical of HF:</b> Breathlessness at rest or on exercise, fatigue, tiredness, ankle swelling.</li>
<li>+ <b>Signs typical of HF:</b> Tachycardia, tachypnea, pulmonary rales, pleural effusion, raised jugular venous pressure, peripheral oedema, hepatomegaly.</li>
<li>+ <b>Objectif evidence of a structural or functional abnormality of the heart at rest:</b> Cardiomegaly, third heart sound, cardiac murmurs, abnormality on the echocardiogram, raised natriuretic (BNP or NT-pro-BNP) concentration.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Classification of HF by ESC: LVEF may be:</b>
<ul>
<li>+ Reduced LV ejection fraction (LVEF ≤ 40%) - Heart failure with reduced ejection function (HFrEF).</li>
<li>+ Preserved LV ejection fraction (LVEF ≥ 50%) - Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF).</li>
<li>+ Mid-range LV ejection fraction (LVEF 41%-49%) - Heart Failure with the LVEF being in the mid-range (HFmrEF).</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li>The prevalence of HF is around 1-2% of adult in the developing countries:
        <ul>
<li>+ The prevalence increased with age, CVRF, Post MI:
                <ul>
<li>Around 1% for those age younger than 55 years,</li>
<li>To &gt;10% in those age older than 70 years old.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>The prevalence of HF in Cambodia is around 3-4% in general population.</li>
</ul>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGIES</h2>
<p><b>A. The common underlying causes of HF in adults are:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Ischemic Heart Diseases (IHD)</li>
<li>Hypertension</li>
<li>Dilated cardiomyopathy-idopathic, familial</li>
<li>Valvular heart disease</li>
<li>Diabetic cardiomyopathy</li>
</ul>
<p><b>B. Other causes of HF include:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Congenital heart disease</li>
<li>Cor pulmonale</li>
<li>Pericardial disease: constrictive pericarditis, cardiac tamponade</li>
<li>Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy</li>
<li>Viral myocarditis</li>
<li>Acute rheumatic fever</li>
<li>Toxic: Alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy e.g. doxorubicin, trastuzumab (Herceptin), cyclophosphamide.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 346 -->

<div>
<ul>
<li>Endocrine and metabolic disorders: thyroid disease, acromegaly, phaeochromocytoma.</li>
<li>Collagen vascular disease: systemic lupus erythematosus, polymyositis, polyarteritis nodosa.</li>
<li>Tachycardia induced cardiomyopathy eg uncontrolled atrial fibrillation.</li>
<li>Infiltrative cardiac disease e.g. amyloid, hyper-eosinophilic syndrome.</li>
<li>High output HF e.g. severe anaemia, large A-V shunts/malformations.</li>
<li>Peripartum cardiomyopathy.</li>
<li>Stress (Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy.</li>
</ul>
<h4>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4>
<p><b>A. Pathophysiology:</b></p>
<p>a. <b>Cardiac Output (CO):</b> Stroke Volume (SV) x Heart Rate (HR): depend on:</p>
<ul>
<li>SV depend on Pre-load, After-load, Myocardial contractility,</li>
<li>Neuro-hormonal activations:
        <ul>
<li>+ Sympathetic nervous system (SNS): Beta-1, Beta-2, Alpha-1,</li>
<li>+ System renin angio-tension aldosterone system (RAAS),</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<div style="text-align: center;">
<h3>Pathophysiology</h3>
<img alt="Flowchart illustrating the pathophysiology of heart failure progression. Myocardial injury leads to Fall in LV performance. This activates RAS, NPS, SNS, ET, AVP. This activation leads to Myocardial toxicity and Peripheral vasoconstriction/Hemodynamic alterations. Both Myocardial toxicity and Peripheral vasoconstriction/Hemodynamic alterations lead to Remodeling and progressive worsening of LV function. Remodeling leads to Morbidity and mortality and Heart failure symptoms."/>
</div>
<p>b. <u>Cardiovascular risk factors:</u></p>
<ul>
<li>HTN,</li>
<li>Prediabetes/DM,</li>
<li>Dyslipidemia</li>
<li>Smoking</li>
<li>Diet, Alcohol, obesity, physical inactivity,</li>
<li>Age, gender, ASCVD</li>
</ul>
<h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<p><b>A. Clinical</b></p>
<p>a. <i>Past medical history of CVDs? CVRF?</i></p>
<p>b. <u>Symptoms:</u></p>
<ul>
<li>Breathlessness,</li>
<li>Orthopnea,</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 347 -->

<ul><li>Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea,</li><li>Cough+/-wheeze</li><li>Reduce exercise tolerance,</li><li>Fatigue,</li><li>Tiredness,</li><li>Increased time to recover after exercise,</li><li>Leg/Ankle/foot swelling,</li></ul><p><b>c. <i>Signs</i></b></p><ul><li>Tachycardia or irregular heart pulse,</li><li>Elevated jugular venous pressure,</li><li>Hepatojugular reflux,</li><li>Third heart sound (gallop rhythm)</li><li>Laterally displaced apical impulse,</li><li>Cardiac murmur,</li><li>Abdominal swelling,</li><li>Rapid weight gain,</li></ul><p><b>d. <i>York Heart Association (NYHA) classification</i></b></p><p>This system groups heart failure into four categories by number. You may see Roman numerals used for these category names.</p><ul><li>NYHA-I: There are no heart failure symptoms.</li><li>NYHA-II: Everyday activities can be done without difficulty. But exertion causes shortness of breath or fatigue.</li><li>NYHA-III: It's difficult to complete everyday activities.</li><li>NYHA-IV: Shortness of breath occurs even at rest. This category includes the most severe heart failure.</li></ul><p><b>e. <i>American College of Cardiology</i></b></p><ul><li>Stage A. risk factors for heart failure but no signs or symptoms.</li><li>Stage B. There is heart disease but no signs or symptoms of heart failure.</li><li>Stage C. There is heart disease and signs or symptoms of heart failure.</li><li>Stage D. Advanced heart failure requires specialized treatments.</li></ul><p><b>f. <i>Left-sided heart failure symptoms include:</i></b></p><ul><li>Paroxysmal nocturnal shortness of breath.</li><li>Shortness of breath during exercise or when lying flat.</li><li>Chronic coughing or wheezing.</li><li>Difficulty concentrating.</li><li>Fatigue.</li><li>Fluid retention causing swelling, or edema, in the ankles, legs and/or feet.</li><li>Lack of appetite and nausea.</li></ul><p><b>g. <i>Right sided heart failure symptoms include:</i></b></p><ul><li>General or inferior limbs oedema,</li><li>Hepatomegalia, hepatalgia</li><li>Turgescence jugular,</li><li>Weight gain and increase abdominal girth.</li></ul><p><b>h. <i>Factors triggered acute HF:</i></b></p><p>Patients with Chronic HF may occasionally develop acute decompensation. The more important causes that need to be recognised and treated appropriately are:</p>

<!-- PAGE 348 -->

<div>
<ul>
<li>Acute myocardial infarction/myocardial ischaemia.</li>
<li>Arrhythmias (e.g. atrial fibrillation).</li>
<li>Hypertensive emergencies.</li>
<li>Infections (e.g. pneumonia).</li>
<li>Non-compliance to medications.</li>
<li>Excessive fluid and salt intake.</li>
<li>Anaemia.</li>
<li>Development of renal impairment.</li>
<li>Adverse effects of drug therapy (e.g. non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs).</li>
</ul>
<h3>Diagnostic algorithm for heart failure</h3>
<p><b>Suspected heart failure</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Risk factors</li>
<li>Symptoms and/or signs</li>
<li>Abnormal ECG</li>
</ul>
<p>If NT-proBNP ≥ 125 pg/mL or BNP ≥ 35 pg/mL:</p>
<ul>
<li>Y: Proceed to Echocardiography.</li>
<li>N: Heart failure unlikely → Consider other diagnoses.</li>
</ul>
<p>Echocardiography</p>
<p>If Abnormal findings:</p>
<ul>
<li>Y: Heart failure confirmed. Define heart failure phenotype based on LVEF measurement.
        <ul>
<li>≤40% (HFrEF)</li>
<li>41–49% (HFmrEF)</li>
<li>≥50% (HFpEF)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>N: Heart failure unlikely → Consider other diagnoses.</li>
</ul>
<p>Heart failure confirmed (after defining phenotype): Determine aetiology and commence treatment.</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 349 -->

<div>
<p><b>B. <u>Investigations</u>:</b></p>
<p>a. <b>ECG:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>To assess heart rate, rhythm, QRS morphologie, QRS duration, QRS voltage, evidence of ischemia, LV hypertrophic and arrhythmia.</li>
</ul>
<img alt="Two ECG strips are shown side-by-side. The left strip (Rong, Lak) shows Sinus tachycardia with prolonged QT interval. The right strip (Chihum, Chan mara) shows Atrial fibrillation."/>
<p>c. <b>Chest X-ray:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>To look for pulmonary congestion, Cardiomegaly and presence of underlying lung pathology, patient with HFpEF may have a cardiac normal size.</li>
</ul>
<p>d. <b>Blood tests:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>FBC, renal function, liver function, serum glucose, lipid profile,</li>
<li>Urinalysis, to look for proteinuria, glucosuria,</li>
<li>Natriuretic Peptides (NP): (. Brain natriuretic petide (BNP) or . N-terminal pro BNP (NTproBNP)): BNP and NTproBNP are a family of hormones secreted by the ventricles in response to wall stress, They are useful in the following situations:
        <ul>
<li>+ In the emergency setting:
            <ul>
<li>&gt; NB are useful as a “ rule out” test for patients presenting with acute dyspnea. A level of &lt; 100pg/ml for BNP and &lt; 300mg/ml for NTproBNT makes the diagnosis of acute HF unlikely. These levels are affected by renal function and gender.</li>
<li>&gt; A high level supports the diagnosis of acute HF and very high levels correlate with the severity of HF and adverse outcome.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>e. <b>Heart Ultrasound (Echocardiography):</b> this will allow access of:</p>
<ul>
<li>Lv chamber size, volume and systolic function.</li>
<li>Lv wall thickness, evidence of scarring and wall motion abnormalities,</li>
<li>Diastolic function of the heart,</li>
<li>Valvular structure and function,</li>
<li>Congenital cardiac abnormalities,</li>
<li>Lv mechanical dyssynchrony</li>
<li>Pulmonary hypertension,</li>
</ul>
</div>

<h3>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Chronic pulmonary disease (COPD), Asthma, Pulmonary fibrosis, Pulmonary hypertension,</li>
<li>Pneumonia, Pleural effusion, Pneumothorax, Aspiration foreign body</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 351 -->

<h2>VII. MANAGEMENT OF HF</h2>
<h3>A. Objectives</h3>
<ul>
<li>Prevention of recurrents: Etiologies treatment and triggered factors</li>
<li>Management of asymptoms LV dysfunction.</li>
<li>Improve quality of life,</li>
<li>Prolongation of life expectancy.</li>
</ul>
<h3>B. Critical signs</h3>
<ul>
<li>Orthopnea, APO</li>
<li>Persistent chest pains or chest discomfort,</li>
<li>Palpitations with optimal treatment.</li>
<li>Cardiac arrest. Persistence of symptom after three months of optimal treatment.</li>
</ul>
<h3>C. Mortality risk factors</h3>
<ul>
<li>Ventricular arrhythmia, Afib with height heart rates,</li>
<li>Multi-lesion coronary artery disease</li>
<li>CKD, HTA, T2D</li>
<li>Anemia,</li>
<li>Hyponatremia and hypokalemia.</li>
</ul>
<h3>D. Out patient management</h3>
<ul>
<li>Patient educations, lifestyle management, call 119 in case emergency.</li>
<li>Regular follow up</li>
</ul>
<h3>E. Medical treatment</h3>
<ul>
<li>To reduce volume overload: Lube diuretic +/- MRA</li>
<li>First line medicine to reduce morbid mortalities: ACE-I/ARB/ARNI, BB, MRA, SGLT2i</li>
</ul>
<h4>Chronic Heart Failures treatment</h4>
<ul>
<li><b>Classic:</b> Digoxin + Diuretics,</li>
<li><b>Modern:</b> Base on the randomized studies: ACE-I/ARB/ARNI + Beta-blocker +/- Diuretics +/- Digoxin.</li>
</ul>
<p>NB: HF treatment: Treatment of activation neuro-hormones.</p>
<p>+ <b>New Guideline HF treatment with LV dysfunction:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Stage 1: ACEI /ARB/ARNI +/- Lube diuretics +/- MRA +/- SGLT2i</li>
<li>Stage 2: ACEI/ARB/ARNI +/- Lube diuretics +/- MRA, Beta-blocker +/- SGLT2i,</li>
<li>Stage 3: ACEI/ARB/ARNI +/- Lube diuretics +/- MRA +/- Beta-blocker +/- SGLT-2 Inhibitors +/- Digoxin</li>
<li>Stage 4: ACEI/ARB/ARNI +/- Lube diuretics +/- MRA +/- Beta-blocker +/- SGLT-2 Inhibitors +/- Digoxin</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 352 -->

<h2>Optimising Drug Therapy In Chronic HFrEF</h2>
<div>
<p><b>Signs and symptoms of Heart failure (LVEF &lt; 40%)</b></p>
<ul>
<li><b>No:</b>
<ul>
<li>In stepwise manner, initiate:
                <ul>
<li>ACE-I (or ARB if ACE-I intolerant)</li>
<li>β-blockers</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Yes:</b>
<ul>
<li>In stepwise manner, initiate:
                <ul>
<li>Diuretics if volume overload/congestion is present (including MRA)</li>
<li>ACE-I (or ARB if ACE-I intolerant) or ARNI</li>
<li>β-blockers if no signs of volume overload/congestion</li>
<li>MRA</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Clinical Improvement</b></p>
<ul>
<li><b>No:</b>
<ul>
<li>Consider:
                <ul>
<li>Switching ACE-I/ARB to ARNI</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Add:
                <ul>
<li>Ivabradine (if sinus rhythm &amp; HR &gt; 70bpm) and/or</li>
<li>Digoxin</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Yes:</b>
<ul>
<li>Continue with:
                <ul>
<li>Diuretics: low maintenance dose</li>
<li>ACE-I/ARB or ARNI: titrate to max tolerated dose</li>
<li>β-blocker: titrate to max tolerated</li>
<li>MRA</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Clinical Improvement</b></p>
<ul>
<li><b>No:</b>
<ul>
<li>See Flow Chart II (Acute HF - Page 29) - Treat with IV - parenteral medications (Consider referral to tertiary cardiac centres)
                <ul>
<li>Loop diuretics + thiazides</li>
<li>Short term parenteral positive inotropes</li>
<li>Consider if suitable:
                        <ul>
<li>&gt; ICD</li>
<li>&gt; CRT</li>
<li>&gt; IABP</li>
<li>&gt; VAD</li>
<li>&gt; Cardiac transplant</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Yes:</b>
<ul>
<li>Continue with:
                <ul>
<li>Diuretics</li>
<li>ACE-I / ARB - Consider switch to ARNI if not on</li>
<li>MRA (if not already on)</li>
<li>β-blockers</li>
<li>Ivabradine</li>
<li>Digoxin</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ul>
<li>HF with CHD,</li>
<li>Diabetes and HF,</li>
<li>HF in pregnancy,</li>
<li>HF in adult congenital heart disease (ACHD),</li>
<li>Arrhythmia-induced HF,</li>
<li>Cardio-oncology and HF,</li>
<li>HF and kidney dysfunction,</li>
<li>HF with desynchronization</li>
<li>Advanced HF/Refractory Hf/Heart transplant,</li>
<li>HF with Mechanical circulatory support,</li>
<li>Palliative and end of life care.</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>The prognostic of HF depends on its comorbid-mortality.</li>
<li>Latest studies have shown that the survival rates of people with chronic HF were:
        <ul>
<li>80% to 90% for one year,</li>
<li>50% to 60% for year five,</li>
<li>Most people with end-stage HF have a life expectancy of less than one year.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>X. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Lifestyle change, patience education,</li>
<li>Vaccination, flux, pneumonias, typhoide, etc.,</li>
<li>Optimal management of LV dysfunction asymptomatic.</li>
<li>Optimal management of HF base on new guideline.</li>
<li>Optimized all causes, IHD, VHD, CHD etc.</li>
<li>Optimized treatment of comorbid-mortality of HF,</li>
<li>Optimized medical treatment of cardiovascular risk factors.</li>
<li>Vaccinations,</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. URGERIES AND DEVICES</h3>
<ul>
<li>Heart surgeries and Intervention cardiology for heart disease that causes HF.</li>
<li>Devices
        <ul>
<li>Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT): biventricular pacing, is used to help improve the heart's rhythm and the symptoms associated with the arrhythmia. In effect, it is “resynchronizing” the heart.</li>
<li>Implantable cardioverter defibrillator (ICD): If an abnormal of heart rhythm is detected, the device will deliver an electric shock to restore a normal heartbeat.</li>
<li>Heart transplantation: remains de gold standard for the treatment of advanced HF in the absence of contraindication.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 357 -->

<h3>KEYS MESSAGES</h3>
<ul>
<li>Patients with HF are classified based on their LVEF. Those with a LVEF between 41% and 49% are defined as 'mildly reduced LVEF (HFmrEF).</li>
<li>Measurement of NPs and echocardiography have key roles in the diagnosis of HF.</li>
<li>ACE-I or ARNI, beta-blockers, MRA, and SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended as cornerstone therapies for patients with HFrEF.</li>
<li>ICDs are recommended in selected patients with HFrEF of an ischaemic aetiology and should be considered in those with a nonischaemic aetiology.</li>
<li>CRT-P/D is recommended in those patients with HFrEF, in sinus rhythm, with a LBBB &gt; 150 ms and should be considered in those with a LBBB &gt;130-149 ms or non-LBBB &gt; 150 ms.</li>
<li>Advanced HF strategies (heart transplantation/MCS) may be appropriate in selected patients.</li>
<li>ACE-I/ARNI, beta-blockers, and MRA may be considered in patients with HFmrEF.</li>
<li>The diagnosis of HFpEF requires objective evidence of cardiac structural, or functional abnormalities as well as elevated plasma NP concentrations consistent with the presence of LV diastolic dysfunction and raised LV filling pressures. A diastolic stress test is recommended when these markers are equivocal.</li>
<li>To date, no treatment has been shown to reduce mortality and morbidity in patients with HFpEF.</li>
<li>Exercise is recommended for all patients who are able, to improve exercise capacity and QOL, and reduce HF hospitalization.</li>
<li>Patients with advanced HF refractory to medical/device therapy and who do not have absolute contraindications should be referred for consideration of heart transplantation. MCS should also be considered as BTT or DT in selected patients.</li>
<li>Patients hospitalized for HF should be carefully evaluated to exclude persistent signs of congestion. Oral treatment should be optimized before discharge.</li>
<li>It is recommended that patients with type II diabetes are treated with SGLT2 inhibitors.</li>
</ul>

<h1>AORTIC REGURGITATION (AR)</h1><p>Asst. Prof. CHHUN Lay Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof CHAN Sokha, Prof. SOK Chour</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>Failure of the aortic valve to close tightly causes back flow of blood into the left ventricle in diastolic.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>The prevalence of rheumatic valvular heart disease in developed countries is declining, with an estimated incidence 41 millions in world wide. The prevalence is higher in developing nations than in US. In Cambodia, the prevalence is more than 35 case per 100000.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><ul><li>Rheumatic fever more than 95%,</li><li>Degenerative,</li><li>Infective endocarditis</li><li>Congenitally bicuspid,</li><li>Prolapse from VSD</li><li>Systemic hypertension,</li><li>Marfan or Marfan-like syndrome</li><li>Malignant carcinoid syndrome,</li><li>Silence Syphilis</li><li>Systemic lupus erythematosus, Whipple disease, Fabry disease, and rheumatoide arthristis.</li></ul><h2>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h2><h3>A. Acute Aortic insufficiency:</h3><p>In acute aortic insufficiency, the retrograde backflow of blood results in a quick rise in the LVEDV. The acute increase in preload and afterload does not allow the time for the LV to adapt to the rapid increase in volume during diastole, and this also results in a sharp rise in LV diastolic pressure. When the LV diastolic pressure rises above the level of LA pressure, premature mitral valve closure and MR can be seen. Additionally, there will be increases in LA pressure and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure that cause pulmonary edema. Compensatory tachycardia may occur to blunt the decline in anterograde stroke volume, and concentric hypertrophy with increased wall thickness can occur.</p><h3>B. Chronic Aortic Insufficiency:</h3><p>In chronic aortic insufficiency, the LV compensates for the diastolic regurgitation of blood from the aorta into the LV by remodeling of the LV via eccentric hypertrophy of the cardiomyocytes and LV dilatation to allow for an increase in LV stroke volume and a lesser increase in wall thickness than that which would be seen in acute aortic insufficiency. However, the left end-diastolic volume and</p>

<!-- PAGE 360 -->

<div>
<p>pressure rise to a high degree such that the sarcomeres can become maximally stretched, LV remodeling and compensation mechanisms fail, and interstitial fibrosis and a drop in LV compliance occur. The composite result of these changes is a decline in the initially compensated and elevated LV stroke volume.</p>
<img alt="Flowchart illustrating the pathophysiology of Aortic Regurgitation (AR). AR leads to Diastolic Regurgitation. This results in increased LV volume, increased stroke volume, decreased aortic diastolic pressure, and decreased effective stroke volume (fatigue). Increased LV volume leads to increased LV mass. Increased stroke volume leads to increased systolic pressure. Decreased aortic diastolic pressure leads to increased LVET. Increased LV mass leads to LV dysfunction. Increased systolic pressure leads to increased myocardial O2 consumption. Increased LVET leads to decreased diastolic time. Decreased effective stroke volume leads to decreased myocardial O2 supply. LV dysfunction leads to increased LVEDP (dyspnea). Increased myocardial O2 consumption and decreased myocardial O2 supply both lead to Myocardial ischemia. Increased LVEDP (dyspnea) and Myocardial ischemia both lead to LV failure."/>
<p>(From Boudoulas H, Gravanis MB: Valvular heart disease. In Gravanis MB [ed]: Cardiovascular Disorders: Pathogenesis and Pathophysiology. St. Louis, CV Mosby, 1993, p 64.)</p>

<h3>V. DIAGNOSIS</h3>
<p><b>A. Discovered diagnostic:</b> Systemic examination, heart auscultation, ECG, heart ultrasound, chest x-ray.</p>
<p><b>B. Clinical presentation:</b></p>
<ol>
<li><b>Symptoms:</b> Aortic Regurgitation are long time tolerance, 20 to 40 years after an episode of rheumatic fever
    <ul>
<li>The most common symptoms are shortness of breath, dyspnea on exertion, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, orthopnea.</li>
<li>Palpitations, chest discomfort, chest pain.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Signs:</b>
<ul>
<li><b>Heart Auscultation:</b> Diastolic murmur</li>
<li><b>Austin Flint murmur:</b> This is believed to occur due to the regurgitant jet of the aortic regurgitation causing premature closing of the mitral valve. This mimics functional mitral stenosis and is described as a low-pitched and rumbling mid to late diastolic or presystolic mitral murmur best heard at the apex.</li>
<li><b>Pulsus bisferiens:</b> A biphasic pulse with two systolic peaks seen on pressure tracings.</li>
<li><b>Corrigan sign:</b> A bounding pulse in large arteries such as the carotids that expands and suddenly collapses and empties between beats.</li>
<li><b>De Musset sign:</b> Head nodding with every heartbeat.</li>
<li><b>Muller sign:</b> Systolic pulsation of the uvula.</li>
<li><b>Quincke sign:</b> Repeatedly alternating blushing and blanching of capillaries in the nail folds upon palpation.</li>
<li><b>Traube sign:</b> Pistol shot sounds heard on the femoral artery upon compression of the artery.</li>
<li><b>Waterhammer Pulse:</b> Peripheral arterial pulses are rapidly dissipated or "bounding". This finding can be accentuated by raising the extremities.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<p><b>C. Test:</b></p>
<p>a. <b>ECG:</b> Sinus rhythm or Sinus tachycardia, or Afib,</p>

<h3>3. Chest X-ray:</h3>
<p>A chest X-ray is a picture of the heart and lungs. It can show whether the heart is enlarged, which can be a sign of certain types of heart valve disease.</p>

<h4><b>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</b></h4>
<ul>
<li>Pulmonary valve regurgitation,</li>
<li>Aortic stenosis</li>
<li>Matral regurgitation,</li>
</ul>
<h4><b>VII. MANGEMENT</b></h4>
<ol>
<li>The goals of aortic valve regurgitation treatment are ease symptoms and prevent complications.
        <ul>
<li>If your symptoms are mild or you don't have symptoms, you may only need regular health checkups. You may need regular echocardiograms to check the health of the aortic valve. Heart-healthy lifestyle changes also are usually recommended.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Prevention recurrent of Acute Rheumatic Fever and Endocarditis (See ARF and Endocarditis)</li>
<li>Medical treatment:
        <ul>
<li>Treat symptoms</li>
<li>Reduce the risk of complications</li>
<li>Lower blood pressure
                <ul>
<li>Volume overload: Loop diuretic with or without MRA, ACEi, ARB (see HF treatment)</li>
<li>Prevention LV remodelling: ACEi, ARB, BB, MRA</li>
<li>Thrombo-embolic prevention: if sinus rhythm undergone ASP-75-81mg/day, if Afib or Fluter: AVK (INR: 2-3) or NOAC,</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 364 -->

<div>
<ul>
<li>Surgery indications: May be needed especially if the condition and symptoms are severe. Asymptom patient and echocardiography showed sever aortic regurgitations (see algorhythm)</li>
<li>Mechanical AVR: undergone AVK (INR: 2-3),</li>
<li>Biological AVR: Sinus rhythm undergone anti-agregant platelats, if Afib undergone anti-coagulation.</li>
</ul>

<ul>

</li>
<li>Stroke: Stroke treatment and HF management.</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Heart failures: First left HF and the right HF,</li>
<li>Ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death,</li>
</ul>

<h1>AORTIC STENOSIS (AS)</h1><p>Asst. Prof. CHHUN Lay Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof CHAN Sokha, Prof. SOK Chour</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>Uncompleted opened aortic valves less than 2cm<sup>2</sup> during LV telesystolic (normal Aortic Surface Area: 2,5 to 3,5cm<sup>2</sup>. Severe AS &lt;0,75cm<sup>2</sup> or &lt;0,50cm<sup>2</sup>/m<sup>2</sup>. Moderated AS: 0,75 to 1,5cm<sup>2</sup> or 0,5 to 1cm<sup>2</sup>/m<sup>2</sup>. Mild AS: 1,5 to 2cm<sup>2</sup>).</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>The prevalence of rheumatic disease in developed countries is declining, with an estimated incidence of 41 million worldwide. The prevalence is higher in developing nations than in US. In Cambodia, the prevalence is more than 35 case per 100000.</p><p>There are large differences in the epidemiology of aortic valve disease between high-income and low-income countries. Rheumatic valvulopathy is most commonly seen in low-income countries. The incidences of aortic stenosis in the developing countries with the population age older than 75 years is high (374 cases per 100,000).</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><ul><li>Rheumatic fever more than 90% (in Cambodia)</li><li>Calcification (in developing countries)</li><li>Congenitally bicuspid,</li><li>Monkeberg disease</li><li>Malignant carcinoid syndrome,</li><li>Systemic lupus erythematosus, Whipple disease, Fabry disease, and rheumatoid arthritis.</li></ul><h2>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY:</h2><p>Left ventricular (LV) obstruction caused by the stenosis of the valve increases LV systolic pressure. It also results in increased LV ejection time (LVET), decreased aortic pressure, and increased LV end-diastolic pressure. The increased afterload, in addition, to an increase in LV volume overload, leads to an increase in LV mass, ultimately leading to LV dysfunction and failure. Myocardial oxygen consumption increases with increased LV systolic pressure, LV mass, and LVET, while myocardial perfusion time decreases with increased LVET. Hence, LV function further deteriorates with increased myocardial oxygen consumption and decreased myocardial oxygen supply.</p>

<!-- PAGE 367 -->

<div>
<img alt="Flowchart illustrating the pathophysiology of Aortic stenosis. Aortic stenosis leads to LV outflow obstruction. LV outflow obstruction causes: ↑ LV systolic pressure, ↑ LVET, ↑ LV diastolic pressure, and ↓ Ao pressure. ↑ LV systolic pressure leads to ↑ LV mass. ↑ LV mass leads to LV dysfunction. ↑ LVET leads to ↑ Myocardial O₂ consumption. ↑ LV diastolic pressure leads to ↓ Diastolic time. ↓ Ao pressure leads to ↓ Myocardial O₂ supply. LV dysfunction leads to ↑ Myocardial O₂ consumption. ↑ Myocardial O₂ consumption leads to LV dysfunction. ↓ Diastolic time leads to ↓ Myocardial O₂ supply. ↓ Myocardial O₂ supply leads to Myocardial ischemia. Myocardial ischemia leads to LV failure. LV failure leads to Myocardial ischemia."/>
<p>(From Boudoulas H, Gravanis MB: Valvular heart disease. In Gravanis MB [ed]: Cardiovascular Disorders: Pathogenesis and Pathophysiology. St. Louis, CV Mosby, 1993, p 64.)</p>
<h2>V. DIAGNOSIS</h2>
<p>Many people with aortic stenosis, or AS, don't experience noticeable symptoms until the amount of restricted blood flow becomes greatly reduced or Aortic surface less than 1cm<sup>2</sup></p>
<p>A. Discovered diagnostic: Systemic examination, heart auscultation, ECG, heart ultrasound, chest x-ray.</p>
<p>B. Clinical presentation:</p>
<p>a. Symptoms:</p>
<ul>
<li>Angina, chest discomfort on exertion</li>
<li>Syncope</li>
<li>Shortness of breath, dyspnea, Symptom</li>
<li>Acute pulmonary oedema.</li>
<li>Palpitations,</li>
</ul>
<p>In severe aortic stenosis with these symptoms indicated the time to surgery, if patients delay surgery will have mortality approximately 100% in five years in coming.</p>
<p>b. Signs:</p>
<ul>
<li>Heart Auscultation:
        <ul>
<li>Systolic murmur: Maximal at left sternum, 2<sup>nd</sup> space of intercostal (ribs), radiation to jaw, apec. The second heart sound may lack a split and can be heard as a single sound during inspiration.</li>
<li>Palpation: Carotid upstroke can be observed. A slow-rising, late-peaking, and a low-amplitude carotid impulse, <i>pulsus parvus et tardus</i>, is an expected finding in severe aortic stenosis and, when present, is specific to aortic stenosis.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>C. Test:</p>
<p>a. ECG: Sinus rhythm or Sinus tachycardia, or Afib,</p>
</div>

<h4><b>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</b></h4>
<ol type="a">
<li>Pulmonary stenosis,</li>
<li>VSD</li>
<li>Mitral regurgitation,</li>
</ol>
<h4><b>VII. MANAGEMENT</b></h4>
<p>A. The goals of aortic valve stenosis treatment are to prevent sudden cardiac death and prevent complications.</p>
<p>If patients symptoms are mild or asymptomatic, they may only need regular health checkups. They may need regular echocardiograms to check the health of the aortic valve. Heart-healthy lifestyle changes also are usually recommended.</p>
<p>B. Prevention recurrent of Acute Rheumatic Fever and Endocarditis (See ARF and Endocarditis)</p>
<p>C. <b>Medical treatment:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Treat symptoms</li>
<li>Reduce the risk of complications,
        <ul>
<li>Volume overload: Loop diuretic with or without MRA. (see HF treatment)</li>
<li>Prevention LV remodelling,</li>
<li>Thrombo-embolic prevention: if sinus rhythm undergone ASP-75-81mg/day, if Afib or Fluter: AVK (INR: 2-3) or NOAC,</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>D. <b>Surgery indications:</b> when patients have symptoms (Angina, syncope, shortness of breath or HF, Acute pulmonary oedema).</p>
<ul>
<li>Mechanical AVR: undergone AVK (INR: 2-3),</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 370 -->

<div>
<p>Biological AVR: Sinus rhythm undergo anti-agregant platelete, if Afib or Flutter undergone anti-coagulation, AVK or NOAC.</p>
<p><b>E. Algorithm:</b></p>
<img alt="Flowchart titled 'Management of patients with severe aortic stenosis'. The flow starts with LVEF &lt; 50%. If Yes (Y), proceed to Symptoms. If No (N), proceed to Physically active. If Physically active is Y, proceed to Exercise test. If Physically active is N, proceed to Indicators of adverse prognosis and low procedural risk. If Exercise test is Y, proceed to Symptoms or sustained fall in BP below baseline. If Exercise test is N, proceed to Heart Team evaluation. If Symptoms is Y, proceed to Intervention likely to be of benefit (after assessment of comorbidity and frailty). If Symptoms is N, proceed to Physically active. If Intervention likely to be of benefit is Y, proceed to Heart Team evaluation. If Intervention likely to be of benefit is N, proceed to Medical therapy. If Symptoms or sustained fall in BP below baseline is Y, proceed to Heart Team evaluation. If Symptoms or sustained fall in BP below baseline is N, proceed to Indicators of adverse prognosis and low procedural risk. If Indicators of adverse prognosis and low procedural risk is Y, proceed to Heart Team evaluation. If Indicators of adverse prognosis and low procedural risk is N, proceed to Educate patient and reassess in 6 months (or as soon as possible if symptoms occur). Heart Team evaluation leads to three outcomes: Patients &lt; 75 years at low-risk for SAVR (STS-PROM/ EuroSCORE II &lt; 4%) OR Unsuitable for TF TAVI and operable; All other patients; Patients ≥ 75 years OR Unsuitable/High risk for SAVR (STS-PROM/ EuroSCORE II &gt; 8%) AND Suitable for TF TAVI. These outcomes lead to final recommendations: Educate patient and reassess in 6 months (or as soon as possible if symptoms occur); SAVR; SAVR or TAVI; TAVI."/>
<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ul>
<li><b>Pregnancy:</b>
<ul>
<li>Mild to moderated AS closely followed, no special medical management.</li>
<li>Severe symptoms, angina, syncope, HF symptoms, acute pulmonary oedema: Closely followed up, HF treatments, cesarean or obortion if need,</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Associated with others VHD:</b> need surgery same time.</li>
<li><b>Coronary artery diseases:</b> need PCI, or CABG with AVR.</li>
<li><b>Stroke:</b> Stroke treatment and HF management.</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Ventricular arrhythmia and sudden cardiac death,</li>
<li>Heart failures: First left HF and then right HF,</li>
</ul>
</div>

<h1>MANAGEMENT OF AORTIC ANEURYSM</h1><p>Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p><b>Aortic dilatation</b>, in clinical practice, aortic root dilatation can be suspected in male adults when aortic diameter is &gt;40 mm and in females at &gt;36 mm or with an indexed diameter/BSA (aortic size index [ASI]) &gt;22 mm/m<sup>2</sup>.</p><p><b>Arterial aneurysm</b> is defined as a diameter &gt;1.5 times (&gt;50%) larger than the predicted one.</p><p><b>Aneurysm</b> is a pathologic dilation of a blood vessel, affecting all three layers of the vessel wall. An aneurysm is a permanent, localized arterial dilation to more than 50% of the normal diameter. True aneurysms involve all three layers, while <b>pseudoaneurysms</b> disrupt intimal and medial layers.</p><p>Aneurysms can be classified by appearance, fusiform or saccular aneurysm.</p><ul><li><input type="checkbox"/> <b>Fusiform:</b> Circumferential widening of the artery</li><li><input type="checkbox"/> <b>Saccular:</b> Localized, typically asymmetric, outpouchings of the artery wall.</li></ul><p><b>Ectasia</b> is an arterial dilatation &lt;150% of normal arterial diameter.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><h3>A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA)</h3><p>Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA) have an estimated incidence of at least 5 to 10 per 100,000 person-years. Aortic root or ascending aortic aneurysms are most common (approximately 60%), followed by aneurysms of the descending aorta (approximately 35%) and aortic arch (&lt;10%).</p><h3>B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA)</h3><p>AAAs occur in 3% to 9% of men older than 50 years and are the most common form of aortic aneurysms. Most AAAs (&gt;80%) arise in the infrarenal aorta.</p><ul><li><input type="checkbox"/> 90% of all abdominal aortic aneurysms &gt;4.0 cm is related to atherosclerotic disease.</li><li><input type="checkbox"/> Risk of rupture increases with size: the 5-years risk of aneurysms &lt; 5cm is 1-2%; whereas it is 20-40% for aneurysms &gt; 5 cm in diameter.</li></ul><h2>III. PATHOGENESIS AND ETIOLOGY</h2><p>Aortic aneurysms result from conditions that cause degradation or abnormal production of the structural components of the aortic wall: elastin and collagen.</p><p>The causes of aortic aneurysms may be broadly categorized as degenerative disorders, genetic or developmental diseases, vasculitis, infections, and trauma.</p><h3>A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA)</h3><p>*Aortic root or ascending aorta:</p><ul><li><input type="checkbox"/> <b>Syndromic:</b> Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Turner syndrome.</li><li><input type="checkbox"/> <b>Non-Syndromic:</b> Bicuspid aortic valve, Sporadic TAA, Familial TAA.</li></ul><p>*Descending aorta:</p>

<!-- PAGE 373 -->

<div>
<ul>
<li>Atherosclerosis</li>
<li>Aortitis (non-infectious): vasculitis disorders (eg, giant cell arteritis, Takayasu arteritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis).</li>
<li>Aortitis (infectious): Syphilis, Infected (mycotic) TAA cause by systemic or local infections (eg, sepsis, pneumonia), lymphangitic spread (eg, tuberculosis).</li>
</ul>
<p><b>B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA)</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Atherosclerosis (majority cause): risk factor: Smoking, age, HTN, Hyperlipidemia, Male sex; Family history of AAA, other cardiovascular disease</li>
<li>Inflammatory aneurysm</li>
<li>Infectious aneurysm</li>
<li>Inherited connective tissue disorders (eg, Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome).</li>
</ul>
<p><b>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</b></p>
<p>A wide variety of pathological factors are associated with aortic aneurysms. These include degenerative diseases, inherited disorders, infections, inflammatory conditions (i.e., vasculitis), and trauma.</p>
<p><b>V. DIAGNOSIS</b></p>
<p><b>1. Clinic</b></p>
<p><b>A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA):</b></p>
<p>Most TAAs are asymptomatic and are discovered incidentally. Less frequently revealed by clinical symptoms:</p>
<ul>
<li>Pain - tearing, radiating to back</li>
<li>Heart failure - due to AR</li>
<li>Thromboembolic (stroke, painful/parenthesis of limbs)</li>
<li>Hoarseness of voice (compression of recurrent laryngeal nerve), dysphagia, plethora and edema from superior vena cava compression</li>
<li>Aorto-esophageal fistula and hemoptysis can also be seen.</li>
<li>Can mimic other acute disorders (AMI, renal colic, pancreatitis)</li>
</ul>
<p><b>B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA):</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Asymptomatic</li>
<li>Incidental finding on abdominal imaging examination: as a palpable, pulsatile, expansile, and nontender mass, frank ecchymosis.</li>
<li>Acute abdominal pain and hypotension occur with rupture of the aneurysm, which requires an emergency operation or endovascular repair.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>2. Investigation</b></p>
<p><b>A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA):</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Chest x-ray: widening of the mediastinal shadow and displacement or compression of the trachea or left main stem bronchus</li>
<li>Echocardiogram or transesophageal echocardiography, can be used to assess the proximal ascending aorta and descending thoracic aorta</li>
<li>Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI are sensitive and specific tests for assessment of aneurysms of the thoracic aorta and involvement of branch.</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 374 -->

<div><p><b>B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm (AAA):</b></p><ul><li>☐ Abdomen x-ray: demonstrate the calcified outline of the aneurysm; 25% not calcified.</li><li>☐ Ultrasonography: screening and surveillance.</li><li>☐ CT or MRI: gold standard's in the pre-operative and post-operative evaluation of AAA.</li><li>☐ Since the presence of mural thrombi may reduce the luminal size, aortography may underestimate the diameter of an aneurysm.</li></ul><p><b>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</b></p><ul><li>☐ Chest pain<ul><li>o Acute myocardial infarction</li><li>o Pulmonary embolism</li><li>o Spontaneous pneumothorax</li><li>o Esophageal rupture</li></ul></li><li>☐ Abdominal pain<ul><li>o Renal/biliary colic</li><li>o Bowel obstruction/perforation</li><li>o Non-dissection-related mesenteric ischemia</li></ul></li><li>☐ Back pain<ul><li>o Renal colic</li><li>o Musculoskeletal pain</li><li>o Intervertebral disc herniation</li></ul></li><li>☐ Focal neurologic deficit<ul><li>o Primary ischemic cerebrovascular accident</li><li>o Cauda equina syndrome</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>VII. MANAGEMENT</b></p><ol><li><b>Objective</b><br/>The goal is to slow the growth of the aneurysm and prevent the rupture or dissection.</li><li><b>Critical signs</b><br/>*Risk of dissection:<ul><li>☐ Diameter &gt; 60mm of ascending aorta</li><li>☐ Diameter &gt; 70mm of descending aorta.</li></ul></li></ol><p><b>A. Thoracic Aortic Aneurysms (TAA):</b></p><p><b>a. Medical therapy:</b></p><ul><li>o Control blood pressure: (target BP&lt;130/80 mmHg for non-diabetic patient and BP &lt; 140/90mmHg for diabetic; target HR: 60bpm.)<ul><li>▪ Beta blocker (Atenolol; Bisoprolol, Metoprolol...)</li><li>▪ ACEi or ARB</li></ul></li><li>o Statin for dyslipidemia target LDL cholesterol &lt;70 mg/dL.</li><li>o Screening 6 months after initial scan then every 12 months unless symptomatic or increased rate of expansion or if size is <b>4.5cm - 5.5cm</b>.</li><li>o Smoking Cessation</li></ul><p><b>b. Percutaneous or surgical intervention:</b></p><p>Indication for surgery:</p><ul><li>o Instable Hemodynamic</li><li>o Symptomatic</li></ul></div>

<!-- PAGE 375 -->

<ul><li>Diameter ≥ 55mm or rate of growth ≥ 1.0cm per year.</li><li>Causing bronchial compression, aortobronchial or aortoesophageal fistulas</li><li>Traumatic, Mycotic</li></ul><p>*Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair (TEVAR) or Open surgery repair.</p><h3>B. Abdominal Aortic Aneurysms (AAA):</h3><ul><li>☐ AAA diameter of <b>25-29 mm</b>, Ultrasound imaging should be considered 4 years later.</li><li>☐ Patient with small diameter (<b>30-55mm</b>), The interval for imaging should be considered:<ul><li>Every <b>3 years</b> for AAA of <b>30-39mm</b>.</li><li>Every <b>2 years</b> for AAA of <b>40-44mm</b> diameter.</li><li>Every year for AAA of &gt; <b>45mm</b> diameter.</li></ul></li></ul><h4>a. Medical Therapy:</h4><ul><li>☐ Control blood pressure: (target BP&lt; 130/80 mmHg for non-diabetic patient and BP &lt; 140/90mmHg for diabetic or CKD; target HR: 60bpm.). Beta blocker is 1st line in HTA drug with AAA. ACEi, ARB and other Antihypertension is drug of choice.</li><li>☐ Statins: reduce the risk of cardiovascular events related to atherosclerosis<ul><li>cardiovascular disease and rupture.</li></ul></li><li>☐ Antiplatelet to reduce intraluminal mural thrombus is controversial but usually use in<ul><li>others indication of CVD.</li></ul></li><li>☐ Smoking Cessation</li></ul><h4>b. Surgical Therapy Indication:</h4><ul><li>☐ Asymptomatic AAA:<ul><li>Diameter &gt;55mm.</li><li>Aneurysm growth &gt;10mm per year.</li></ul></li><li>☐ Symptomatic AAA<ul><li>In case of ruptured AAA, emergency repair is indicated.</li><li>In case of symptomatic but non ruptured AAA, urgent repair is indicated.</li></ul></li></ul><h4>AAA repair methods:</h4><ul><li>☐ Open aortic aneurysm repair</li><li>☐ Endovascular aortic aneurysm repair (EAVR)</li></ul><h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3><p>Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) is the most common congenital cardiac abnormality. A thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is present ≈ 50% of BAV patients, who also have an 8-fold higher risk of aortic dissection than the general population.</p><h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3><ul><li>☐ Thoracic abdominal aneurysms (TAA) enlarge an average of 3 to 5 mm/year.</li><li>☐ Risk factors for rapid enlargement include larger size of aneurysm, location in the descending aorta, and presence of mural thrombi.</li><li>☐ The risk of rupture appears to rise abruptly as TAAs reach 6 cm in diameter.</li><li>☐ Survival rate of patients with untreated large TAAs is 54% at 5 years.</li><li>☐ TAA rupture has a mortality of 97%.</li><li>☐ Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAAs) typically enlarge at a rate of 10%/year, but some</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 376 -->

<div>
<p>enlarge exponentially; about 20% remain the same size indefinitely.</p>
<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Rupture or Dissection</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Thrombus embolism.</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Lower Limb ischemia.</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Infected (mycotic) aneurysms</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Aorto-enteric fistulas, Aorto-caval fistulas</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<ul>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Stringent control of hypertension</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Lipid profile optimization</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Smoking cessation</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Other atherosclerosis risk reduction measures.</li>
<li><input type="checkbox"/> Avoid isometric exercises</li>
</ul>

<h1>MITRAL REGURGITATION (MR)</h1><p>Asst. Prof. CHHUN Lay Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof CHAN Sokha, Prof. SOK Chour</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>Is the heart valve condition in which the flaps of the mitral valve do not close properly, causing a backward flow of blood back to the left atrium.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>MR is the most common valvular abnormality worldwide, affecting over 2 to 3% of the total population and has a prevalence that increases with age.</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><h3>A. Primary MR:</h3><ol type="a"><li><b>Infectious/Rheumatic:</b><ul><li>Rheumatism valvular heart disease is most common cause of VHD, more than 95% of total VHD in the developing country,</li><li>Endocarditis</li></ul></li><li><b>Degenerative:</b><ul><li>Mitral valve prolapses,</li><li>Myxomatous degenerative,</li><li>Maorfanc syndrome</li></ul></li><li><b>Congenital:</b><ul><li>Congenital malformations of the mitral valve,</li></ul></li></ol><h3>B. Secondary MR:</h3><ol type="a"><li><b>Papillary Muscle Rupture:</b><ul><li>Papillary muscle rupture is a very rare condition seen in 1% to 2% of patients after myocardial infarction (MI)</li><li>or infective endocarditis. It leads to severe mitral regurgitation due to dysfunction of the papillary muscles,</li></ul></li><li><b>Ischemic MR (IMR):</b><ul><li>IMR results from prior MI associated with normal mitral valve leaflets and chordae. Ischemia of the segments underlying the papillary muscles results in remodeling. This phenomenon causes papillary muscle displacement, which results in a more apical position of the leaflets known as a “seagull sign”.</li></ul></li><li><b>Congestive heart failure (CHF) Associated:</b><ul><li>Cause by annulus dilation</li><li>Remodeling of left LV</li></ul></li><li><b>Chronic Atrial Fibrillation,</b></li><li><b>Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy</b></li><li>Other rare causes of MR such as prolonged use of certain medications can cause MR,</li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 378 -->

<h4>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h4>
<h5>A. <i>Pathophysiology mechanism:</i></h5>
<ul>
<li>The definition of mitral regurgitation is a retrograde flow from the left ventricle into the left atrium.</li>
<li>Mitral regurgitation leads to left ventricular volume overload due to increased stroke volume, caused by an increase in blood volume within the left atrium and hence an increased preload delivered to the left ventricle during diastole.</li>
<li>In chronic progressive MR, ventricular remodeling occurs, allowing maintenance of cardiac output, and an initial increase in ejection fraction (EF) is usually observed.</li>
<li>However, depending on the regurgitant fraction, the effective EF can be considerably lower. Over time, there is a positive feedback loop by which volume overload from MR causes ventricular dilatation, widening of the mitral annulus, and diminished coaptation of leaflets, leading to further worsening of MR.</li>
<li>Eventually, volume overload becomes so severe that excitation-contraction coupling becomes impaired and wall stress-related afterload on the left ventricle leading to dilatation and decreased contractility, resulting in a reduction of EF.</li>
</ul>
<h5>B. <i>Anatomy pathology: Any disease affection these anatomies can cause MR,</i></h5>
<ul>
<li><b>Mitral leaflets (anterior and posterior)</b></li>
<li>Mitral valve annulus,</li>
<li>Chordae teninease</li>
<li>Papillary muscle</li>
<li>LV remodeling,</li>
</ul>
<div>
<img alt="Diagram showing the anatomy of the mitral valve, including the anterior and posterior leaflets, chordae tendineae, papillary muscles, and annulus."/>
<img alt="Diagram showing the mitral valve in relation to the aortic valve, coronary cusps, and the Aortic Mitral Curtain, illustrating the commissures and leaflet segments (A1, A2, A3, P1, P2, P3)."/>
</div>
<h5>C. <i>Carpentier classification:</i></h5>
<ul>
<li>Type I: Normal leaflet motion
        <ul>
<li>+ annular dilation, leaflet perforation</li>
<li>+ regurgitation jet directed centrally</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Type II: Excessive leaflet motion
        <ul>
<li>+ papillary muscle rupture, chordal rupture, redundant chordae,</li>
<li>+ eccentric jet, directed away from involved leaflet.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Type III: restricted leaflet motion,
        <ul>
<li>+ IIIa: leaflet motion restricted in both systole and diastole,
                <ul>
<li>rheumatic heart disease,</li>
<li>jet may be centrally or eccentrically directed,</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>+ IIIb: leaflet motion restricted in diastole
                <ul>
<li>papillary muscle dysfunction, LV dilation,</li>
<li>jet may be centrally or eccentrically directed.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 379 -->

<div>
<h2>Carpentier's Classification</h2>
<img alt="Diagram illustrating Carpentier's Classification of Mitral Regurgitation (MR) into four types: Type I (Normal leaflet motion), Type II (Excessive leaflet motion), Type IIIa (Restricted opening during systole &amp; diastole), and Type IIIb (Restricted closure during systole). Each type is shown with a corresponding cross-sectional view of the mitral valve."/>

<h3>V. DIAGNOSIS</h3>
<p><b>A. Clinical presentation:</b> normally patients asymptomatic for long decade for mild or moderated chronic MR (inferior than grad III)</p>
<p><b>B. Symptoms:</b></p>
<ol>
<li>Acute severe MR:
        <ul>
<li>Palpitation, chest discomfort,</li>
<li>Dyspnea NYHA III, IV,</li>
<li>Orthopnea, Acute pulmonary embolism,</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Chronic Rheumatic severe MR:</b>
<ul>
<li>Long term compensated</li>
<li>For severe chronic Rheumatic MR superior than grade III,
                <ul>
<li>+ Fatigue,</li>
<li>+ Shortness of breaths (dyspnea) on exertion, grade by NYHA</li>
<li>+ Orthopnea, Acute pulmonary embolism.</li>
<li>+ Palpitations,</li>
<li>+ Chest discomforts,</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<p><b>C. Signes:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>+ Heart Auscultation: Holosystolic murmur, maximum apex, radiated to axillary,</li>
<li>+ Galop of S3 or Galops,</li>
<li>+ Tachycardia: regular (sinus rhythm) or irregular (Atrial Fibrillation)</li>
<li>+ Enlarge of chock point to the left apex due to LV dilations,</li>
<li>+ Lung auscultation: Crackle if APO or acute bronchitis.</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 380 -->

<div>
<p><b>D. Test:</b></p>
<ol>
<li><b>ECG:</b> Sinus rhythm or Sinus tachycardia, or Afib,</li>
</ol>
<img alt="Two ECG strips are shown side-by-side. The left strip (Trevik, Suk chan) shows a normal sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 75 bpm. The right strip (Chitun, Chan mura) shows atrial fibrillation (AFib) with a heart rate of 62 bpm."/>
<ol>
<li><b>Echocardiographie:</b> (Key exam to diagnose MR)
<ul>
<li>Quantification of severity of MR by PISA</li>
<li>Certified etiologic of MR</li>
<li>Evaluation of LV function and LV dilation,</li>
<li>Estimate PAP,</li>
<li>Selected patient for indications interventional surgery and opened heart surgery.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<img alt="Four echocardiography images are displayed. Top left: A color Doppler image showing flow across the mitral valve. Top right: A color Doppler image showing turbulent flow in the left atrium. Bottom left: A schematic diagram illustrating the Proximal Isovelocity Surface Area (PISA) method for quantifying mitral regurgitation. Bottom right: A continuous wave Doppler trace showing the velocity profile of the mitral regurgitant jet."/>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 381 -->

<div>
<p><b>3. Chest X-ray:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>A chest X-ray is a picture of the heart and lungs. It can show whether the heart is enlarged, which can be a sign of certain types of heart valve disease.</li>
</ul>
<img alt="Two chest X-ray images showing the heart and lungs."/>
<p>4. Blood test: CBC, Diabetes screening (Fasting Glucose, HbA1C), Kidney function (Iono, urea, creat), Uric acide, TC, HDL, LD, TG, liver functions (Transaminases, GGT, Bilirubines, PAL, Albumine), TSH, T4, Cortisol, Calcium, Magnesium,</p>
<h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<ul>
<li>Aortic stenosis (AS)</li>
<li>Tricuspid Regurgitation (TR)</li>
<li>Obstructive Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (OHCM)</li>
<li>Congestive heart failure</li>
</ul>
<h4>VII. MANAGEMENT: MR IS LONG TERM TOLERANCE</h4>
<ul>
<li><i>Mild to Moderate:</i> Follow up and prevention of endocarditis and RAA.</li>
<li><i>Sever chronic MR symptomatic:</i>
<ul>
<li><i>Medical treatment:</i>
<ul>
<li><i>Prevention of endocarditis and RAA.</i>
<ul>
<li><i>Sinus rhythm:</i>
<ul>
<li>+ Volume overload: Loupe diuretic (Furosemide) +/- MRA (Spironolactone or Eplenone)</li>
<li>+ LV remodeling and LV dysfunction or LV dilated: HF management,</li>
<li>+ Thrombo-embolic prevention: Antiplatelet: ASP-81/day</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><i>Afib or Flutter: Antithrombotic:</i>
<ul>
<li>+ Heparin standart or henoxaparin, Antivitamin-K: Warfarin, Sintrom, or NOAC. etc.</li>
<li>+ Heart rate controle: Digoxine, Betablocker etc.</li>
<li>+ Volume overload: Loupe diuretic (Furosemide) +/- MRA (Spironolactone or Eplenone),</li>
<li>+ LV remodeling, LV dysfunction, LV dilated: HV management.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><i>Surgery:</i>
<ul>
<li>The first choice is conservative surgery: mitral valves repair if feasible, Mitral Valve Annuloplasthies:</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 382 -->

<div>
<p>- <b>MVR</b> (Biologic or Mechanical) (see Algorithm),</p>
<p>+ <b>Biologic MVR:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Sinus rhythm: Antiplatelet, ASP-81/day</li>
<li>AFib or Flutter: Antivitamin-K: Warfarin, Sintrom, etc</li>
<li>Optimal management of HF,</li>
</ul>
<p>+ <b>Mechanical MVR:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Antivitamin-K: Warfarin, Sintrom, etc.</li>
<li>Optimal management of HF,</li>
</ul>
<p>+ <b>Interventional repair</b> (Mitral valve clip) if contra-indication for opened heart surgery.</p>
<p><b>Algorithm:</b></p>
<img alt="Flowchart titled 'Management of patients with severe chronic primary mitral regurgitation'. The process starts with Symptoms. If Symptoms are present (Y), proceed to Operative risk judged by the Heart Team. If Symptoms are absent (N), check LVEF &lt;= 60% or LVESD &gt;= 40 mm. If LVEF &lt;= 60% or LVESD &gt;= 40 mm is true (Y), proceed to Operative risk judged by the Heart Team. If LVEF &lt;= 60% or LVESD &gt;= 40 mm is false (N), check New onset of AF or SPAP &gt; 50 mmHg. If New onset of AF or SPAP &gt; 50 mmHg is true (Y), proceed to Operative risk judged by the Heart Team. If New onset of AF or SPAP &gt; 50 mmHg is false (N), check High likelihood of durable repair, low surgical risk, and LA dilatation. If High likelihood of durable repair, low surgical risk, and LA dilatation is true (Y), proceed to Surgical mitral valve repair. If High likelihood of durable repair, low surgical risk, and LA dilatation is false (N), proceed to Follow-up. From Operative risk judged by the Heart Team, if Inoperable or at high surgical risk (Y), proceed to TEER if anatomically suitable/extended HF treatment. If Inoperable or at high surgical risk (N), proceed to Surgery (repair whenever possible). If High risk of futility (Y), proceed to Palliative care."/>
<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ul>
<li>Pregnancy (see VHD with pregnancy)</li>
<li>Associated with others valvular heart diseases, may have concomitant surgery.</li>
<li>Coronary Heart Disease may need PCI or CABG,</li>
<li>Stroke (see stroke management with VHD)</li>
<li>MI with mechanical complications</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>MR long term tolerance</li>
<li>Severe MR if no medical management evolute to be HF, supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmia, bad prognosis,</li>
<li>Severe MR:
        <ul>
<li>Even though optimal medial management evolute to be HF and other complication</li>
<li>Surgery on time good prognostic (see algorithm).</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 383 -->

<div><p><b>X.</b> <b>COMPLICATION</b></p><ul><li>HF, Acute Pulmonary Oedema (APO),</li><li>Supraventricular arrhythmia: Afib, Flutter,</li><li>Ventricular arrhythmias: Ventricular tachycardia (VT), Ventricular Fibrillation (VF),</li></ul><p><b>XI.</b> <b>PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</b></p><ul><li>Prevention of endocarditis, RAA by good management pharyngitis and other infectious diseases,</li><li>Closely follow up, optimal management of HF, surgery indication on time.</li></ul><p><b>XII.</b> <b>REFERENCES</b></p><ol><li>ESC 2021 guideline on the management of valvular heart disease,</li><li>Baumgartner H, Falk V, Bax JJ, De Bonis M, Hamm C, Holm PJ, et al. <h1>MITRAL STENOSIS (MS)</h1>
<p>Asst. Prof. CHHUN Lay Dr. LIM Eakstrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Asst. Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst. Prof CHAN Sokha, Prof. SOK Chour</p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Mitral stenosis (MS) is a form of valvular heart disease, characterized by narrowing of mitral valve orifice in diastole. Today, the most common cause of MS is rheumatic fever, but the stenosis usually appears clinically relevant only after several decades.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>The prevalence of rheumatic disease in developed countries is declining, with an estimated incidence of 1 in 100000. The prevalence is higher in developing nations than in US. In Cambodia, the prevalence is more than 35 case per 100000.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li>Rheumatic fever more than 95%,</li>
<li>Calcification of mitral valve leaflets,</li>
<li>Congenital heart disease,</li>
<li>Mitral annular calcification,</li>
<li>Endomyocardial fibroelastosis,</li>
<li>Malignant carcinoid syndrome,</li>
<li>Myxom of mitral valves</li>
<li>Systemic lupus erythematosus, Whipple disease, Fabry disease, and rheumatoid arthritis.</li>
</ul>
<h2>IV. PHYSIOPATHOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li>The normal mitral valve orifice area is 4 to 6cm<sup>2</sup>. If mitral valve areas less then 2cm<sup>2</sup> cause and impediment to the blood flow from the LA int LV. This creates a presser gradient across the MV. As the gradient across the MV increases, the LV requires the atrial kick to fill with blood.</li>
<li>MS causes an increase int LA pressure. The normal LV diastolic pressure is 5 mmHg. A pressure gradient across the MV of 20 mmHg due to severe MS will cause a LA pressure of about 25 mmHg. This LA pressure is transmitted to the pulmonary vasculature resulting in pulmonary hypertension.</li>
<li>A LA pressure remains elevated, the LA will increase in size. As the LA increases in size, there is a greater chance of developing Afib. If Afib develops, the atrial kick is lost.</li>
<li>Thus, the LV filling depends on the atrial kick in severe MS. With the loss of the atrial kick, there is a decrease in cardiac output and sudden development of CHF.</li>
<li>MS progresses slowly from initial signs of mitral stenosis to NYHA functional class II symptoms to Afib to NYHA functional class III or IV symptoms.</li>
</ul>

Left Atrial Enlargement leads to Atrial Arrhythmias. ↑ Pulmonary Venous Pressure leads to Pulmonary Edema. Pulmonary Edema leads to Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension. </div>
