<h3>C. Anatomy pathology:</h3>
<h4>Mitral Valve Anatomy According to the Wilkins Score</h4>
<p><b>Grade 1</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Mobility: Highly mobile valve with only leaflet tips restricted</li>
<li>Thickening: Leaflet near normal in thickness (4 mm to 5 mm)</li>
<li>Calcification: A single area of increased echo brightness</li>
<li>Subvalvular Thickening: Minimal thickening just below the mitral leaflets</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Grade 2</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Mobility: Leaflet mid to base portions have normal mobility</li>
<li>Thickening: Mid leaflets normal, considerable thickening of margins (5 to 8 mm)</li>
<li>Calcification: Scattered areas of brightness confirmed to leaflet margins</li>
<li>Subvalvular Thickening: Thickening of chordal structures extending to one of the chordal lengths</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Grade 3</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Mobility: Valve continues to move forward in diastole, mainly from the base</li>
<li>Thickening: Thickening extending through the entire leaflet (5 mm to 8 mm)</li>
<li>Calcification: Brightness extending into the mid portions of the leaflets</li>
<li>Subvalvular Thickening: Thickening extended to the distal third of the chords</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Grade 4</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Mobility: No or minimal forward movement of the leaflets in diastole</li>
<li>Thickening: Considerable thickening of all leaflet tissue (more than 8 mm to 10 mm)</li>
<li>Calcification: Extensive brightness throughout much of the leaflet tissue</li>
<li>Subvalvular Thickening: Extensive thickening and shortening of all chordal structures extending down to the papillary muscles.</li>
</ul>

<h3>V. DIAGNOSIS</h3>
<p><b>A. Clinical presentation:</b></p>
<p>a. Symptoms: MS is 20 to 40 years after an episode of rheumatic fever</p>
<ul>
<li>The most common symptoms are orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea,</li>
<li>Palpitations, chest pain, hemoptysis, thromboembolism when the LA is increased</li>
<li>Ascites, edema and hepatomegaly if right side HF develops.</li>
<li>There is also an increase in symptoms of fatigue and weakness with exercise and pregnancy.</li>
</ul>
<p>b. Signs:</p>
<ul>
<li>Heart Auscultation:
        <ul>
<li>Normal sinus rhythm: diastolic murmur, Eclat zB1 and B2</li>
<li>In irregular heart beat and tachycardia: difficult.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Palpitation, cat shacking,</li>
<li>Lung auscultation: crackle, sibilente,</li>
<li>Right heart failure signs,</li>
</ul>
<p><b>B. Test:</b></p>
<p>a. <b>ECG:</b> Sinus rhythm or Sinus tachycardia, or Afib,</p>

<img alt="ECG strip showing a regular rhythm, likely sinus tachycardia."/>
</div>
<p>b. <b>Heart ultrasound:</b> key diagnosis of MS</p>
<ul>
<li>Quatification of severity of MS,</li>
<li>Certified etiology, of MS</li>
<li>Estimated of PAP,</li>
<li>Selection patient for surgery indications</li>
</ul>

<h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<ul>
<li>Aortic stenosis (AS)</li>
<li>Tricuspid Regurgitation (TR)</li>
<li>Obstructive Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (OHCM)</li>
<li>Management: MR is long term tolerance</li>
<li>Mild to Moderate: Follow up and prevention of RAA,</li>
<li>Sever MR symptomatic (send to the reference heart center).</li>
</ul>
<h4>VII. MANGEMENT</h4>
<ol>
<li>Prevention recurrent of Acute Rheumatic Fever and Endocarditis (See ARF and Endocarditis)</li>
<li>Mild and moderated MS, MSA ≥1.5cm2: Medical treatment and preventrion
<ul>
<li>Prevention recurrent of Acute Rheumatic Fever and Endocarditis,</li>
<li>Sinus rhythm: Rhythm and rate control by betablocker, systemic thrombo-embolic prevention by anti-agregent plaquettar, ex. Aspirin-81 mg or Clopidogrel-75/day,</li>
<li>Afib: Rate control with Anticoagulant, AVK ex. Warfarin or Sintrom,</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Sever MS, MSA &lt;1.5cm2
<ul>
<li>Asymptomatic patient: medical treatment, prevention of thrombo-embolic and endocarditis.</li>
<li>Symptoms or any complications related with MS:
<ul>
<li>Surgery indications: (see algorhythm)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Percutaneous balloon valvular Plasty if favorable (See Wilking and Cormier Classification and surgical selection)</li>
<li>Opened heart commissurotomy if favorable (See Wilking and Cormier Classification and surgical selection)</li>
<li>Mitral valve replacement:
<ul>
<li>Mechanical valve replacement: Under life anticoagulations, AVK</li>
<li>Biologic valve replacement: Aspirin if SR, anticoagulation AVK if Afib.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<p>Medical treatment:</p>
<ul>
<li>Volume over load: Lope diuretic + MRA</li>
<li>Sinus tachycardia:
<ul>
<li>Betablocker: propranolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, metoprolol.</li>
<li>Thrombo-embolic prevention: Antiplatelet: ASP-81 or CLOPIDOGREL/day.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Afib or Flutter: Antithrombotic: Heparin standart or henoxaparin, Antivitamin-K: Varfarin, Sintrom. Heart rate controle: Digoxine, Betablocker (propranolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, meteprolol)</li>
</ul>
</div>

<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ul>
<li>Pregnancy:
        <ul>
<li>Mild to moderate MS, MSA ≥ 1.5cm<sup>2</sup>: can keep pregnancy, have child bird, systemic embolic prevention,</li>
<li>Severe MS, MSA &lt; 1.5cm<sup>2</sup>, Grdmean: 15mmHg, PAPs &gt; 50mmHg with symptoms relate to MS: Should have pregnancy Abortions,</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Stroke: It is a seriously conditions and most frequently ischemic stroke,
        <ul>
<li>Mild to moderate MS, MSA ≥ 1.5cm<sup>2</sup>: undergone ASP-81 associate Clopidogrel-75/day.</li>
<li>Severe MS, MSA &lt; 1.5cm<sup>2</sup>, with Sinus rhythm or Afib: undergone AVK (Warfarin or Coumadin).</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. COMPLICATION</h3>
<ul>
<li>Arrhythmia: Atrial flutter, Afib.</li>
<li>Systemic thrombo-embolism: Ischemic stroke, others organism ischemic,</li>
<li>Heart failures: Left heart failure and right heart failure,</li>
<li>Signs of pulmonary effusions, frequency fo bronchitis,</li>
<li>Infectious endocarditis.</li>
</ul>

<h1>MANAGEMENT AND SURVEILLANCE OF PROSTHETIC VALVES</h1>
<p><i>Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Prosthetic heart valves are designed to replicate the function of native valves by maintaining unidirectional blood flow and can be separated into two broad categories, mechanical and bioprosthetic (also called tissue) valves, each with different advantages and disadvantages.</p>
<p>Mechanical heart valves (MHV) are made entirely from non-biological (artificial) materials including metals (titanium, cobalt), pyrolytic carbon, and polymers in order to provide mechanical stability and durability.</p>
<p>Bioprosthetic valves (BPV) are, at least in part, made from animal (e.g., porcine, bovine or equine) (heterograft or xenograft) or human (homograft or allograft) tissue mounted onto a metal or polymer supporting structure with three pillars (also called struts or posts) and have a trileaflet configuration that resembles the geometry of a native aortic valve.</p>
<h2>II. SELECTION OF PROSTHETIC VALVES</h2>
<p>The choice between a mechanical and a bioprosthetic valve is a complex decision based on prosthetic valve characteristics, patient-related factors (e.g., comorbidities) and patient preferences such as wishes and expectations.</p>
<table>
<caption>Table 1. Factors to be considered for the choice of prosthetic heart valve</caption>
<thead>
<tr>
<th>In favor of a bioprosthesis</th>
<th>In favor of a mechanical valve</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>For AVR: age &gt;65 years</td>
<td>For AVR: age &lt;60/50 years</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>For MVR: age &gt;70/65 years</td>
<td>For MVR: age &lt;65 years</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Anticoagulation contraindicated, not desired, or cannot be monitored</td>
<td>Other indication for anticoagulation (e.g., atrial fibrillation)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Desired pregnancy<br/>Limited life expectancy</td>
<td>Small aortic root size (preclusion of future transcatheter valve-in-valve [VIV] implantation for failed aortic bioprosthesis)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Patient preference (avoidance of risk or inconvenience of anticoagulation)</td>
<td>Patient preference (avoidance of risk of reintervention)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h2>III. BASELINE ASSESSMENT AND FOLLOW-UP</h2>
<p>All patients with prosthetic valves require lifelong follow-up to detect early deterioration in prosthetic function or ventricular function, or progressive disease of another heart valve. Clinical assessment should be performed <b>yearly</b> or as soon as possible if new cardiac symptoms occur. TTE should be performed if <b>any new symptoms occur</b> or if complications are suspected. After transcatheter, as well as surgical implantation of a BHV, echocardiography, including measurement of transprosthetic gradients, should be performed within 30 days after valve implantation (i.e. baseline), at 1 year, and annually thereafter.</p>

<!-- PAGE 393 -->

<div>
<p>Many clinicians in the United States use 4–6-week INR follow-up intervals for these patients. However, the 2012 American College of Chest Physicians’ guidelines suggested a 12-week INR follow-up interval may be appropriate.</p>
<h3>IV. ANTITHROMBOTIC THERAPY</h3>
<h4>1. Mechanical heart valves</h4>
<p>The term antithrombotic therapy refers to anticoagulant, antiplatelet therapy or both. All mechanical valves require lifelong oral anticoagulation using a vitamin K antagonist (VKA) (Class I). It is preferable to specify a single international normalised ratio (INR) target median value for each patient and to concede that the acceptable range includes 0.5 INR units either side of this target. There are no data to support the use of non-vitamin K oral anticoagulants (NOACs) in patients with MHVs.</p>

<h4>2. Adjunctive antithrombotic pharmacotherapy in bioprosthetic valves</h4>
<ul>
<li>VKA for 3 months should be considered in all patients with a mitral or tricuspid BHV and ASA or VKA should be considered for 3 months after surgical implantation of an aortic bioprosthesis.</li>
<li>OAC is recommended lifelong for patients with surgical BHVs who have other indications for anticoagulation. The evidence supporting the use of NOACs in preference to VKA has increased.</li>
</ul>
</div>

<h3>V. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ul>
<li>Combination of oral anticoagulant (OAC) with antiplatelet drugs: this combination may be considered in patients with coexistent atherosclerotic (e.g., peripheral artery, coronary artery or cerebrovascular) disease (Class IIb)</li>
<li>Interruption of anticoagulant therapy for planned invasive procedure: bridging therapy during interruption of oral anticoagulation for planned invasive procedures is a complex issue (discussed in “Vitamin K antagonism in surgery” section)</li>
<li>Management of vitamin K antagonist (VKA) overdose and bleeding (Table 3)</li>
</ul>
<table border="1">
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>INR &gt;4.5 with bleeding</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>The VKA should be discontinued</li>
<li>10 mg vitamin K should be administrated by slow i.v, infusion and repeated every 12 h if needed</li>
<li>Until the anticoagulation effect is reversed, administration of prothrombin complex concentration (PCC) and/or fresh frozen plasma (FFP) therapy should be initiated according to body weight and pre-treatment INR.</li>
<li>Monitored by re-check of INR at 30 min and every 4–6 h until normalization.</li>
<li>The optimal time to restart anticoagulation should be discussed in relation to location of the bleeding event and interventions performed to stop bleeding and/or to treat an underlying cause.</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>INR &gt; 10 without bleeding</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>The use of PCC and/or FFP therapy is not recommended</li>
<li>The VKA must be stopped</li>
<li>oral vitamin K (2.5–5 mg) prescribed, while the INR must be monitored on a daily base for 2 weeks</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>INR 4.5 to 10 without bleeding</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>The VKA should be stopped temporarily, and a small dose of oral vitamin K (1–2 mg) can be considered on an individual basis balancing between the risks</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>INR &lt;4.5 and asymptomatic</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Requiring careful down-titration and/or skipping one or more doses.</li>
<li>In all patients with MHVs, VKAs must be resumed once the INR achieves the therapeutic range or is slightly elevated</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<ul>
<li>Mechanic heart valves (MHV) in pregnancy:
        <ul>
<li>The need for anticoagulation increases maternal and foetal mortality and morbidity due to the risk of MHV thrombosis and high risk of bleeding during pregnancy and delivery.</li>
<li>The potentially teratogenic VKAs cross the placenta and have a dose-dependent relationship with adverse outcomes, including foetal wastage and embryopathy.</li>
<li>It is very challenging to manage the anticoagulant during pregnancy for the safety of mother and child as well as avoiding the complications.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 396 -->

<h4>VI. COMPLICATIONS</h4>
<ul>
<li>Structural failure (bioprosthetic valves): resulting in thickening, calcification, tearing, or disruption of the prosthetic valve (PV) with eventual haemodynamic dysfunction, manifesting as stenosis, regurgitation or a combination of both.</li>
<li>Thrombosis and thromboembolism: leading to prosthetic valve dysfunction and embolism.</li>
<li>Pannus formation: leading to prosthetic valve dysfunction</li>
<li>Paraprosthetic regurgitation</li>
<li>Bleeding related to antithrombotic therapy</li>
<li>Intravascular haemolysis</li>
<li>Infectious endocarditis</li>
<li>Heart failure</li>
</ul>
<h4>VII. PATIENT EDUCATION</h4>
<p>Patients should be educated about</p>
<ul>
<li>Prosthetic valve outcomes,</li>
<li>The need for proper care (including optimal dental care, the need for antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures, and when required, appropriate antithrombotic therapy)</li>
<li>Seeking prompt medical attention for any new sign or symptom that might be related to a valve complication such as a significant change in the audible click of a mechanical prosthesis, persistent or recurrent fever, decrease in exercise tolerance, ischemic cerebral events, or palpitations.</li>
<li>The relation of VKA and diet</li>
<li>Follow-up and checking PT and INR regularly with his/her doctor.</li>
<li>Not to start, stop, or change the dose of any medicine or supplement without checking with his/her doctor.</li>
<li>Telling his/her doctor, nurse, and pharmacist about all medicines he/she takes. This includes prescription or over-the-counter medicines, natural products, and vitamins. (As in Cambodia, prescribed-VKA patient should not take other medication without consulting his/her doctor due to medication interaction).</li>
<li>Birth control and if she has an accidental pregnancy, should inform her follow-up doctor and not to stop taking VKA without consultation.</li>
</ul>

<h1>DEEP VENOUS THROMBOSIS</h1>
<p><i>Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is the formation of blood clot (thrombus) in a deep vein, typically in the legs.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>DVT is a significant global health issue, affecting around 1 in 1000 people annually. The incidence increases with age and risk factors include immobility, surgery, trauma, cancer, and genetic clotting disorders. DVT is more common in women due to risk factors like pregnancy and oral contraceptive use.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<p>The etiology of DVT involves a combination of factors that promote blood clotting in the veins. These include <b>immobility</b> (e.g after surgery or long flights), <b>trauma</b> to the vein, <b>hypercoagulability</b> (due to genetic disorders like Factor V Leiden), and <b>vascular injury</b>. Additional risk factors include <b>cancer</b>, use of <b>oral contraceptives</b>, <b>pregnancy</b> and <b>obesity</b>.</p>
<h2>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h2>
<p>The pathophysiology of DVT involves Virchow's triad, which consists of three key mechanisms: <b>venous stasis</b>, <b>endothelial injury</b>, and <b>hypercoagulability</b>. Venous stasis, often caused by prolonged immobility, reduces blood flow, promoting clot formation. Endothelial injury from trauma or surgery triggers clotting at the injury site, while hypercoagulability – whether from genetic disorders, cancer or hormonal changes – increases the blood's tendency to clot. Together, these factors lead to thrombus formation in deep veins, usually in the legs.</p>
<h2>V. DIAGNOSIS</h2>
<ol>
<li>Clinical assessment:
        <ul>
<li>Assess symptoms (leg pain, swelling) and use a clinical prediction tool like the <b>two-level modified Well's Score</b> (Annex 1) to determine the likelihood of DVT</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>D-dimer Test:
        <ul>
<li>For patients with <b>DVT unlikely</b>, a <b>D-dimer</b> blood test is performed. If the D-dimer is negative, DVT is ruled out. If positive, further imaging is required.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Imaging with Venous Ultrasound:
        <ul>
<li>For patients with <b>DVT likely</b> or <b>positive D-dimer</b>, compression venous ultrasound is the first-line imaging test.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Further Imaging:
        <ul>
<li>If the ultrasound results are unclear or DVT involves unusual locations (e.g. pelvic veins), advanced imaging like <b>CT venography</b> or <b>MR venography</b> may be used.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 398 -->

<div>
<p>5. Follow-up:</p>
<ul>
<li>In patients where initial tests are inconclusive but suspicion remains, <b>repeat ultrasound after 5 – 7 days may be performed to confirm or exclude DVT.</b></li>
</ul>
<h4><b>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</b></h4>
<p>Several conditions that present with similar symptoms such as leg pain and swelling:</p>
<ol>
<li>Cellulitis: a bacterial skin infection that cause redness and swelling</li>
<li>Muscle strain or tear: injury to muscle can lead to localized pain and swelling</li>
<li>Baker's cyst: a fluid-filled cyst behind the knee that can rupture, causing pain and swelling</li>
<li>Lymphedema: swelling due to lymphatic obstruction can mimic DVT</li>
<li>Chronic venous insufficiency: persist swelling and skin changes due to poor vein function, often confused with acute DVT</li>
</ol>
<h4><b>VII. MANAGEMENT</b></h4>
<ol>
<li>Initial assessment: risk stratification is crucial. Categorize patients as low, intermediate or high risk based on clinical presentation and underlying conditions</li>
<li>Initial treatment (first 5 – 21 days)
        <ul>
<li>Initiate anticoagulation in most patients unless contraindicated</li>
<li>Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) such as apixaban or rivaroxaban are preferred for most <b>non-cancer patients</b></li>
<li><b>LMWH (Low molecular weight heparin) or unfractionated heparin (UFH)</b> is used for certain patients (e.g. cancer, renal impairment, high bleeding risk).</li>
<li><b>VKA (Vitamin K antagonists): second-line therapy.</b> VKA are often considered when DOACs are contra-indicated or unsuitable, such as
                <ul>
<li>In patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR &lt; 30 ml/min)</li>
<li>In patients on certain medications that interact with DOACs, reducing their efficacy or increase bleeding</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Compression stockings</b> are recommended to reduce symptoms like swelling and prevent post-thrombotic syndrome.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<ol>
<li>Long-term management (first 3 – 6 months)
        <ul>
<li>Continue anticoagulant to prevent clot extension and recurrence. The choice of anticoagulant is based on patient's characteristic
                <ul>
<li>DOACs are first-line for <b>non-cancer patients</b></li>
<li>LMWH is preferred in <b>cancer patients</b></li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Monitor for bleeding risks</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Extended treatment (&gt; 6 months)
        <ul>
<li>For patients at <u>high - risk of recurrence</u> (e.g. those with active cancer, recurrent DVT, or persistent risk factors), anticoagulation may be extended indefinitely, balancing the risk of bleeding</li>
<li>For patients with lower recurrence risk, anticoagulation may be stopped after 3 – 6 months, with follow-up imaging to assess for clot resolution.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 400 -->

<h5>5. Algorithm for deep venous thrombosis assessment and management</h5>
<div>
<p><strong>Lower limb DVT suspicion</strong></p>
<p>Clinical probability assessment (two-level modified Wells score)</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>DVT unlikely</strong>
<ul>
<li>D-Dimers</li>
<ul>
<li>Negative → No DVT → No AC</li>
<li>Positive → Venous US</li>
</ul>
</ul>
</li>
<li><strong>DVT likely</strong>
<ul>
<li>Venous US</li>
<ul>
<li>Proximal DVT
                <ul>
<li>At least 3-months AC (NOACs in non-cancer patients)</li>
<li>Immediate (&lt;24hrs) compression</li>
<li>Assess indication to reperfusion</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>IDDVT
                <ul>
<li>High risk patient → 3-months AC</li>
<li>Low risk patient
                        <ul>
<li>Short term LMWH (full or lower dose)</li>
<li>Or venous US surveillance</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<p>3-months assessment</p>
<ul>
<li>Venous US, risk/benefit, compliance and patient's preference, PTS</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>Stop AC</li>
<li>Continue or not compression</li>
<li>Extend AC</li>
<li>Yearly evaluation</li>
<li>Continue or not compression</li>
</ul>
</div>
<h5>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h5>
<ul>
<li><strong>Pregnancy-Related DVT:</strong> due to physiological changes and compression of pelvic veins. Use Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) for treatment.</li>
<li><strong>Cancer-Related DVT:</strong> due to increased coagulability associated with malignancy, treatment (chemotherapy) and immobility. Management often involves long-term anticoagulation with LMWH or DOACs.</li>
<li><strong>Post-surgical DVT:</strong> Common in orthopedic and abdominal surgeries. Prophylactic measures (e.g. early mobilization, compression stockings) and anticoagulation may be initiated perioperatively.</li>
<li><strong>Upper extremity DVT:</strong> often associated with central venous catheters or repetitive trauma. Management focus on catheter removal and anticoagulation.</li>
<li><strong>May-Thurner Syndrome:</strong> compression of the left common iliac vein by the right common iliac artery leading to DVT. Management includes stenting or surgical intervention alongside anticoagulation.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 401 -->

<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Immediate risk: DVT can lead to serious complications such as pulmonary embolism (PE) especially in acute phase</li>
<li>Long-term outcomes: many patients may experience resolution of symptoms, but some develop post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS), characterized by chronic pain and swelling</li>
<li>Recurrence: the risk of recurrent DVT varies based on individual risk factors (e.g. cancer, history of thrombosis), with rates ranging from 10 – 30% in 10 years</li>
<li>Appropriate anticoagulation and monitoring improve outcomes, reducing the risk of complications and recurrences.</li>
</ul>
<h3>X. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Pulmonary embolism (PE)</li>
<li>Post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS): resulting from damage to veins and valves</li>
<li>Recurrent DVT</li>
<li>Chronic venous insufficiency: long-term damage to veins lead to varicose veins and skin ulcer</li>
<li>Phlegmasia Cerulea Dolens: a rare, severe condition where extensive thrombosis causes blue discoloration of the limb, leading to tissue ischemia and necrosis.</li>
<li>Venous gangrene: a rare but critical complication (death of tissue due to compromised blood flow)</li>
</ul>
<h3>XI. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<ul>
<li>Identify individuals at high risk (e.g. surgery patients, those with cancer, or prolonged immobilization) to tailor prevention strategies</li>
<li>Use compression stocking to promote venous return during hospitalization or surgery</li>
<li>Pharmacological prophylaxis: administer anticoagulant (LMWH or DOACs) for high-risk patients</li>
<li>Early mobilization: encourage early mobilization after surgery or during prolonged hospitalization</li>
<li>Patient education: inform patients about DVT symptoms and the important of prevention measures particularly after surgery or during long travel.</li>
</ul>

</ol>

<h1>PREVENTION OF DEEP VENOUS THROMBOSIS</h1>
<p><i>Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</i></p>
<h2>I. INTRODUCTION</h2>
<p>The prevention of deep venous thrombosis (DVT), a common and potentially serious condition, is a critical component of clinical care.</p>
<p>Effective DVT prevention begins with identifying patients at risk:</p>
<ol>
<li><b>Risk factors:</b>
<ul>
<li>Medical conditions: Cancer, heart failure, stroke, acute infection</li>
<li>Immobilization: Prolong bed rest, paralysis, or travel</li>
<li>Surgery: orthopedic (hip and knee) or major abdominal/pelvic surgeries</li>
<li>Previous DVT or pulmonary embolism (PE)</li>
<li>Thrombophilias: inherited or acquired conditions (e.g. Factor V leiden, antiphospholipid syndrome)</li>
<li>Others: obesity (BMI &gt; 30), pregnancy, hormonal therapy (oral contraceptives, or hormonal replacement)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Assessment tools</b>
<ul>
<li>Padua Prediciton Score (for hospitalized medical patients)</li>
<li>Caprini Risk Score (for surgical patients)</li>
<li>IMPROVE Bleeding Risk Score (risk assessment for bleeding)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<h2>II. RISK ASSESSMENT AND PROPHYLACTIC RECOMMENDATION FOR MEDICAL PATIENTS</h2>
<h3>1. PADUA prediction score (PPS)</h3>

<h2>2, Risk Stratification and Prophylactic Recommendation of Medical Patients</h2>
<table border="1">

<th>Category</th>
<th>Recommendation</th>

<td>Early mobilization or mechanical prophylaxis</td>
</tr>
<tr>

</tbody>
</table>
<h3>III. RISK ASSESSMENT AND PROPHYLACTIC RECOMMENDATION FOR SURGICAL PATIENTS</h3>
<h4>1. CAPRINI Risk Score</h4>

<h4>IV. ISK ASSESSMENT FOR BLEEDING</h4>
<ol>
<li><b>Improve Bleeding Risk Score</b>
<p>The IMPROVE bleeding risk score is a validated tool for assessing the risk of bleeding in hospitalized patients who may require pharmacological prophylaxis for DVT / PE</p>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Risk Factor</th>
<th>Points</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Active gastroduodenal ulcer</td>
<td>4</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Bleeding within 3 months before admission</td>
<td>4</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Platelet count &lt; 50 x 10<sup>9</sup>/L</td>
<td>4</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Age ≥ 85 years</td>
<td>3</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Hepatic failure (INR &gt; 1.5)</td>
<td>2</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Severe renal failure (eGFR &lt; 30 ml/min)</td>
<td>2</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>ICU or critical care unit stay</td>
<td>2</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Central venous catheter</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Rheumatic disease</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Current cancer</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Male sex</td>
<td>1</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</li>
<li><b>Scoring and Risk category</b>
<ul>
<li>Score ≥ 7: High risk of bleeding (pharmacological prophylaxis should be used cautiously or avoided). Mechanical prophylaxis may be alternative.</li>
<li>Score &lt; 7: Low risk of bleeding (pharmacological prophylaxis is safe and recommended)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<h4>V. METHOD OF PROPHYLAXIS</h4>
<ol>
<li><b>Mechanical Prophylaxis:</b>
<p>Mechanical methods promote venous blood flow and are primarily used for patients at high bleeding risk or as an adjunct to pharmacological prophylaxis</p>
<ul>
<li>Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC): inflatable sleeve applied to the legs to promote venous return and useful in surgical and ICU patients with high bleeding risk</li>
<li>Graduated Compression Stocking (GCS): Elastic stockings that apply pressure to the legs, reducing venous stasis.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Pharmacological prophylaxis</b>
<ul>
<li>Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH):
        <ul>
<li>Enoxaparin 40 mg (SC) daily</li>
<li>Enoxaparin 20 mg (SC) daily (for renal impairment with eGFR 15 – 30 ml/min)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Unfractionated Heparin (UFH): 5000 units (SC) every 8 – 12 h, preferred in patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR&lt; 30 ml/min)</li>
<li>Direct Oral Anticoagulant (DOA):
        <ul>
<li>Rivaroxaban: 10 mg orally once daily (avoid if eGFR &lt; 15 ml/min)</li>
<li>Apixaban: 2.5 mg orally twice daily (avoid if eGFR &lt; 15 ml/min)</li>
<li>Dabigatran: 110 mg orally on the first day, then 220 mg once daily (avoid if eGFR &lt; 30 ml/min).</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 406 -->

<h2>VI. TIMING AND INITIATION OF PROPHYLAXIS</h2>
<h3>1. Medical patients</h3>
<ul>
<li>Indication: prophylaxis is indicated for hospitalized medical patients with a Padua Prediction Score ≥ 4</li>
<li>Timing:
        <ul>
<li>Initiate on admission and continue throughout hospitalization</li>
<li>Avoid prophylaxis in patients with active bleeding or high bleeding risk</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Option: LMWH is preferred (Enoxaparin)</li>
</ul>
<h3>2. Surgical patients</h3>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Clinical situation</th>
<th>Prophylactic agents</th>
<th>Timing of initiation</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>General Surgery</td>
<td>LMWH: Enoxaparin 40 mg OD</td>
<td>12 – 24 h post-op</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td rowspan="2">Orthopedics<br/>Hip/Knee replacement<br/>Hip Fracture</td>
<td>LMWH: Enoxaparin 40 mg OD</td>
<td>12 – 24 h post-op</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Rivaroxaban 10 mg OD</td>
<td>6 – 10 h post-op</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h2>VII. DURATION OF PROPHYLAXIS</h2>
<h3>1. Medical patients</h3>
<ul>
<li>Duration: Until the patient is fully ambulatory or discharged from hospital</li>
<li>Extended prophylaxis: not routinely recommended after hospital discharge unless they are at very high risk of venous thromboembolism and low risk of bleeding</li>
</ul>
<h3>2. Surgical patients</h3>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Indication</th>
<th>Duration</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><b>Major General Surgery</b></td>
<td>Until hospital discharge (7 – 10 days)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><b>Orthopedic Surgery</b></td>
<td>Minimum duration: 10 – 14 days<br/>Extended duration: up to 35 days</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Hip/Knee Replacement</td>
<td>post-operatively is recommended</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Hip Fracture repair</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<h1>INFECTIOUS ENDOCARDITIS</h1>
<p><i>Dr. SOK Monghak, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHM AO Pichmanil, Dr. KHUON Rithy, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst.prof. CHAN Sokha, Asst.prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Infectious Endocarditis (IE) refers to infection of the endocardial surface of the heart; it usually refers to infection of one or more heart valves or infection of an intracardiac device.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li>The incidence of infective endocarditis is estimated between 30 and 80 cases per million inhabitants and per year in the general population in industrialized countries.</li>
<li>Incidence increases after the age of 60 and Staphylococcus is now the most frequent responsible microorganism.</li>
<li>Infective endocarditis was native (NVE) in 1764 (56.6%) patients, prosthetic (PVIE) in 939 (30.1%), and device-related (CDRIE) in 308 (9.9%). Infective endocarditis was community-acquired in 2046 (65.66%) patients.</li>
</ul>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY AND RISK FACTORS</h2>
<ul>
<li>Risk factors for native valve infective endocarditis (IE) include cardiac factors or non-cardiac risk factors.</li>
<li>It is most often from bacteria and more rarely a fungus from</li>
</ul>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Bacteria</th>
<th>Source of Infection</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Staphylococcus aureus</td>
<td>Skin</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Oral Streptococcus, HACEK</td>
<td>Oral, dental</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Group D Streptococcus</td>
<td>Gastro-intestinal tract (Coloscopy)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Enterococcus</td>
<td>Gastro-intestinal tract (Coloscopy), Urinary tract</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Cardiac risk factors</th>
<th>Non-cardiac risk factors</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Previous infective endocarditis</li>
<li>Valvular heart disease</li>
<li>Prosthetic heart valve</li>
<li>Central venous or arterial catheter</li>
<li>Transvenous cardiac implantable electronic device</li>
<li>Congenital heart disease</li>
</ul>
</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Central venous catheter</li>
<li>People who inject drugs</li>
<li>Immunosuppression</li>
<li>Recent dental or surgical procedures</li>
<li>Recent hospitalization Haemodialysis</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<!-- PAGE 408 -->

<h4>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4>
<div>
<p>Risk factors (Source of Infection)</p>
<p>Risk of Heart disease</p>
<ul>
<li>Vegetations
        <ul>
<li>Systemic Embolism</li>
<li>Pulmonary Embolism</li>
<li>Other Infection (Splen abscesses, renal abscesses, arthritis, meningitis, etc.)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Valve destruction
        <ul>
<li>Regurgitations (Leak) of Valvular or paraprosthetic</li>
<li>Intracardiac fistulas</li>
<li>Acute heart failure (Pulmonary edema, Cardiogenic shock)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Disinsertion of prosthesis
        <ul>
<li>AV Block</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Abscess
        <ul>
<li>AV Block</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Inflammation
        <ul>
<li>Alteration of general condition</li>
<li>Septic shock</li>
<li>Vasculitis systemic inflammation</li>
<li>Infectious aneurysms (mycotic)</li>
<li>Hemorrhages (Cerebral and others)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<ol>
<li>Clinical Manifestations
        <ul>
<li><b>Symptoms:</b> Fever is the most common symptom of IE
                <ul>
<li>It is often associated with chills, anorexia, and weight loss.</li>
<li>Other common symptoms: Malaise, headache, myalgias, arthralgias, night sweats, abdominal pain, tooth pain and dyspnea.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Signs:</b> A new or changing cardiac
                <ul>
<li>Supportive signs: splenomegaly, petechiae or splinter hemorrhages.</li>
<li><b>Relatively uncommon manifestations highly suggestive of IE:</b>
<ul>
<li>Janeway lesions</li>
<li>Osler nodes</li>
<li>Roth spots</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Investigation for Endocarditis
        <ul>
<li>Blood cultures: At least two sets of blood cultures should be obtained from separate venipuncture sites prior to initiation of antibiotic therapy.</li>
<li>Cardiac imaging:
                <ul>
<li>Trans thoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the first diagnostic test for patients with suspected IE.</li>
<li>Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) has higher sensitivity than TTE and is better for detection of cardiac complications.</li>
<li><b>Cardiac CT:</b> May be helpful for cases in which definitive evidence of IE and its complications cannot be demonstrated with TEE, and/or for planning surgery in patients with extra valvular complications.</li>
<li>Additional evaluation for IE source or complications: ECG, chest radiography, other radiographic imaging tailored to clinical manifestations, and dental evaluation.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Definitions of the 2023 European Society of Cardiology modified diagnostic criteria of infective endocarditis</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 409 -->

<div>
<h3>Major criteria</h3>
<ol>
<li>Blood cultures positive for IE
        <ol type="a">
<li>Typical microorganisms consistent with IE from two separate blood cultures: Oral streptococci, Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis), HACEK group, S. aureus, E. faecalis.</li>
<li>Microorganisms consistent with IE from continuously positive blood cultures:
                <ul>
<li>≥ 2 positive blood cultures of blood samples drawn &gt;12 h apart.</li>
<li>All of 3 or a majority of ≥4 separate cultures of blood (with first and last samples drawn ≥1 h apart).</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Single positive blood culture for C. burnetii or phase I IgG antibody titre &gt;1:800.</li>
</ol>
</li>
<li>Imaging positive for IE:
        <p>Valvular, perivalvular/periprosthetic and foreign material anatomic and metabolic lesions characteristic of IE detected by any of the following imaging techniques:</p>
<ul>
<li>Echocardiography (TTE and TOE)</li>
<li>Cardiac CT</li>
<li>[<sup>18</sup>F]-FDG-PET/CT(A)</li>
<li>WBC SPECT/CT</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<h3>Minor criteria</h3>
<p>Predisposing conditions (i.e. predisposing heart condition at high or intermediate risk of IE or PWIDs)</p>
<p>Fever defined as temperature &gt;38°C</p>
<p>Embolic vascular dissemination (including those asymptomatic detected by imaging only):</p>
<ul>
<li>Major systemic and pulmonary emboli/infarcts and abscesses.</li>
<li>Haematogenous osteoarticular septic complications (i.e. spondylodiscitis).</li>
<li>Mycotic aneurysms</li>
<li>Intracranial ischaemic/haemorrhagic lesions</li>
<li>Conjunctival haemorrhages</li>
<li>Janeway's lesions</li>
</ul>
<p>Immunological phenomena:</p>
<ul>
<li>Glomerulonephritis</li>
<li>Osler nodes and Roth spots</li>
<li>Rheumatoid factor</li>
</ul>
<p>Microbiological evidence:</p>
<ul>
<li>Positive blood culture but does not meet a major criterion as noted above.</li>
<li>Serological evidence of active infection with organism consistent with IE.</li>
</ul>
<h3>IE Classification (at admission and during follow-up)</h3>
<p><b>Definite:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>2 major criteria.</li>
<li>1 major criterion and at least 3 minor criteria.</li>
<li>5 minor criteria.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Possible:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>1 major criterion and 1 or 2 minor criteria.</li>
<li>3–4 minor criteria.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Rejected:</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Does not meet criteria for definite or possible at admission with or without a firm alternative diagnosis.</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 410 -->

<h2>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h2>
<p>The differential diagnosis for endocarditis is broad and should be considered based on two clinical categories: presence of bacteraemia in the absence of valvular vegetation and presence of valvular vegetation(s) in the absence of bacteraemia.</p>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Presence of bacteraemia in the absence of valvular vegetation</th>
<th>Presence of valvular vegetation(s) in the absence of bacteraemia</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Intravascular catheter infection</li>
<li>Cardiac device infection</li>
<li>Prosthetic joint infection</li>
<li>Hematogenous osteomyelitis</li>
<li>Septic thrombophlebitis</li>
<li>Infected arterial aneurysm</li>
</ul>
</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Culture-negative endocarditis or sterile vegetation(s) (marantic endocarditis or Libman-Sachs endocarditis) due to a noninfectious etiology or antiphospholipid syndrome.</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<h3>1. Antimicrobial therapy:</h3>
<ul>
<li>Penicillin-susceptible oral streptococci and <i>Streptococcus gallolyticus</i> group and Oral streptococci and <i>Streptococcus gallolyticus</i> group susceptible, increased exposure or resistant to penicillin</li>
</ul>

<h2>2. Indications and timing of surgery in the presence of heart failure in infective endocarditis:</h2>
<p>Timing of surgical intervention in patients with IE complicated by HF should be decided by the Endocarditis Team, although surgery should not be delayed by Endocarditis Team discussions in patients requiring emergency operations. The presence of HF leads to recommendation for surgery in the majority of patients and is the principal indication for urgent surgery in IE patients.</p>
</div>

<h3>VIII. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Relapse is a repeat episode of IE caused by the same microorganism and represents a failure of treatment and mandates a search for a persistent focus of infection and an evaluation towards surgical therapy.</li>
<li>Reinfection is an infection caused by a different microorganism, usually more than 6 months after the initial episode.</li>
<li>Once antibiotic treatment has been completed, blood cultures should be performed.</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 416 -->

<ul><li>Patients discharged after the first episode of IE should remain under close surveillance for potential long-term complications.</li></ul><h3>IX. COMPLICATIONS</h3><p>Complications of infective endocarditis (IE) include cardiac, metastatic, neurologic, renal, musculoskeletal, and pulmonary complications as well as complications related to systemic infection (including embolization, metastatic infection, and mycotic aneurysm). More than one complication can occur simultaneously.</p><table border="1"><thead><tr><th>Cardiac complications</th><th>Metastatic infection</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><ul><li>Heart failure</li><li>Perivalvular abscess</li><li>Pericarditis (suppurative or nonsuppurative)</li><li>Intracardiac fistula (eg, aorta-atrial or aorta-ventricular)</li></ul></td><td><ul><li>Forms of metastatic infection include Septic embolization, metastatic abscess, and mycotic aneurysm.</li><li>Embolism can occlude or damage virtually any vessel in the systemic or pulmonary arterial circulation:<ul><li>Stroke</li><li>Paralysis (due to embolic infarction of either the brain or spinal cord)</li><li>Blindness (due to embolism or due to endophthalmitis as a result of bacteremic seeding)</li><li>Ischemia of the extremities</li><li>Splenic or renal infarction</li><li>Pulmonary embolism</li><li>Acute myocardial infarction</li></ul></li></ul></td></tr></tbody></table><h3>X. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3><p>Measures for prevention of IE include:</p><ul><li>Maintenance of oral hygiene</li><li>Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to invasive dental or invasive oral procedures</li><li>Timely treatment of infections with pathogens likely to cause endocarditis</li><li>Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to surgery reduces the risk of surgical site infection, as discussed separately, and has been postulated to reduce the risk of subsequent endocarditis.</li><li>Closure of a patent ductus arteriosus or ventricular septal defect.</li></ul><h3>XI. <h1>INFECTIOUS ENDOCARDITIS</h1>
<p><i>Dr. SOK Monghak, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHM AO Pichmanil, Dr. KHUON Rithy, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Asst.prof. CHAN Sokha, Asst.prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Infectious Endocarditis (IE) refers to infection of the endocardial surface of the heart; it usually refers to infection of one or more heart valves or infection of an intracardiac device.</p>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li>The incidence of infective endocarditis is estimated between 30 and 80 cases per million inhabitants and per year in the general population in industrialized countries.</li>
<li>Incidence increases after the age of 60 and Staphylococcus is now the most frequent responsible microorganism.</li>
<li>Infective endocarditis was native (NVE) in 1764 (56.6%) patients, prosthetic (PVIE) in 939 (30.1%), and device-related (CDRIE) in 308 (9.9%). Infective endocarditis was community-acquired in 2046 (65.66%) patients.</li>
</ul>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY AND RISK FACTORS</h2>
<ul>
<li>Risk factors for native valve infective endocarditis (IE) include cardiac factors or non-cardiac risk factors.</li>
<li>It is most often from bacteria and more rarely a fungus from</li>
</ul>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Bacteria</th>
<th>Source of Infection</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Staphylococcus aureus</td>
<td>Skin</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Oral Streptococcus, HACEK</td>
<td>Oral, dental</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Group D Streptococcus</td>
<td>Gastro-intestinal tract (Coloscopy)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Enterococcus</td>
<td>Gastro-intestinal tract (Coloscopy), Urinary tract</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Cardiac risk factors</th>
<th>Non-cardiac risk factors</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Previous infective endocarditis</li>
<li>Valvular heart disease</li>
<li>Prosthetic heart valve</li>
<li>Central venous or arterial catheter</li>
<li>Transvenous cardiac implantable electronic device</li>
<li>Congenital heart disease</li>
</ul>
</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Central venous catheter</li>
<li>People who inject drugs</li>
<li>Immunosuppression</li>
<li>Recent dental or surgical procedures</li>
<li>Recent hospitalization Haemodialysis</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<h4>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4>
<div>
<p>Risk factors (Source of Infection)</p>
<p>Risk of Heart disease</p>
<ul>
<li>Vegetations
        <ul>
<li>Systemic Embolism</li>
<li>Pulmonary Embolism</li>
<li>Other Infection (Splenic abscesses, renal abscesses, arthritis, meningitis, etc.)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Valve destruction</li>
<li>Disinsertion of prosthesis
        <ul>
<li>Regurgitations (Leak) of Valvular or paraprosthetic</li>
<li>Intracardiac fistulas</li>
<li>Acute heart failure (Pulmonary edema, Cardiogenic shock)</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Abscess
        <ul>
<li>AV Block</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Inflammation
        <ul>
<li>Alteration of general condition</li>
<li>Septic shock</li>
<li>Vasculitis systemic inflammation</li>
<li>Infectious aneurysms (mycotic)</li>
<li>Hemorrhages (Cerebral and others)</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<ol>
<li>Clinical Manifestations
    <ul>
<li><b>Symptoms:</b> Fever is the most common symptom of IE
        <ul>
<li>It is often associated with chills, anorexia, and weight loss.</li>
<li>Other common symptoms: Malaise, headache, myalgias, arthralgias, night sweats, abdominal pain, tooth pain and dyspnea.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Signs:</b> A new or changing cardiac
        <ul>
<li>Supportive signs: splenomegaly, petechiae or splinter hemorrhages.</li>
<li>Relatively uncommon manifestations highly suggestive of IE:
            <ul>
<li>Janeway lesions</li>
<li>Osler nodes</li>
<li>Roth spots</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Investigation for Endocarditis
    <ul>
<li>Blood cultures: At least two sets of blood cultures should be obtained from separate venipuncture sites prior to initiation of antibiotic therapy.</li>
<li>Cardiac imaging:
        <ul>
<li>Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the first diagnostic test for patients with suspected IE.</li>
<li>Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) has higher sensitivity than TTE and is better for detection of cardiac complications.</li>
<li>Cardiac CT: May be helpful for cases in which definitive evidence of IE and its complications cannot be demonstrated with TEE, and/or for planning surgery in patients with extra valvular complications.</li>
<li>Additional evaluation for IE source or complications: ECG, chest radiography, other radiographic imaging tailored to clinical manifestations, and dental evaluation.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>

<!-- PAGE 419 -->

<h3>3. Definitions of the 2023 European Society of Cardiology modified diagnostic criteria of infective endocarditis</h3>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th colspan="2">Major criteria</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>1. Blood cultures positive for IE</td>
<td>(a) Typical microorganisms consistent with IE from two separate blood cultures: Oral streptococci, Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis), HACEK group, S. aureus, E. faecalis.<br/>(b) Microorganisms consistent with IE from continuously positive blood cultures:<ul><li>≥2 positive blood cultures of blood samples drawn &gt;12 h apart.</li><li>3 j ≥4 w w ≥1 apart).</li></ul>(c) Single positive blood culture for C. burnetii or phase I IgG antibody titre &gt;1:800.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>2. Imaging positive for IE:</td>
<td>Valvular, perivalvular/periprosthetic and foreign material anatomic and metabolic lesions characteristic of IE detected by any of the following imaging techniques:<ul><li>Echocardiography (TTE and TOE)</li><li>Cardiac CT</li><li>[<sup>18</sup>F]-FDG-PET/CT(A)</li><li>WBC SPECT/CT</li></ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th colspan="2">Minor criteria</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Predisposing conditions (i.e. predisposing heart condition at high or intermediate risk of IE or PWIDs)</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Fever defined as temperature &gt;38°C</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Embolic vascular dissemination (including those asymptomatic detected by imaging only):</td>
<td><ul><li>Major systemic and pulmonary emboli/infarcts and abscesses.</li><li>Haematogenous osteoarticular septic complications (i.e. spondylodiscitis).</li><li>Mycotic aneurysms</li><li>Intracranial ischaemic/haemorrhagic lesions</li><li>Conjunctival haemorrhages</li><li>J w ’</li></ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Immunological phenomena:</td>
<td><ul><li>Glomerulonephritis</li><li>Osler nodes and Roth spots</li><li>Rheumatoid factor</li></ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Microbiological evidence:</td>
<td><ul><li>Positive blood culture but does not meet a major criterion as noted above.</li><li>Serological evidence of active infection with organism consistent with IE.</li></ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th colspan="2">IE Classification (at admission and during follow-up)</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Definite:</td>
<td><ul><li>2 major criteria.</li><li>1 major criterion and at least 3 minor criteria.</li><li>5 minor criteria.</li></ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Possible:</td>
<td><ul><li>1 major criterion and 1 or 2 minor criteria.</li><li>3–4 minor criteria.</li></ul></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Rejected:</td>
<td><ul><li>Does not meet criteria for definite or possible at admission with or without a firm alternative diagnosis.</li></ul></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<h2>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h2>
<p>The differential diagnosis for endocarditis is broad and should be considered based on two clinical categories: presence of bacteraemia in the absence of valvular vegetation and presence of valvular vegetation(s) in the absence of bacteraemia.</p>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Presence of bacteraemia in the absence of valvular vegetation</th>
<th>Presence of valvular vegetation(s) in the absence of bacteraemia</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Intravascular catheter infection</li>
<li>Cardiac device infection</li>
<li>Prosthetic joint infection</li>
<li>Hematogenous osteomyelitis</li>
<li>Septic thrombophlebitis</li>
<li>Infected arterial aneurysm</li>
</ul>
</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Culture-negative endocarditis or sterile vegetation(s) (marantic endocarditis or Libman-Sachs endocarditis) due to a noninfectious etiology or antiphospholipid syndrome.</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<h2>2. Indications and timing of surgery in the presence of heart failure in infective endocarditis:</h2>
<p>Timing of surgical intervention in patients with IE complicated by HF should be decided by the Endocarditis Team, although surgery should not be delayed by Endocarditis Team discussions in patients requiring emergency operations. The presence of HF leads to recommendation for surgery in the majority of patients and is the principal indication for urgent surgery in IE patients.</p>
<div>
<img alt="Flowchart titled 'Surgical timing for patient with left-sided infective endocarditis'. The flowchart starts with three initial conditions: Heart failure, Uncontrolled infection, and High risk of embolism or established embolism. Each condition leads to a subsequent decision point (purple box). 1. Heart failure leads to Cardiogenic shock or pulmonary oedema. A 'Y' path leads to Emergency surgery (Class I). An 'N' path leads to Poor haemodynamic tolerance. 2. Uncontrolled infection leads to Local complications (abscess, false aneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation). A 'Y' path leads to Urgent surgery (Class I). An 'N' path leads to Persistent positive blood cultures^a. 3. High risk of embolism or established embolism leads to Vegetation ≥10 mm and emboli despite appropriate antibiotic therapy. A 'Y' path leads to Urgent surgery (Class I). An 'N' path leads to Vegetation ≥10 mm and other reason for surgery^b. The flow continues based on subsequent decisions: - Poor haemodynamic tolerance: 'Y' leads to Urgent surgery (Class I); 'N' leads to Non-urgent surgery (Class I). - Persistent positive blood cultures^a: 'Y' leads to Urgent surgery (Class IIa); 'N' leads to Resistant bacteria^c or fungi. - Vegetation ≥10 mm and other reason for surgery^b: 'Y' leads to Urgent surgery (Class I); 'N' leads to Vegetation ≥10 mm and no evidence of embolus. - Resistant bacteria^c or fungi: 'Y' leads to Urgent or non-urgent surgery (Class I)^d; 'N' leads to PVE caused by S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negative bacilli. - Vegetation ≥10 mm and no evidence of embolus: 'Y' leads to Urgent surgery (Class IIb); 'N' leads to Antibiotic therapy and continued observation. - PVE caused by S. aureus or non-HACEK Gram-negative bacilli: 'Y' leads to Urgent surgery (Class IIa); 'N' leads to Non-urgent surgery (Class I)."/>
</div>
<p><small>Proposed surgical timing for infective endocarditis. HACEK, Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, and Kingella; PVE, prosthetic valve endocarditis. Surgery timing: emergency, within 24 h. Urgent, within 3–5 days. Non-urgent, within same hospital admission. a Despite appropriate antibiotic therapy for &gt;1 week and control of septic embolic foci. b E.g. patients with significant valvular dysfunction that is, or is not, a direct result of endocarditis process. c S. aureus (methicillin resistant and non-methicillin resistant), vancomycin-resistant enterococci, non-HACEK Gram-negative bacteria and fungi. d Urgent for S. aureus, non-urgent for others.</small></p>

<!-- PAGE 426 -->

<h3>VIII. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<ul>
<li>Relapse is a repeat episode of IE caused by the same microorganism and represents a failure of treatment and mandates a search for a persistent focus of infection and an evaluation towards surgical therapy.</li>
<li>Reinfection is an infection caused by a different microorganism, usually more than 6 months after the initial episode.</li>
<li>Once antibiotic treatment has been completed, blood cultures should be performed.</li>
<li>Patients discharged after the first episode of IE should remain under close surveillance for potential long-term complications.</li>
</ul>
<h3>IX. COMPLICATIONS</h3>
<p>Complications of infective endocarditis (IE) include cardiac, metastatic, neurologic, renal, musculoskeletal, and pulmonary complications as well as complications related to systemic infection (including embolization, metastatic infection, and mycotic aneurysm). More than one complication can occur simultaneously.</p>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Cardiac complications</th>
<th>Metastatic infection</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Heart failure</li>
<li>Perivalvular abscess</li>
<li>Pericarditis (suppurative or nonsuppurative)</li>
<li>Intracardiac fistula (eg, aorta-atrial or aorta-ventricular)</li>
</ul>
</td>
<td>
<ul>
<li>Forms of metastatic infection include Septic embolization, metastatic abscess, and mycotic aneurysm.</li>
<li>Embolii can occlude or damage virtually any vessel in the systemic or pulmonary arterial circulation:
<ul>
<li>Stroke</li>
<li>Paralysis (due to embolic infarction of either the brain or spinal cord)</li>
<li>Blindness (due to embolism or due to endophthalmitis as a result of bacteremic seeding)</li>
<li>Ischemia of the extremities</li>
<li>Splenic or renal infarction</li>
<li>Pulmonary embolism</li>
<li>Acute myocardial infarction</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h3>X. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<p>Measures for prevention of IE include:</p>
<ul>
<li>Maintenance of oral hygiene</li>
<li>Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to invasive dental or invasive oral procedures</li>
<li>Timely treatment of infections with pathogens likely to cause endocarditis</li>
<li>Antibiotic prophylaxis prior to surgery reduces the risk of surgical site infection, as discussed separately, and has been postulated to reduce the risk of subsequent endocarditis.</li>
<li>Closure of a patent ductus arteriosus or ventricular septal defect.</li>
</ul>

<h1>PERICARDITIS</h1>
<p><i>Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</i></p>
<h2>I. DEFINITION</h2>
<p>Pericarditis refers to the inflammation of the pericardial layers with or without pericardial effusion.</p>
<h3>Type of pericarditis</h3>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th></th>
<th>Definition of Pericarditis According to the Time of Presentation</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Acute</td>
<td>Even lasting &lt;4 weeks</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Incessant</td>
<td>Even lasting &gt;4 to 6 weeks without remission<br/>But &lt;3 months</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Recurrent (20-30%)</td>
<td>Symptoms occur about 4 to 6 weeks after an episode of acute pericarditis with no symptoms in between</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Chronic constrictive</td>
<td>Lasting &gt;3 months</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Acute pericarditis is diagnosed in 0.2% of all cardiovascular in-hospital admissions and is responsible for 5% of emergency room admissions for chest pain.</p>
<h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2>
<ul>
<li>Idiopathic is most common: presumed to be viral</li>
<li>Infectious
        <ul>
<li>Tuberculosis</li>
<li>Viral: Coxsackie virus A, B (most common), echovirus</li>
<li>Bacterial: S. pneumoniae, S. aureus</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Post-MI: acute (direct extension of myocardial inflammation, 1-7 d post-MI), Dressler's syndrome (autoimmune reaction, 2-8 weeks post-MI)</li>
<li>Post-cardiac surgery (e.g. CABG), other trauma</li>
<li>Metabolic: uraemia/CKD, hypothyroidism</li>
<li>Neoplasm: Hodgkin's, breast, lung, renal cell carcinoma, melanoma</li>
<li>Collagen vascular disease: SLE, polyarteritis, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma</li>
<li>Other: drugs (e.g. hydralazine), radiation, infiltrative disease (sarcoid)</li>
</ul>
<h2>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h2>
<p>Due to the parietal layer's rich innervation, any inflammatory process mediated by an infectious, autoimmune or traumatic insult can result in severe retrosternal chest pain, as is commonly seen in acute pericarditis. This explains why the vast majority of presentations (&gt;90%) have chest discomfort. In cases of pericardial effusion, the pericardial compliance can increase in response to slowly</p>

<!-- PAGE 429 -->

<div><p>accumulating fluid, allowing the pericardial sac to dilate over time without compressing the cardiac chambers. This means that the rate of fluid accumulation (and resulting pressure changes, as in pericardial compliance) is often more important than the volume in determining the hemodynamic sequelae affecting the heart.</p><h4>V. DIAGNOSIS</h4><h5>Symptoms</h5><p>Chest pain is the most common symptom of pericarditis (&gt;95%). It usually feels sharp or stabbing, and some patients having achy or pressure-like chest pain.</p><p>The pain:</p><ul><li>Usually occurs behind the breastbone or on the left side of the chest</li><li>Spread to the left shoulder and neck</li><li>Get worse when coughing, lying down or taking a deep breath</li><li>Get better when sitting up or leaning forward</li></ul><p>Other signs and symptoms of pericarditis may include:</p><ul><li>Cough</li><li>Fatigue or general feeling of weakness or being sick</li><li>Leg swelling</li><li>Low-grade fever</li><li>Palpitation</li><li>Shortness of breath when lying down</li><li>Swelling of the belly (abdomen)</li></ul><h5>Investigations</h5><ul><li>ECG: initially diffuse elevated ST segments ± depressed PR segment, the elevation in the ST segment is concave upwards → 2-5 d later ST isoelectric with T wave flattening and inversion</li><li>Chest X-ray</li><li>Heart ultrasound: performed to assess for pericardial effusion</li><li>CT or MRI: when located pericardial effusion, pericardial thickening or masses, constrictive pericarditis</li></ul><div><img alt="Four ECG strips illustrating the stages of pericarditis. Stage 1 shows PR depression and generalized ST segment elevation. Stage 2 is transitional, showing early and late phases where J points flatten before T waves. Stage 3 shows T wave inversion. Stage 4 shows normalization of ECG."/><table><tbody><tr><td>• PR depression</td><td colspan="2">Transitional</td><td>T wave inversion</td><td>Normalization of ECG</td></tr><tr><td>• Generalized ST segment elevation</td><td colspan="4">J points on the base line before T waves begin to flatten</td></tr></tbody></table></div></div>

<!-- PAGE 430 -->

<h4>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSES</h4>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Common</th>
<th>Less common</th>
<th>Rare</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Myocardial infarction<br/>Acute gastritis<br/>Gastroesophageal reflux disease<br/>Pleuritis<br/>Pneumonia</td>
<td>Esophageal spasm<br/>Pulmonary embolism<br/>Pneumothorax</td>
<td>Aortic dissection<br/>Esophageal rupture</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<h4>VII. TREATMENT</h4>
<ul>
<li>Anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDs/ASA, steroids)</li>
<li>Colchicine</li>
<li>Treat the underlying disease</li>
</ul>
<table border="1">
<thead>
<tr>
<th>Drug</th>
<th>Dose</th>
<th>Duration</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Aspirin*</td>
<td>750-1,000 mg every 8 h</td>
<td>1-2 weeks</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Ibuprofen*</td>
<td>600-800 mg every 8 h</td>
<td>1-2 weeks</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Colchicine</td>
<td>0.5-1.2 mg in one or divided doses</td>
<td>3 months</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p>* Tapering once inflammatory markers have normalized</p>
<h4>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h4>
<ul>
<li>Inpatient investigation and more intensive evaluation for a non-viral etiology should be considered where there is:
        <ul>
<li>Any fever &gt;38°C</li>
<li>Gradual onset</li>
<li>Large effusion (&gt;20 mm) or tamponade</li>
<li>Lack of response to 1 week of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs</li>
<li>Any history of trauma, immunosuppression/deficiency or oral anticoagulant use</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>If pericarditis is caused by a bacterial infection, treatment may include antibiotics and drainage, if necessary.</li>
<li>If pericarditis causes fluid buildup around the heart, a surgery or other procedure may be needed to drain the fluid (pericardiocentesis).</li>
</ul>
<h4>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h4>
<p>The prognosis of acute pericarditis largely depends on the underlying aetiology. It is excellent in cases of idiopathic pericarditis. Prompt diagnosis and appropriate treatment of acute pericarditis may reduce the risk of acute complications and recurrences.</p>
<h4>X. COMPLICATION</h4>
<ul>
<li>Pericardial effusion</li>
<li>Constrictive pericarditis</li>
<li>Cardiac tamponade (this life-threatening condition requires emergency treatment)</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 431 -->

<h2>XI. PREVENTION</h2><p>Acute pericarditis can't be prevented. We can take steps to reduce your chance of having another acute episode, complications or chronic pericarditis. These steps include getting prompt treatment, following your treatment plan and getting ongoing medical care as needed.</p><h2>XII. Available from: <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431080/">https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK431080/</a></li><li><a href="https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/pericarditis/prevention-and-treatment-ofpericarditis#:~:text=Can%20pericarditis%20be%20prevented%3F,ongoing%20medical%20care%20as%20needed">https://www.heart.org/en/health-topics/pericarditis/prevention-and-treatment-ofpericarditis#:~:text=Can%20pericarditis%20be%20prevented%3F,ongoing%20medical%20care%20as%20needed</a></li></ol><h3>Abbreviation:</h3><p>ASA: aspirin<br/>CABG: coronary artery bypass graft<br/>CKD: chronic kidney disease<br/>CT: computed tomography<br/>DE: delayed enhancement<br/>LV: left ventricle<br/>MI: myocardial infarction<br/>MRI: magnetic resonance imaging<br/>NSAIDs: nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs<br/>PE: pericardial effusion</p>

<h1>CONSTRUCTIVE PERICARDITIS</h1><p>Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOR Sokhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. SRENG Dina, Ass Prof. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Ass Prof CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</p><h2>I. DEFINITION</h2><p>Constrictive pericarditis (CP) is a chronic inflammatory process, often characterized by chronic scarring, fibrosis and calcification of the pericardium associated with diastolic dysfunction, eventually leading to low cardiac output and heart failure.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>Complication of acute CP is a relatively rare complication of viral or idiopathic acute pericarditis (&lt;0.5%) but, in contrast, is relatively frequent for specific etiologies, especially bacterial. In Asian series, TB pericarditis is reported to be the underlying etiology in 20-80% of cases</p><h2>III. ETIOLOGY</h2><ol><li><b>Common causes:</b><ul><li>Complication of acute idiopathic pericarditis</li><li>Post cardiac surgery or post chest radiotherapy</li><li>Infection (viral or bacterial)<ul><li>Tuberculosis</li><li>Bacterial infections that lead to purulent pericarditis</li></ul></li></ul></li><li><b>Less common causes:</b><ul><li>Infection (fungal)</li><li>Neoplasms</li><li>Uremia</li><li>Connective tissue disorders</li><li>Drugs (e.g: procainamide and hydralazine)</li><li>Trauma</li><li>Myocardial infarction (with past medical history of Dressler syndrome and hemopericardium)</li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 433 -->

<div>
<h4>IV. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY</h4>
<p>Pericardial non-compliance creates a stiff ventricular-pericardial unit,</p>
<p>limiting ventricular relaxation and determines ventricular diastolic pressure, resulting in elevated, equalized diastolic pressures in all chambers</p>
<p>decreasing the LV end diastolic volume (LV preload) and therefore left-sided stroke volume.</p>
<p>Clinically, predominantly as right-sided congestion (jugular venous distention, edema, and ascites) as well as elevation in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure and a decreased cardiac output response to exercise (given inadequate ventricular filling) results in dyspnea and effort intolerance</p>
<h4>IV. DIAGNOSIS</h4>
<ol>
<li><b>Initial assessment:</b>
<ul>
<li>The low prevalence of CP makes identifying key physical examination and historical features an important initial step in the diagnostic process.</li>
<li>History of cardiac surgery, radiation or <b>tuberculosis</b> should heighten clinical suspicion in the presence of edema, abdominal distention and exertional dyspnea.</li>
<li>In early stage: symptoms secondary to a reduction in cardiac output including fatigue and exertional dyspnea</li>
<li>In late stage, the filling pressures become significantly elevated, and systemic venous pressure rises, signs of overt RHF develop such as jugular venous distention, edema, ascites, pleural effusion.</li>
<li>Elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP) is present in virtually all patients:
<ul>
<li>Kussmaul's sign</li>
<li>Rapid x- and y-descents seen in the JVP of a patient with constrictive pericarditis. These are appreciated as rapid inward "flicking"/collapsing deflections in the presence of an elevated JVP.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Other findings: diastolic apex beat or diastolic precordial impulse, high-pitched early diastolic pericardial knock in heart auscultation.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>Investigations:</b>
<ol type="a">
<li><b>Laboratory testing:</b> nonspecific in constrictive pericarditis.</li>
<li><b>Echocardiography:</b> As an initial diagnostic test, echocardiography can confirm the diagnosis of CP in most cases if pre-test probability is sufficiently high.
<ul>
<li>The pathognomonic finding is respirophasic septal shifting, detected by either M mode or 2D imaging and abnormal beat-to-beat septal motion, or "shudder," due to differential rapid early diastolic filling of the right and then left ventricle.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
</li>
</ol>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 434 -->

<ul><li>The inferior vena cava is universally plethoric in the absence of hypovolemia; a sensitive but nonspecific feature of CP.</li><li>The exaggerated respiratory preload changes are also exemplified by an inspiratory decrease in mitral valve inflow Doppler and an increase in tricuspid valve inflow Doppler.</li></ul><p><b>c. Cardiac radiology:</b></p><ul><li>In CP, chest x-rays can demonstrate pericardial calcification, a pathognomonic finding in the presence of clinical heart failure and elevated JVP. Chest CT is more sensitive for pericardial calcification than chest x-ray.</li><li>Chest CT and MRI allow for precise measurement of pericardial thickness, with MRI in particular demonstrating excellent accuracy (93%) in detection of pericardial thickening &gt;4 mm.</li></ul><h2>VI. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS</h2><p>The differential diagnosis of constrictive pericarditis (CP) includes conditions with similar symptoms such as <b>restrictive cardiomyopathy</b>, <b>cardiac tamponade</b>, <b>systolic or diastolic congestive heart failure (CHF)</b>, <b>Right-sided valvular abnormalities</b>, <b>Right-sided atrial tumors</b>, and <b>Superior vena cava syndrome and nephrotic syndrome</b>. These can present with dyspnea, edema, ascites, pleural effusion, jugular vein distention mimicking CP. Careful evaluation of clinical history, laboratory finding and diagnostic imaging (echocardiography, cardiac CT or MRI) is essential to differentiate CP from these conditions.</p><h2>VII. MANAGEMENT</h2><ol><li><b>Objective:</b><ul><li>Improving cardiac function, reducing inflammation and congestion.</li><li>The primary etiology be identified and managed accordingly</li><li>The definitive cure for CP is primarily surgical in the form of complete pericardiectomy, where feasible.</li></ul></li><li><b>Critical signs:</b><p>End-stage disease can include cachexia, markedly reduced resting cardiac output (cardiac index ≤1.2 L/m<sup>2</sup> per min), hypoalbuminemia due to protein-losing enteropathy, and/or congestive hepatopathy including cardiac cirrhosis.</p></li><li><b>Outpatient management</b><p>Outpatient care may be appropriate during the early stages of the disease, particularly when the diagnosis is still uncertain and symptoms are relatively stable. It is important to emphasize and encourage a <b>low salt and fluid-restricted diet</b> as these are probably beneficial in order to avoid congestion and exacerbations of heart failure symptoms. Although no specific restrictions are needed, activity can often be severely limited by symptoms. However, decreased daily activities may be recommended in some patients.</p></li><li><b>Pharmacologic therapy:</b><p>Medical treatment may be considered as a trial of two to three months as conservative treatment if it is transient CP. The following specific treatment modalities should be considered for each of the special situations highlighted.</p><ul><li><b>Subacute CP</b> may respond to <b>steroids</b> if treated before pericardial fibrosis develops.</li><li><b>Diuretics</b>, particularly loop diuretics, are the mainstay to <b>relieve congestion</b> and to optimise clinical volume status; however, they may decrease preload to the point of reducing cardiac output and thus <b>require closer monitoring</b>.</li><li>Any other medications used to treat patients with CP should be specifically directed to the underlying aetiology of the pericardial disease.</li></ul></li></ol>

<!-- PAGE 435 -->

<ul><li>Any therapy directed towards the <b>causative disease</b>, e.g., antituberculosis therapy, is appropriate.</li><li>CP-related complications require their own specific therapy as appropriate, e.g., atrial arrhythmias.</li><li>In general, <b>beta-blockers</b> and <b>calcium channel blockers</b> should be avoided.</li><li>Patients with advanced cardiac symptoms related to constriction may derive little benefit from surgery, as these are often the high surgical risk group.</li></ul><h3>Drug therapy in acute and recurrent pericarditis for adult patients</h3><table border="1"><thead><tr><th>Drug</th><th>Antiinflammatory dose</th><th>Duration of initial or maintenance dose*</th><th>Tapering regimen</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td colspan="4">First-line therapy for most patients:Δ</td></tr><tr><td>Aspirin</td><td>650 to 1000 mg orally 3 times daily</td><td>1 to 2 weeks</td><td>Decrease dose by about 250 mg per week</td></tr><tr><td colspan="4">or</td></tr><tr><td>Ibuprofen</td><td>600 to 800 mg orally 3 times daily<sup>S</sup></td><td>1 to 2 weeks</td><td>Decrease dose by 200 mg per week</td></tr><tr><td colspan="4">or</td></tr><tr><td>Indomethacin</td><td>25 to 50 mg orally 3 times daily</td><td>1 to 2 weeks</td><td>Decrease dose by 25 mg per week</td></tr><tr><td colspan="4">plus</td></tr><tr><td>Colchicine</td><td>0.5 to 0.6 mg orally 2 times daily</td><td>3 months (acute)<br/>6 months or more (recurrent)</td><td>Usually not tapered</td></tr><tr><td colspan="4">Second-line therapy (for refractory cases or patients with a contraindication to NSAID therapy):</td></tr><tr><td>Prednisone</td><td>0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg daily</td><td>2 to 4 weeks (acute or recurrent<sup>†</sup>)</td><td>Gradual tapering over 2 to 3 months; refer to UpToDate topic review of treatment of acute pericarditis, section on glucocorticoids</td></tr><tr><td colspan="4">plus</td></tr><tr><td>Colchicine</td><td>0.5 to 0.6 mg orally 2 times daily</td><td>3 months or more<br/>(acute)<br/>6 months or more (recurrent)</td><td>Usually not tapered</td></tr><tr><td></td><td></td><td>Colchicine is generally continued for 4 weeks or more after discontinuation of glucocorticoid</td><td></td></tr></tbody></table>

<!-- PAGE 436 -->

<h3>5. Pericardiectomy</h3>
<p>Pericardiectomy: a pericardiectomy remains the definitive therapy and a potential cure in most CP patients</p>
<p><b>Indication</b> — We suggest pericardiectomy for patients with chronic constrictive pericarditis who meet all of the following criteria:</p>
<ul>
<li>Symptoms and signs have persisted despite at least 4 to 12 months of IL-1 inhibitor therapy.</li>
<li>Symptoms are moderate to severe (New York Heart Association [NYHA] functional class III or IV (table 2).</li>
<li>Constrictive pericarditis has not progressed to "end-stage." (See 'Patients unlikely to benefit from pericardiectomy' below.)</li>
<li>There is no concomitant restrictive cardiomyopathy</li>
</ul>
<p><b>Patients unlikely to benefit from pericardiectomy:</b> Due to the complex nature of the surgery and the associated operative mortality, surgery should be carefully considered in patients who may not benefit from the procedure.</p>
<ul>
<li>Mild disease</li>
<li>End-stage disease</li>
<li>Mixed constrictive-restrictive disease</li>
<li>Other high-risk groups – Mortality after pericardiectomy is also high in individuals with end-stage kidney disease or ventricular systolic dysfunction.</li>
</ul>
<h3>6. Mortality risk factors of pericardiectomy</h3>
<p>Detrimental outcomes of pericardiectomy include progressive heart failure or advanced heart failure symptoms (NYHA III-IV), sepsis, renal failure, respiratory failure, arrhythmia, prior mediastinal radiotherapy as the primary cause of constriction, and other concomitant severe comorbidities.</p>
<p>Preoperative myocardial atrophy or fibrosis is as well one of the causes of peri-operative mortality due to reduced ventricular mobility, particularly the RV free wall, are associated with acute RV dilatation related to subsequent increased preload to the RV, to increased venous return which then leads to acute RV failure and decreased cardiac output, function and subsequent death. Extensive pericardial calcification might have prognostic implications, which make pericardiectomy more extensive and complex.</p>

<!-- PAGE 437 -->

<h2>7. Algorithm</h2>
<h3>Diagnostic Algorithm for patient with suspected constrictive pericarditis</h3>
<p><b>Figure 1</b></p>
<div>
<p>The diagnostic algorithm starts with the central diagnosis: <b>Constrictive pericarditis</b>.</p>
<p>Initial assessment steps (blue boxes) include:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>History</b>, which leads to considerations of <b>Cardiac procedures</b>, <b>Radiation</b>, and <b>Connective tissue disease</b>.</li>
<li><b>Physical exam</b>, which leads to <b>JVP</b>. JVP findings may indicate <b>Infection (TB)</b> (with associated <b>¹Y, ¹X</b>) or <b>Kussmaul's sig</b>.</li>
<li><b>Lab/ECG/X-Ray</b>, which can lead to a <b>Nonspecific</b> result.</li>
</ul>
<p>Further evaluation includes:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Advanced cardiac imaging</b>, which involves <b>Echocardiography</b>, <b>Cardiac MRI</b>, and <b>Cardiac CT</b>. These imaging modalities are linked to <b>Anatomy</b> and <b>Physiology</b>.</li>
<li><b>Invasive hemodynamics</b>, which is linked to <b>Anatomy</b> and <b>Physiology</b>.</li>
</ul>
<p>Findings related to <b>Anatomy</b> (red box) include:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>¹Pericardial thickness</b></li>
<li><b>Pericardial calcification</b></li>
<li><b>ericardial effusion</b></li>
</ul>
<p>Findings related to <b>Physiology</b> (red box) include:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Imaging correlates of ¹ventricular interdependence</b></li>
<li><b>Pericardial Inflammation</b></li>
</ul>
<p>Final diagnostic criteria (green boxes) derived from the above assessments are:</p>
<ul>
<li><b>Discordant respirophasic Ventricular pressure changes</b></li>
<li><b>Intrathoracic-intracadiac dissociation</b></li>
</ul>
</div>

<h2>Diagnosis and therapeutic approach for relapsing pericarditis</h2>
<div>
<p><b>Relapsing CP, criteria:</b></p>
<ol>
<li>Acute pericarditis, chest pain with one of the following: Fever, pericardial friction rub, ECG changes, pericardial Effusion or elevated acute phase markers (WCC, ESR, CRP)</li>
</ol>
</div>
<table>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="text-align: center; vertical-align: top;">
<p><b>YES</b></p>
<p>ASA or other NSAIDS ± Colchicine<br/>NO steroids implicated</p>
<p>Multiple relapses</p>
<p>Add steroids (prednisone, preferably) OR immunosuppression therapy</p>
<p>Followed by slow tapering of steroids</p>
<p>If therapy fails, then consider surgery, complete pericardiectomy</p>
</td>
<td style="text-align: center; vertical-align: top;">
<p><b>NO</b></p>
<p>Consider further tests to exclude the Primary etiologies:<br/>Do Echo, CT scan, MRI</p>
<p>If persistent large pericardial effusion,<br/>Need for pericardiocynthesis</p>
</td>
</tr>
