<h2>Approach to treatment of subacute constrictive pericarditis in adults</h2>
<div>
<p><b>Initial treatment: NSAID plus colchicine</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Good response:
        <ul>
<li>Continue treatment for 2 to 3 months</li>
<li>Then slowly taper NSAID as</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>Patient tolerates NSAID taper
                <ul>
<li>Discontinue colchicine once NSAID is tapered off</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Symptoms or signs Recur during taper
                <ul>
<li>Switch to a Glucocorticoid plus Colchicine</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Inadequate response:
        <ul>
<li>Switch to a Glucocorticoid plus Colchicine</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>Good response:
                <ul>
<li>Continue treatment for 2 to 3 months</li>
<li>Then slowly taper glucocorticoid as</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>Patient tolerates Glucocorticoid taper
                        <ul>
<li>Discontinue colchicine once glucocorticoid is tapered off</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Symptoms or signs Recur during taper
                        <ul>
<li>Switch to an IL-1 inhibitor</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Inadequate response:
                <ul>
<li>Switch to an IL-1 inhibitor</li>
</ul>
<ul>
<li>Good response:
                        <ul>
<li>Continue treatment for at least 4 to 12 months</li>
<li>Then slowly taper IL-1 inhibitor as tolerated</li>
<li>If symptoms or signs recur during taper, restart IL-1 inhibitor</li>
<li>If response to a second course of IL-1 inhibitor</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Inadequate response:
                        <ul>
<li>Refer for pericardiectomy</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>
<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<p>Due to high prevalence of Tuberculosis in Cambodia (WHO's estimated TB incidence in Cambodia is 302 per 100,000 population in 2018), in a case of constrictive pericarditis, Tuberculosis should be investigated as one of potential causes.</p>
<h3>IX. EVOLUTION AND PROGNOSIS</h3>
<p>Long-term survival after pericardiectomy for constrictive pericarditis is inferior to that of an age- and sex-matched population, although in many patients this is likely related to comorbid conditions. In one series, the 5- and 10-year survival rates were 78 and 57 percent, respectively.</p>
<h3>X. PREVENTION AND RECOMMENDATION</h3>
<p>The conditions which are primarily the leading causes of CP should be adequately managed to prevent the occurrence of CP as listing in Etiology Section above.</p>

<!-- PAGE 440 -->

<h2>XI. COMPLICATIONS</h2><p>Constrictive pericarditis if left untreated will lead to heart failure due to myocardial atrophy or fibrosis (diastolic et systolic dysfunction), Abnormal heart rhythm, liver and kidney dysfunction, which result in severe congestion in limbs, ascites, pleural effusion and dyspnea.</p><h2>XII. <h1>MANAGEMENT OF CARDIOVASCULAR DISEASES DURING PREGNANCY</h1><p>Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</p><h2>I. INTRODUCTION</h2><p>Today the number of pregnancy woman complicated by cardiovascular disease (CVD) is increasing worldwide. In western industrialized countries such patients represent 0.2-4% of all pregnancies. Counselling and management of women of childbearing age with suspected cardiac disease should start before pregnancy occurs; they should be managed by interdisciplinary teams; high risk patients should be treated in specialized centers; and diagnostic procedures and interventions should be performed by specialists with great expertise in the individual technique and experiences in treating pregnant patients.</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><p>Hypertensive disorder are the most frequent cardiovascular events during pregnancy, occurring in 6-8% of all pregnancies.</p><p>In the western world, congenital heart disease is the most frequent cardiovascular disease present during pregnancy (75-82%). Congenital heart disease represents just 9-19% outside Europe and North America.</p><p>Rheumatic valvular disease dominates in non-western countries, including our country, Cambodia, comprising 56-89% of all cardiovascular disease in pregnancy.</p><p>Cardiomyopathies are rare, but represent sever causes of cardiovascular complication in pregnancy. Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is the most common cause of severe complications.</p><h2>III. HEMODYNAMIC, HEMOSTATIC AND METABOLIC ALTERATIONS DURING PREGNANCY</h2><p>Pregnancy induces changes in the cardiovascular system to meet the increased metabolic demands of the mother and fetus: <b>increases in blood volume and cardiac output (CO), and reductions in systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure (BP):</b></p><ul><li>Plasma volume reaches a maximum of 40% above baseline at 24 weeks gestations.</li><li>A 30-35% increase in CO in normal pregnancy</li><li>Heart rate starts to rise at 20 weeks and increases until 32 weeks</li><li>Systemic BP (SBP) typically falls early in gestation and diastolic BP (DBP) is usually 10mmHg below baseline in the second trimester: caused by active vasodilation. In the 3<sup>rd</sup> trimester, the DBP gradually increases and may normalized to non-pregnant values by term.</li><li>The heart can increase its size by up to 30%</li></ul>

<p><b>Figure 1.</b> Hemodynamic changes in pregnancy</p>
<p><b>Hemostatic changes:</b> tend to hypercoagulability and increase risk of thrombo-embolic due to increases in concentration of coagulation factors, fibrinogen, and platelet adhesiveness, as well as diminished fibrinolysis.</p>
<p>Maternal glucose and homeostasis may change and cholesterol levels increase in adaptation to fetal-maternal needs.</p>
<p>These changes can affect absorption, excretion, and bioavailability of all drugs.</p>
<p>Uterine contractions, positioning (left lateral vs. supine), pain, anxiety, exertion, bleeding and uterine involution cause significant hemodynamic changes during labor and post-partum.</p>
<h4>IV. ARDIOVASCULAR DIAGNOSIS IN PREGNANCY</h4>
<p>□ History and clinical investigation</p>
<ul>
<li>Family history:
        <ul>
<li>Asking about possible sudden deaths in the family can identify some disease such as: Marfan syndrome, congenital heart disease, juvenile sudden death, long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic VT or Brugada syndrome.</li>
<li>Asking for the history or family history of hypertension or pre-eclampsia</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Clinical assessment:
        <ul>
<li>dyspnea: important for diagnosis a prognosis of valve lesions and for heart failure.</li>
<li>Auscultation: to detect new murmur, changes in murmur</li>
<li>Oximetry: should be performed in patients with congenital heart disease</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<h2>V. INTERVENTION IN THE MOTHER DURING PREGNANCY</h2>
<div>
<p><b>SYMPTOMS</b></p>
<p>NYHA class ≥ II *</p>
<p><u>Suggestive of Heart Failure:</u></p>
<ul>
<li>Dyspnea</li>
<li>Mild orthopnea</li>
<li>Tachypnea</li>
<li>Asthma unresponsive to therapy</li>
</ul>
<p><u>Suggestive of Arrhythmia:</u></p>
<ul>
<li>Palpitations</li>
<li>Dizziness/syncope</li>
</ul>
<p><u>Suggestive of Coronary Artery Disease:</u></p>
<ul>
<li>Chest pain</li>
<li>Dyspnea</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div>
<p><b>VITAL SIGNS</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Resting HR ≥110 bpm</li>
<li>Systolic BP ≥140 mm Hg</li>
<li>RR ≥24</li>
<li>Oxygen sat ≤96%</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div>
<p><b>RISK FACTORS</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Age ≥40 years</li>
<li>African American</li>
<li>Pre-pregnancy obesity (BMI ≥35)</li>
<li>Pre-existing diabetes</li>
<li>Hypertension</li>
<li>Substance use (nicotine, cocaine, alcohol, methamphetamines)</li>
<li>History of chemotherapy</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div>
<p><b>PHYSICAL EXAM</b></p>
<p><b>ABNORMAL FINDINGS</b></p>
<p>Heart: Loud murmur or Lung: Basilar crackles</p>
</div>
<div>
<p>≥ 1 Symptom + ≥ 1 Vital Signs Abnormal + ≥ 1 Risk Factor <b>or</b> ANY COMBINATION ADDING TO ≥ 4</p>
</div>
<div>
<p>Consultation indicated: MFM and Primary Care/Cardiology</p>
</div>
<div>
<p>Obtain: EKG and BNP</p>
<ul>
<li>Echocardiogram +/- CXR if HF or valve disease is suspected, or if the BNP levels are elevated</li>
<li>24 hour Holter monitor, if arrhythmia suspected</li>
<li>Referral to cardiologist for possible treadmill echo vs. CTA vs. alternative testing if postpartum</li>
</ul>
<p>Consider: CXR, CBC, Comprehensive metabolic profile, Arterial blood gas, Drug screen, TSH, etc.</p>
<p>Follow-up within 1 week</p>
</div>

<p>Results negative</p>
<p>Signs and symptoms resolved<br/>Reassurance and routine follow-up</p>
</div>

<p><b>Figure 2. Cardiovascular disease assessment in pregnant and postpartum women</b></p>
<h3>5.1. Percutaneous therapy</h3>
<ul>
<li>the best time to intervene is considered to be after the fourth month in the second trimester: organogenesis is complete, the fetal thyroid is still inactive, and the volume of the uterus is still small (greater distance between the fetus and the chest).</li>
<li>Fluoroscopy and cineangiography times should be short and the gravid uterus should be shielded from the radiation.</li>
<li>Heparin should be given 40-70 U/Kg, keep ACT between 200-300s.</li>
</ul>
<h3>5.2. Cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass</h3>
<ul>
<li>Cardiac surgery is recommended only when medical therapy or interventional procedures ail and the mother's life threatened.</li>
<li>The best period for surgery is between the 13<sup>th</sup> and 28<sup>th</sup> week (surgery during the first trimester carries a higher risk of fetal malformations and during the third trimester is a higher incidence of pre-term delivery and maternal complication)</li>
<li>Cesarean delivery may be considered before cardiopulmonary bypass if gestational age is &gt; 26 weeks.</li>
<li>Before surgery a full course (at least 24h) of corticosteroids should be administered to the mother, whenever possible.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 445 -->

<ul><li>During cardiopulmonary bypass, fetal heart rate and uterine tone should be monitored in addition to standard patient monitoring.</li><li>Keep pump flow &gt; 2.5L/min/m2 and perfusion pressure &gt; 70mmHg, maternal hematocrit &gt; 28% is recommended to optimize the oxygen delivery.</li></ul><h4>VI. IMING AND MODE OF DELIVERY: RISK FOR MOTHER AND CHILD</h4><p>6.1. Labor induction</p><ul><li>Oxytocin and artificial rupture of the membrane are indicated when the Bishop score is favorable (avoiding long induction time)</li><li>Dinoprostone is contraindicated in active CVD (has profound effect on BP and risk of arrhythmia)</li><li>Mechanical methods such as a Foley catheter would be preferable to pharmacological agents, particularly in the patient with cyanosis where a drop in systemic vascular resistance and/or BP would be detrimental.</li></ul><p>6.2. Vaginal or caesarean delivery?</p><ul><li>The preferred mode of delivery is vaginal and should be take place in a tertiary center with specialist multidisciplinary team care: less blood loses and infection risk, lower risk of venous thrombosis and thrombo-embolism.</li><li>Caesarean delivery is reserved for obstetric indications: no consensus regarding absolute contraindications to vaginal delivery as this is very much dependent on maternal status and the time of delivery and the anticipated cardiopulmonary tolerance of the patient.</li><li>Caesarean delivery should be considered:<ul><li>For the patient on oral anticoagulants</li><li>Marfan syndrome and an aortic diameter &gt; 45mm or between 40-45mm</li><li>Patients with acute or chronic aortic dissection</li><li>Patients in acute intractable heart failure</li><li>Women with sever aortic stenosis</li><li>Women with severe form of pulmonary hypertension (including Eisenmenger syndrome), or acute heart failure</li><li>Patient with mechanical heart valve prothesis</li></ul></li></ul><p>6.3. Anesthesia/analgesia and labor</p><ul><li>Lumbar epidural analgesia is often recommendable: it reduces pain related elevation of sympathetic activity, reduces the urge to push and provides anesthesia for surgery.</li><li>However, it can cause systemic hypotension and must be used with caution in patients with obstructive valve lesion.</li><li>Labor position: the woman should be placed in a lateral decubitus position to attenuate the hemodynamic impact of uterine contractions.</li><li>Delivery should be assisted by low forceps or vacuum extraction, without maternal pushing to avoid the unwanted effects of the Valsava manoeuvre.</li></ul><h4>VII. ISK ESTIMATION: CONTRAINDICATION FOR PREGNANCY</h4><ul><li>Pre-pregnancy counselling: a risk assessment should be performed prior to pregnancy and drugs reviewed so that those which are contra indicated in pregnancy can be stopped or changed to alternatives where possible</li><li>All women with heart disease should be assessed at least once before pregnancy and during pregnancy and hospital delivery should be advised.</li></ul>

<h3>mWHO I</h3>
<ul>
<li>Uncomplicated, small or mild pulmonary stenosis, PDA, mitral valve prolapses</li>

</ul>
<p>⇒ <i>Risk is very low, cardiology follows up during pregnancy may be limited one or two visits.</i></p>

<li>Repaired coarctation</li>
</ul>
<p>⇒ <i>Follow up every trimester is recommended.</i></p>

<ul>

<ul><li>Aortic dilatation 45-50mm in aortic disease associated with bicuspid aortic valve<br/>⇒ <i>High risk of complications, follow up monthly or bi monthly during pregnancy with cardiologist and obstetrician is recommended.</i></li></ul><p><b>mWHO IV (pregnancy contraindicated)</b></p><ul><li>Pulmonary arterial hypertension of any cause</li><li>Sever systemic ventricular dysfunction (LVEF &lt; 30%, NYHA III – IV)</li><li>Previous peripartum cardiomyopathy with any residual impairments of left ventricular function</li><li>Sever mitral stenosis, sever symptomatic aortic stenosis</li><li>Marfan syndrome with aorta dilated &gt; 45mm.</li><li>Aortic dilatation &gt; 50mm in aortic disease associated with bicuspid aortic valve</li><li>Native sever coarctation</li><li>⇒ <i>Advised against pregnancy, if pregnancy occurred consider termination of pregnancy. If they will not consider termination, monthly or bi-monthly review is recommended.</i></li></ul><p><b>VIII. METHODS OF CONTRACEPTION</b></p><p>Monthly injectable that contain <u>medroxyprogesterone acetate</u>: <i>not recommended</i> in patient with <i>heart failure</i> because of risk of fluid retention.</p><p>Oral contraceptive containing 20mcg of ethinyl estradiol are safe in women with a low thrombogenic potential but not in women with complexes vascular disease.</p><p><b>Barrier method (condom) and IUD is the safest and most effective method</b> in women with cyanotic congenital heart disease and pulmonary vascular disease (caution with this method: 5% of patients experience vasovagal reactions at the time of implant). It is contraindicated in cyanotic women with Ht &gt; 55% (risk of intrinsic hemostatic defects that will cause excessive menstrual bleeding)</p><p><b>II. CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE AND PULMONARY HYPERTENSION</b></p><p><b>1. Maternal high-risk conditions (mWHO III-IV)</b></p><p><b>1.1. Pulmonary hypertension</b></p><p>Pulmonary hypertension defined as mean PAP ≥ 25mmHg at rest. It encompasses a group of disease with different pathophysiologies which include PAH, pulmonary hypertension related to left heart disease, to lung disease and/or hypoxia, chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, idiopathic, heritable forms of the disease as well as pulmonary hypertension associated with congenital heart disease, with or without previous corrective surgery.</p><p>• <b>Management:</b></p><ul><li>If pregnancy occurs, termination should be offered.</li><li>If patients choose to continue pregnancy despite the risk, they should be managed in a center with expertise in PAH with all therapeutic options available.</li><li>Goal is to maintain circulating volume, avoid systemic hypotension, hypoxia and acidosis which may precipitate refractory heart failure.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 448 -->

<ul><li>Supplemental oxygen therapy, IV prostacyclin or aerosolized iloprost are occasionally used antenatally and peripartum to improve hemodynamic during delivery.</li><li>In patients who are already taking drug therapy for PAH before becoming pregnant, continuation of this therapy should be considered, but patients should be informed about the teratogenic effects of some therapies, such as bosentan.</li><li>In the patients where the indication of anticoagulation outside pregnancy is established, anticoagulation should be maintained during pregnancy.</li><li>Type of the anticoagulation that can be used during pregnancy: UFH, LMWH, VKA need to be decided on an individual basis.</li><li>In PAH associated with portal hypertension, anticoagulation is not recommended.</li></ul><p><b>Delivery:</b></p><ul><li>The mode of delivery should be individualized.</li><li>Planned caesarean delivery and vaginal delivery are favored over emergency caesarean delivery.</li></ul><h3>1.2. Eisenmenger syndrome</h3><p><b>Management:</b></p><ul><li>If pregnancy occurs, termination should be offered (to be noted, termination also carries a risk)</li><li>If patients choose to continue pregnancy despite the risk, care should be based in a specialist unit.</li><li>Bed rest may be beneficial.</li><li><u>Anticoagulant</u>: prevention for thrombo-embolism should be considered after hematology review and investigations for blood hemostasis (anticoagulation should be use with caution, as patients with Eisenmenger syndrome are also prone to hemoptysis and thrombocytopenia).</li><li><u>Diuretic</u> should be used in patients with heart failure at the lowest effective dose (to avoid hemoconcentration and intravascular volume depletion)</li><li><u>Supplement oral or IV iron</u>: use in case of microcytosis and iron deficiency.</li></ul><p><b>Delivery:</b></p><ul><li>An early caesarean delivery should be planned if the maternal or fetal condition deteriorates.</li><li>Incremental regional anesthesia may improve maternal outcome.</li></ul><h3>1.3. Cyanotic heart disease without pulmonary hypertension</h3><p><b>Management:</b></p><ul><li>Women with an oxygen saturation below 85% at rest should be advised against pregnancy.</li><li>Restriction of physical activity and supplemental oxygen (monitoring oxygen are recommended)</li><li>Use of compression stocking and avoiding the supine position to prevent venous stasis.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 449 -->

<ul><li>Prophylactic heparin administration should be considered (after hematology review and investigations for blood hemostasis.</li><li>Diuretic and iron therapy are indicated and manage in the same way as in patients with Eisenmenger syndrome.</li></ul><p><b>Delivery:</b></p><ul><li>Vaginal delivery is advised in most cases.</li><li>If the maternal or fetal condition deteriorates, an early caesarean delivery should be planned.</li><li>Incremental regional anesthesia may improve maternal outcome.</li></ul><h2>2. Maternal low and moderate risk conditions (mWHO I, II and III)</h2><h3>2.1. Atrial septal defect (ASD)</h3><ul><li>Pregnancy is well tolerated by most women with an ASD</li><li>The only contraindication is the presence of PAH or Eisenmenger syndrome</li><li>Maternal risk includes: trombo-embolic complications ~ 5%, arrhythmia especially in unrepaired ASD, ASD closed at older age and the pregnant woman is &gt; 30 years old.</li></ul><p><b>Management:</b></p><ul><li>Follow up twice during pregnancy is sufficient</li><li>Catheter device closure can be performed during pregnancy but is only indicated when the condition of the mother is deteriorating</li><li>Prevent of venous stasis with using of compression stockings and avoiding the supine position to reduce the risk of paradoxical embolism.</li><li>Early ambulation after delivery, in case of prolonged bed rest, prophylactic heparin administration should be considered.</li></ul><p><b>Delivery:</b></p><ul><li>Spontaneous vaginal delivery is in most case appropriate.</li></ul><h3>2.2. Ventricular septal defect (VSD)</h3><ul><li>For large VSD with pulmonary hypertension, manage as pulmonary hypertension</li><li>Small peri membranous VSDs without left heart dilatation have a low risk of complications during pregnancy</li><li>Follow up twice during pregnancy is sufficient and spontaneous vaginal delivery is appropriate.</li></ul><h3>2.3. Atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD)</h3><ul><li>After correction, pregnancy is usually well tolerated when residual valve regurgitation is not severe and ventricular function is normal.</li><li>Patients with severe (residual) left atrioventricular (AV) valve regurgitation with symptoms and/or impaired ventricular function should be treated surgically pre-pregnancy.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 450 -->

<ul><li>AVSD with pulmonary hypertension =&gt; manage as pulmonary hypertension in above section.</li></ul><p><b>Management</b></p><ul><li>Follow up during pregnancy at least once each trimester.</li><li>Clinical and echocardiographic follow up is indicated monthly or bimonthly in patients with moderate or severe valve regurgitation or impaired ventricular function.</li><li>Prevention the risk of paradoxical thrombo-embolism.</li></ul><p><b>Delivery:</b></p><ul><li>Spontaneous vaginal delivery is in most case appropriate.</li></ul><h3>2.4. Coarctation of the Aorta (CoA)</h3><ul><li>After repair, the pregnancy is often well tolerated.</li><li>Those women with unrepaired native CoA and those repaired who have residual hypertension, residual CoA, or aortic aneurysms have an increased risk of aortic rupture and rupture of a cerebral aneurysm during pregnancy and delivery.</li></ul><p><b>Management:</b></p><ul><li>Close surveillance of BP is warranted, and regular follow up at lease every trimester is indicated.</li><li>Hypertension: should be treated but avoid an aggressive treatment to avoid placental hypoperfusion.</li><li>PCI for re-CoA is possible during pregnancy but it carries higher risk of aortic dissection than outside pregnancy. It should be performed if sever hypertension persists despite medical therapy and there is maternal or fetal compromise (the use of cover stent may lower the risk of dissection).</li></ul><p><b>Delivery:</b></p><ul><li>Spontaneous vaginal delivery is preferred with use of epidural anesthesia particularly in hypertensive patients.</li></ul><h3>2.5. Pulmonary valve stenosis and regurgitation</h3><p><b>Management:</b></p><ul><li>Mild and moderated PS are regarded low-risk lesions and follow up once every trimester is sufficient.</li><li>In patient with sever PS, cardiac evaluation by echocardiography should be performed monthly or bi-monthly to determine clinical status and for surveillance of RV function.</li><li>Percutaneous valvuloplasty can be undertaken in severely symptomatic PS not responding to medical therapy and bed rest during pregnancy or in severe pulmonary stenosis (peak Doopler gradient &gt; 64m) Hg) pre-pregnancy.</li></ul><p><b>Delivery:</b></p>

<!-- PAGE 451 -->

<ul><li>Vaginal delivery is favored in patients with non-severe PS or severe PS in NYHA class I/II</li><li>Caesarean section is considered in patients with severe PS and in NYHA class III/IV despite medical therapy and bed rest, in whom percutaneous pulmonary valvulotomy cannot be performed or has failed.</li></ul><h3>2.6 Tetralogy of Fallot</h3><p><b>Management:</b></p><ul><li>Follow up every trimester is sufficient in the majority of women</li><li>In women with severe PR, monthly or bi-monthly cardiac evaluation with echocardiography is indicated.</li><li>Diuretic and bed rest: if RV failure occurs during pregnancy</li><li>Transcatheter valve implantation or early delivery should be considered in those who do not respond to conservative treatment.</li></ul><p><b>Delivery:</b></p><ul><li>The preferred mode of delivery is vaginal in almost all cases.</li></ul><h3>2.7 Ebstein's anomaly</h3><ul><li>In women with Ebstein's anomaly without cyanosis and heart failure, pregnancy is often tolerated well.</li><li>Symptomatic patients with cyanosis and/or heart failure should be treated before pregnancy or counselled against pregnancy.</li><li>In severe symptomatic TR, repair should be considered pre-pregnancy.</li></ul><p><b>Management:</b></p><ul><li>Follow up</li><li>Even severe TR with heart failure can usually be managed medically during pregnancy</li><li>Prevention of paradoxical emboli (in case of interatrial shunting that can develop shunt reversal and cyanosis)</li></ul><p><b>Delivery:</b></p><ul><li>The preferred mode of delivery is vaginal in almost all cases.</li></ul><h2>III. AORTIC DISEASE</h2><p>Several heritable disorders affect the thoracic aorta, pre-disposing patients to both aneurysm formation and aortic dissection:</p><ul><li>Marfan syndrome</li><li>Bicuspid aortic valve</li><li>Ehlers-Danlos syndrome</li><li>Turner syndrome</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 452 -->

<div><p>All women with genetically proven Marfan syndrome or other familial aortic pathology should have counselling on the risk of dissection and the recurrence risk, and have a complete evaluation including imaging of the entire aorta before pregnancy.</p><p>► <b>Management</b></p><ul><li>Follow up: aortic diameter should be monitored by echocardiography at 4-12 weeks intervals throughout pregnancy and 6 months post-partum</li><li>β-blockers is recommended to use in patients with Marfan syndrome during pregnancy to prevent dissection.</li><li>* Celirolol is recommended in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV</li><li>Fetal growth should be monitored when the mother is taking B-blockers.</li><li>Intervention before pregnancy is recommended if ascending aorta ≥ 45mm in patients with Marfan syndrome or other syndromes with high risk of dissection, otherwise intervention should be done pre-pregnancy when the ascending aorta ≥ 50mm or &gt; 27mm/m<sup>2</sup> for small woman.</li><li>When progressive dilatation occurs during pregnancy, before the fetus is viable, aortic repair with the fetus in utero should be considered.</li><li>When the fetus is viable, caesarean delivery followed directly by aortic surgery is recommended.</li></ul><p>► <b>Delivery</b></p><ul><li>If the woman is taking β-blockers during pregnancy they should be continue in the peripartum periods</li><li>If the ascending aorta diameter is 40-45mm, vaginal delivery with expedited second stage and regional anesthesia is advised to prevent BP peaks or Caesarean delivery could be considered based on the individual situations.</li><li>Caesarean section should be considered when the aortic diameter exceeds 45mm and should be performed early especially in women with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV.</li></ul><table border="1"><caption>Table 3. Different aortic pathology and its complication during pregnancy</caption><thead><tr><th></th><th>Marfan</th><th>Bicuspid aortic valve</th><th>LoeysDietz</th><th>Turner</th><th>Vascular Ehlers-Danlos</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Location of aneurysm/dissection</td><td>Everywhere (sinus of Valsalva)</td><td>Ascending aorta</td><td>Everywhere</td><td>Ascending aorta, arch and descending aorta</td><td>Everywhere</td></tr><tr><td>Risk of dissection</td><td>High: 1-10%</td><td>Low: &lt;1%</td><td>High: 1-10%</td><td>High: 1-10%</td><td>High: 1-10%</td></tr><tr><td>Comorbidity</td><td>Dural abnormalities, Mitral regurgitation, heart failure, arrhythmias</td><td>Aortic stenosis or regurgitation</td><td>Dural abnormalities, Mitral regurgitation.</td><td>Low height, infertility, hypertension, diabetes, bicuspid aortic valve, Coarctation</td><td>Dural abnormalities, uterine rupture</td></tr><tr><td>Advise not to become pregnant</td><td>Ascending aorta &gt; 45mm (or &gt;40mm in family history of dissection or sudden death)</td><td>Ascending aorta &gt; 50mm</td><td>Ascending aorta &gt; 45mm (or &gt; 40mm in family history of dissection or sudden death)</td><td>ASI &gt; 25mm/m<sup>2</sup></td><td>All patients</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

<!-- PAGE 453 -->

<h4>IV. ALVULAR HEART DISEASE</h4>
<p>Rheumatic heart disease remains a major problem in developing countries. Stenotic valve disease carries a higher pregnancy risk than regurgitant lesion, and left sided valve disease have a higher complications rate than right sided valve lesions.</p>
<p>Specific problems, mainly related to anticoagulant therapy, are present in women with mechanical valve prostheses.</p>
<h5>1. Mitral stenosis</h5>
<ul>
<li>The risk of decompensation depends on the severity of MS.</li>
<li>Heart failure occurs frequently in pregnant women with moderate to severe MS (valve area &lt; 1.5cm<sup>2</sup>), particularly during the second and third trimesters, even in previously asymptomatic women.</li>
<li>AF carries the additional risk of thrombo-embolic events.</li>
</ul>
<h6>Management</h6>
<ul>
<li>All patients with moderate to severe MS even when asymptomatic should be counselled against pregnancy.</li>
<li>Intervention should be performed pre-pregnancy, favoring percutaneous interventions.</li>
<li>Clinical and echocardiographic follow up is indicated monthly or bi-monthly depending on hemodynamic tolerance for moderate to severe MS. For mild MS, evaluation is recommended every trimester and prior to delivery.</li>
<li><b>In patients with symptoms or pulmonary hypertension</b> (estimated systolic PAP &gt; 50mmHg), <i>restricted activities and B1-selective blockers are recommended.</i></li>
<li><b>Diuretics are recommended (avoiding high dose) when congestive symptoms persist despite B-blockers</b></li>
<li><b>Therapeutic anticoagulation</b> is recommended in the case of paroxysmal or permanent AF, left atrial thrombosis, or prior embolism or spontaneous echocardiographic contrast in the LA, large left atrium (≥ 40mL/m<sup>2</sup>), low CO or congestive heart failure.</li>
</ul>
<h6>Intervention</h6>
<ul>
<li>Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy is preferable performed after 20 weeks gestations.</li>
<li>It is indicated in women with <i>NYHA class III/IV and/or estimated systolic PAP &gt; 50mmHg despite optimal medical treatment</i>, in the absence of contraindications and if patient characteristics are suitable.</li>
</ul>
<h6>Delivery</h6>
<ul>
<li><u>Vaginal delivery</u>: in patient with mild MS and in patients with moderate to severe MS in NYHA class I/II without pulmonary hypertension.</li>
<li><u>Caesarean section</u>: in patients with moderate or severe MS who are in NYHA class III/IV or have pulmonary hypertension despite medical therapy.</li>
</ul>
<h5>2. Valvular aortic stenosis</h5>
<p>Cardiac morbidity during pregnancy is related to severity of AS and symptoms. Asymptomatic mild or moderate AS, pregnancy is well tolerated. Also, patients with severe AS, may sustain pregnancy well, as long as they remain asymptomatic during exercise testing and have a normal BP response during exercise.</p>
<h6>Management</h6>
<ul>
<li>All symptomatic patients with severe AS or asymptomatic patients with impaired LV function (LVEF &lt; 50%) or a pathological exercise test should be counselled against pregnancy.</li>
<li>Valvuloplasty or surgery should be performed pre-pregnancy.</li>
</ul>

<!-- PAGE 454 -->

<ul><li>Regardless of symptoms, pre-pregnancy surgery should be considered in patients with ascending aorta &gt; 50mm (27.5mm/m<sup>2</sup>).</li><li>Monthly or bimonthly cardiac evaluation including echocardiography are advised to determine symptom status, progression of AS, or other complications.</li><li><b>Restricted activities</b> are indicated for patients developing signs or symptoms of heart failure during pregnancy.</li><li><b>Diuretics</b> are indicated in case of congestive symptoms.</li><li><b>β-blocker</b> or a <b>non-dihydropyridine calcium channel antagonist</b> or <b>digoxin</b> should be considered for rate control in AF.</li></ul><p><b>Intervention</b></p><ul><li>Percutaneous valvuloplasty is indicated in severely symptomatic patients not responding to medical therapy in non-calcified valves with minimal regurgitation.</li><li>If this is not possible and patients have life-threatening symptoms, valve replacement should be considered after early delivery by caesarean section.</li></ul><p><b>Delivery</b></p><ul><li>In severe AS=&gt; caesarean delivery should be preferred with endotracheal intubation and general anesthesia.</li><li>In non-severe AS=&gt; vaginal delivery is favored, avoiding a decrease in peripheral vascular resistance during regional anesthesia and analgesia.</li></ul><h3>3. Mitral and aortic regurgitation</h3><p>Left sided regurgitant valve lesions carry a lower pregnancy risk than stenotic valve lesion because the decreased systemic vascular resistance reduces regurgitant volume.</p><p>Severe regurgitation with LV dysfunction is poorly tolerated, as is acute severe regurgitation.</p><p><b>Management</b></p><ul><li>Pre-pregnancy valve repair surgery should be done in patients with severe regurgitation and symptoms or compromised LV function or LV dilatation.</li><li>Follow up every trimester in mild/moderate regurgitation and more often in severe regurgitation (needed to be individualized)</li><li>Symptoms of fluid overload can usually be managed medically</li><li>In acute severe regurgitation with therapy-refractory heart failure, surgery sometimes is unavoidable.</li></ul><p><b>Delivery</b></p><ul><li>Vaginal delivery is preferable, in symptomatic patients, epidural anesthesia and shortened second stage is advisable.</li></ul><h3>4. Valvular atrial fibrillation</h3><p>Prevention of thrombo-embolic risk is important. UFH / LMWH can be used in the first and last trimester.</p><p>LMWH should be given in weight adjusted therapeutic dose (twice daily) until 36h prior to delivery.</p><p>OACs (VKA) or LMWH can be used in the 2<sup>nd</sup> trimester.</p><p>INR should be kept between 2.0 and 2.5 (to minimize the risk for the fetus).</p><h3>5. Bio prothesis</h3><p>Pregnancy is generally well tolerated in women with a failed functioning bio prosthesis. Pre-pregnancy assessment and counselling as well as follow up, medical treatment, and indications for intervention are comparable with those for pregnancies with native valve dysfunction.</p>

<!-- PAGE 455 -->

<p><b>Delivery</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Planned vaginal delivery is usually preferred with prior switch to heparin.</li>
<li>A planned cesarean section may be considered in patient with high risk of valve thrombosis (aim to keep the time without OACs as short as possible).</li>
<li>Caesarean delivery should be performed if labor onset occurs while the patient is still on OACs.</li>
</ul>
<h3>V. CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE AND ACUTE CORONARY SYNDROME</h3>
<p>ECG and measurements of troponin level are recommended when a pregnant woman has a chest pain.</p>
<p><b>Primary coronary angioplasty is recommended as the preferred reperfusion therapy for STEMI during pregnancy.</b> The safety of DES in pregnant woman is still unknown and they should be avoided because it requires prolonged DAPT.</p>
<p>In <b>non-ST-elevation ACS / NSTEMI</b>, an <i>invasive management should be considered in only patient with risk criteria</i>, otherwise a <b>conservative management should be considered</b>.</p>
<p>The use of ACEi / ARBs and renin inhibitor is contraindicated during pregnancy.</p>
<p><b>β-blockers and low dose aspirin</b> are considered to be <i>relatively safe</i>.</p>
<p>Clopidogrel should only be used when strictly needed (after stenting) and for the shortest duration possible.</p>
<p><b>Breastfeeding is not recommended in mother who take antiplatelet agents other than low dose aspirin</b> due to lack of data.</p>
<h3>VI. ARDIOMYOPATHIES AND HEART FAILURE</h3>
<p>It is recommended to <b>treat women with HF during pregnancy according to current guideline for non-pregnant patients, respecting contraindications for some drugs in pregnancy</b></p>
<img alt="Flowchart titled 'AHF during pregnancy'. The process starts with 'Induction of lung maturation &gt;23 + 5 weeks initiated without delaying patient transfer to tertiary center'. This leads to 'Status and prognosis of the foetus'. If 'Foetus non viable', the path leads to 'Delivery' and then 'Maximal advanced AHF therapy Supportive psychotherapy'. If 'Foetus viable', the path leads to 'Parents' wish Maternal and fetal status'. If 'Pregnancy continued', the path leads to 'Monitoring mother/foetus tailored HF Therapy Consider advanced AHF therapy'. If 'Delivery' (from Foetus viable), the path leads to 'Maximal advanced AHF therapy'."/>
<p>Figure 5. Rapid interdisciplinary workup and treatment of mother and foetus</p>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 457 -->

<div>
<p>In patients with PPCM and DCM, subsequent pregnancy is not recommended if LVEF does not normalize, counselling for recurrent risk during subsequent pregnancy is recommended in all cases, even after recovery of LV function.</p>
<p>In this case <b>bromocriptine treatment may be considered to stop lactation and enhance recovery (LV function).</b></p>
<p>Due to the high metabolic demands of lactation and breastfeeding, preventing lactation may be considered in patients with severe heart failure.</p>
<p><b>β-blocker is recommended to continue</b> in women who used them before pregnancy or <b>install them with caution in heart failure, in HCM or in arrhythmia.</b></p>
<p>Cardioversion should be considered for persistent atrial fibrillation.</p>
<p><b>Therapeutic anticoagulation with LMWH or VKA</b> according to stage of pregnancy is recommended for patients with atrial fibrillation or with intracardiac thrombus detected by imaging or with evidence of systemic embolism.</p>
<img alt="Flowchart titled 'Management of acute heart failure during/after pregnancy'. This then leads to Recovery? If yes, Transplantation; if no, Weaning. Stabilized AHF branches into Antepartum and Postpartum. Antepartum HF therapy includes Hydralazine, Nitrates, Beta-blocker, Consider diuretics, and Consider delivery (vaginal delivery with PDA). Both Antepartum and Postpartum lead to Consider WCD therapy if LVEF ≤35%, which then leads to Continue HF therapy."/>

Bradyarrhythmias</h3><p>□ Sinus node dysfunction:</p><ul><li>sinus bradycardia may appear as a reflex cardiac slowing (Valsava maneuver) during delivery.</li></ul></div>

<ul><li>Rare case of bradycardia cause symptoms of hypotension, if occur =&gt; change the position of the mother to a left lateral decubitus position.</li><li>For persistent symptoms, a temporary pacemaker may be necessary.</li></ul><p>☐ AV blocks</p><ul><li>1<sup>st</sup> degree AV block can be observed during pregnancy in the absence of underlying heart disease</li><li>Temporary pacing during pregnancy is recommended in selected women with complete heart block and symptoms due to the risk of bradycardia and syncope.</li><li>Implantation of permanent pacemaker can be performed safely, especially if the fetus is beyond 8 weeks gestations (with echo guidance).</li></ul><h3>VIII. HYPERTENSIVE DISORDERS</h3><p>Hypertension is the most common medical problem in pregnancy, complicating up to 15% of pregnancies and accounting for about a quarter of all antenatal admission.</p><p>☐ Diagnosis and risk assessment</p><ul><li>Lab test: urine analysis, blood count, hematocrit, liver enzyme, serum creatinine and serum uric acid, 24hour proteinuria, urine metanephrine and normetanephrine</li><li>Ultrasound of the adrenals</li><li>Doppler ultrasound of uterine arteries (to detect uteroplacental hypoperfusion), which is associated with a higher risk of pre-eclampsia and intra uterine growth retardation.</li></ul><p>☐ Definition and classification of hypertension in pregnancy</p><ul><li>The definition of hypertension in pregnancy is based on absolute BP value (SBP ≥ 140mmHg or DBP ≥ 90mmHg).</li><li>Mildly hypertension: 140-159/90-109mmHg</li><li>Severely hypertension: ≥ 160/110mmHg</li></ul><p><b>Pre-existing hypertension:</b> hypertension that either precedes pregnancy or develop before 20 weeks of gestation. This is usually persists &gt; 42 days post-partum.</p><p><b>Gestation hypertension or pregnancy induced hypertension:</b> develop after 20 weeks gestations and resolves in most cases within 42 days post-partum. It is characterized by poor organ perfusion.</p><p><b>Pre-existing hypertension plus superimposed gestational hypertension with proteinuria.</b></p><p><b>Antenatally unclassifiable hypertension:</b> when BP is first recorded after 20 weeks gestations and hypertension is diagnosed.</p><p><b>Pre-eclampsia is a pregnancy specific syndrome</b> that occurs after mid-gestation: de novo appearance of hypertension with new onset of significant proteinuria &gt; 0.3g/24h.</p><p><b>Signs and symptoms of pre-eclampsia</b></p><ul><li>Right upper quadrant/epigastric pain due to liver oedema +/- hepatic hemorrhage</li><li>Headache +/- visual disturbance (cerebral edema)</li><li>Occipital lobe blindness</li><li>Hyperreflexia +/- clonus</li><li>Convulsion (cerebral edema)</li><li>HELLP syndrome</li></ul><p>☐ Pharmacological Management</p>

<!-- PAGE 460 -->

<ul><li>Low dose aspirin (100-150mg daily) is recommended in women at high or moderate risk of pre-eclampsia from week 12 to weeks 36-37.</li><li><b>Methyldopa, labetalol and calcium antagonists</b> are recommended for the treatment of hypertension in pregnancy.</li><li><b>IV Nitroglycerine</b> is recommended in case of <i>pre-eclampsia with pulmonary edema</i>, infusion of 5mcg/min and gradually increase every 3-5mins to a maximum dose of 100mcg/min.</li><li><b>IV labetalol or oral methyldopa or nifedipine</b> is recommended in severe hypertension.</li><li>ACE inhibitors, ARBs or direct renin inhibitor are not recommended.</li><li>Diuretic should be avoided because they may decrease blood flow to the placenta.</li></ul><p>In women with gestational hypertension or pre-existing hypertension superimposed by gestational hypertension, or with hypertension and sub clinical organ damage or symptoms, initiation of drugs treatment is recommended at SBP &gt; 140mmHg or DBP &gt; 90mmHg. In all other cases, initiation of drug treatment is recommended if SBP ≥ 150mmHg or DBP ≥ 95mmHg.</p><p><b>SBP ≥ 170mmHg or DBP ≥ 110mmHg in a pregnant woman is an emergency and hospitalization is recommended.</b></p><h4>□ Delivery</h4><ul><li>In women with gestational hypertension or mild pre-eclampsia, delivery is recommended at 37 weeks.</li><li>Induction of delivery is recommended in gestational hypertension with proteinuria with adverse conditions such as visual disturbances, coagulation abnormalities, or fetal distress.</li></ul><h3>IX. VENOUS THROMBO-EMBOLISM</h3><h4>1. Prevention</h4><ul><li><b>Early mobilization and avoidance of dehydration.</b></li><li><b>Using compression stoking</b></li></ul><p>In case of anticoagulation is needed:</p><ul><li><b>Enoxaparin 0.5IU/KG body weight or</b></li><li><b>Dalteparin 50IU/Kg body weight twice daily.</b></li></ul><p>Please see Table 7 and Table 8 to stratify venous thrombo-embolism and indication for anticoagulant prophylaxis.</p><p><b>Table 7. Management of acute venous thrombo-embolism</h2><h3>□ Pulmonary embolism</h3><ul><li>Clinical presentation (same as in non-pregnant state): dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, haemoptiysis, and collapse.</li><li>Diagnosis:<ul><li>D-dimer levels increase physiologically in pregnant women with each trimester, thus a positive D-dimer test base on the conventional cut-off level is not necessarily indicated of VTE, but it helps to rule out VTE in the case of negative D-dimer.</li><li>Bilateral compression ultrasonography is indicated follow by measurement of D-dimer.</li><li>MRI may be used to rule out iliac vein thrombosis</li><li>CT pulmonary angiography should be performed with the diagnosis cannot be confirmed or excluded with the above-discussed tool.</li></ul></li><li>Treatment:<ul><li>LMWH:<ul><li>Enoxaparin 1mg/kg body weight bid.</li><li>Dalteparin 100iu/kg body weight bid.</li></ul></li></ul></li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 462 -->

<ul><li>Aiming for 4-6h peak anti Xa values of 0.6-1.2 IU/mL</li><li>UFH (used in patients with renal failure and when urgent reversal of anticoagulation by protamine is needed, as well as in the acute treatment of massive pulmonary emboli:<ul><li>Loading dose of 80U/Kg followed by</li><li>IV continuous fusion of 18U/Kg/h</li><li>Therapeutic target aPTT ratio 1.5-2.5 times the average laboratory control value</li><li>The aPTT has to be determine 4-6h after the loading dose, 6h after any dose change and then at least daily when in the therapeutic range.</li></ul></li></ul><p>When haemodynamics are improved and the patient is stabilized, UFH can be switched to LMWH in therapeutic dose and maintain during pregnancy.</p><ul><li>LMWH should be switched to i.v. UFH at least 36h before the induction of labour or caesarean delivery.</li><li>UFH should be discontinued 4-6h before anticipated delivery and restarted 6h after a vaginal birth or 12h after caesarean delivery if there are no bleeding complications.</li><li>UFH and LWMH are not contraindicated to breastfeeding.</li><li>VKA may be started on the second day after delivery and continued for at least 3 months or for 6 months if pulmonary embolism occurred late in pregnancy.</li><li>INR should be between 2 and 3 and needs regular monitoring, ideally once every 1-2 weeks.</li><li>Thrombolysis: Relatively contraindicated during pregnancy and peripartum =&gt; should only be used in high-risk patients with severe hypotension or shock.</li><li>Other anti-coagulants: Fondaparinux and Rivaroxaban are not recommended to use in pregnancy (due to transplacental passage of the drug)</li></ul><h3>Acute deep vein thrombosis</h3><h4>Clinical presentation:</h4><ul><li>leg swelling (&gt; 85% left sided due to compression of the left iliac vein by the right iliac artery and the gravid uterus),</li><li>isolated pain in the buttock, groin, flank or abdomen (in case of isolated iliac vein thrombosis)</li></ul><h4>Diagnosis:</h4><ul><li>D-dimer (see diagnosis in pulmonary embolism)</li><li>Compression ultrasound leg vein imaging</li></ul><p>In women with <u>high pre-test probability</u>, a positive D-dimer and a normal initial compression ultrasound =&gt; <b>magnetic resonance venography</b> may be considered to exclude isolated pelvic DVT.</p><p>Women with <u>low pre-test probability</u> and normal D-dimer should undergo serial compression ultrasonography on day3 and after 1 week without anti-coagulation.</p><h4>Treatment</h4><ul><li>LMWH:</li></ul>

<h1>CARDIOVASCULAR DRUGS AND PREGNANCY</h1>
<p>Dr. SRENG Dina, Dr. SAN Samrany, Dr. SOK Sorkhan, Dr. KHMAO Pichmanil, Dr. KIRY Samnang, Dr. LIM Eaksrong, Dr. SUY Sovannara, Dr. MEN Sengleap, Dr. PHOUY Sonaroth, Dr. THENG Youdaline, Dr. SAING Leang, Dr. LIM Sivutha, Dr. SOK Phang, Dr. CHAN Sokha, Ass Prof. CHHUN Lay, Prof. SOK Chour</p>
<h2>I. GENERAL PRINCIPLES</h2>
<p>There are no uniform recommendations for the treatment of pregnant women yet. As drug treatment in pregnancy concerns the mother and the fetus, optimum treatment of both must be targeted. In case of emergency, drugs that are not recommended by the pharmaceutical industry during pregnancy and breastfeeding should not be withheld from the mother. The potential risk of a drug and the possible benefit of the therapy must be weighed against each other.</p>
<p>Before pharmacological treatment in pregnancy is started, it is recommended to check table below (Table 2) for clinical safety data.</p>
<p>In the absence of clinical safety data, it is recommended to check the electronic drug table (www.safefetus.com) for pre-clinical safety data.</p>
<p>In the absence of adequate human safety data, decision-making should be based on individual drug efficacy and safety profiles, and the available animal data, and the decision must be made together with the patient.</p>
<p>Decision making based on former US Food and Drug Administration (FAD) categories alone is no longer recommended.</p>
<table border="1">
<caption><b>Table 1. FDA Drug Classifications</b></caption>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Rating A</td>
<td>Controlled study in women fall to demonstrate a risk to the fetus in the first trimester; no evidence of a risk</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Rating B</td>
<td>Either animal-reproduction studies have note demonstrate a fetal risk but there are no controlled studies in pregnant women or animal-reproduction studies have shown adverse effect (other than a decrease in fertility) that was not confirmed in controlled studies in women in the first trimester (and there is no evidence of a risk in later trimesters)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Rating C</td>
<td>Either studies in animals have revealed adverse effects on the fetus (teratogenic, embryocidal, or other) and there are no controlled studies in women or studies in women and animal are not available. Drugs should be given only if the potential benefits justify the potential risk to the fetus.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Rating D</td>
<td>There is positive evidence of human fetal risk, but the benefits from use in pregnant women may be acceptable despite the risk (eg, if the drug is needed in a life-threatening situation or for a serious disease for which safer drugs cannot be used or are ineffective).</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Rating X</td>
<td>Studies in animals or human beings have demonstrated fetal abnormalities, there is evidence of fetal risk based on human experience, or both, and the risk of the use of the drug in pregnant women clearly outweigh any possible benefit. There drug is contraindicated in women who are or may become pregnant.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<!-- PAGE 465 -->

<h2>II. RECOMMENDATION FOR DRUGS USES</h2><p><b>Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB)</b> are pregnancy category D drugs because of the risk of reduced fetal renal function and increased fetal and neonatal morbidity and death, especially with use during the 2<sup>nd</sup> and 3<sup>rd</sup> trimester. Women taking ACE inhibitors or ARB who desire to become pregnant should be advised to <u>stop taking these drugs before conception</u> to minimize the risk of fetal abnormality.</p><p><b>β-Blockers</b> have a favorable safety profile, and no teratogenic risk have been reported with their use. They have been associated with an increase in small-for-gestational-age infants and neonatal bradycardia and hypoglycemia but in practical terms are considered safe to use. Atenolol has been associated with low birth weight and therefore is not the β-blocker of choice during pregnancy.</p><p>The <u>routine use of diuretics</u> is <u>discouraged</u> because of the potential reduction in maternal plasma volume early in gestation that is potentially harmful to the fetus. <b>They should be used judiciously.</b></p><p><b>Amiodarone</b> has been associated with a 9% incidence of fetal hypothyroidism and a 21% incidence of intrauterine growth retardation and should be reserved for cases of <u>refractory ventricular arrhythmia</u>.</p><p>Drugs listed as category X include the following:</p><ul><li><b>Anticoagulants:</b> <u>Vitamin K antagonist</u> cross the placenta and are potentially fetotoxic. They are commonly used in women with mechanical valves, and the risk and benefits associated with their use should be discussed with the patient before pregnancy is completed.</li><li><b>Endothelin receptor antagonists</b> (bosentan, ambrisentan, and macitentan)</li><li><b>Statin:</b> although inadvertent exposure to statin during early pregnancy appears unlikely to increase the risk of adverse pregnancy outcome, theoretical considerations concerning the role of cholesterol in embryo development and the lack of demonstration benefit of treating hyperlipidemia during gestation are reasons for not recommending statin during pregnancy.</li></ul><table><caption>Table 2. <h1>CARDIAC EVALUATION BEFORE NON-CARDIAC SURGERY (NCS)</h1><p>Ass Prof. Suy Sovannara, Dr. Sok Sorkhan, Dr. Khmao Pichmanil, Dr. Kiry Samnang, Dr. San Samrany, Dr. Lim Eaksrong, Dr. Sreng Dina, , Dr. Men Sengleap, Dr. Phouy Sonaroth, Dr. Theng Youdaline, Dr. Saing Leang, Dr. Lim Sivutha, Dr. Sok Phang, Ass Prof. Chan Sokha, Ass Prof. Chhun Lay, Prof. Sok Chour</p><h2>I. DEFINITIONS OF SURGICAL TIMING AND RISK</h2><table border="1"><thead><tr><th>TIMING</th><th>DEFINITION</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Emergency</td><td>Immediate threat to life or limb without surgical intervention, where there is very limited or no time for preoperative clinical evaluation, typically &lt;2 h.</td></tr><tr><td>Urgent</td><td>Threat to life or limb without surgical intervention, where there may be time for preoperative clinical evaluation to allow interventions that could reduce risk of MACE or other postoperative complications, typically ≥2 to &lt;24 h.</td></tr><tr><td>Time-sensitive</td><td>Surgery may be delayed up to 3 months to allow for preoperative evaluation and management without negatively impacting outcomes.</td></tr><tr><td>Elective</td><td>The surgical procedure can be delayed permitting a complete preoperative evaluation and appropriate management.</td></tr></tbody></table><table border="1"><thead><tr><th>RISK CATEGORY</th><th>DEFINITION</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Low risk</td><td>Combined surgical and patient characteristics predict a low risk of MACE of &lt;1%.</td></tr><tr><td>Elevated risk</td><td>Combined surgical and patient characteristics predict an elevated risk of MACE of ≥1%.</td></tr></tbody></table><p>* MACE: Major Adverse Cardiac Events (Death, Heart Attack, Heart failure, Arrhythmia, Stroke)</p><h2>II. EPIDEMIOLOGY</h2><ul><li>Each year, approximately 14.4 million inpatient and 19.2 million ambulatory surgeries are performed in the United States, with an estimated 313 million surgeries performed worldwide. Cardiovascular risk factors and disease are prevalent among adults undergoing NCS, and perioperative cardiovascular complications are an important cause of morbidity and mortality.</li><li>In a large retrospective analysis of adults ≥45 years undergoing in-hospital surgery, perioperative death, myocardial infarction (MI), or ischemic stroke occurred in 1 of every 33 surgical admissions, corresponding to &gt;150,000 annual perioperative events in the United States. Although orthopedic</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 470 -->

<div>
<p>(40.0%), general (21.4%), and vascular (10.7%) surgeries were the most performed, patients undergoing vascular, thoracic, and solid organ transplantation surgeries had the highest incidence of cardiovascular events. Irrespective of the surgical subtype, perioperative cardiovascular complications are associated with prolonged inpatient hospitalizations, significantly higher medical costs, and increased mortality.</p>
<h3>III. PREOPERATIVE CARDIOVASCULAR DIAGNOSTIC TESTING</h3>
<ul>
<li><b>ECG:</b> For patients with known coronary heart disease, significant arrhythmia, peripheral arterial disease, cerebrovascular disease, other significant structural heart disease, or symptoms of CVD undergoing elevated risk surgery (COR:2a)</li>
<li><b>ECHOCARDIOGRAPHY to assessment of ventricular function:</b> In patients undergoing NCS with new dyspnea, physical examination findings of HF, or suspected new/worsening ventricular dysfunction (COR: 1)</li>
<li><b>STRESS TESTING:</b> Vasodilator pharmacological stress imaging, Exercise stress testing, Dobutamine stress echocardiography</li>
<li><b>CARDIOPULMONARY EXERCISE TESTING:</b> in whom objective functional capacity is reduced. Reduced cardiorespiratory fitness increases the risk of postoperative complications.</li>
<li><b>CORONARY COMPUTED TOMOGRAPHY ANGIOGRAPHY:</b> In patients with acute chest pain and no known CAD, CCTA may be useful to exclude atherosclerotic plaque and obstructive CAD and is recommended as an alternative to invasive angiography.</li>
<li><b>INVASIVE CORONARY ANGIOGRAPHY:</b></li>
</ul>
<h3>IV. APPROACH TO PERIOPERATIVE CARDIAC TESTING</h3>
<img alt="Flowchart titled 'Approach to Perioperative Cardiac Testing'. The flow starts with 'Patient With Cardiovascular Risk Factors*, Disease, or Symptoms Scheduled for NCS'. If NO, proceed to surgery. If YES, check 'Emergency surgery?'. If YES, proceed to surgery. If NO, check 'Does the patient have?' (Acute coronary syndrome, Unstable cardiac arrhythmias, Decompensated heart failure). If YES, management of acute cardiac condition and multidisciplinary team discussion for deferral of surgery, noninvasive treatment, or palliation. If NO, proceed to 'Estimation of perioperative risk'. This leads to checking if the patient has any of the following risk modifiers: Severe valvular heart disease (Section 6.4), Severe pulmonary hypertension (Section 6.3.2), Elevated-risk congenital heart disease (Section 6.3.3), Prior coronary stents/CABG (Sections 6.1.1 &amp; 7.5), Recent stroke (Section 6.7), CIED (Pacemaker/ICD) present (Section 6.6), Frailty (Section 3.3). If YES, use 'Risk calculator for adverse cardiovascular events (2a)'. If NO, proceed to 'Consider appropriate team-based consultation regarding timing of NCS and perioperative diagnostic testing and management'. If risk modifier present with any calculated risk, consider echocardiography for suspected moderate/severe valvular stenosis/regurgitation, new dyspnea, or suspected new/worsening ventricular dysfunction (1/2a) (Sections 4.2, 6.4.1, and 6.4.3). If no risk modifiers, proceed to 'Consider 12-lead ECG in elevated-risk asymptomatic patients without established CVD (2b) (Section 4.1)'. If elevated calculated risk and no risk modifiers, consider GDMT initiation for long-term cardiovascular risk reduction and disease management, as applicable (Section 7). If low calculated risk and no risk modifiers, proceed to surgery. If poor or unknown functional capacity (DASI ≤34, METs &lt;4) (2a), proceed to surgery if NO. If YES, check 'Will further testing impact decision-making/perioperative care?'. If NO, proceed to surgery or consider alternative strategies: deferral of surgery, noninvasive treatment, or palliation. If YES, consider GDMT initiation for long-term cardiovascular risk reduction and disease management, as applicable (Section 7)."/>

<h3>V. CARDIOVASCULAR COMOBDITIES AND PERIOPERATIVE MANAGEMENT</h3>
<ul>
<li><b>CORONARY ARTERY DISEASE:</b> In patients with ACS being considered for elective NCS, coronary revascularization as appropriate and deferral of surgery is recommended to reduce perioperative cardiovascular events. (COR:1C)</li>
<li><b>HYPERTENSION:</b>
<ul>
<li><b>Pre-operative:</b> In most patients with hypertension planned for elective NCS, it is reasonable to continue medical therapy for hypertension throughout the perioperative period. Except, poorly controlled hypertension (systolic blood pressure [SBP] ≥180 mm Hg or diastolic blood pressure [DBP] ≥110 mm Hg before the day of surgery), deferring surgery may be considered to reduce the risk of perioperative complications.</li>
<li><b>Intraoperative Blood Pressure Management:</b> In patients undergoing NCS, maintaining an intraoperative mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥60 to 65 mm Hg or SBP ≥90 mm Hg is recommended to reduce the risk of myocardial injury.</li>
<li><b>Postoperative Blood Pressure Management:</b>
<ul>
<li>In patients undergoing NCS, treatment of hypotension (MAP &lt;60-65 or SBP &lt;90 mm Hg) in the postoperative period is recommended to limit the risk of cardiovascular, cerebrovascular, renal events, and mortality.</li>
<li>In patients with hypertension undergoing NCS, it is recommended that preoperative antihypertensive medications be restarted as soon as clinically reasonable to avoid complications from postoperative hypertension.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li><b>HEART FAILURE:</b>
<ul>
<li>In patients with HF undergoing elective NCS, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) should be withheld for 3 to 4 days before surgery when feasible to reduce the risk of perioperative metabolic acidosis.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 472 -->

<ul><li>it is reasonable to continue <b>GDMT</b> (Guideline Direct Medical Therapy) (excluding SGLT2i) in the perioperative period, unless contraindicated, to reduce the risk of worsening HF.</li></ul><p><b>&gt; HYPERTROPHY CARDIOMYOPATHY:</b></p><ul><li>For patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) undergoing NCS, factors that aggravate or trigger dynamic outflow obstructions (Ex, positive inotropic agents, tachycardia, or reduced preload) are harmful and should be avoided to reduce the risk of hemodynamic instability.</li><li><b>If hypotension develops:</b><ul><li>Prioritize intravenous fluid administration to correct hypovolemia.</li><li>Use alpha-agonists, such as phenylephrine or vasopressin,<sup>7</sup> rather than beta-agonists, which can worsen LVOT obstruction.</li><li>Consider intraoperative echocardiography to evaluate LVOT obstruction in the setting of hypotension.</li><li>In selected cases, intravenous beta-blockade may be necessary to reduce LV myocardial contractility and relieve LVOT obstruction.</li></ul></li></ul><p><b>&gt; PULMONARY HYPERTENSION:</b></p><ul><li>In patients receiving stable doses of targeted medical therapies, continue these agents.</li><li>In patients with severe<sup>†</sup> PH undergoing elevated-risk NCS, Referral to or consultation with a specialized PH center and invasive hemodynamic monitoring.</li></ul><p><b>&gt; ADULT CONGENITAL HEART DISEASE</b></p><ul><li>Preoperative consultation with an adult congenital heart disease (ACHD) specialist is recommended before the surgery.</li></ul><p><b>&gt; VALVULAR HEART DISEASE</b></p><ul><li>Patients with severe valvular heart disease should be evaluated for the need for valve intervention before elective NCS.</li><li>In asymptomatic patients with moderate or severe AS and normal LV systolic function as assessed by echocardiography within the past year, it is reasonable to proceed with elective low-risk NCS.</li></ul><p><b>&gt; ATRIAL FIBRILLATION</b></p><ul><li>Treat potential underlying triggers contributing to AF and rapid ventricular response (Ex, sepsis, anemia, pain).</li><li>Initiation of postoperative anticoagulation therapy can be beneficial after considering the competing risks associated with thromboembolism and perioperative bleeding.</li></ul>

<!-- PAGE 473 -->

<div>
<p>➤ <b>PREVIOUS STROKE OR TRANSIENT ISCHEMIC STROKE</b></p>
<ul>
<li>it is reasonable to delay elective NCS for ≥3 months after the most recent cerebrovascular event to reduce the incidence of recurrent stroke, MACE, or both.</li>
</ul>
<p><b>VI. PERIOPERATIVE MEDICAL THERAPY</b></p>
<ul>
<li>➤ <b>STATINS:</b> Continuation of statin therapy is recommended to reduce the risk of MACE.</li>
<li>➤ <b>RENIN-ANGIOTENSIN-ALDOSTERONE SYSTEM INHIBITORS:</b> Omission 24 hours before surgery may be beneficial to limit intraoperative hypotension.</li>
<li>➤ <b>ANTIPLATELET THERAPY AND TIMING OF NCS IN PATIENT WITH CAD</b>
<ul>
<li>Timing of NCS after PCI:
<ul>
<li>In patients with recent coronary artery balloon angioplasty without stent placement, elective NCS should be delayed for a minimum of 14 days to minimize perioperative MACE.</li>
<li>In patients with DES-PCI placed for ACS who require elective NCS with interruption of ≥1 antiplatelet agents, surgery should ideally be delayed ≥12 months to minimize perioperative MACE.</li>
<li>In patients with DES-PCI placed for CCD who require elective NCS with interruption of ≥1 antiplatelet agents, it is reasonable to delay surgery for ≥6 months after PCI to minimize perioperative MACE.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Perioperative Antiplatelet Management Post PCI
<ul>
<li>In patients with prior PCI undergoing NCS, it is recommended to continue aspirin* (75-100 mg), if possible, to reduce the risk of cardiac events.</li>
<li>In patients with CAD who require time sensitive NCS within 30 days of PCI with BMS or &lt;3 months of PCI with DES, DAPT should be continued unless the risk of bleeding outweighs the benefit of the prevention of stent thrombosis.</li>
<li>In patients with prior PCI in whom OAC monotherapy must be discontinued before NCS, aspirin should be substituted when feasible in the perioperative period until OAC can be safely reinitiated.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>Perioperative Antiplatelet Management in Patients Without Prior PCI
<ul>
<li>In patients with CCD without prior PCI undergoing elective NCS, it may be reasonable to continue aspirin in selected patients when the risk of cardiac events outweighs the risk of bleeding.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>➤ <b>ORAL ANTICOAGULANT:</b> multidisciplinary team-based approach to time-based interruption is recommended to balance the competing risks of thromboembolism and perioperative bleeding.</li>
</ul>
</div>

<!-- PAGE 474 -->

<div>
<p>&gt; <b>BETA BLOCKER:</b> beta blockers should be continued through the perioperative period as appropriate based on the clinical circumstances.</p>
<h3>VII. MANAGEMENT OF POSTOPERATIVE STEMI/NSTEMI</h3>
<ul>
<li>&gt; Patients who develop STEMI after NCS should be considered for GDMT, including consideration of ICA, balancing bleeding, and thrombotic risks with the severity of the clinical presentation.</li>
<li>&gt; Patients who develop NSTEMI after NCS should receive medical therapy as recommended for patients with spontaneous MI but after consideration of postoperative bleeding risks and hemodynamic status.</li>
</ul>
<h3>VIII. SPECIAL CASES</h3>
<ul>
<li>&gt; <u>Preoperative evaluation before liver and kidney transplantation</u>: Data from the U.S. Renal Data System and Medicare claims reported that more frequent invasive or noninvasive CAD testing in the year before kidney transplantation was not associated with lower rates of 30-day posttransplant death or acute MI.</li>
<li>&gt; <u>Obesity and bariatric surgery</u>: careful attention to history and risk factors during preoperative assessments is essential, because:
        <ul>
<li>patients who underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass or sleeve gastrectomy, prior cardiac history was associated with greater risks of perioperative cardiac arrest and 30-day mortality.</li>
<li>patients with obesity undergoing bariatric surgery reported that a history of ACS or HF was associated with increased risks of perioperative cardiovascular complications.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
